textfield_comment_value:
Si l'on met à part le phénomène Magic, les Colons de Catan sont le plus remarquable succès commercial du jeu de société des dix dernières années. Rien d'étonnant à cela: la thématique était dans l'air du temps, et le jeu est excellent.
Les Colons de Catan, c'est un peu la version moderne et politiquement correcte du Risk. Un Risk où l'on ne guerroie pas pour conquérir des territoires, mais où l'on commerce et l'on rivalise pacifiquement pour construire des routes, des colonies et des cités. Un Risk où l'on n'occupe pas les terres du voisin mais où l'on colonise un continent vierge, sans le moindre indigène à massacrer ou à réduire en esclavage. Les colons de Catan, c'est le fantasme d'une histoire européenne à l'eau de rose, d'une histoire faite par des bâtisseurs, des explorateurs et des marchands. D'un simple point de vue sociologique, c'est déjà intéressant, et ce n'est sans doute pas par hasard que ce jeu nous vient d'Allemagne.

Les colons de Catan c'est aussi un très bon jeu, aux règles simples, au matériel agréable, qui mèle harmonieusement tactique, chance et interaction. Chaque joueur démarre avec deux colonies et deux tronçons de route. À Chaque tour de jeu, un jet de dés détermine lesquelles des territoires en jeu rapporteront des ressources aux colonies adjacentes. Ces ressources - brique, bois, laine, roche, blé - sont nécessaires pour construire de nouvelles routes, installer de nouvelles colonies, bâtir des cités. Dans ce jeu, en effet, on construit mais on ne détruit jamais. Chacun a donc des ressources différentes, mais peut éventuellement se procurer ce qui lui fait défaut en commerçant avec les autres joueurs. Cités, colonies et quelques bonus annexes rapportent des points, et le premier à dix points est vainqueur. C'est tout, c'est simple, cela laisse une certaine place au calcul mais n'est jamais vraiment prise de tête. Petit plus, qui est sans doute aussi pour beaucoup dans l'extraordinaire succès du jeu, le plateau de jeu, constitué d'une structure d'hexagones disposés aléatoirement, est différent à chaque partie. Seul défaut du jeu, il est assez fréquent qu'un joueur, du fait d'une mauvaise position initiale et d'une malchance en début de partie, se retrouve rapidement hors course.

Que dire de plus? Pendant presque un an, je n'ai joué quasiment qu'aux colons de Catan, et après quelques années de break dues à la saturation, je l'ai redécouvert avec ses nouveaux scénarios, ses nouvelles variantes, et toujours autant de plaisir.
Comme toujours, le succès commercial a en effet entrainé la parution d'une foule d'extensions et de produits dérivés - et même d'une édition promotionnelle pour une marque de whisky dans laquelle les joueurs bâtissent des distilleries.

La boite de base ne permet de jouer qu'à 3 ou 4, et une extension est nécessaire pour le jeu à 5 ou 6. Celui-ci est cependant moins intéressant, ne serait-ce que parce que le défaut indiqué plus haut est encore plus prononcé.
L'extension maritime - Les Marins de Catan - est en revanche très intéressante, enrichissant le jeu de nouveaux mécanismes et d'une foultitude de variantes pour tous les goûts. Ouvrant le jeu, elle rend plus satisfaisant le jeu à 5 ou 6 - mais il vous faudra alors le jeu de base, l'extension 5-6 joueurs, l'extension maritime et l'extension 5-6 joueurs à l'extension maritime. Cela commence à faire cher.
L'extension "Cités et Chevaliers" alourdit sensiblement un jeu qui n'en avait nul besoin, au point de le dénaturer, et je la déconseille donc.
Il y a beaucoup de texte, et malheuresement en allemand, dans le très beau "livre des colons de Catan". Ce recueil de scénarios s'adresse à ceux qui, comme moi, apprécient le jeu de base et l'extension maritime, et ignore totalement l'extension Cités et Chevaliers. 200 pages de scénarios donc, accompagnés d'une petite boite contenant les éléments - voies ferrées, volcans, jungle, etc - nécessaires pour les jouer et, surtout, pour imaginer votre propre version des colons. Ce livre développe en effet l'une des grandes qualités des colons de Catan, son caractère ouvert et modulaire. Avec la boite de base, l'extension Seefahrer, le matériel pour six joueurs et le livre, vous avez tout ce qu'il faut pour imaginer à l'infini scénarios et variantes, produisant pour chaque partie un jeu différent - mais on réservera quand même le livre à ceux qui lisent l'allemand, et se sentent le courage de jouer chaque fois à un nouveau jeu.
Les variantes "historiques" s'adressent aussi avant tout aux inconditionnels du jeu. Sont parus pour l'instant Die Siedler von Nuernberg, une première boite de deux scénarios historiques, La pyramide de Cheops et Alexandre le Grand, et une seconde boite de deux scénarios, La Muraille de Chine et La Guerre de Troie. La Guerre de Troie, dans lequel les joueurs sont disvisés en deux camps, partisans de Troie et de Mycène, sans savoir quels sont leurs alliés et leurs adversaires, est sans doute la meilleure déclinaison des Colons de Catan, et sans conteste la melleure manière d'y jouer à 6 joueurs. C'est un achat indispensable pour tous les amateurs de Catan.
Je signale par ailleurs aux collectioneurs quelques curiosités typiquement américaines publiés par des maisons spécialisées : un scénario chrétien Settlers of Canaan, et un scénario mormon, Settlers of Zarahemla. C'est drôle et exotique, mais pas vraiment indispensable.
Les Colons de l'âge de pierre et Settlers of America ont chacun droit à leur fiche dans la ludothèque idéale, car ce sont des jeux à part entière, même si leurs concepts de base sont empruntés aux Colons de Catan. Il en va de même de la version spatiale et d'Elasund, qui en sont encore plus éloignés.
----
Except for the Magic the Gathering frenzy, the Settlers of Catan series is the biggest hit in the game business for these last ten years. This is not surprising: the game theme was in the air, and the game itself is very well designed.
The Settlers of Catan are like a modern and politically correct Risk. Instead of fighting to conquer territories, players peacefully compete one with another to build roads, settlements and cities. Instead of occupying the neighbour's land, players colonize a new continent, with no native to slaughter or enslave. The Settlers of Catan are the fantasy of a mawkish european history, a history made by builders, explorators and merchants. On a pure historical and sociological point of view, this is already interesting, as is interesting the fact that this game comes from Germany.

The Settlers of Catan, however, is also a very good game, with simple rules, with nice components, with a balanced mix of tactic, strategy, luck and interaction. Each player starts with two settlements and two road sections. Each turn, a die roll decides which lands will produce commodities given to the owners of the neighbouring cities and settlements. These commodities - brick, wood, wool, rocks and wheat - are used to build new roads, new settlements, new cities. In this game, players build but never destroy anything. Each player has different commodities, but they may get what they lack by trading one with another. Cities, Settlements and a few extra bonuses award victory points, and the first player with ten victory points wins the game. That's all, it's simple, there is some recknoning but never brain teasing. The game board modular structure, made of 19 different hexes, makes every game different, and this also made a lot for the game's appeal. The only problem with the Settlers is that a player with a bad starting position and bad die rolls in the first turns may be very soon out of the race for victory. 

What more? For about one year, I played and played the settlers. I probably played it too much, and resigned for a few years, but I've recently rediscovered it, with its new scenarios and variants, and been enthralled again.
As usual, the outstanding commercial success of the Settlers gave way to many, too many, variants and expansions. There is even a "whisky-settlers" edition in which players build distilleries instead of settlements.

The basic set allows for only 3 or 4 players, and an expansion set is requested to play with 5 or 6. The game with more players, however, is far less exciting because it tends to drag on and on, and the "out of the race" problem comes more often.
On the opposite, the Seafarers expansion is very interesting, introducing new ideas, new mechanisms, and, most of all, the possibility to build your own scenarios and variants. Since it opens new horizons to the game, it also makes it much better with five or six players.... but the basic set, the seafarer expansion, the 5-6 players expansion and the 5-6 players sefarers expansion, this begins to be expensive, and for the price you can buy four other games.
The Cities and Knights expansion is very dispensable, since it only makes the game heavier and more complicated. You can pass on this one.
Theres' much text, german text, in the "Settlers of Catan book", so it's only for german-speaking settlers addicts. This compendium of scenarii has been written for the players who, like me, use the basic set and the Seafarers expansion, and like to design their own scenario. 200 pages with various ideas and scenarii, and a little box with all the components (railtracks, jungle, volcanoes…) you need to play them and to design your own. The book emphasizes on the greates quality of the Settlers of Catan, a quality it shares only with Cosmic Encounter and Magic the Gathering, it's openness and modularity. With the basic set, the Seafarers, the six players expansions and the book, you have all you need for unnummerable scenarii and variants, making each game a new and different game. If that's what you want from Settlers, go for it.
The historical scenarii were clearly designed for players who already know the game well, and each one of them brings some new and interesting mechanisms into the game. Die Siedler von Nürnberg is the most complex. The two boxes of two scenarios - Troy & the Great Wall ; Cheops & Alexander the Great - are less ambitious, but the Troyan War scenario is a real gem, a must buy for all Settlers players - it is also the best way to play Settlers of Catan with 6 players. In the Trojan War, players are divided in two teams, Mycena and Troy, but noone knows who for sure who is on what side, and this brings a real new dimension in the game.
There are also two typically american editions, one aimed at the christian market - Settlers of Canaan - and one for Mormons family - Settlers of Zarahemla. They are also fun and exotic collector items.
As for Settlers of the Stone Age and Settlers of America, probably the very best follow-ups of the Catan series, they have their own entry in the ideal game library, since they clearly deserves it. Their basic systems come from Catan, but there's much more in the game, and they feel really different. It's even more true of the Space Settlers game and of Elasund.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The designer for Settlers of Catan, Klaus Teuber, passed away a few days ago on April 1st, 2023. The game needs no introduction here on BGG. I have touched Catan only sporadically over the past two decades. Probably about half a dozen times with the most recent game about 2 years ago. Even though the game often gets mixed reviews from hobby gamers, this is CATAN we are talking about – the foundational game that is at least partially if if not mostly responsible for the explosion of Euro-style board games around the world. Whatever misgiving one may have of the game, it seems wrong not to own a copy of the classic. I have kept the original Mayfair Settlers of Catan in my collection since day one of my board gaming journey and while other titles have come and gone, I have never seriously entertained the idea of selling the entire lot, including the expansions. Call it nostalgia, hype or hoarding, it just never crossed my mind to get rid of the one game that has defined the hobby.

Catan started with a bang

The gap between Catan sessions grew larger right after I was done with graduate school. Up till then, we played and enjoyed the plain vanilla Catan. While I wouldn’t say we were avid Catan fans, everyone was poor and owning a copy of Catan meant many nights of fun that didn’t cost us a dime. In short, we had a good time bonding of the game. At some point, toward the end of my time in school, I made the mistake of getting the 5-6 player expansion and introduced it to a bunch of newbies. A BIG mistake. That game session soured many, myself included as it dragged for hours. Even though details of the actual day are sparse, I am quite sure that everyone left with a bitter taste in their mouth. I never saw much of Catan after that session. Part of that was because I left school and the other part was just the growth of my board game collection, thanks in part to the amazing games published by Rio Grande Games.

The dice do not always roll in your favor

Still, Catan stayed on my shelf and waited patiently for its turn. The couple of times I played in the intervening years further convinced me that the game has a limited audience, at least within my gaming circle. It did not help that at least half of my group was not enamored by the game. There is no doubt that the single source of frustration is the inability to catch up once you fall behind in building settlements and collecting resources. Sitting there round after round, looking at the board without making any progress can feel stifling and frustrating. There have been many strategy articles written about how the game is all about mitigating luck. I cannot deny that with superior strategy, one can still eke out a victory even though conditions are tough. But due to the small sample size, the game is still ultimately bound by the dice rolls. You only get to roll a handful of times each game and if the dice gods do not favor your settlements, there is very little you can do about it. Probabilities be damned.

Yet, the millions of people who have enjoyed Catan can’t possibly be wrong, can they? Because of Teuber’s recent passing, I wanted to pull out the two designs of his that are in my collection: Catan and Lowenherz. I decided that my 8 year old should be old enough to grasp the rules and intricacies of Catan that it was worth a try. With my kid, any game has the potential for a hit or miss. I have noticed some trends in her gaming preferences, but overall, I know she enjoys gaming more than any game itself. She may have favorites, but she does not pine for them, nor care if she loses. Sure, at times she will sulk, but I think that is true even for adult players.

Simple rules

The first thing that struck me after such a long hiatus from Catan is the simplicity of the rules. My kid’s attention span is fleeting especially when it comes to listening to the rules before play. She can absorb the rules, but enjoy learning through experience. With Catan, it was not an issue. It took me 10 minutes after set up to properly explain the basic rules and after a short Q&A, we were off to the races. In not thinking about Catan after all these years, I was pleasantly reminded of how accessible the game was for my daughter, and likely true for all the casual gamers out there who have embraced the game because of the easy to digest rule set. The winning conditions are intuitive: be the first to reach 10 points through building cities/settlements, longest road, largest army or getting VP cards. That’s it. You don’t have a plethora of choices to score points, which means all your efforts are focused on these 4 options. Beyond that, the most difficult part to explain are the building restrictions on the map and perhaps, the impact of moving the robber around the board. I have been somewhat jaded by rules explanation for the current crop of mid-weight games that I have resorted to watching how-to-play videos – something which I rarely do. In contrast, teaching Catan was a joy. Never mind that the rulebook in the Mayfair edition came in three parts and contains an “almanac” – teaching Catan reminded me of the biggest reason why I still love the “OG” (original German) designs.

A different type of joy

It occurred to me when playing Catan with my partner and my kid, that this was the first time I have played Catan with 3 players and with someone so young. After a few cycles around the table chucking dice, I saw one thing that always makes the gamer in me smile- my kid was eagerly anticipating the outcome of each dice roll, particularly during her turn. She is asking for the dice and hollering at her folks to hurry up. She is reaching across the table to grab the dice and is asking for trades even before her turn. This happens rarely with other dice games in my collection. Sadly to say, most dice games from Knizia fail to elicit the same response, perhaps with the exception of 5 player Excape. Don’t get me wrong, she will gladly play and enjoys Pickomono or High Score or Into the Deep, but that extra ummph isn’t present. It is unclear to me why Catan engages her this way. Perhaps winning might have something to do with it. But I suspect length, theme and agency in deciding where to build cities or settlements has a huge role in creating the extra excitement. There is a secret sauce in Catan and this is Teuber’s masterpiece for a reason.

The contrast in my kid’s excitement with each roll of the dice could not be more stark from my partner’s grimace. We played back to back games and in each session, some poor rolls caused her to miss out on the premium locations for construction. Of course once that happens, there is a slow spiral into non-competitiveness which can be hard to catch up. Since this was family gaming, she was not particularly bothered, and neither was I when my kid rolled snake eyes twice in the final few turns to win the game. The whooping and hollering from her more than made up for it. My kid won both games over the Easter weekend and she was ecstatic. To be clear, we NEVER throw games. Ever. She earns all her victories.

In short

Seeing my daughter win Catan – twice- over the weekend made me appreciate that not every player cares about the unevenness of luck in a game. In fact, probably most casual players don’t. The fact that sometimes luck plays a role in crowning the victor will be appealing to some folks, most likely the casual gamer who is already indirectly handicapped compared to hobby gamers from the get go. The same applies with kids. Games like Catan levels the playing field just by a tad, giving the inexperienced a fighting chance to win even though experience will ultimately triumph. I am ok with that.

After seeing my partner’s reaction and knowing my game group, Catan is unlikely to ever make another appearance on our game night. In fact, I am not even sure I would pick Catan with so many other quality games waiting in the wings. And yet, that is perfectly fine as there will always be a place for Catan on many other tables, including ours. I am quite sure my kid will ask for more Catan in the upcoming weeks and months. The game maybe the same, but a different crowd brings with it a different type of gaming joy, but joy nonetheless. We should be so lucky to cherish what Catan brings to the table as is, as opposed to what it could or should have been.

In the mean time, save that old copy of Catan that you have been meaning to trade. Bring it out and try it with your neighbor or colleague that has never gamed before. You might be surprised. For the rest of us grizzled veterans, there is always Teuber’s other underrated masterpiece – Lowenherz.

Final word: Good
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Most Over-Hyped BoardGame of the Modern BoardGame Era .. Please Avoid & Don't Use as an Intro Game

○ Short Why This Review :

I want more people to like board gaming...  this bad game turns people off board gaming.

Run, .. run very fast...  don't say you weren't warned.

○ Short Synopsis :

Way, way, way too much luck for such a long, laborious, & way overpriced game (for $68+ w expansion, you can get one or more games that are way, way, way more fun.)

○ Why This Review :

Pre-pandemic, I ran the largest irl board gaming group in NJ...  I think board games are a healthy way to have fun & socialize, and I would love for board gaming to become even more popular.

Catan is a dated game, that easily turns meeples off gaming; and should 'never' be used as an intro to board gaming game.  But even if you're not new to gaming, you shouldn't waste your time & money on this game.

○ Synopsis :

Catan pretty much fails at every level, & only excels in two categories:

• Schadenfreude
• Masochism

○ Detailed Review:

So let's take a tour of all the failures :

#1 Failure :-))  Way, way, way too much luck for the length of the game!

Games with a heavy luck component aren't inherently bad "per se"...  to each their own, no?

But, "in general", games with heavy luck are shorter, games with less luck are longer.  This also tends to mirror the goals of the game for the different player demographics.  Short/lucky/light gamers aren't looking for complex rules and/or playing experiences .. they want a light fun experience (usu while waiting for another game and/or while doing something else.)  Conversely, long/strategic/heavy gamers are usually looking for minimal luck, because they want their decisions to matter & they want their investment in time to be worth it.

Catan is broken no matter which way you look at it...  it's a luck game that's too long, or it's a strategy game with too much luck.  There's luck in the dice rolling for resources, there's luck in which development cards you draw (no choice), and if all the players are equal level - good luck with the completely broken trading mechanism.  Have a great strategy?..  managed to get lumber & brick on an 8!.. ? ... watch the Schadenfreude of the other players as 8 fails to get rolled during the course of a game! ? ... so, not only are you having a miserable time, but because these critical resources are now constrained, watch as the whole game slows to a crawl & trading becomes non-existent.

#2 Failure :-))  No catch-up mechanism...  

So after 30 min, you realize you've 60 min to go & no chance of winning...  does this sound like fun to you?..  if yes, well I did say this game excelled in Masochism .. if not, well, there's probably another person turned off board gaming ?

I'm not saying that every game needs to have a catch-up mechanism, nor am I saying that every game which does, does it well.  The closest Catan has, is the trading mechanism...  but that's not a good catchup mechanism, as it only works with equally talented & advanced gamers that can see the weighted value of a trade .. (and of course, even if they do weight it correctly luck can completely upend any careful planning).  Plus, the more restricted trading is, the slower the game; which if you're not in a position where you can actually win, just makes the game more painful.

#3 Failure :-))  Various mechanics "were" cutting edge...

You might think this is a positive, and if you traveled back in time, it was.  But another way to think of it, in today's terms; many of the mechanics were an "early alpha" release.  And many, many games have taken the mechanics in Catan and tweaked/evolved/re-combined them to make much, much better games.

#4 Failure :-))  Some mechanics don't really work...

The trading is the biggest failure in Catan...  there's no real structure given to it, & the resources are so scarce it makes trading painful at best.  What success there can be, is completely up to the player "group", and not wrt the game.  And in a cutthroat game, of equal level players, trading often falls apart completely contributing to the length of the game.

The board layout (when done randomly) is often unbalanced ... you can often determine "who's in the running" & who's not simply by this alone.  So imagine playing a 90 minute game, & having almost no chance to win due to skill, right from the start!..  I've seen a player there, & they were so frustrated, I never saw them board game again.

The "robber" makes a bad game worse by having the players attack one another...  and most games aren't fun with this aspect as an aside, unless the act of attacking other players is directly designed to be fun (The Dragon & Flagon) comes to mind.  And since the robber is on a 7, it's the most frequent action.

## History :-))  Ok, here's where Catan has value.

Do you like to goto Museums?..  Do you like to use old 8-bit tech, to relive the "Glory Days" of your youth?..  Ok then there's no doubt Catan, like the Neanderthal or the Dodo, have a place in history.  One could argue, it was the 'first' mainstream euro board game to reach zeitgeist in pop culture.

So while it deserves a place in history, as does Monopoly & it's 275 million copies (as of 2015), that doesn't make it a good game worth playing in modern times.

## Honorable Mention :-))  But what about the expansions?...

One of the common refrains I hear from meeples who've drank the Catan Kool-Aid is that, "ok, granted there are some aspects of the game that aren't that great; but the expansions help."

First, I really dislike a game where it 'requires' an expansion...  when that's the case, the base game should just include the expansion.  Secondly, you're throwing more money after bad; Catan is already overpriced (MSRP: $55.00, but usu seasonally averaging $32 or $46) plus then either of the two commonly recommended/overpriced expansions of Cities & Knights (MSRP: $55.00, but usu seasonally averaging $37 or $43) or Seafarers Expansion (MSRP: $55.00, but usu seasonally averaging $36 or $44).  To them, I challenge, you're telling me that for $68+ the 'best' you can do for gaming value is Catan + Expansion?.?..

Also I will note that even the most fervent Catan cultist when giving the above defense, will say "help" & not "fix"...  so in the end, you're looking at $68+ for a "meh" ? game.

** $68+ :-))  Hmmm...

This is off the top of my head...

TransAmerica $33
Armadora $20
Love Letter $9
Sushi Go! $6

... not a definitive, list, just top of the head stuff / first thing to pop in my mind...  but way more fun, & all of which are better for beginners.  

** Only saving grace :-))  It comes with two dice...

Here's my recommendation, take the two dice, & everyone rolls off...  highest total wins.  In case of tie, all repeat the roll (go catchup mech!) until only one player has the highest total.  Then make a cool game with the components, and/or use the components to replace missing pieces from other games.

Was it fun?..  I don't know, but at least you saved 89 minutes of your life for a game, after which you'll ask yourself, "was it fun", and probably still have the same average answer of "meh" ?.

I'll end with a favorite quote of mine...

“A strange game. The only winning move is not to play.” -- Joshua/WOPR -- WarGames (1983)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] Like many people, Catan one of the boardgames that got me into the hobby. I loved it, then I liked it, then I was indifferent about it, and then I sold it before I felt any worse about it. Finding games on Board Game Arena for Catan is quite literally instantaneous; well, as long as you have Premium, because there seem to be dozens of non-Premium players waiting for a game at any time. 

Catan should not take a long time; however, turn-order immediately put me into some terrible spots off-the-bat, and players were taking minutes to perform each of their turns. Frankly, I should not be surprised, but I am surprised how much starting a game of Catan feels like voluntarily walking into a hostage situation. Also, in the first five turns, double-6 showed up twice. That was also when I steadily came to realize that I accidentally forgot to take anything that gave me Bricks... so, uh, a win would be a miracle. By the mid-game, it was clear that one player who immediately got a second settlement in the middle of the board was going to win - the Robber naturally just kept alternating between their two Brick deposits.  

Hilarious is how obnoxious the trading phase is: the many pop-ups for "X wants Brick" from one player regularly got a laugh out of me. 

"Y wants Sheep" is probably the funniest so far because they literally just asked for a Sheep without offering anything at all.

People saying that Catan works best when players are willing to trade miss what I believe to be a key point: many people are bad at trading, and far people keep offering terribly one-sided trades. Everyone needs that Brick, everyone needs the late-game Wheat, everyone needs the late-game Brick, no one wants the Bricks when no one wants the Bricks.

Initial placement in Catan is extremely important. In some rare cases, players can potentially get away with using the 2:1 trades (which assumes they have the Brick to reach it) or the 3:1. Worse, though, is that players can get boxed-in by players with enough roads because their Brick and Wood supply was simply superior. To be fair, in my most recent game, securing a 3:1 with a powerful wood supply nearly got me a win off a Church card, most Knight cards, and longest road (I thought I could have stood a chance at winning until a few lucky dice rolls loaded two other players with crazy amounts of wood). I really got into the tail-end of that match: if only I just got a single Wheat card, I'll score big, I tell ya'! My 3-settlement 8-tile Wood supply was going to win me the game if the Robber was not blocking my stupid wheat tile!

----- X -----

Really, Catan has survived the test of time: it is great. For how dry of a Euro it feels to me (or as miserable of an experience as it feels), I still remember how amazing the feeling of playing it in my first year of playing boardgames. I ran out and bought my own copy that went unused for years - reason being, almost everyone I knew already owned copies. It *feels* like it has depth, it *feels* like it's competitive, and it *feels* like everyone is involved in the process. Catan does not induce a heavy amount of brain-burn, Perhaps the low downtime plays into that since turns consist of rolling dice and collecting resources; compared to something like Space Base or Dice Forge, Catan is far less fiddly and much easier to engage with (simpler iconography, simpler resources, many types of resources that are all relatively intuitive). It is also one of the games I can personally attest to having gotten many people into the hobby, let alone having convinced many people to sit around and play any boardgame at all who otherwise my not have. The Robber probably lives rent-free in many peoples' heads, especially when rolling it on your own turn after picking up a dozen resources - I rolled into it 3 times with 8 cards in my hand each time, which was just enough to trade for a City... I never got that City by the end-game. 

Some guy lamented that I decided the game by using a Robber and stealing from them. Sorry, but I needed a resource they likely had more than another player. Well, I am not actually sorry - that game had been going on for over an hour, and they won anyway because someone else accepted a trade at the last minute that gave said player the victory. Catan is prone to king-making in my experience, and it is largely obvious when it happens - unless the dice roll in my favor, sometimes taking obviously-bad trades is the only way to stay in the running. If two players trade, one player gets more ahead than the other, and this will be at the detriment of all other players in the game. Comes with the experience, which is also why I am not a fan of actually playing Catan anymore. This is one of those games that I have actually turned-down a match of on more than one occasion (see also: Munchkin, which I cannot even say I played 'once' as the games I played never reached a conclusion before everyone left the table). I have somewhere over a dozen plays of Catan over my life, which feels like a lot for me - one of my opponents had 50 games logged, another had 250, and the person whining had 800 of Catan alone. Please. Unlike when a friend tries to tell me that I will "never achieve mastery of a game like those other people unless I play it hundreds of times", I do not derive joy in that - I burned myself out of Catan with only a bit over a dozen over the course of a few years. Personally, there are many games that I can see myself playing hundreds of times, and Catan is nowhere near that list.

I will say: Ticket to Ride is just the better game. No questions asked on that front. There's just something about Catan which, well, works, for the most part and for most people. Despite feeling like a captive forced to an hour of Catan, I will admit I was on the edge of my seat an hour later begging for that stupid 8-tile to score me the Wood I need to get the Wheat I need to get the City I need to get more Wheat to get those last victory points... NO, ANYTHING BUT THE ROBBER!

textfield_comment_value:
Not bad, and inspired a movement, but just not all that good.  They hit nicely on a formula that works with no major flaws and which improves upon classic titans like Monopoly in every way.  I've played the game many times including most expansions.  When I was first introduced to it before I'd played many euros or "new age" games I thought it was fun and the group I played with was good.  

The board is modular and the theme is nice and charming.  There is some good strategy to how you set up your initial pieces, although the length of the game can allow for some whack odds that throw off your strategy (not enough rolls for the odds to even out).  It ends up being a choice of going for a wide spread of resources and numbers and playing a very conservative game, or going for gold and either hitting big (easy win) or being screwed (sitting there doing nothing for an hour).  Neither of these are particularly satisfying really, for obvious reasons.  There are a few different ways to win and trying them each out can last you a good handful of games, but it gets very dry after that and only the social interaction aspect can save it.  Game is too long for what it is, so I suggest a house rule of starting with one town and one city to speed things up.  

Thus this game depends heavily on a good group that all understand the game and play to stop the current leader from winning so as to better their own chances, while cleverly manipulating each other.  Unfortunately you can play with people who are too soft, too random, or prejudiced about the take-that and trading action and it kind of ruins it.  In other words, the game has a high and obvious luck factor with the die rolls and mitigating this to make the game fun requires that people play properly.  It really can ruin it if people do not play strategically and engage in group discussions.  Otherwise it becomes a luck-fest that is way too long to be a fun luck-fest, a la Monopoly.  

A really good game involves everyone debating about who is winning and who has better potential while trying to convince everyone that you aren't the threat.  If you allow creative trades it improves this formula.  While this is somewhat fun, it can really make the game drag on and become a matter of who can wear the others down by being the better (more aggressive?) business negotiator.  While I like that sort of thing, it can be done much better in a much shorter period of time in games that don't bother with all the fiddling with a euro game structure, such as in The Resistance.  Basically what I'm saying is after a while the whole game is just about the negotiating anyway, so you may as well do away with the the rest of the game.  

After not long my group played only with the Cities and Knights expansion (best expansion) as vanilla Catan was just too dry.  After that group parted ways due to people moving, I moved on and rarely played Catan again but now and again newer players ask if you have it and beg for a play.  I don't mind as I have the nice wooden box edition and it is cool to pull it out now and then, but I am always quickly reminded of how I'd rather be playing something else.  I try to push for Cities and Knights to at least make it interesting, but newer players are concerned that it will complicate things, and even some seasoned players that somehow still like Catan will refuse it as they feel it ruins the purity for them and they just want what's familiar.  This game has become so big that there are many die-hards that know it very well but somehow do not know other strategy games (aren't really gamers), and will always favour Catan.  

While it is not a bad game, it is unfortunate in a way that it became quite so popular as many non-gamers choose it over better games due to the infamous "I already know this game" disorder.  This is where I try to explain that they had to learn Catan at some point and loved it so maybe it is worth learning a newer game that I promise is better.  It is kind of that game that won't go away as too many people got hooked on it and it is just too well known.  This, combined with the lightness of the strategy and simplicity of play while offering some minor depth and the feeling you are playing a proper game makes it consistently appealing to many who want to play a real game but don't really want to play anything heavy.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
Endlich sind meine Kinder so weit, um sie in die Welt der "guten" Spiele einzuführen. „Die Siedler von Catan“ ist eines dieser Spiele, welches für einen solchen Übergang sehr gut geeignet ist.
Die Spieler bauen in diesem Spiel Siedlungen und erweitern diese später zu Städten auf einer Insel, genannt "Catan".

Durch Würfelwürfe am Zugbeginn, erhalten alle Spieler Erträge der Landschaften, an denen ihre Siedlungen angrenzen. Auf diese Weise wird Getreide, Holz, Wolle, Erz und Lehm gesammelt und für Straßen, Siedlungen, Städte und Entwicklungskarten ausgegeben werden. Siedlungen und Städte geben neben den Ressourcen die wichtigen Siegpunkte.
Runde um Runde breiten sich die Spieler weiter auf der Insel aus, bis es einem Spieler gelingt 12 Siegpunkte zu erreichen und damit gewinnt.

„Catan“ - wie es heute heißt - ist immer noch ein gutes Spiel aus der alten Zeit. Sehr wichtig ist, dass sich die Spieler auf den Handel untereinander einlassen und ihre Ressourcenkarten miteinander tauschen, um Interaktion stattfinden zu lassen. Außerdem erhält damit jeder Spieler eine faire Chance zu gewinnen und das Spiel wird insgesamt beschleunigt. Ohne dieses Verhandlungselement ist es ein großes Glücksspiel, da es nur darauf ankommen würde, wessen Zahlen im richtigen Moment gewürfelt werden.
Auch mit dem Verhandlungselement ist das Spiel klar vom Zufall bestimmt, der durch die Häufigkeit der Würfelwürfe ausgeglichen werden sollte. Mich hat "Catan" als Jugendlicher begeistert, als es 1995 auf den Markt kam. Heute hat es ein wenig Charme verloren, kommt aber dennoch immer mal wieder auf unseren Spieltisch.

Die „Seefahrer“ Erweiterung variiert die Karte auf der gespielt wird. Die Spieler müssen mit Holz und Wolle Schiffe bauen, um auf andere Inseln zu gelangen. In der Anleitung sind viele verschiedene Szenarien enthalten, lässt den Spielern aber auch selbst noch eine Menge kreativen Freiraum.
Mir gefällt die Erweiterung ganz gut, da sie das Spielfeld vergrößert und insgesamt mehr Variabilität ins Spiel bringt.
In der Sonderedition "Kolonien" wird die Regel der Schifffahrt geändert. Jeder Spieler hat lediglich drei Schiffe zum Bau zur Verfügung, dafür werden diese nicht mehr als Route aufgestellt, sondern bewegen sich tatsächlich über das Feld. Beim Entdecken der neuen Kolonien wird das entsprechende Schiff zu einem Außenposten auf das Feld gesetzt, welcher später den Bau einer Siedlung erlaubt. Die Landschaften der "Kolonien" produzieren lediglich kleine Plättchen, die mit Schiffen zur Hauptinsel zurückgebracht werden müssen, wo sie in Punkte oder Ressourcen umgewandelt werden können.
Diese Erweiterung greift die Thematik der Kolonialzeit auf, welcher derzeit sehr umstritten ist. Leider erklärt weder das Spiel selbst, noch die Anleitung die damalige Ausbeutung der "Kolonien". Abgesehen davon hat mir dieses Szenario sehr gut gefallen, da mit den Schiffen 'realitätsnah' umgegangen wird und sie immer wieder über das Meer gefahren werden müssen.
Die „Städte und Ritter“ Erweiterung erhöht die Komplexität des Spiels in einem guten Maß nach oben. Mit ihr kommen Ritterfiguren, die für die Sicherheit der Insel und all ihrer Bewohner sorgen. Sie sind nötig, um die regelmäßigen Barbarenüberfälle zurückzuschlagen, die "Catan" heimsuchen, wobei der ruhmreiche Siedler mit Bonussiegpunkten belohnt wird. Außerdem erwirtschaften die Städte in dieser Erweiterung nicht mehr das Doppelte an Ressourcen. Vielmehr werden die Handelsgüter Münzen, Tuch und Papier eingeführt, die zum internen Ausbau der Städte und schlussendlich zum Erwerb der neuen Entwicklungskarten genutzt werden. "Städte und Ritter" ist für meinen Geschmack die bessere Erweiterung, da sie das Spiel in den oberen Kennerbereich anhebt. Es gibt mit ihr wesentlich mehr Optionen, was mit den Ressourcen auf der Hand angestellt werden kann und erlaubt den Spielern einen besseren Ausbau seines Königreichs mit individuellen Sonderfähigkeiten in ihren Metropolen.
Es gibt noch viele weitere Erweiterungen, die weitere Szenarien und Spielmodi einführen, aber für mich reichen die ersten beiden vollkommen aus. Lediglich der 'Ereignisse auf Catan' Kartenstapel aus der "Atlantis" Erweiterung finde ich spannend, da durch ihn der Zufall der Würfel weitestgehend herausgenommen wird und die Schriftgröße der Ertragszahlen auf den Landschaftsfeldern endlich ihrer Bestimmung nachkommt.
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
A interação entre os jogadores é certamente o aspecto mais marcante e divertido de Catan, característica esta que pode também fazer as partidas demorarem um pouco além do que diz na caixa caso os jogadores sejam muito insistentes e/ou lentos na hora de negociar. A forte dependência de sorte na produção de matéria-prima também pode fazer as partidas ficarem arrastadas dependendo da situação dos jogadores no tabuleiro (ex. se um determinado recurso estiver frequentemente faltando à todos na mesa e ao mesmo tempo ninguém tiver porto). Caso a partida seja com tabuleiro aleatório, é importante auxiliar bastante os novatos na Fase de Fundação, pois se posicionarem mal suas aldeias iniciais, terão uma péssima experiência do jogo.

O manual diz que quando os jogadores estiverem experientes pode-se ignorar a regra de só poder construir após a fase de negociação. Eu achei melhor sem esta regra mesmo, pois ela deixa o jogo mais travado, porém a retirada dela também pode aumentar o downtime, já que os jogadores poderão fazer mais ações em seus turnos.

O tempo de partida com quatro jogadores gira entre 40 minutos (partida considerada bem rápida) e 1h40min (tempo máximo).

Muita gente critica o Catan ferrenhamente, comparando-o com inúmeros outros jogos atuais, mas na maioria das vezes a comparação é péssima porque não consideram um simples e notório elemento que o diferencia dos outros: a possibilidade de negociação. A real é que, ainda hoje, poucos jogos possuem esse mecanismo, pois é um elemento extremamente difícil de fazer bem feito e Catan o implementa com maestria. Um detalhe que acho importante frisar é que em Catan não se pode dar um recurso a outro jogador sem receber algum outro recurso em troca. Me parece algo importante de ressaltar porque já vi até produtor de conteúdo dizendo que se pode fazer isso e dizendo inclusive que sempre jogou assim e que é isso que faz o jogo ser divertido. Catan é um jogo que tem alguns detalhes de regra cruciais para manter a competitividade, e não duvido nada que muitas dessas avaliações negativas venham de experiências ruins de partidas jogadas com regra errada como esta.

Um erro grave que ouço pessoas comentarem que fazem, por exemplo, é sortear as fichas numeradas no tabuleiro. Não faça isso! Pois o espaçamento entre os números é importante e garantido pela colocação correta das fichas. Esse equívoco além de não estar nas regras, ainda desbalanceia o jogo. Catan possui um setup bastante espeficio (mesmo aleatorizando os tiles) e aleatorizar as fichas numeradas não faz parte dele.

Uma dica para melhorar a fluidez do jogo (embora possa diminuir a transparência) é, no momento da produção, todos pegarem seus recursos ao mesmo tempo.

Uma sugestão para melhorar a transparência em mesas muito competitivas é convencionar entre os jogadores que no momento de construir, ao invés de descartar os recursos de volta no monte, eles devem ser descartados em uma área separada de descarte.

Ainda sobre transparência, uma dica em relação à carta de progresso Monopólio (que pode facilmente ser alvo de trapaça por obrigar todos os jogadores a lhe entregar todas as cartas da matéria-prima do tipo que você escolher) é: caso você desconfie que alguém está roubando, basta fazer a contagem das cartas no monte. É um procedimento simples e que pode ser aproveitado inclusive para conferência das cartas em jogo. Mas não faça esse procedimento sem motivos. Faça somente em sua vez, quando jogar a carta (Monopólio), e se desconfiar que alguém está omitindo cartas que deveria lhe entregar.

No final das contas a diversão proporcionada suplanta todas as críticas que fiz, e acaba sempre sendo uma experiência muito prazerosa, principalmente quando todos na mesa aprenderam bem o jogo. Sempre saio TENSO das partidas de Catan, principalmente quando ganho. Porque a qualquer momento alguém pode "bater" na sua frente. \o/

textfield_comment_value:
La puntuación que le doy es de dos puntos.

Resulta difícil tratar de escribir algo acerca de un juego tan popular como el Catán, y más si es en contra, pues no es un juego que crea bien desarrollado ni construido, pero poco a poco, trataré de argumentarlo a continuación:

En el juego asumiremos los papeles de colonos en una tierra virgen, donde deberemos hacernos fuertes estableciendo rutas comerciales entre nuestras ciudades para llegar a ser la más próspera del reino, o lo que es lo mismo, alcanzar siete puntos. Si bien es cierto que no pretende nada en absoluto, la sensación, no está lejos de ser, si quiera, una sensación. Si en lugar de comerciar con ovejas, henos de trigo o arcilla, lo hiciéramos con contenedores de bicicletas, ordenadores y iPods, pues nos daría lo mismo. Con lo cual, el tema es totalmente irrelevante.

Para la mecánica principal del juego voy a hablar de dos conceptos principales: el azar y la buena voluntad de las personas. El primero es muy sencillo de analizar, pues se basa en el manejo de la probabilidad. Tiraremos los dos dados y la suma nos dará un número; si en la casilla que marcan los dados tenemos un pueblo o una ciudad, obtendremos el beneficio indicado (ovejas/madera/trigo/piedra/arcilla), y si no, pues nada.

Como se puede ver en la tabla, el resultado más probable es el siete (6), siendo el central,  y conforme nos alejamos hacia los extremos, la probabilidad decrece en una unidad, hasta el dos y el doce respectivamente (1). Pues bien, el resultado central, el siete, está reservado para el ladrón, que es una figurita que se va moviendo por las casillas y robando a los jugadores que tengan presencia en la misma. Eso nos dice que los siguientes resultados más probables, serán el ocho y el seis, que pasarán a ser las losetas más solicitadas. El problema aquí reside en el propio azar. Y es que éste es perfecto en el infinito. Lo que quiere decir, que a pesar de que resulte obvio que los jugadores vayan llenando el mapa de acuerdo a lo que nos dice la estadística, puede darse el caso, de que se den veinte tiradas seguidas de resultado doce. ¿Que qué os cuento nuevo? Nada, pero recordad que si no sale vuestro número, no tenéis recurso, y sin ellos, tampoco comerciáis, lo que quiere decir, que directamente, no jugáis.

El segundo, en cambio, es un poco más difícil de valorar ya que es totalmente subjetivo. Me refiero a que el juego permite comerciar, es decir intercambiar materiales entre los jugadores de la forma en la que ellos estimen oportuna, sin reglas de ningún tipo. Esto presupone muchas cosas. La primera puede resultar evidente, pero hay que decirla, y es que todos quieran ganar.

Sin embargo esto puede darse al comienzo de la partida, pero se va desvirtuando con el transcurso de la misma, ya que, saldrán a relucir algunas cosas nada deseables. Un ejemplo de las mismas, puede ser el hecho de que alguien, fuera de la victoria, decida hacer ganador a otro, por simple afinidad personal. Como también pudiera serlo, aquello que decía el Joker de Batman, de “yo sólo quiero ver el mundo arder”, y dedicarte a machacar a alguien en particular o a todos en general. Eso ya va a gusto del consumidor.

A la pregunta de si volvería a jugarlo, respondo casi sin pensar: la verdad es que no lo creo. La alta dependencia del azar sumada, al tener que depender de mostrar un perfil bajo, de no sobresalir para que los golpes se los lleve otro, la verdad es que no me gusta en absoluto. Y, sin embargo, es esto mismo lo que creo que lo hace tan popular. Me recuerda mucho a las carreras del Mario Kart, en las que cualquiera pueda ganar, menos el que va primero, ese se lleva todo el amor del resto de jugadores sin que pueda el pobre hacer nada.

Voy a terminar, diciendo que opino como alguien que ha conocido el juego en 2018, con lo cual, no le concederé el beneficio del tiempo, creo que éste es un juez lo suficientemente exigente, para hablar de vigencia o calidad.  La experiencia que me ha ofrecido, en mi opinión ni es divertida, ni recomendable, lo que me hace decir que es un juego que se quedará en mi colección, pero no por mérito propio, si no por estar dedicado por la persona que me lo regaló.

textfield_comment_value:
Settlers is great for its accessibility to new players and the way the game encourages player interaction. The variable board setup adds replayability and long-term interest, while the (mostly) static number arrangement ensures the probabilities are always balanced, even when some resources are scarce. The element of luck can be overly strong at some times, particularly if one player gets a string of bad rolls at the beginning of the game. In other games (Tigris & Euphrates, Puerto Rico, etc.), the player can always take some productive action even when luck is not on his side; in Settlers, the player simply cannot act. I would like to see an official way to mitigate bad luck, but some version of the '[url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/150443/the-famous-welfare-variant]welfare variant[/url]' should work well enough. While I appreciate that trading keeps players engaged, I do not enjoy the mechanic as much as other modes of player interaction, as I feel like I have to 'act' in order to play well. For this reason, the game isn't at the top of my list, but I do enjoy playing it with the right group. [8] (2012-03-23)

After many more plays of Settlers, my appreciation for the game -- and rating -- has improved greatly. Strings of good/bad luck can still hurt, but with good placement (diverse numbers) and repeated play, I don't see it as a major flaw in the game; rather, it is most often the result of a flaw in a player's initial placements. Sometimes it's not, but that's to be expected in a game with dice, and it's not likely to happen again in the next game (or if it does, it's an indication that the fault may in fact be with the player). I will now gladly recommend Settlers and will play it any time I am offered the chance to do so, especially with 4 players (3 is also ok; 5 and 6 work but 4 is preferable). I appreciate the fact that though the game is fairly simple (very few rules) and repetitive (each turn offers the same single mandatory action and few voluntary actions, compared to worker placement or role selection games), the game is still tense and exciting due to the competition for key settlement spots, the need to make a critical trade, and the fear of letting one player get too much of a lead before others are positioned to catch up. A great design worthy of all the praise it has received. [8 -> 10] (2014-01-22)

After many, many, [b]many[/b] more plays of this game, I still think it is quite brilliant, but a couple flaws have emerged which sour the experience a bit for me. First, the ability of players to target each other has emerged as a fairly significant flaw. When players accurately read the board and play within the game, this is fine, but repeated plays with the same group(s) tends to lead to "You win all the time, so I'm blocking you" -- regardless of board state, etc. Other times, someone is blocked early just because ... well, [i]someone[/i] has to be. The ability to screw an individual player is fine, but here, due to fairly constrained opportunities to ameliorate the ramifications of being robbed, this can -- and does -- lead to games where one player is denied a chance to meaningfully compete from an early stage. This is less than ideal when it is just bad luck (someone had to be blocked, and a 7 wasn't rolled for a long time), but incredibly demoralizing when done out of consideration for factors outside the current game (e.g., past wins). Second, trading effectively can, at times, feel like social manipulation / politicking, especially in certain play groups. This is a sub-game I'm increasingly less interested in playing. This is still a great game, but I feel I may have drained it a bit dry... [10 -> 8] (2020-02)
Title: CATAN

textfield_comment_value:
The crimes of Catan are these:

1. With the random board setup and the rolling of dice there's simply too much randomness in acquiring resources for my liking. Even if you could find a path to gain wheat, it could be on a tile that only produces on a 3. I like modular boards, but Clash of Cultures at least starts the same for all players until you factor in the expansion. Mage Knight has a progression of tiles. Catan looks like it does because somebody stopped stirring the gumbo. Starting position can be painfully obvious for a starting player who has played the game enough, or I could see it being an AP nightmare for a newer player.

2. And about that dice rolling for resources. There's the chance you roll and other people get resources, but you don't. Since you received no resources, you might not be able to build anything nor trade for anything. This happened multiple times in the game for me. I just think a player's turn should be an advantage and in a number of cases nothing happened for me and other players gained resources.

"But you can gain resources when it isn't your turn."

Still doesn't take away the crap feeling of a dead turn. I dislike Acquire for when you have to place a tile out in an open area but at least you can buy stocks. Catan? You get nada during a dead turn. If I were to make a creed for game design, the lack of a dead turn has to be listed. It feels inexcusable for a gateway.

3. The robber.

This issue was low for me this time. I wasn't hit much with it, but it was placed in a couple of spots a lot during the game and even one player mentioned at least once how it was being placed in their area to a fault. It's basically a randomized take on bash the leader.

Significant for its influence versus its game play these days. Even if you are picking gateway games, 7 Wonders beats this and even that's slowly growing on me. We simply make better games now. Okay, we made better games before Catan but bygones.

Rating Potential: 6-6.5. I really don't see this moving up. 7 Wonders alone scratches virtually the same itch and does it without the random factor of the robber. Takenoko is similar in that they are both gateways, but I find it more enjoyable despite its flaws. Again, not that similar, but Keyflower is another game from a design standpoint that really beats this into the ground.

Update. I think it is stuck in the 6.01 range. Expansions might give it enough legs to bump it up, but I don't see the base game going to a 7. I see no need to buy it for the obvious lack of need to due to quality and somebody else will have a copy anyway so that's the 0 in the score. After that it is merely how often I want to play it, and I'm guessing this will sneak in a once a year kind of play even if I'm going "Why am I not playing  pretty much anything else I would bring instead?"

I might prefer this as a 5-6 player game with the additional special build phase. I'll have to see how it plays as a 4-player game. Really not worth playing as a 3-player game. Trading is too difficult to make it fun. Can be more AP prone, see The Longest Turn meme, than I would like for a gateway.

2nd play of 6 player game. Yeah, um no. I fully accept the fact that I took a risk in my initial placement of my second settlement and road so I didn't give up on longest road from the start, but I was instantly blocked and thus vastly did nothing the whole game. I started on a spot for gold with a 9 on it, and it ended up being one of the lesser numbers rolled. I seriously do not get the hype for the game. 1 good play in 5 has me wondering if this shouldn't go lower. Actually, updated to a 5. I'll debate putting it at a 4.

[COLOR=#006600][b]Comments: [/b][/COLOR]

We [b][i]always[/b][/i] play with a variant I found on an old version of Herr Teuber's site.  (I haven't seen this particular variant listed anywhere in the years since.)  As in "Poverty Is No Dishonor", a player who receives no resource on any single dice-roll receives a chip.  On his turn, if he has as many chips as he has visible points, he must trade them in to the bank for a resource of his choice.  This mitigates luck and helps less as a player's position becomes stronger.  I would not rate this game so highly if we did not play with this variant.

[COLOR=#006600][b]Why we own it: [/b][/COLOR] 

This game is comfort-food for my gamer's soul.  In all the years since discovering Settlers, I think it's fair to say that almost all of our game purchases have been in the hopes of finding other games that please us as much as Settlers.

[COLOR=#006600]Instructions: [/COLOR]It's been years since I've read the rules, but I do recall feeling daunted by the separate rules and almanac booklets in the third edition.  That much printed material made the game seem more complex than it actually is.  I do appreciate the distinction between rules (for learning the game) and almanac (for clarifying details).  The fourth edition was printed in color, making the illustrations that much more helpful.
[COLOR=#006600]Learning Curve: [/COLOR] Rather involved, yet intuitive.  In only a couple of rounds, a new player will have the gist. (Best to learn from an experienced player, rather than from the rulebook.)
[COLOR=#006600]Depth: [/COLOR]Placement and expansion are quite strategic, but the social aspects dominate.
[COLOR=#006600]Luck: [/COLOR]Dice can be cruel, so initial placement is crucial.
[COLOR=#006600]Downtime: [/COLOR]Production and trading affect all players on all turns, so downtime is minimal.  Some friends have complained that the game bogs down during the trading phase.

textfield_comment_value:
This was my second ‘genuine’ boardgame I ever played (after Avalon Hill’s Civilization), and the experience was not pleasant. I played with 3 players, and we were soon leafing through the rules to establish whether we’d done anything wrong. We were rolling dice and growing, but there wasn't any sense of progression or challenge. I then played a few games with 4 players, and became intimately familiar with the rather annoying phenomenon of getting no useful resources for a long period of time simply because the dice (of course) didn’t land on their expected values. The standard reply is that you need to trade to alleviate this problem, and that the leaders should be excluded from trade. And that brings me to the heart of the issue I have with Settlers. It's not really the fact that 2D6 determine which resources get produced; no, it's that the game relies on people actively recognising that someone is doing too well, and then simply excluding him from participation in the game to a considerable extent until they catch up. I want to feel engaged, not given the proverbial cold shoulder until the rest have decided that it's okay to play with me again.

A second though lesser issue I have is that the game also doesn’t give you a meaningful choice what to with the dice as in, for example, Yspahan or Troyes. Settlers is all about reacting in a fairly uninteresting manner to a completely random input. Your only choice deals with whom to trade, and perhaps, guesstimating considerably, where to place a house. I know of lots of games which [i]do[/i] present me with interesting choices along the way.

Settlers deserves humoungous credit for its relative simplicity, the introduction of resources and being able to trade them with others to the general public, and presence of dice—which are a quite familiar and necessary element to many non-gamers; and so opening the eyes of quite a lot of people to the availability of games other than Monopoly or Risk. But as a [i]game[/i] I find it boring because there is very little to do and grating because I am expected to bash leaders in the most obvious of ways.

If, on the other hand, you and your group like to negotiate... then this title is fairly staple material.

[b]Update[/b] Auctioned off with the rest of the Settlers boardgame paraphernalia. It feels like a great burden has been lifted off my shoulders. 

[b]Update 2[/b] Very unexpectedly I was sitting behind a bunch of game material looking suspiciously like Catan's. It was... somewhat interesting, but also very boring. I got into a resource rut from which I could not pull out; trade just meant accelarating the competition's VP outlook more than mine. Even though I did score a non-neglegible amount of VPs I could not ever become a competitor for the win. The experience taught me that high relative frequencies of dice results mean nothing if you cannot link to a matching harbour to make the n : 1-trade more efficient; and that actually it's not really too bad to accept a lower relative frequency for resources which are more directly tied to VPs. You're safer from the Robber, and you're not limited by inefficient 4 : 1- or even 3 : 1-trades. But even so... the pauses of non-activity in this game plus the random clobbering by the Robber are really Not Fun; and I think that this is what after all this time sours me the most about Settlers. Its enduring popularity remains somewhat of a mystery.

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Settlers of Catan[/b] - Slovenian Edition (3rd 2007)

2-4 players (5-6 with expansion)

Has seen countless plays. Great game. I suppose my opinion might not last forever, its sheen may dull, but when? If one plays too often? It has been fun on a consistent basis, and am almost always willing to play it, which I cannot say for all games.

[b]The Pros[/b]
-lots of player interaction due to negotiation/diplomacy/trading 
-usually little down time (use a timer when playing with slow players!)
-opponents' plans can be disrupted in various ways
-multiple paths to victory
-multiple game variants (expansions)
-modular board =every game will be different
-very easy to learn
-not an overlong game, allowing 2 or more games to be played in one game night evening

[b]The Cons[/b]
Some might complain about the usage of dice. If dice are not your thing, you could use a [url=https://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgameexpansion/20038/catan-event-cards]dice deck[/url] to replace them. It is included within the event cards in [thing=27760][/thing].

However, I think luck usually doesn't play a major role. The "randomness" of the dice roll doesn't automatically mean luck rules this particular game.

For one, the usage of two dice lessens the randomness, making some number totals more statistically probable than other totals (ex. totals of six are much more probable than totals of two, because there are more possible combinations of the dice rolls. Whereas 3 and 3, 1 and 5, 4 and 2 all equal 6, only 1 and 1 equal 2). See: http://wizardofodds.com/gambling/dice/

As you gain experience, you learn to avoid building on those provinces, which will statistically provide less resources. A frequent mistake committed by novices. And if the best provinces have already been taken during the initial setup, an experienced player knows how to use the sea ports to his advantage (exchanging resources 2:1 or 3:1).

Even if one player does indeed have more luck with the dice, and beats the statistic probability overwhelmingly, this usually tends to balance itself out: 1) with the other players creating alliances against him, 2) with the brilliant Robber mechanism, which steals from those too rich with resources, 3) the clever usage of sea ports, and 4) trading with your allies as much as possible. The key is to make those trades, which benefit you more than your opponent.

A degree of randomness challenges one's ability in adapting to changing circumstances. Real life is all about this. But for those who do not like it, there are always the dice cards mentioned above.

Whereas strategy is the overall plan, tactics are the actual means used to gain an objective. This game has both. But of course this is not one of the heavy, deep or complex games, which I do like as well.

Interesting thoughts on board game design:

textfield_comment_value:
A classic that should be in the top ten. Many NEWNEWNEWBUYBUYBUYERS find this game 'dated', which is absurd really. Dated in what sense? How? Not only do I owe Settlers my entire existence as a game hobbyist, but it is a fantastic game that manages to appeal to both the strategic gamer and those who have only played mainstream games. As the groupthink wheel slowly turns and the NEWNEWNEWERS get sick of the 10-mechanics-and-a-pasted-theme Euros, when the simple, elegant loveliness of the classic Euros comes back in fashion, Settlers will return, slaughter the suitors and reclaim its crown. 

I love the dice. They add a tension and risk management to what might otherwise have been a dull resource conversion game (as if we need another one of those). 

COPY AND PASTE FROM MY GEEKLIST RANT:

Settlers of Catan's slide towards the bottom of the top 100 is proof again of the silliness of BGG's ratings system and its bias in favor of new-and-shiny games over the classics. Like Monopoly (which is also much better than BGG gives it credit for), Chess, and dozens of other older games, Settlers of Catan's popularity, age, and ubiquity work against it having a higher rating, but it is still one of the best introductory games and one of my favorite Eurogames. 

The saturated, consumerist board game market, with dozens of new releases every week, encourages players to shallowly rate games after one or two plays--which makes no sense since it often takes several plays to internalize the rules for even a simple game to the point where a player can focus on actually playing the game well. Market saturation encourages us to "take his word for it" and rate with the group (many members of which will be doing the same thing) so we that can unwrap the next package. 

Coupled with the saturated market is BGG's stranglehold on board game culture. The dominance of one information-outlet is not conducive to a free thinking environment, even in the case of user-generated content websites like BGG. A glimpse through the comments section for any top-100 game shows that raters are often repeating or paraphrasing the comments and judgements of other raters. Absolute democracy, which under-informed (because few of us have time enough to play any but our favorite games more than once or twice), user-generated content websites often resemble, encourages groupthink and the tyranny of the single persuasive voice. The practice that a few well known "game critics" have of passing judgement or rating games after a single play is intellectually dishonest and ethically suspect. 

Don't get me wrong, I love BGG and spend too much time here looking for new games, but the ratings system has never been much use to me beyond providing a starting point for game research. Giving anything but the most minor significance to which game lies where on the scale is the equivalent of basing judgements of worth and value on the results of a popularity contest. 

A thousand unwise voices rolled into one do not necessarily become one wise voice. It's too bad that Settlers may not show up on the first page of the top 100; it is a fantastic game, and one that I will play any time and anywhere.

textfield_comment_value:
We have played this approximately 12-15 times before I started logging plays. 

I think luck is an important part of many games, as it can level the playing field a little (the same player won't always win). Catan's dice rolling however, exceeds my optimal amount of luck. Based on how lucky we are the game takes between one and two hours for us.

Variable setup appears to be a strength of this game to improve replayability. However, I think some random setups are not well balanced and turn order in selecting starting locations can lead to one player being very likely to win or one player being very unlikely to win, due to unbalanced starting positions.

Many people seem to love the trading aspect. Perhaps we are too conservative. Trading occurs in our games, but is not a big part. Especially in the second half of the game or where someone is getting something very useful. This is probably something that works better with four players than our usual three. In many of our games it is just a waste of time: Does anyone want to trade X for Y, no but I'll trade Y for 2X + Z... No thanks. Keep repeating each round until the initial person has enough to trade with a port or the bank.

I don't buy the argument that the dice rolls are probabilistic and so even out in the end. The early dice rolls are much more important than later ones. A player whose placement matches well with the early dice rolls in the game can expand rapidly and hence get more opportunities for successful rolls in future rolls. Whereas a player who has bad luck early can find themselves boxed in or with the limited and often poor expansion options taken by the time they get going. Even with the robber and "trading" as catchup mechanisms, our games often see the rich i.e. those who got a good start getting richer and the poor getting left further behind. 

In a three player game, it is often not a three horse race by half way through, either one player is out in front or one player has been left behind (worst scenario). If you have been left behind the second half of the game takes a long time, especially if every round you seem to get a bit less than everyone else and your requests for trade are ignored because the other players  are confident of getting what they need anyway.

This one is on the slide. As we get more games, the bar is lifted as I see the variety and quality of gaming experiences available. I suspect I would have rated it an 8 or 9 in early 2017, I rated it a 6 in Mar 2018, and a 5 in Feb 2019. I don't think it will fall further than that.

Although this sounds quite negative, I'm very glad we got Catan. It is the game that influenced us to becoming a board gaming family more than any other. It offered a far more immersive gaming experience than any game we had played before. We followed this with ticket to ride Europe and then the shackles were off, we were hooked.

From what I've read, many others have played this a lot more than us and still love it. That's great for them, but we have other games we enjoy more. We'll try and play it once a year or so to see if the magic returns for us.

Settlers was for me, like many others I'm sure, THE gateway game, and will always hold a very special place in my heart.  I actually learned Settlers in 10th grade, every week I would go to a club at Cornell University where a bunch of the college students gathered to play games, almost exclusively Magic: The Gathering. I had been going for a couple years and would continue going for a couple more years, and throughout most of that time I mostly just played/traded Magic, spending far too much money in the process.  One fateful evening, I looked over and saw people playing this rather odd boardgame. Up until that point in my life I'd only played Monopoly, Risk, Life, Backgammon, etc. It looked so strange and interesting, I actually tore myself away from Magic for a few moments to watch. I became so engrossed that I watched the entire game. In fact, up until last year I'd never even read the rule book for Settlers, I simply learned by watching that game very closely. So throughout the years I started to play Settlers from time to time at that club at Cornell.  Eventually I even bought my own copy, which I found at the local comic book store; I bought the old brown Mayfair edition.  And I played this, and I played it some more, actually I played it for years and years.  All the time never stopping to realize that there might be more games out there like this one.  I loved Settlers, but somehow it didn't occur to me that there were other games of the same or similar ilk.  Fast forward a bit, I move to Chicago and go to college, I meet a couple good friends, and show them Settlers, the three of us end up playing Settlers almost every week together, and all this time, never think that there could be any other games out there I should be checking out.  So then I leave the country to study abroad, and while I'm away one of the friends I'd been playing Settlers with tells me about this board game fair on Navy Pier in Chicago and how he found out about and saw all these neat board games somewhat like Settlers but different and great, and they even had a giant life-size 3D version of Settlers.  I'm very jealous, but my interest is piqued.  Shortly thereafter, that same friend goes to California to visit someone, and comes back raving about this incredible game called Carcassonne that he was introduced to and that I just have to play. I'm like Carca-what?  He's like, you haven't heard of it?  I thought you were all into board games, isn't that your thing? And I'm like, uhh, no, I like Settlers, but haven't really ever played any other good games.  Anyway, I blame it all on him (or rather I thank him profusely) because from that point on I decided that maybe board games should be my thing, so I got Carcassonne shortly thereafter, played it, and fell in love with it.  My collection began to grow very quickly indeed, and now I'm as addicted as ever.  So it was Settlers that I played first, and Settlers will probably always be the game that I played most, I still can't believe it didn't occur to me for so long to see if there were more games I might like.
