textfield_comment_value:
Encore un jeu de plombier, un de ces jeux où les joueurs doivent poser côte à côte, en les faisant se correspondre, des cartes carrées ou hexagonales représentant des portions de tuyaux. Les tuyaux sont parfois remplacés par des rails. Cette fois-ci, ce sont des chemins serpentant autour de la cité de Carcassonne.

Encore un jeu de plombier, donc, mais sans doute le meilleur du genre. Il n'est pas trop prise de tête, les cartes étant assez faciles à poser, et un ingénieux système de score lui confère originalité et variété. Les cartes délimitent en effet non seulement des chemins, mais aussi des abbayes, des cités et des fermes. Les joueurs posent des voleurs sur les chemins, des moines dans les abbayes, des chevaliers dans les cités, des paysans dans les fermes, et chaque type de personnage permet de marquer des points d'une manière différente, ce qui rend les interactions relativement complexes, et permet des stratégies très variées.

La plupart des jeux de plombiers tournent vite au puzzle ou au casse-tête. Ce n'est pas le cas de Carcassonne, qui reste un jeu léger, agréable, rapide, faisant autant de place à la chance qu'à la tactique, tournant aussi bien à deux joueurs qu'à cinq.

Ceux qui veulent un jeu plus tactique pourront essayer les deux variantes suivantes: • chaque joueura une main de trois tuiles. À son tour, il en joue une, puis en pioche une. • le premier joueur pioche deux tuiles. Il en joue une, puis passe l'autre à son voisin de gauche, qui en pioche une seconde, et ainsi de suite.

D'innombrables extensions de ce jeu ont été publiées, et j'avoue ne plus suivre depuis quelques temps.
La Rivière, se compose d'une quinzaine de tuiles destinées à modifier la disposition initiale du jeu. Distribuée gratuitement lors du salon d'Essen 2001, elle est aujourd'hui difficile à trouver.
La deuxième extension, appelée... l'extension, ajoute un sixième joueur, quelques tuiles nouvelles et d'amusants "géants", des pions plus gros qui comptent double. Je ne pense pas qu'elle soit vraiment nécessaire, mais si vous aimez le jeu, elle renouvellera agréablement vos parties sans pour autant les complexifier.
La troisième extension, Marchands et Architectes, dans une boite rouge, s'efforce d'introduire dans le jeu de base quelques unes des meilleures innovations de la version préhistorique... autant acheter directement la boite verte.
Roi et Éclaireur, la toute dernière extension, est comme la première une petite boite d'une douzaine de tuiles distribuée gratuitement à Essen, mais que l'on peut trouver en vente ici et là; destinée aux inconditionnels du jeu, elle introduit de nouvelles tuiles tant pour le Carcassonne médiéval, bleu, que pour la version préhistorique, verte. Il y en a eu encore d'autres depuis, avec un Comte, avec des princesses et des dragons, mais je ne suis plus. - quand je veux jouer à Carcassonne, je sors ma boite verte préhistorique.

Carcassonne a été un grand succès commercial, et c'est pour entretenir ce succès que l'éditeur a commandé à Klaus-Jürgen Wrede un "Carcassonne bis". Le contrat était difficile à remplir, car Carcassonne 2 devait être assez différent de l'original pour renouveler le jeu, et assez proche pour ne pas dépayser les habitués. Il a été rempli avec brio. La boite verte de "Carcassonne - Chasseurs et Cueilleurs" se distingue aisément de la boite bleue du jeu original. L'action de ce Carcassonne 2 se situe quelques milliers d'années avant l'érection de la cité éponyme, et les joueurs posent désormais des cueilleurs dans les forêts, des pécheurs au bord des rivières et des lacs, des chasseurs dans les plaines. On y retrouve tous les principes et toutes les règles du jeu de base, mais avec quelques ajouts et réglages astucieux - des huttes sur pilotis, des tuiles de bonus permettant de rejouer quand on complète une forêt, des pions moins nombreux - qui réussissent à rendre le jeu à la fois plus mouvementé et plus tactique.

Si vous aimez le jeu de base, vous ne pouvez qu'adorer cette nouvelle version qui est indiscutablement plus aboutie. Si vous envisagiez d'acheter Carcassonne, et pouvez vous débrouiller avec des règles en angle ou en saxon, préférez la boite verte à la boite bleue.

Carcassone - La Cité est une variante bien plus stratégique, et que j'ai estimée suffisamment différente pour lui faire une entrée spécifique dans la ludothèque idéale.
---
One more plumber game, one of these games in which player must match the sides of square or hexagonal tiles with stretches of pipe on them. Most of the recent games of this kind only replaced pipes with rails. This time, no pipes, no rails, but stretches of road in the great plain around the mediaeval city of Carcassonne.

One more plumber game, for sure, but may be the best one. Since the tiles are rather easy to match, the game is not too brain teasing. It's original score system makes for most of the game originality and variety. The tiles do not only build roads, but also cloisters, cities and open fields. Players can play thieves on the roads, monks in cloisters, knights on cities and farmers in fields, and each kind of character has a different way of scoring points, which makes for some interesting and sometimes complex interactions, and for very different strategies.

Most plumber games are puzzles disguised as games. Carcassonne is a true game, a rather light, enjoyable, fast paced one, with a good luck-skill balance, which can be played as well with two or with five players.

For a more tactical game, you can playwith the following variant rules: • each player has a "hand" of three tiles. On his turn, he plays one, then draws one. • The first player draws two tiles. He plays one, and gives the other one to the next player, who draws a second one, and so on.

Many expansions have been published, and I must admit that I've not looked at the very last ones. The river is made of a dozen new tiles that only change the initial setup of the game. It was given for free at the 2001 Essen fair, and is now hard to find - though it has been included in the last reprint of the us edition.
The second expansion, called... the expansion, adds pawns for a sixth player, some new tiles and "giant" pawns, who count as two standard people. Though it is absolutely not necessary to enjoy the game, it brings some more variety in it for the Carcassone addicts.
The third expansion, Merchants and Architects, implements in the original game some of the best new ideas from the prehistoric edition - so better buy directly the green box.
King and Scout, like the River, is a small pack of a dozen tiles that was given for free at the Essen fair, but it can still be bought on some web sites. Since it has tiles for both the mediaeval and the prehistoric game, it is clearly intended only for the game addicts. And there are some more now, with a count, with dragons and princesses, but these are only for real Carcassonne addicts. As far as I am concerned, when I want to play a game of Carcassonne, I take my green prehistoric box.

Carcassonne was a commercial hit. In order to keep the sales going, the publisher asked Carcassonne designer, Klaus-Jürgen Wrede, for a new version of Carcassonne. Hard challenge: the new game had to be different enough from the old one to feel really new, and to be similar enough not to disorient the Carcassonne addicts. The challenge has been brilliantly fullfilled. The Carcassonne green box, called "Carcassonne - Hunters and Gatherers" is easy to distinguish from the blue original. The action takes place many thousand years before the city was built, and the players now place hunters in the plains, gatherers in the forests, fishers on the rivers. All the basic rules and systems of the original Carcassonne are still there, with a few clever twists and adjustments (huts built on stilts on the lakes, bonus tiles that make you play again when you complete a forest, less people per player) that make the game both more dynamic and more tactical.

If you like the basic game, you will love the new version, which has been better tuned and finalized. If you were already thinking of buying Carcassonne, better buy the green box than the blue one.

Carcassonne - The City is a meatier version of the game, and is original enough to deserve its own entry in the ideal game library.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] I have not played much Carcassonne, but I was always largely indifferent to it. I had tried it once in person, and I had played a moderate bit with an old Android APK in a Humble Bundle sold many years ago. The main detail that I retain in my brain is that Carcassonne popularized the meeple; the second detail that I try to retain in my brain is that it is spelled with one more letter 's' than I am comfortable writing, usually. I tried it on Board Game Arena without expansions and with all expansions available on the site (The River, Inns & Cathedrals, Traders & Builders, The Princess & The Dragon) to see the extent of Carcassonne's gameplay. 

-----X-----

In the base game, players can use their meeples to occupy road segments, cities, monasteries, and fields, each with slightly different scoring conditions. Any tile placed must be legal - for example, a road segment cannot be placed in such a way that it extends into a field or a city at the other end. One rule clarification that annoyed me when I was learning this game: players cannot place meeples into cities that are already occupied by other meeples, although they can place meeples into city tiles and then connect those cities together. People talk about sneaking a city; what about sneaking a 24-tile field with a 2-farmer majority? In one of my games, my opponent stole the farm with their majority, and I could not do anything to contest it - inexperience, really. 

I'm sure that, with experience, base Carcassonne gets better. In my first match, my opponent had 2200 games played; in my second match, my opponent had 4500 games played. For example, some of that would stem from knowing the distribution of tiles in a game of Carcassonne - for example, knowing how many of those 3-way intersection tiles would be great. There is no denying that experience trumps all in Carcassonne - as much as I'd like to point to lucky tile draws as being the reason for my losses, my opponents were strategizing their meeples to gain majority in certain areas through careful precision. 

Frankly, I don't see enough here for me to sink my teeth into, largely because I personally get bored very quickly. While some others argue that it does not overstay its welcome, I am spending half the game thinking to myself, "Just how many tiles are left in this pile?" There are other tile-placement games that I have greatly enjoyed of varying complexities, such as Terraforming Mars and The Castles of Burgundy to Azul, Patchwork, and Kingdomino. I saw some comment mention that Castles of Mad King Ludwig and Cascadia are strictly better in their experience, but I  have not tried either. I recently picked up Isle of Skye and hope to get that to the table eventually. That excludes the several polyomino games that I have tried and enjoyed. Then, there is the fantastic card-laying game from Button Shy Games called Sprawlopolis. Really, I do not see why Carcassonne would be among any of those beyond accessibility (outside of Board Game Arena, anyway) and heritage - sadly, that is not enough to warrant me wanting to keep playing.

-----X-----

Adding the expansions listed brought the tile count from ~72 (if I am not mistaken) to ~152 (again, if I am not mistaken). Players form a river to establish some preliminary amount of the map, which I think is kind of neat. The fairy came into play and I have to admit that it was more chaotic than I cared to understand - from what I could ascertain, players can move the fairy to a pre-existing . Wheat? Wine? Cloth? DRAGONS KILLING MY MEEPLES!? (My opponent swooped in and stole my city worth 12 due to the stupid dragon and a lucky draw... nope, no thanks.). Large meeples? Builders allow multiple tile placements? Pigs? That game went on -forever-, except it was (only...) 44 minutes. I cannot say I understood much of what was happening - I, uh, lost by 2 points (285 to 287) to a player with 3008 games because... farmers and the stupid pig, it seems? Truthfully, I did let them get away with a dozen-odd two-point closed road segments and I lost 3 of those points in the last turn of the game because the dragon got steered right into one of my meeple, so I basically threw away an easy victory. 

Non-ramble on a per-expansion basis: 
- River is just a river, though it helps speed up some of the early tile-placing by forcing players to establish the river.
- Inns & Cathedrals introduces the big meeple that, frankly, just annoys me, although many of the new tiles added seem neat.
- Traders & Builders adds the builder that, frankly, just annoys me, as well as the traders and the pig which, frankly, just irritate me, although many of the new tiles seem neat. Really, I found the trading aspect especially unnecessary to the base experience - in my case, I just kind of stumbled my way into wealth.
- The Princess & The Dragon add both the fairy and the dragon which - no. no. no. nonononono. Keep them out of Carcassonne. Awful, awful, awful, awful, awful. The fairy solely serves to provide incentive to scoring larger cities and road structures instead of small, immediate scoring options; however, in many cases, this just meant that it was several dozen +3s over the course of a game to both players (unless someone was sitting on several farmers with their meeples). The dragon should likewise not exist: personally, Carcassonne already has enough ways to be mean by blocking opponents from ever being able to place the necessary tile to score a territory and return their meeple to their supply - it definitely did not need the dragon causing massive swings during the game, some of which ended up being oddly helpful by allowing some players to return meeples to their supply after messing up. If anything, players messing up and running out of meeples is a problem caused by the game length, worsened by adding so many tiles to the game. 

Some discussion in the thread titled "First ever game - Base only or add in some expansions" from August 2nd (literally a week ago as I write this) highlights some interesting repercussions of playing with expansions. Namely, the base game presents players with many complex aspects to keep track of in such an otherwise simple experience - the knowledge of tile distributions, the key features present on each of those tiles, and the complex math that the designer had to use to balance the game in developing the base experience that has survived 23 years at this point. Plus, one person highlighted that the expansions can be more forgiving by just making everything much more muddled down in the many rules additions and individual elements. I could see myself playing with the River expansion after awhile to shuffle up the base game experience, and the Inns & Cathedrals expansion can be worth adding as it does not largely alter the base experience. 

-----X-----

Put simply, I do not think I will revisit Carcassonne (except for perhaps the Hunters and Gatherers standalone as it is implemented on Board Game Arena). Instead, I will likely just keep looking for other tile-laying games, even if many of them may simply be 'cult of the new'.

I will admit that the Strategic variant (which Board Game Arena specifies as players having 3 cards in hand at all times) might be more interesting, although I would be more inclined to just playing any of the other games previously mentioned.

(As an aside: playing Carcassonne just made me realize how much Gaïa was a sort of bootleg Carcassonne. It modifies the tile-laying to represent individual biomes that, when adjacent in certain ways, allow the placement of cities. It also introduced power cards, which... at best, are an unbalanced and frustrating mess. This game was so influential, yet I get the impression that Carcassonne and many of its descendants are best when the game is 'pure', i.e. lighter on complexity with simple mechanisms that mix to create a game that is high in strategy rather than trying to force interaction via special rules and unnecessary mechanisms).
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Board Game Revolution - ~2005[/b] 
One of the first games my wife and I bought when we got married.  I still enjoy the puzzle like feel of building the city of Carcassonne.  Since then we've added most of the base game's expansions to our collection.  Easy game to teach and play with the kids.

[b]Expansions owned:[/b]
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/2591/carcassonne-river][i]Carcassonne: The River[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2005[/b] 
I don't know if I'd consider this an "expansion" as it came with the base game.  But the added river through the countryside visually adds to the game and helps spread out all the players so we're not quite so congested.
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/18836/carcassonne-river-ii][i]Carcassonne: The River II[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2007[/b] 
Starting out with an extra long river adds to the game.  We like to mix all the river tiles together.  I like to include the lake (end) in the bag so that we never know if we'll have a long river or a short one.  This house rule adds to the replay-ability of this expansion.
-------[b]Update 1/13/15: New idea for use of the river tiles[/b]
Start with all the tiles in the bag except one spring tile and the plain lake tile.  When/if the lake tile gets drawn.  The next player adds the spring (river starting) tile where applicable and continue drawing river tiles adding to the new river. At end cap off the river with the lake tile set aside.
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/12903/count-carcassonne][i]Carcassonne: The Count of Carcassonne[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2008[/b] - Just don't think it adds too much to the game.  It's nice to share points with another player, but I'd rather work on expanding my own city/road/abbey. Part of main expansion 6.
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/2993/carcassonne-expansion-1-inns-cathedrals][i]Carcassonne: Expansion 1 - Inns & Cathedrals[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2006[/b] 
I think the best addition this expansion adds to the game are the Inns allowing players to double the points of their roads from 1/tile to 2/tile.  The two cathedrals are nice to get early on in the game for bookoo points; but drawn later on in the game they become more of a nuisance. Great idea to "force" players to finish their bonus building/road, otherwise all that time was wasted and you don't get any points for any of those tiles.
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/5405/carcassonne-expansion-2-traders-builders][i]Carcassonne: Expansion 2Traders & Builders[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2011[/b] 
The builder meeple adds A LOT to the game.  Being able to draw two tiles at a time is great!  Just be sure to not trap your builder into a city/road that cannot be expanded.  It is near impossible to get him back otherwise, unless you're playing with the dragon.  BUAH HA HA!  :)
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/15158/carcassonne-princess-dragon][i]Carcassonne: Expansion 3 - The Princess & the Dragon[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2012[/b] 
This is by far our family's favorite expansion to the base game.  We all try to keep the dragon away from us, but love eating the other's meeples!  My youngest son will often eat his own meeples simply because he can.  We do, however, often forget to give the bonus point for the fairy, so we usually leave that part out.
- [geekurl=/boardgameexpansion/21385/carcassonne-tower][i]Carcassonne: Expansion 4 - The Tower[/i][/geekurl] - [b]Board Game Revolution - ~2012[/b] 
At first I was skeptical about this expansion, but being able to take other player's meeples prisoner is awesome!  The only downside is when you are unable to capture the other person's meeple and do a prisoner exchange.  :(  But you can always award that player 3 points to get it back. [b]tl;dr[/b] — Potentially light and mild, it's a great social game when played in 30ish minutes, but sags if it goes longer.  Expansions are the seasoning and so should be used sparingly to create the game that suits your current mood.  Terribly cruel when played to win, though.

[microbadge=10153]

Neat for what it is, a kids' game that can be played for blood (farm wars, anyone?).  The vanilla version is a pleasant-enough pastime.  Where [i]Carc[/i] really shines, though, is as a game system—the mix 'n match expansions allow you to complicate or flavor the game as you will.

UPDATE:  Revising down from a 7 to a 6.  This was shockingly novel at first, being only the second Eurogame I'd ever seen, but now...  And another thing:  The 8,000,000,000 different farm-scoring schema make for bizarre parallel-dimension gaming where some people at the table have evil goatees and some don't, leading to the disastrous overlay of competing realities, some where farmers lie on their backs and gaze at duck-shaped clouds scudding by and others where you can only get promoted by stabbing your boss in the neck.*

[size=7]*So, 12 years later, it looks like this has settled down—the standard seems to be German 3rd Edition rules with "farm-centric" scoring of cities for three points each.  I like the simplification—as well as the change making the tiny two-bit mini-cities worth four points instead of two, eliminating a rules exception, always a good thing.[/size]

UP-UPDATE:  This is the game that made me realize that most expansions are crap—they just add plaque that calcifies a decent game into an immobile, spiky mess.  (Or, to go to the other extreme, bloats it out so it can't even wear pants anymore.)   Expansions, in general, are a terrible idea unless:

a) It was a part of the original game (as designed) that got peeled off to make the base game simpler/cheaper,

b) Actually adds an element that enhances repeat plays, or

c) Fixes one or more broken elements that really shoulda been caught during playtesting.

Only three expansions for [i]Carc[/i] fit any of that—[thing=2591]The River[/thing], [thing=2993]Inns & Cathedrals[/thing] and [thing=5405]Traders & Builders[/thing].  Everything else is dessicated mummy-crap.

UP-UP-UPDATE:  Resurrecting this as a mild social activity; as a [i]game[/i] game it gets a 5, when consumed as a small bowl of whipped cream it's a 6.  The deal with the expansions is to understand that every tile added into the mix is another turn—and if you've got multiple axes to consider (with several expansions at once) then those turns can become very long indeed.  The game works best when it comes in well under an hour; it [i]wants[/i] to be short.**  I can honestly only see using one expansion at a time...

[size=7]**The closer to 30 minutes the better.[/size]

I forgot what an awful little game this can be:  so much grief, so many ambitious building projects that will never be completed, so many farmers stabbing each other in the tummy with pitchforks from the backs of rage-donkeys.

I'm not sure how the rest of world plays this, but man, we are just plain [i]mean[/i] to each other.

[i]Me likey.[/i]

UP-UP-UP-UPDATE:  Back up to a 7 where I expect it to stay.  When grokked and played accordingly—as a shortish social activity with one big and maaaybe one small expansion at a time it's a pip.

[b]CODA:  GROINS IMPLY BOOTS[/b]

The sheer ruthlessness required to play the game competitively is entirely at odds with the presentation:  cutesy li'l squares of bucolic cartoons, and the meeples themselves, adorable and nonthreatening, the very symbols of "points without pain" Eurogaming.  If the package reflected the truth of it the art would be dark and violent:  fields strewn with fresh grave-mounds, dangerous roads to nowhere festering with spleen-stabbing thieves, sprawling slums with gaping holes in the walls patrolled by gangs of baby-stomping kingsmen.

This is what you must do to win:  sucker your opponents into fights that you either dominate or walk away from (leaving them overextended), place tiles to ensure their followers are trapped in projects that will never be completed, and never share points unless you are so far ahead it doesn't matter... and even then, hook yourself in for +1 at the last minute to steal the "joint effort" for yourself.

You must crush dreams, snap their bones and suck the marrow.  You must be prepared to engineer fallen crests and hopelessness.  I'll be honest:  I felt like a complete jerk at first, as playing to win in [i]Carc[/i] is really about [i]making everyone else lose[/i], and the constant pooping in the punchbowl can suck the fun right out of the party.  But if you wish to do your best then that tile [i]must[/i] be placed where it maximizes both personal gain [i]and[/i] does the most harm to your opponents.

In the end the countryside puzzle we are constructing is a façade that does nothing to conceal the suffering of the nameless, numberless peasants who are too small to see from our lofty perches of intrigue.

[i]Carcassonne[/i] is an assassin in clown paint.

Rating bumped up to an 8.

:thumbsup: [b]POSITIVE POINTS:[/b]

++ Good light weight tile-laying gateway game that can scale from family game to a more medium-weight strategic game by adding some expansions (also using some house rules/variants to make it "friendlier" or more "cutt-throat").
++ Simple, elegant tile-laying / worker placement mechanisms.
++ Good replayability due to the random order tiles are drawn and also due to the high number of expansions you can add.
++ To reduce the luck of the draw and to make it more strategic several house rules/variants can be used easily and effectively:
* You can draw 2 or 3 tiles that you keep in your hand, and after playing one, you redraw (this also speed up the analysis time of the tiles drawn since you already have your tiles durings the other players' turn).
* You can have some tiles (between 3 to 5) facing up near the scoring board and players must choose from these tiles. Chosen tiles are replaced immediately (like cards in Ticket To Ride).
++ Easy to teach, fast to set-up and fast to play.
++ There are severeral expansions available for this game (which is useful to refresh the game when we have overplayed it).


:thumbsdown: [b]NEGATIVE POINTS:[/b]

-- The luck of the draw can be frustrating at time, but this can be made a more strategic game with some variants.
-- The area control part of this game can make this game too cutt-throat when playing against casual players or wife! (thus some house rules have been made)
-- Since I hate sorting tiles when adding or removing an expansion, we always plays with all the tiles, but not all the rules (before the game we state with which expansion we desire to play and ignore some icon on some tiles) but this make the game longer that it should (thus our variant to randomly remove a handful of tiles from the draw bag at the beginning of the game).

Hundreds of reviews for Carcassonne can be found on BGG. These reviews pretty much covers the entire spectrum of the game. Love it or hate it, I am quite sure you will find an appropriate review for it. There is really nothing much to add other than my personal opinion and rate the game through the lens of playing it with my child who recently came of age to join the board gaming world.

Carcassonne is the poster child for a tile-laying game. As far as I can remember, Carcassonne is synonymous with tile laying. The term meeples can probably be traced back to Carcassonne. Players pick a tile and play a tile to form cities, roads or fields. With each tile, players have the option to put meeples either as farmers on fields, knights on cities or robbers on roads. Points are scored when structures are completed and importantly, players have a chance to work together or against each other to complete the structures.

Obviously, Carcassonne can be played cooperatively to score points by jointly completing building, roads or fields. I have also played a cutthroat version of Carcassonne where players go all out to foil each other to complete structures. Believe me, both versions are day and night and the cutthroat version is not for everyone. It was incredibly frustrating to play and brutal.

At present, there are so many expansions for Carcassonne I have lost track. This must be a constant evergreen for title for Jurgen-Wrede. There are constant reprints, big boxes, anniversary editions for Carcassonne that there is no way you can miss it. For me, my modified base game consists of Carcassonne plus The River, Inns and Cathedrals and Traders and Builders.

The game is such a classic that I feel it’s a crime to sell it. I have tried, but somehow it is sticking around. Mechanistically speaking, the game is relatively unique and unparalleled. It is easy to pick up and play and certainly has some longevity. But it is definitely not something you play over and over, though I suspect there are some hard core fans out there. It is charming, inoffensive (if played cooperatively) and a fine way to pass time, I think it is rightfully considered a staple of gaming in modern households.

Final word: Average
Kids Corner

6 years and 4 months: All hail Carcassonne! My six year old just picked up the game and is now fully immersed in it. She can play the full game but we have omitted farmers for scoring. That is still the hardest part of the game for her to grasp. We include inns and cathedrals but not traders and builders. That will happen in due time. For now, I am excited that she is excited to play the game. I think there is really nothing to prevent kids from playing the game. I think the sharing of buildings can still be tricky concept to learn but I do see something click in her head. I think Carcassonne is an excellent gateway game for kids. For younger kids, one can even omit scoring and focus on just building structures for fun. That works too. While I haven’t tried Carcassonne kids, I don’t think the regular Carcassonne is out of reach for a 5-6 year old.

Egy játék alapján (amiben az alapjátékot és a kereskedő kiegészítőt használtuk (az építész és a disznók nélkül)) alapvetően tetszett. Szerettem azon gondolkozni, hogy hova is lenne a legjobb letenni az adott lapot, ugyanakkor kicsit olyan érzésem támadt, hogy nincs igazi választási lehetőségem: ha odaillik valahova, ahova nekem jó, akkor oda kell letenni, ha meg nem, akkor pedig nagyjából mindegy. Szóval nem éreztem eléggé, hogy a saját döntéseim alakítanák a játékot, túl nagy volt annak az aránya, hogy a játék önmagát játszotta a két játékost bábként felhasználva.
Kevésnek éreztem a játékosok közti interakciót. Nehéz elérni, és nem is igazán törekszik rá az ember, hogy az adott mezőn/várban/úton többségbe kerüljön, ha más is odavetődik; mi inkább csak magunknak játszottunk, szinte passziánszoztunk. Ezen lehet majd javítani a gróf és a sárkány kiegészítőkkel, kíváncsi vagyok mennyit javul velük a véleményem.
Szóval így elsőre nekem túl egyszerű ez a játék, amiben lehetne ugyan sokat gondolkozni minden egyes lépésen, de ez valószínűleg nem sokkal növelné a játékélményt. Nem igazán lehet a másik játékára hatni, csak nagyon közvetett módon, ami vagy összejön, vagy nem. Direkt kölcsönhatás a játékosok között gyakorlatilag nincs, ennek a hiányát erősen éreztem.

A társasjátékokkal többször játszva mindig javulni szokott róluk a véleményem, hisz jobban megismerve őket jobban meglátom az értékeiket, a szépségüket, és valószínűleg ennél is ez fog történni. Első játék után kb. 7 pont, aztán majd meglátjuk!

Update: Játszottam 3 személlyel is, teljesen jól működik így a játék. Játszottam a netes verzióban egy rakás kiegészítővel (sárkányos, építész és kereskedő, kocsmás, király és vándor), azok is teljesen jól működnek, pluszt adnak a játékhoz. 7 -> 7.5 pont.

Update2: Rá kellett jönnöm, hogy ez egy férfiaknak való játék. A barátnőmmel játszottunk, és az volt a gond, hogy míg ő békésen építkezve játszott volna, addig én agresszív voltam: több félkész városát is elfoglaltam, majd végül a nagy mezőjét is. Rosszul esett neki, úgy érezte, én nem építek, hanem csak rombolok. Én viszont nem vagyok képes másképp játszani, mint győzelemre törekedve a játékszabályok maradéktalan betartásával és kihasználásával, ráadásul szerintem épp a városokért/utakért/mezőkért folyó kis csatározások adják meg a játék ízét, nélkülük ez a játék unalmas és interakció nélküli. Számomra csodás érzés küzdeni a többség kialakításáért vagy megtartásáért egy-egy nagyobb városban vagy mezőn. Az egyszerűsége mellett pont ez az, amivel együtt szerintem megérdemli az év játéka díjat, és amitől annyi rajongója van.
Női aggyal játszva (konfrontációt kerülve simán csak építkezve) semmilyen potenciált nem látok a játékban, nem érzem, mi lehet benne úgy a jó. Így aztán vegyes nemű társaságnak vagy nőknek nem javaslom, fiútestvéreknek vagy férfi baráti társaságnak viszont annál inkább, lehetőleg kiegészítőkkel együtt.

Update3: Jó játék ez: 7.5 -> 7.7 pont.

Update4: Újrapontozom a játékokat aszerint, hogy melyikkel mennyire szívesen játszanék mondjuk ma este. Ez alapján: 7

textfield_comment_value:
Jogo pequeno, leve, rápido e bom. Quarenta minutos de partida, com mesa cheia, já incluindo a contagem final de pontos. Para iniciantes a parte mais difícil será a pontuação dos fazendeiros, mas nada que os ótimos exemplos do próprio manual não resolva.

É um jogo que exige do jogador uma certa habilidade de projeção, um bom golpe de vista, para olhar a peça em sua mão e visualizar suas várias alternativas possíveis na mesa. O fato é que muita gente simplesmente não tem essa habilidade muito desenvolvida e isso pode fazer com que essas pessoas sintam até mesmo dificuldade em jogar, mesmo tendo entendido bem a proposta e a malícia existente no jogo.

O jogo possui um nível de sorte variável de acordo com a quantidade de jogadores: com dois é quase um xadrez, onde você consegue ter bastante controle do seu jogo, desenvolver profundas estratégias e marcar bastante o seu adversário. Já com cinco a sorte pesa bastante e neste cenário muitos vão se frustrar com o jogo. Mas não desista dele antes de testar estas diferentes contagens entre dois a cinco jogadores.

A regra original diz que cada jogador deve pegar sua peça apenas em seu turno e jogá-la, mas depois que fiquei sabendo que nos campeonatos oficiais usam uma variante onde o jogador pode pegar sua próxima peça logo após jogar a atual, não vi mais sentido em continuar seguindo o manual neste ponto específico, e passei a adotar isso como regra padrão. Não deu outra, o jogo melhorou significativamente. Ficou mais dinâmico e imediatamente diminuiu AP e downtime, pois desta forma os jogadores podem ir pensando em sua jogada com antecedência. É um caminho sem volta. Nunca mais joguei sem isso.

Mais um detalhe dos campeonatos que vale a pena ressaltar é que ao iniciar o turno, o jogador deve revelar a peça que está em mãos antes de jogá-la. Esta simples mudança contribui ainda mais para melhorar o AP e Downtime, pois ajudam os jogadores adversários a ir se preparando para a próxima jogada.

A única coisa que não entendo mesmo é a editora deste jogo ficar lançando sucessivas edições dele (já estamos na terceira) fazendo apenas mudanças estéticas no jogo, quando se tem essas evoluções claras da regra usadas nos próprios campeonatos oficiais. A regra original favorece AP e Downtime desnecessariamente, e ninguém gosta disso, muito menos os jogadores casuais.

To me, it's all in there.

This is another game Mrs Mo actually enjoys (in it's "vanilla" form) but our girls don't as much.  I really wish my wife would play 2P games with me, because this one would be our go to.  It's fairly simple (the farmer scoring seems to mess a little with the people I play with).  It looks good on the table as you build the landscape with various cities and roads.  It's got meeples!  It has strategy but in that light (vanilla Carc) to light-mid (with I&C added) range.

If you want to go crazy, there are numerous expansions that add all kinds of things.  I am content with Inns & Cathedrals as it adds just that little extra strategy and gameriness (how's that for a made up word) to make it that much more fun and challenging.

[u]24-Jan-2014[/u]: Still my favorite game despite not really having anyone to play against.  I play a lot using the iOS app vs various AIs so that kind of gives me my fix.  Otherwise, I play mostly with various solo variants.  Just really enjoy this game.

[u]The Solo Variants[/u]:
[listitem=1129534]SoloPlay Variant[/listitem]
This is my favorite way to play solo.  The SoloPlay variants aren't for everyone as some of them have some funky setups and additional rules for gameplay and scoring, but I really enjoy them.  This one can be used with just the base game, or with one or both of the first two expansions (I&C and T&B), or with or without the River.  So lots of options. textfield_comment_value:
RULES: ***** - The rule set is terrific. You can easily get the flow of the game in mere minutes. Of course, there are known issues with farmer scoring, but 4th edition rules are fairly intuitive and easy to grasp.
STRATEGY: ** - There is a possibility to have a vague plans of what you are going to do next, but you honestly can't plan much before the game, it's a lot more about reacting correctly to the current events.
TACTICS: **** - This game would be a perfect tactical game, but it isn't just because you have only one tile a turn to place and you can't choose which one it is, hence the choices get somewhat limited by your tile draw.
LUCK: *** - Most of the time you can find a proper place for the drawn tile to be placed, however, sometimes it gets very frustrating when you can't draw anything but roads while someone steals your city. Having a hand of three tiles would have been a lot better, and a lot more evil... But that's just thinking aloud.
PLAYER INTERACTION: ***** - Believe me when I say this game can get evil. Tension is high and fights for the biggest cities and largest farms can get mad. Furthermore, the turns are short and the pace is fast.
REPLAYABILITY: *** - Without expansions, I'd say the game is very fun, but the fun doesn't last long enough and the game does get repetitive after a while. A couple of better expansions to expand your opportunities will easily fix this though.
THEME: ** - It is an abstract. It has almost nothing to do with city or road building or farming. It could use any other theme and be just as succesful. However, I can't deny that all those cute cartoonish graphics on tiles do add some needed flavour, so the theme, however thin, does provide a nice touch.
BALANCE: **** - The cities and farms seem to be the hugest point sources in the game, leaving cloisters and roads in a supportive role. I would rather this was fixed, and I believe that certain expansions address that problem fairly succesfully. Anyway, the game is quite good without any expansions as well, it's just that you have to concentrate on cities more.
DOWNTIME: ***** - None! Grab a tile, place a tile, place a meeple, score! There is almost no place for analysis and the game flow is awesome. You will never feel bored while playing the game (not speaking of repetitiveness kind of boredom, of course).
ACCESSIBILITY: **** - Anyone can play the game. I mean it. You can teach your Grandma play it, and she is very likely to like it. It's easy, it's fast, it's fun. My biggest complaint is that the game absolutely sucks with more than three players, because it gets too chaotic. Otherwise, you can't ask for a better game to fit everyone's taste.

Nach Ankauf der [thing=5405] 2ten Erweiterung Händler und Baumeister[/thing] sind die Karten in den blauen Stoffbeutel gekommen. Ich finde das Ziehen aus dem Beutel am praktischsten. Den Turm aus der 4ten Erweiterung [thing=21385]Der Turm[/thing] finde ich dagegen nicht wirklich praktisch (der Turm als Kartenhalter sieht halt nur interessant aus).

Die folgenden Erweiterungen habe ich standard in das Grundspiel integriert: 
[thing=2591]Der Fluss[/thing] diese kleine Mini-Erweiterung gab es als Beigabe zum PC-Spiel. Die Flusskarten sehen schön aus, ändern das Grundspiel aber nicht dramatisch. Da diese Karten eine andere Rückseite haben sind sie leicht heraus zu sortieren.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
I am 21 years late to the Carcassonne party, but happy to have finally arrived.  One of the easiest modern board games I have learned, the edition I purchased included The River and The Abbot mini expansions.  The stripped down base game is instantly fun and gratifying as one schemes how to horn in on others’ territory to share and steal points.  After a few plays, the different tiles and their distribution become more familiar and one learns how to avoid painting oneself into a corner and running out of meeples.  Once all players grasp the fundamentals, it becomes painfully obvious that luck of the draw dictates the outcome of the average game: it is nearly impossible to beat the person at the table who keeps drawing monasteries, especially when you repeatedly draw roads.  It is also very frustrating when you draw ten tiles in a row that you cannot use because your meeples are all stuck on the board and only certain tiles can free them.  This heavy luck element prevents a victory from feeling truly satisfying.  Only once did I play using “farmers,” which seemed to shift the entire focus of the game to fighting for control of one massive field.  The river expansion is also underwhelming as it immediately establishes a leader and underdog(s) based on luck of the draw, since about half the river tiles are valuable.  When playing with the abbots, the game will simply be won by whoever is fortunate enough to keep drawing flower beds and monasteries.  These experiences will prevent me from buying any future expansions.  The original Carcassonne is a small and simple game that plays quickly and offers some interesting choices, perfect for introducing new players to the hobby or for when no one can agree upon which game to play.  

Update: I’ve played many rounds with various setups and player counts since writing the above review, and my opinion remains largely the same.  However, I recently began experimenting with the unofficial three-tile hand variant that many have clamored about, and it has breathed new life into Carcassonne for me.  This variant enhances the tactical nature of the game by allowing some planned attacks and calculated risks, though luck-of-the-draw can still swing a game.  And I cannot begin to express how much of a relief it is to draw a monastery, see that you have no meeples left, and then realize that you can just save that tile for later.  Revolutionary.  If Carcassonne has gone stale for you, try the three-tile hand variant.

2/10/09
-------------------------------

[i]Carcassonne[/i] is a tile-laying game that plays in 45 minutes and is very easy to understand. You place a tile, and then you place a ‘follower’ on a feature on the tile, with the aim of ‘completing’ features to get points. The game plays 2-5 people, and is probably better with fewer players; achieving the best results at the minimum of 2. As you add more players, the ratio of decisions to time decreases dramatically, and can become quite boring, as this a game that can be prone to analysis paralysis.

I wouldn’t call this game for everyone, as it can wear out rather quickly I find. Even though the large amount of tiles and combinations seem exhaustive at first, the games seem to repeat themselves rather often, and by that I mean that they seem the same, even though they are not. This is due to the lack of interesting decisions in the game it around the 10-20 plays mark. Even the limited player conflict cannot prevent this from occurring. The one exception to this is the two player game, which I find to be rather tense under the circumstances; however it also feels rather repetitive.

The actual gameplay itself is dictated by luck, but sufficient contingency planning should be able to eliminate this, but it is still not uncommon for an experienced player to lose to a newer one on luck alone. For the first couple of plays, it may seem like there is little interaction, but many people discover the method of interfering with other people’s plans fairly soon. Towards the end of the game, the completion of your features and the placing of your farms gives the game a nice tense atmosphere, but as noted above, this does not remain for too many plays.

To conclude, [i]Carcassonne[/i] is a fun game for the first few times you play it, and is good for introducing new people to the world of gaming, but I would not dwell on it too long, at least, not without the expansions. Also, try to stay away from games with more than four players, as they can get boring very quickly unless someone is marching the game through at breakneck pace.

[b]Pros[/b]
- Simple to teach and learn
- Good gateway game
- Equal opportunity to win
- Plenty of expandability

[b]Cons[/b]
- Lacking in continued playability
- Analysis paralysis prone 
- Decisions lose interest after a while
- Games feel the same quite often
- Lack of accommodation for large numbers of players

textfield_comment_value:
Is Carcassonne a bland co-op or cut throat jigsaw puzzle?  That, my friends, is up to you.

Carcassonne is simple.  A bunch of tiles show parts of cities and roads surrounded by green fields and containing the occasional abbey.  The components are quite lovely.

On their turn a player draws a tile and places it, puzzle like, next to a previously played tile.  Roads and Cities spill over onto multiple tiles and as the game progresses.  After placing a tile a player can place a meeple (the rules call them "followers") on any structure in that tile.  If that tile, however, expands a pre-existing structure, a road for example, that already has a meeple on it, then no new meeple can be played on that structure.

When a tile completes a structure, ending a road for example, any meeples on it are removed from the board and the owning players score points based on the size of the structure.  The game ends when all the tiles are drawn at which time end game points are awarded and the person with the most points wins.

Now the rules state that on a turn a player is supposed to draw a tile and discuss with the other players how best to play it.  Two words: BO RING.

Here's how you should play Carcassone: 

First draw your tile at the end of your turn so you can think about where to play when your next turn begins.  

Second, it's possible for cities, roads and fields with meeples already on them to grow together.  If they do, the player or players with the most meeples on the structure get the points.  Yes, you can steal points from other players this way!

Third, unless a structure gets completed a player can't get their meeples back.  They are stuck on the board.  Clever tile play can lock up other players meeples and reduce their scoring opportunities.

On one hand Carcassonne provides many of the fun puzzle solving elements that one can find in jigsaw puzzles.  But it can also be played in a competitive fashion.  These two elements combined make it one of the best family games out there.  It's simple to play, fast and full of interaction.

I've heard complaints on BGG about down time issues in multiplayer games.  I've never experienced such a problem, presumably because we always play such that a player draws a new tile at the end of their turn rather than at the beginning.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
When I discovered this game, I quickly became a huge fan. I was drawn in by how the game centers around topology: whether certain areas are connected or not, and whether or not they close.

What makes this game interesting is that there are different ways to earn points, and they all involve different levels of investment with a general dynamic of more risk, more reward. The risk takes the form of having to place a man with the possibility of not getting one of your mans back. Traders on the roads are low-risk, low-reward. Knights in cities and monks in monestaries are moderate-risk, moderate-reward. Farmers are high risk, as you never get them back, but can be very high reward in some games.

The game rewards efficiency, if you are able to set up multiple things going at once so you can play a single tile and have it increase your points for multiple mans on the board.

The game also rewards balance, in that you need to place enough different types of mans and place them in different enough locations, such that any tile you draw, you'll be able to utilize it.

But there's also an element of antagonizing, blocking, and even stealing points. Some games can get competetive, cutthroat even. You can place tiles to make it impossible for an opponent to close something they started, so one of their mans is permanently stuck on the board. You can even drop multiple mans to out-compete a player and steal points from a city or farmland, but doing so requires a clever, indirect approach of starting on initially-unconnected tiles and later connecting them, which of course, players can thwart by keeping the sections disconnected on their turn, if they are luck enough to draw tiles to allow it.

Over the years though I have come to tire of it somewhat. I think what led me to tire of it is that there are more or less a finite, and quite small number of dynamics that can play out with each game. This game was very fun until I had played it maybe 10-12 times or so, after which it started feeling less strategically interesting. By contrast, a number of other games I own have had much higher replay value.

Is this game worth buying? I don't know. Personally, I'd give it up if someone else really wanted it. Perhaps some others like it more than I do. I still think it's a decent game.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
An excellent tile-laying game, children also enjoy the game play and medieval theme immensely.  2001 SDJ winner.  Best with just two players.  House-rule of having three tiles in hand is worth considering when playing with more than two players, to make the game more strategic and less dependent on luck-of-the-draw.  At the very least, draw your tile after your turn, so that players can plan their move and avoid downtime.  

Recommended: play with [url=http://www.riograndegames.com/uploads/Game/Game_48_gameRules.pdf]third edition rules[/url], where scoring is more consistent:
- 2 tile cities are worth 4 points (i.e. all cities and pennants score 2 points per tile)
- farmers scoring works by scoring each field, not each city (i.e. calculate which farmers control a field, and then that field scores 3 points per completed city touching that field)
These 3rd Edition rules score fields just like all other features: (a) points go to the players with the most followers in the feature; (b) remove followers, score next.  
See [url=http://boardgamegeek.com/thread/319545]here[/url] for discussion on 1st vs 3rd edition rules.

Expansions I own:

[gameid=2591] - Came as part of my Carcassonne game.  Starting with the River tiles gives a good, broad starting area with more choices, and helps break up fields. (note: the farm goes around the spring, as discussed [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/thread/383180]here[/url]).

textfield_comment_value:
We are talking about THE CLASSIC.

Much like how mocha coffee has been for most of us a gateway to coffee, "cIgGAReTtes aRE A GaTEwaY to DrUGs" for our parents, and avocado toast is a gateway to millennial existential crisis, this game has been the gateway for most into serious board game hobbyism and hoard-ism.

A quintessential board game that creeps into most board gamers' collections only to be dusted off every now and then when you feel the waves of nostalgia, or when your preteen brother comes over for a visit or that friend who was always resistant to joining your board game cult-call decides to give one game a try. But, that should not stand as a diminishing statement to its value!

We are talking about the Michelangelo David of Eurogames, the perfect representation of simple yet effective game mechanics, language-independent, replay-ability, quick learning curve but with allowance for more competitive and strategic gameplay. It's a game that you can play both casually with your family, friends and/or coworkers, or go pro and compete in international tournaments.

It doesn't stop there, we are talking about a game, that is essentially so flexible, it allows for mods, for supreme customisation. I have not yet come across any other game that it supports modding (though I am sure they exist). On the official ZMAN webshop you can buy the tile cardboard components to print on it your own custom tiles with your own custom house rules. You can go as crazy as you want, make it as fun and as personal as your heart desires.

There's numerous expansions which all add different game mechanics and more tiles and you can pick and choose which ones you want to adopt into your main game. I currently have six expansions, some I'll probably never purchase because I don't much care or need the mechanics they introduce but some have added an extra spice flavour to the gameplay.

I can't overstate how much this game is a board game in a class above the rest. I can rave for hours. It's perfect for beginners, and even for mid- and pro- players who feel like (re-)experiencing the sensation of playing something that is so simple and pure and perfect in its game design.

textfield_comment_value:
„Carcassonne“ habe ich schon ewig nicht mehr gespielt. Jetzt gab es zu viert eine Partie mit zwei Kindern. Dazu kamen die Erweiterungen „Fluss 2“, „Wirtshäuser und Kathedralen“ und „Händler und Baumeister“, von denen ich nur den Fluss (aber die Nummer 1) kannte. Gegenüber dem Grundspiel hat sich wenig geändert: Plättchen ziehen. Fluchen, dass das Plättchen nicht zu dem passt, was ich gerade weiterbauen will. Plättchen anlegen und ggf. eine Figur darauf legen. Das geht meist flott, sodass keine hohe Downtime entsteht. Und es macht sogar Spaß, den Mitspielerinnen „sinnvolle“ Tipps zu geben, wo deren Plättchen denn passen könnte.

Die Erweiterungen machen nichts außergewöhnlich anders, bis auf den Baumeister. Wenn ich diesen auf eine eigene Stadt oder Straße gesetzt habe und in einem späteren Zug die Stadt oder Straße erweitere, darf ich noch ein Plättchen ziehen und anlegen. Das ist natürlich extrem glücksbetont, dieser extra Zug hat mir aber sehr gut gefallen, da ich damit einfach mehr bauen kann. Die Händler hatten kaum Auswirkung bei uns, was aber auch damit zu tun hatte, dass drei Spielerinnen eine riesige Stadt zusammen aufbauten, diese aber nie vollendeten. Daher fand ich die Mehrheitenwertung bei Spielende etwas witzlos, weil von jedem Rohstoff nur ein oder zwei vor den Spielerinnen lagen und die 10 Siegpunkte für ein einziges Plättchen irgendwie zu unbalanciert wirkten. Die Wirtshäuser veränderten ebenso wenig am Spielgefühl, es gab halt 2 Punkte pro Wegstück bei der Vollendung. Die Kathedralen dagegen nutzten wir vor allem als Ärgerfaktor, um einer Person die Stadt so groß zu machen, dass sie diese nicht abschließen kann und dann aufgrund der Kathedrale auch bei Spielende keine Punkte dafür bekommt. Und den Fluss finde ich immer gut, um einen variablen Startaufbau zu haben.

Die Spielzeit verlängert sich ein bisschen durch die drei Erweiterungen, aber aufgrund der geringen Wartezeit zwischen meinen Zügen waren es unterhaltsame anderthalb Stunden. Daher spiele ich gerne wieder mit – vor allem, wenn ich so klar mit 121:86:75:? gewinnen darf, was vor allem an der unfertigen Stadt meiner drei Mitspielerinnen lag.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
This is a quick, simple, and yet challenging game.  I found newcomers were able to pick it up quickly and it's fast enough that you can play a few times in a row to get the hang of it.  I bought it for a friend who occasionally plays board games with us and her and her boyfriend absolutely love playing it.

There are always pivotal decisions to be made over where and when to place workers and turns generally move quickly.  You always feel like you are in control of you play and you won't find yourself waiting long  for your next turn.

The random tile draw can make developing a strategy difficult, but by counting tiles, you can usually make some informed bets on whether or not a strategy will work. It can be frustrating when it doesn't work out, but the tension of finding out is half the fun of the game.

Despite this, it's a lot of fun to build up the map and there are enough big payoffs throughout to make you feel that you've played successfully.  It's a good, quick game that newbies will take to with ease.  It's great to play as a time-filler when waiting for somebody to show up or when you don't have a lot of time for a longer game.

However, there are a couple places where the game can really slow down.  Figuring out what fields are attached and who owns them can interfere with placing workers.  Also, the points often aren't clear until the end of the game, at which point it can take several minutes to add up the score while everybody else waits.  It does make for a suddenly slow ending to an otherwise fast-paced game.

I recommend this as a game for younger kids, for playing with new gamers, and for a quick game when deeper games just aren't appropriate.  If you prefer more strategy, you may find this game gets old after a while, but it's simple enough to explain and get the hang of for new comers to quickly take to it and the game offers plenty of depth to keep strategists entertained.

Over a year since getting this, several of my friends now have their own copies. I've also introduced many non-gamers to it and they absolutely loved it. This is a great gateway game!

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Tipo:[/b] Competitivo // [b]Interacción:[/b] Baja // [b]Azar:[/b] Alto // [b]Rejugabilidad:[/b] Media
[b]Cartas:[/b] No



[b]OPINIÓN PERSONAL:[/b]
El padre de todos los juegos de colocación de losetas, estupendo para iniciar a alguien en los juegos de mesa (aunque para la primera partida recomiendo encarecidamente hacerle caso a las instrucciones y jugar SIN granjeros).

Es un juego que a primera vista parece no tener casi interacción entre jugadores, pero según vas jugando te das cuenta de que (aun sin ser su fuerte) sí que hay "puteo"... y es que no hay nada como ir ampliando una y otra vez la ciudad del rival para que nunca llegue a terminarla, o quitarle una gran urbe/camino colocando estratégicamente a tus meeples. Se podría decir que la interacción es un poco sutil, pero desde luego es un punto clave para alzarte con la victoria (un jugador que nunca fastidie a su rival no tiene nada que hacer contra un oponente más "agresivo").

En cuanto al azar, está claro que tiene un peso importante, pero los grandes jugadores pueden llegar a controlarlo (memorizando cuántas losetas hay de cada tipo y calculando cuántas quedan por salir/qué probabilidad hay de que salga una en concreto). Si no tienes una mente superdotada, siempre puedes añadir alguna regla casera para limitar un poco el azar (como la de tener una mano de dos losetas, y que en tu turno robes una y elijas cual echar de entre las tres)... aunque personalmente creo que para este juego concreto, el azar (y saber cómo adaptarte a él) es uno de sus encantos. Y eso que a mí no suele gustarme nada el azar.

No recomiendo comprar demasiadas expansiones, pues me parece que solo complican (innecesariamente) el juego con miles y miles de pequeñas reglas, pero si se hace quizás sea recomendable quitar unas cuantas losetas antes de empezar a jugar para que la partida no se alargue demasiado (cada ampliación suele añadir unas cuantas losetas, y la partida no se termina hasta que se colocan todas).

textfield_comment_value:
Nagyon sok ideig az egyik kedvenc játékom volt, és még mindig elég gyakran előkerül. (Fontos hogy itt csak az alapjátékról beszélek)

Előnyök:
- Nagyon újító játék volt amikor megjelent, elötte nem nagyon voltak ilyen lapka lehelyezős, térkép építős játékok.
- A játé menete nagyon egyszerű és könnyen tanítható, ezért remek élmény az új játékosoknak is, és a szerencse miatt még nyerni is van esélyük, a tapasztalt játékosokkal szemben.
- Rengeteg kiegészítője van melyek mind színesítik az alapjátékot.
- Ha valaki nagyon sokat játszott vele akkor már kb. tudja a lapkákat, így csökken a szerencse szerepe.
- Kifejezetten jó a kettő mini kiegészítő ami ebben a kiadásban van (folyó és apátok)
- Ez tipikusan az a játék amit lehet nagyon békésen is játszani, de ha olyan a társaság akkor helyenként már-már háborúba csap át az egyes városok irányítása.

Hátrányok:
- Nem ad túl sok döntési lehetőséget a játék, a felhúzott lapkát általában egyértelmű hogy hova "kell" letenni hogy minél többet érjen. E miatt egy idő után unalmassá válhat
- Ha jól tudja kezelni a társaság akkor előny viszont családok esetén nem annyira hogy nagyon direktbe lehet "támadni" a másikat.
- Sokkal jobb, és modernebb játékok vannak a kategóriájában.

Összességében:
Elöszőr is minden tisztelet meg kell adnom ennek a játénak mert egy fantasztikus műfajt teremtett meg. Már csak e miatt is legalább egyszer mindenkinek játszania kell vele. Viszont vitathatatlan hogy számomra nem öregedet szépen, túlságosan kevés döntést hagy nekem, ami még 2 fővel oké, mert elég sokszor kerülök sorra de 5-en (kiegészítővel 6-an)esélyem sincs hosszú távra tervezni. Ennek ellenére a mai napig szoktam vele játszani, és ez az egyetlen játék amit háziszabályozni szoktam (nyilván csak ha mindenki ismeri már a társaságban a szabályokat és beleegyeznek. Ez pedig annyi hogy mindig van egy "piac" ahol két lapka van fel fedve, ezek közül választhat az aktuális játékos, majd utána feltöltjük a piacot.

textfield_comment_value:
At some point, I had to ask myself if owning an entry level game on the grounds that "everybody" knew it was worth me never being really thrilled to open the box. While it features some moderately non-boring decisions ("Should I close the city of that opponent?", "Is this farm likely to score a lot down the line?", "How long is that meeple likely to be committed to the board?"), the minute-to-minute gameplay is more often luck-of-the-draw and opportunism than rewards for good planning. (Cloisters are particularly egregious in this regard.) As a consequence, some mismatch between the casual audience the gameplay is going for and fairly unintuitive aspects for beginners, such as visualising the exact surface of a farm or remembering the scoring method for each feature, which sometimes differs depending on whether we're talking completion of feature or endgame.

If you want to play the game “seriously”, though, parsing the exact range of options for each tile placement or proceeding to a meticulous accounting of the tiles are yet to be drawn (or are already depleted) is a bit too bothersome. I personally know several households who switched to a video game implementation that takes care of those issues, and haven't opened their physical box since. I could say “problem solved”, but that would mean that I’m now rating Carcassonne as a video game; a domain in which the poor thing is woefully outmatched. Instead I’ll postulate that the digital adaptation is not a strict upgrade, because it loses in translation the primal appeal of original: manually matching a puzzle of tiles together. I guess it’s just hard to put the genie of convenience back in the lamp.

Speaking of fields in which this game struggles to stay relevant: given how (more) chaotic it becomes as the player count increases, Carcassonne is in practice mostly competing against my favourite 2-player games; where it really doesn't stand much of a chance.

textfield_comment_value:
2008-07-10
This was my introduction to boardgaming along with Illuminati. Still enjoying it.

2016-02-08
In many ways I regard Carcassonne one of the most versatile games of all time that fits almost any situation or group. It can be played with novices, kids and hardcore gamers alike. It takes only about 45-60 minutes, which you usually have at your disposal. There is a significant amount of skill involved but the luck of draw makes every game different and gives the less experienced players a chance. The game scales to all player numbers, although the more players the more chaotic and luck driven it becomes.

For its graphical design, Carcassone is great with all the necessary information clearly visible. The rules are fairly simple, except for the scoring of fields, and this is my biggest criticism towards the game. It is just a pain in the ass to figure out who has the majority for each city and it is even more difficult to explain this to new player, especially since most of the people who are new to Carcassonne are rather green with boardgames in general. The solution they came up with in Carcassonne Hunters and Gatherers is much more elegant and intuitive.

Another minor thing with C is that once two players share a city or a road, neither of them has an incentive close it, especially in two player games. This has also been fixed in Carcassonne H&G by introducing the gold nuggets and bonus tiles into the game.

Carcassonne can also be expanded with a myriad of expansions. Personally I deem the base game the best with maybe the one or two of the first expansions thrown in at max. You still want to have a rather compact experience and using too many expansions will just make to whole game too convoluted and away from all the fun.

I'll be happy to play Carcassonne any time but my personal choice is the H&C version of the game, since the problems have been fixed in it and H&G needs no expansions.

textfield_comment_value:
Works well as a gateway game and definitely requires quite a bit of spatial analysis, but it's just so bland, regardless if you're playing draw 1 tile or hand of 3. It's just different ways to score points and is really abstract. Now I like Patchwork which is also a very Euro-ey, spatial aspect required, abstract game, but I like the economic button aspect of Patchwork too, along with the theme, the artwork, and that it doesn't feel as point-salady, whereas Carcassonne's multiple, somewhat arbitrary scoring methods doesn't integrate well thematically to me.

EDIT: Tried this more since I've realized I've liked other games that have either area control that has a focus besides just plurality, or games with a shared map tile placement rather personal board tile placement of say Glen More or Vikings. I like it quite a bit more at the beginning of the game when you are cordoning off your own territory, but once things becomes sprawling and less of a knife fight in a phone booth I like it a lot less. Second, I don't like the all or nothing scoring of the fields, so vastly prefer the game with 2, so as long as you don't win a field by more than 1 it is functionally the same as everyone scoring per meeple, once you consider that only score difference matters. Third, the tile draw isn't that random, but it is kind of the middle of making the most of what you have of Kingdom Builder, vs. the greater control of an abstract, and I would prefer one or the other. Fourth, games aren't long but are still more turns than other games that scratch the same itch (14-35 turns, compared to ~10 for Kingdom Builder, ~10 for Iwari, 12- for Taluva, 15- for Babylonia, 11 for Cacao).
Also, the rules for this game aren't many, but the game explains things in a very disorganized manner, such as separating out how you score things, and that only the person with the most in a region scores that thing.

textfield_comment_value:
It was mid 2021, when I'd been back in the hobby for a few years, that I realized I'd skipped straight over one of the hobby's classics: Carcassonne. I purchased it second-hand with very few expectations, if only so I could further my never-ending board game education.

I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this game, to the point where I don't think I'll ever see it leaving my collection. The rules are dead simple (provided you're not playing with those pesky farmers) and gameplay it so short and delightfully snappy. Would introduce this game to just about anyone.

I enjoy the semi cooperative nature of building out your French countryside. It's incredibly pleasant and satisfying. The placement of your meeples and the ability to join someone else's city or road to share in the points (or even better, gain meeple majority and steal them) makes for fun and engaging gameplay all the way through the short playtime.

For my money, Inns and Cathedrals is an essential expansion. Primarily it balances roads and makes them viable (as the base game offered paltry VPs for them compared to cities) and Cathedrals can turn cities into gargantuan VP behemoths by tripling their score. It's a lot of fun to fight over. And the best part? If you don't finish a feature with an inn or cathedral you don't score anything for it, meaning you have to commit to finishing what you started.

Traders and Builders fell flat for me, despite many recommending it as an expansion as quality as Inns and Cathedrals. It nearly doubled the length of my game and adds a set collection aspect I found a little awkward, fiddly, and at odds with the snappy pace of the game. As it stands, the game doesn't see regular rotation anymore and Inns and Cathedrals is the experience I want whenever Carcassonne makes it off the shelf these days.

My relations with Carcassonne are of love-hate type that averages on mediocre. First it was Ok, but got boring very quickly. Then after a long break I tried it again with my wife and surprisingly liked it. We played it more and it quickly flipped to other extreme.
Now I don't mind playing it and appreciate simplicity and (even today!) freshnest of game mechanics, it's cute look and zen-ness, but eventually it's too random and lacks enough interesting decisions for my taste.
Carcassonne highly customizable with expansions (and this box has ones of the best), you can always find something more to your liking, but they detract from purity of base game and don't change it's feel that much anyway.
I'm still keeping it though. If anything it still is a classic.

My feelings had another turn. Throwing in all expansions I own, though totally crazy, brought game to another level. If you have a few expansions mixed in, the game is dominated by that expansion-specific mechanics. But you have a lot in the mix, their impact spreads thinner and often competes with another expansion, creating tension and harmony. You want to build bigger cities and roads to get King/Robber, but now there is threat of towers and dragon, so what do you do? The towers are diluted by other expansions and are not ever-present threat, and if you do get knocked out, you still have an option to take it back with Count's help. And so on. The game becomes epic. So does play time, setup and takedown, but so far it's my favourite way to play and elevates game to 7/10.

Vanilla Carcassonne grew on me a little. It's not a good game, but it's an enjoyable experience. And at least it plays fast, Carcassonne with all expansions is way too time consuming.

textfield_comment_value:
Carcassonne was probably the game that introduced me to the hobby (and it was the first game I got as a gift) and I have introduced other players to the hobby with this game. And for that alone it has my greatest respect as a game. Later I played this game too much and my view of it has faded quite a bit. Usually I prefer to play games with players that are experienced in the game, but this is not true for this game, since I found that people that know too much about the distribution of tiles (and even tile counting). There are measures that can be made against it (by playing several expansions and remove tiles), but it is not what I usually do. With more plays, many moves seem to be automatic or random since you don’t know what will come up in the next tile draw.

There is a wide appeal for this game for mainly two reasons I think. First it looks stunning when completed. There is something satisfying building the landscape in the game and is something completely different from more traditional games. Secondly, the rules are quite simple, where you pick a tile, place it and if you want to place a follower on the tile.

Many expansions are available, but I prefer to not play with too many of them for the reason that it takes an elegant game and bloat it. I much like the simplicity of the main game.

I usually play this as a two player game with my girlfriend and it works great. You can choose to either build your own stuff or try to sabotage (something I rarely do however). It also works great with three or four players. With more players the game tends to be more chaotic and more competition and helping to completing large areas. I don’t recommend playing the game with five players, since I found it to be too chaotic.

Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Game in a Nutshell: Build cities, roads, and farms by laying one tile at a time. Then place a marker (meeple) to claim it as your own so long as it doesn't belong to someone else. Finish your claims and score points or mess with other people trying to finish theirs. Most points win.

Played as: 2,3,4,5 player (xbox live: 2,4,5)

Played with: Plain; Inns & Cathedrals; Traders & Builders; Inns & Cathedrals + Princess & the Dragon; Inns & Cathedrals + The River II; Inns & Cathedrals + Princess & the Dragon + The River II.

Pros: Big love to a light quicker game that plays well with a smaller group (2-3). My favorite part of the game is how any tile can be used for your gain or an opponents demise. And it's up to you to weigh out so many options in a wide open environment. Few games feel like art in motion, this is one of them as you watch the board grow with every tile. It's like the swiss army knife of games: use it as a fill-in while waiting for a larger crowd to gather for a meatier game; play back-to-back with a friend, you name it and this game will work for the occasion.

Cons: Like most tile-laying games (abstract by nature), it didn't have that instant click that makes a person excited to try it again. This, I think, somewhat diminishes its gateway appeal as compared to SoC or TTR. 

Other: The least luck-based of all the euro gateways. With it's less appealing abstract nature strongly countered by a less luck driven, more intimate (better with less players) feel, this is really a gateway game of a different less social breed. The game's interest will die off if played casually while longer life can be achieved with aggressive play.

Best Use: Works for almost any occasion-- warm-up, filler, 2-3 player gateway, single session time killer, etc.
Title: Carcassonne

textfield_comment_value:
Whilst this is a good game, it's far from being the best of the Carcassonne series.  It's historical importance to gaming is large and I will normally be up for a game of it, since it's a lot of fun (esp if you play with everyone always having a tile in hand to speed it up). Hunters and Gatherers is a better game because the forests are less fiddly than the cities, the rivers allow for better scoring than the roads, and (most importantly), the meadows are not likely to be as sprawling as the farms.

But, let's be clear here - this is the first of a series of superb gateway games.  I'd rank the best of the series right up there with Ticket to Ride - and much better than Settlers (but then again, I don't like Settlers at all, so I'm biased there). Art is good and to play it at its best you need to throw in at least a couple of expansions - esp with 4/5 players.  TBH though, this is better with 2-4 players.

I will state though that even on the first play, I did see a problem with the  the endgame in particular. Despite not having any Cloister tiles in a four player game (and thus lagging behind as those tiles are a real boon to pick up), I still won because at the end, I drew a tile I needed to connect an extra meeple to a HUGE farm that I was equalling the control of. This enabled me to win the game, scoring a decisive 40 points.

It seems to me that at the end, you can either draw such a lucky tile, or you can draw rubbish.  Similarly, if you draw no Cloisters and then also draw badly at the end, you will have no chance of winning.

So, I enjoy the game, BUT H and G IS more balanced and better at the end and The Castle is more cerebral (although it's only 2 player).  Haven't tried The City, but that may well be wonderful...

:arrowE: [u]Synopsis[/u]:
This game popularized the now-ubiquitous meeple and remains a great time even after I've played lots of heavier fare. Pick up a tile and lay it down, slowing creating lovely bits of the countryside, like roads, cities, farms, and monasteries.  Committing meeples to incomplete projects ties them up until the project is finished, meaning that enterprising enemies can block you in, cutting your chances of completing and abandoning your meeples on the board. Points are awarded for completed projects, and expansions add additional elements like big meeples, shepherds, bonuses for scoring roads and cities, and lots of very cooky (but fun!) stuff.

:arrowE: [u]What I like most[/u]:
There is something just utterly satisfying and cathartic about building the eventual sprawl of the French countryside which I can't find in any other game. Tile laying is enjoyable just for being tile laying, but the simple set of rules built around it, such as committing meeples and attempting to snipe projects started by other players, makes it especially interesting.

This is still my preferred gateway game.

:arrowE: [u]What I like least[/u]:
The obsession to play nasty. This game can be really rough if your intention is to shut down your opponents. I honestly like it the most when it's played more passively. I'm not going to give my opponents the tiles they need at no benefit to myself, but I'm not out to get them.

Número de Jogadores: 2 a 5
