textfield_comment_value:
“You choo choo choose me?" - Ralph Wiggum

GAMEPLAY
One of the most well-known designer board games out there it has recently seen a huge influx of players with a very well done ios version of the game. The game turn consists of three simple choices. Pick up cards, play a train route by playing cards, or get more route cards. It's great because rounds go very quickly and no one feels left out. There is no direct interaction between players, but it is possible to block others from connecting routes.

COMPONENTS
The board is a good quality card stock and the cards are smaller than playing cards so small hands won’t have a problem. Days of wonder includes some extra trains of each color in case you lose some. Make sure to count out your trains before each game. The art throughout is wonderful, The trains themselves leave something to be desired, I would like to see wooden trains but that's nitpicking.

THEME
The base game uses a map of America which has about 40 cities on it. Connecting routes throughout the country is simple and resonates with most people as a traveling adventure. The small disconnect is that the players don’t have to connect the routes in sequence. This abstraction doesn’t distract from the enjoyment.

WHO IS IT FOR?
This game is for everybody. Really. I entertained three nephews ages 15, 16, and 18 recently. None of them gamers and they all had a great time. Families with children as young as 8 will have a great time with games lasting about 45 minutes. Even power gamers will enjoy it once in a while; there is light strategy based on your route cards and blocking the other players. For established gamers use it as a gateway for your friends you would like to engage in your hobby.

textfield_comment_value:
The hype train, excuse the pun, was so strong on this game for so long that I deliberately passed on playing for many years... However, having finally bit the bullet I'm pleased to say the praise is very well-deserved, it is truly a great game design. 

The base USA map is lots of fun, looks great, and the "dual carriageway" rules for higher player counts is a good balancing mechanic. The USA map definitely makes TtR casual in the sense that if you miss a single critical one-train link for your route(s) you can end up with a large point swing due to the ruling that if you don't complete your routes you end up having points deducted instead of added. Also, the strategy whereby you ignore routes altogether to aim for the higher-scoring long-train sections is a little bit too strong vs playing traditionally. My other criticism would be that route draw randomness has a bit too much of an effect on final outcomes, in particularly some routes involving Miami can be irksome to complete.

My favourite map I've played so far is India, as the shorter train sections make route completion a bigger part of the game, and the multiple ways of completing routes means that the game is more balanced. Very much enjoy India map (moreso than USA or Europe mainstream options). 

Despite the clear 'casual' elements of the base game, it also gets points for implementing a decent degree of strategy into a gateway game, and also the theme and intuitive ruleset which makes TtR a very easy sell for nascent gamers. 

Overall, the "why-didn't-I-think-of-that" game design speaks volumes to the accessibility and plain enjoyability of TtR and earns a solid 8 out of 10 from me for the series.

textfield_comment_value:
Basically, you draw cards and lay tracks.  You can't foil anyone as there are virtually a million paths to every destination.  So then it comes down to drawing cards and placing trains.  This has to be the most over-hyped game ever.  

If you are looking for a game where you drink beer and occasionally pay attention to what's going on, this is it.


I once saw a guy draw a circle on his white board then toss small sticky balls (about an inch is size) at it for hours.  I thought he would grow tired of this painfully dull act after a day or so.  A year later he still does it as he finds it most relaxing and fun.  I realized that this is how some people meditate (whether they know it or not).  They focus on the easy task at hand and clear the mind.  The easier the task, the more euphoria the brain experiences.  This game is popular because satisfies the same requirement.  A very simple, zero strategy game that sends the brain in to an easy mediative state.  This euphoria elevates when the brain discovers that it could complete a route and did not have to work - thus fulfilling one the the laws of physics that states everything seeks is lowest energy level.  

For that, I give it a 10.  But for gaming, I give it a 1.  I have played this 11 or 12 times now.  After the first 4 (trying to find something I may have been missing) I mostly observed the other players - a very interesting experiment (try it sometime!).  They had the same happy look on their faces as the guy with the sticky balls.  Don't think me negative, I too now like the sticky balls (heh heh).  But for this type of game, I prefer Risk or Monopoly - a tad more excitement with the dice.

textfield_comment_value:
I was and still am dissappointed with this game. It should/could be a 9 for me. Let me explain why. I feel very strongly that the bonuses for completing your rail links between cities is too small. In game play terms I'd add about a 25-50% to the value of the bonus to every city card. You could do this by adding 5 to every card or use a percentage as above. If you added say 30% a 10 would be worth 13. As the game sits its mainly about getting a east to west rail line using as many 5 or 6 link sections as you can. There is virtually no way you can win without using large links. I played a game where I drew mainly north south runs in the east. I completed 7 of 8 but as it turns out even if I'd completed 8 of 8 I still would have lost. This just doesn't seem right. A train game should primarily reward you for building clever rail lines not just a big sections where ever. If you wish you can overlook this completely and play it as a pure strategy game and have fun but I think it still limits the strategic options to one rather than two.

New Idea: I might try a strategy which is to keep two small runs which you can complete easily and focus on playing a mainly defensive strategy to stop others from connecting their big runs. If you get help from one or two other players who may also try this strategy, then completing a big run becomes difficult. This should nicely balance things out. If you really mess with one guy early he will have no choice but to join you in stopping someone else when he is not going to make his big runs. Then this can landslide to 3 or 4 people stopping the last one or two people trying for the big connection.

This is a great gateway game. Also, aside of Magic the Gathering, it is the most played game I own (counting all expansions together).
The core of the game is to fulfill set of tickets - connect two cities on the ticket with the train route. You do this by collecting train cards of different colors and claiming routes by placing number of trains according to their length. 
This is the core set of the game with no additional rules covering USA territory. The strategy is usually to connect the west with east to make one long route ideally. I strongly recommend to add USA 1910 expansion and play megagame variant - shuffling all tickets together and having 10p bonus for longest track and 15p for the most tickets completed.

What I like:
- easy, not brain burning, perfect for the new people in the hobby, Ideal game to pick when you want to introduce board gaming.
- You feel you have actually building something, and when completing all your tickets, it feels somehow good.
- Nice components, artwork is great (in all maps in series general)
- this version I pick when I just need to relax, play without any additional rules introduced in later versions.

What I dislike:

This issue can be partially overdone by good planning and preparing your tracks for the future.
- As this is light gateway game, don't expect some hard brain work, the gaming experience is very casual.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
Has become a staple in our family since we got it in December 2011. Very simple to teach but surprisingly difficult to master, as you need to adjust your strategy based on the tickets you get - do you go for longest cross country routes or do you have bad tickets for that which forces you to do blocking and going for random 6 car routes? Do you start completing your tickets early to seize critical routes or do you hoard cards so as not to tip your hand before you have all the needed cards? When do you force the game to end? The optimal answers to these questions differ with each game and better players will win the vast majority of the time, despite the randomness associated with drawing tickets, drawing cards, and whether you end up competing heavily for certain routes.

Another fun aspect to this game is aesthetic as routes criss cross the board. One game ended with such a beautiful pattern that I literally snapped a picture and made it my phone's lock screen for a couple months.

My only complaint is the variability associated with drawing tickets - it is possible to be at a huge disadvantage out of the gate if you draw poor initial tickets. So we've been experimenting with variants like starting with 6 tickets and keeping at least 3, or starting with 4 tickets and keeping at least 2, etc.

Our family loves gateway games that are light-to medium rules complexity with medium depth to them, and this game fits the bill perfectly, right along with Pandemic and Settlers of Catan. This game's terrific reputation as an awesome gateway game is well deserved.
Title: Ticket to Ride

textfield_comment_value:
I remember learning about this game from SU&SD in my early days of gaming and hearing Paul say that Ticket to Ride is fun and he'd have a good time with it, but given the opportunity to play a board game with friends, he'd rather play about any other SU&SD recommended game. While I think that is a bit harsh on TTR, there is some truth to that. 

I really do like TTR. It's a safe choice that you never really forget how to play even if you only pull it out once or twice a year. Building out your routes and placing your trains is bound to be hailed as clean fun by everyone at the table. As a family game and a gateway game, this is a classic. Really! I genuinely like this game. However, as my tastes have adjusted and my preferences have emerged, there are just other games that fit this same family/gateway niche that I find more compelling. And that's the main problem with TTR. It's not compelling enough to make me suggest it for a game night. Of course there's the trade off between accessibility and compelling gameplay. The more intertwined and obtuse the gameplay, the less accessible it becomes. TTR errs on the side of "uncontroversial" and wants to be a crowd pleaser. For what it aims to do, it is great! I would say it's excellent, but in my opinion the game is a bit too long for the decision space it provides. Although the pace of the game is perfect, I wish it ended about 15 minutes sooner each time we play. Still such a great game but I just don't need it on my shelf. There are other "snappier" and more compelling family games that I prefer over this.

textfield_comment_value:
(Play it digital)

Ticket to Ride is one of the "you have to play it at least once" game, the kind that introduced many people to the modern board game.
It's very easy to explain the rules and to start to play. No need for a previous experience at this game or at any game to know what you want to do. You take cards from the color you need, or try to be lucky with the top deck card. That's very easy. 
The game is quite fast-paced, as each player can play in a few seconds, but from the start to the end it can last quite long, for a "medium-light" game. And most of the time, you just take cards, take cards, take cards, and from time to time, you spend them to claim the railway. And then again, take cards... It lacks variety in action, and you need to do a lot of the same action A before doing action B. For example, in Takenoko, which is also a gateway medium-light game, each turn can be different, as you have to choose between 5 different actions.
Overall, Ticket to Ride has good and bad points. Everybody can play it and understand what's going on. You can plan a """strategy""". The turns are quick, but the game is long, and during your endless journey to victory, you will draw cards over and over again, hoping that nobody else is gonna steal your railway... but what can you do ? You need 3 more blue cards, and they aren't showing up ! Also, the negative points for uncompleted objectives can really hit hard, especially when you just needed one or two more cards. I have played this game with my niece at least 6 or 7 times just this past week. I have also played it with a few adults who aren't very interested in games and it has gone down quite well. Some people might think that it is boring because it isn't a "proper" train game, whatever that may be. There isn't a lot of heavy strategy going on in this game which is nice. Sure there are a lot of ways to connect the different routes, which adds a little to the strategy. Do you try to play in an obvious manner and claim routes in a line, or are you a little sneaky, and try to hope that it all coalesces towards the end of the game? I can imagine that with more players it would become quite intense as there are more players potentially competing for the same routes. 
Sure there is a little downtime while everyone is just taking two (or one if you get the up facing locomotive!) cards. However, in this game you can really crush someones dream. I had to laugh at my niece because she would always celebrate when she got certain cards, and I would think that was funny. If you lose friends over playing a game like this, then maybe you should look at the type of company that you keep? Seriously, if your friends cannot take losing in a game as simple and light as this, then maybe that does say more about you than the game. Overall, I really like this series of games. I think it would appeal mostly to children and non-gamers. I would consider this game as a great gateway game for kids who have only played Cluedo and Monopoly.

textfield_comment_value:
When I tell people I play board games for a hobby, there's always the stigma that they think I spend hours and hours playing games like Monopoly and Candy Land. Not so. And if you're on this site reading this review, you probably know what I mean. So, in an effort to share our wonderful hobby we sometimes need those games that bridge the gap between the hardcore enthusiast, and the person who thinks Clue is a brain burner.

Enter Ticket to Ride! This is one of my go-to gateway games. You can teach it in about 5 minutes, and the game can be played within an hour...depending on your players of course.

And it's a pretty easy sell to. A train game of building railroads across the country. Connecting cities from one coast to another. There are all sorts of different sizes of tracks, that when claimed, give you victory points. This is a set collection game (i.e. you collect different sets of different colored train cars to claim routes). But the key to victory is in each players specific "tickets." These tickets are hidden information, for your eyes only. On them are two cities that you need to connect with a continuous railroad. At the end of the game, you score more points for completing these tickets. But beware, you will also go back that many points for NOT completing them!
This game is perfect for families. And the last few rounds always provide nail-biting tension that just seems to make the game enjoyable as you're all desperately trying to finish routes. Oh, and route blocking is perfectly legal!

I honestly don't understand the popularity of this game. at all. It is such a boring mediocre game. I would never recommend it as a gateway game either, because if I were new to boardgameing and got introduced this game, I will not come back to boardgaming again.

The game is essentially rummy variant. You spend many turns drawing two cards - oh dear. There is very little player-interaction in this game. It costs too much to block your opponents. So blocking happens rather randomly. This sort of random personal attack is my least favorite aspects in the player-interaction. You can, but don't need to care about other people's hand in this game because blocking is rare as the map has many alternative routes.

Destination cards have too much luck and huge swing between completion or incompletion - positive or negative. This is too rough and seems very unbalanced. Also tickets are valued merely by the length and, needless to say, they are quite unbalanced.

I must mention that the scoring scheme is extremely artificial. 1,2,4,7,10,15? What kind of sequence is that?
http://www.research.att.com/~njas/sequences/A027384
Long segments (5 or 6) clearly has huge advantage because they are far more economical. So of course everyone just keeps drawing cards until they get a set of 5 or 6.

I prefer Santa Fe for Moon's railroad game. As a train game (connection game), Trans America is much better than this. Something similar to Ticket to Ride that I much prefer will be Looting London and Marco Polo.

You have to give Mr. Moon some credit here. Of the big four gateway games (Ticket, Settlers, Ra, Carcassonne), his wins out. After dissecting every materially different starting draw (base set only - with a larger, expansion-inundated deck of Tickets the game is much worse because players can never infer if certain tickets remain in the deck as well as the probability and necessity of getting them) and how players would thus begin the game, one should figure out that a spinal route is usually optimum. (The route extends from Calgary to L.A. to Pitt to Miami, with endpoints truncated if necessary, e.g. tickets in New York or Montreal. A secondary route folds back on itself slightly to encompass Duluth, and requires the black six to coexist with the aforementioned.) The only other possibilities include central tendencies of geography in either the west or east (these players need to acquire some strategic routes to pinch the spinal folks) or two "big" tickets that are almost exactly the same route. (Lucky contestants here can simply come on down, there's not much you can do to prevent SEA-NY + VAN-MON and the brevity with which they can be completed.) I even mapped out the optimum routes for all west/east as well as basic countermeasures against traditional players and break points where routes can be shortened given the absence of tickets to cities like Santa Fe or Chicago. As you may have expected, this game has lost its luster for me, but hey - at least it's not Ra.

Il suffit d’une partie des Aventuriers du rail pour comprendre qu’il ait remporté toutes les récompenses ludiques les plus prestigieuses en 2004/2005. Extrêmement accessible avec ses principes expliqués clairement en quelques minutes, il reste remarquablement fluide grâce à son unique action à chaque tour de jeu, y compris à quatre ou cinq joueurs, pour des parties rapides offrant pourtant ce qu’il faut de questionnements tactiques, sur les missions que l’on accepte, le blocage de ses adversaires au détriment de ses propres trajets, l’accumulation de petits segments ou la préférence pour de longs segments, plus rentables mais plus longs à construire…

Cela en fait un excellent jeu familial, satisfaisant encore parfaitement aux standards contemporains, et dont je ne suis pas étonné que d’autres titres s’inspirent directement de l’élégance.

Sa dimension pédagogique (on y apprend la localisation de nombreuses villes) ajoute encore à son charme, et est renforcée par la présence de multiples extensions, promettant mille voyages et découvertes.

L'intégralité de la critique des Aventuriers du Rail et de son extension Japon/Italie est lisible sur VonGuru : https://vonguru.fr/2020/03/31/les-aventuriers-du-rail-voyagez-aux-etats-unis-au-japon-et-en-italie-depuis-votre-salon/

Solo Player Value = Excellent. Playing solo with a single character is rough. I like to use two characters. A single player can manage two character easily.

Two Player Value = Excellent. Pandemic scales flawlessly.


Pandemic is a very well designed cooperative game that scales nicely from being played solo to being played with many. With a single player the game is absolutely fantastic. The single player can play as a single roll or as multiple rolls allowing for more choices.

Essentially Pandemic has been built as a solo solitaire game that has a strong win or lose victory condition with the player fighting against the game itself. More players can play the game because the game is solitaire based and the players are cooperatively fighting against the game. 

This multi-player solitaire against the game works well in Pandemic and actually changes the games difficulty. The game gets more difficult with more players as each player then gets fewer turn. In the solo game this is the player playing multiple rolls.

Playing against the game is accomplished by a player taking a turn for himself, followed by taking a turn as the game; after which it is the next players turn to follow the same pattern. The game's turn is fairly scripted and pre-set making it easy and clean to run the game.

Since Pandemic is designed to be played as the players versus the game the players can strategically work together for victory. This leads to some wonderfully tight strategic choices for the players that can truly make the difference in victory or defeat. Every choice feels like it is important.


Pros - 
- Great design
- Scales well
- Excellent strategic choices for the players
- Suits many players from solo to four

Cons - None

**This game is scored using the expansion


[b]-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------[/b]


Here I will discuss the Pandemic expansion [thing=40849][/thing].

This is truly a wonderful expansion.  If only all expansions could be this good.

This is the first expansion that I can remember which offers multiple expansion components inside the single expansion.  Basically, in this expansion are three separate and individual expansions that can be added to the base game in any combination.  This is a great idea and goes a long way to improve the game longevity.

Due to that I will discuss each piece of this expansion separately.  

------------------

The Virulent Strain is the first piece of this expansion.

With this piece a single disease becomes more powerful and deadly.  That particular disease then has extra rules to govern it which are somewhat random and unpredictable.  This does a lot to increase the difficulty of the game.  

This new difficulty makes the players re-think the games strategy.  The players must now come up with a way to keep the Virulent Strain from quickly spinning of control, while maintaining control over the other three diseases.  This is often much harder than it sounds as the Virulent Strain is designed to cause the players problems.

------------------

The Mutation is the second piece of the expansion.

With this piece a fifth disease is added to the game, called the Mutant Strain.  The Mutant Strain has half as many cubes as regular diseases which make it twice as deadly.  This really cranks up the games difficulty.

The Mutant Strain is governed by special cards which are in both the player draw deck and the disease deck.  This makes the Mutant Strain spread quickly.  Dealing with the Mutant Strain often take precedence due to its lethality, but players must still contend with the other four diseases as well.

------------------

For a real challenge players might want to play with both the Virulent Strain and the Mutant Strain together.

Dealing with both of these disease at the same time is both fun and challenging and offers a huge step up in difficulty.

------------------

The third piece of this expansion is the Bio Terrorist.

This is the first game I can remember that takes a cooperative base game and turns it in a competitive game.  Many games now offer this ability with expansions and I think Pandemic was ahead of its time in this manner.

In this expansion one player becomes a Bio Terrorist and works against the other players.  The Bio Terrorist controls the Mutant Strain and decides how and where the Mutant Strain moves and grows.  The Bio Terrorist gets a turn like normal players but has actions geared toward spreading the Mutant Strain and damaging the players.

While this is a fantastic idea, I think this fails in practice.  The actions the Bio Terrorist can take are limited and weak and somewhat diminish the potency of the Mutant Strain.

Also, this expansion has an element of Scotland Yard to it.  The Bio Terrorist remains, and plays his turns, hidden.  Finding and capturing the Bio Terrorist greatly slows him down.  I don't think this adds anything fun to the game and even confuses the other mechanics.  

-----------------

I think two out of the three new pieces are absolutely fantastic.  The third piece I simply do not like.

Because this expansion so greatly changes the base game I think I should re-score the game.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Longtemps, les jeux de coopération sont restés un genre mineur, généralement destiné aux enfants. En 2000, avec son grand jeu du Seigneur des Anneaux, Reiner Knizia a entièrement renouvelé le genre et pratiquement inventé le jeu de société coopératif pour adultes. Nombre d’auteurs s’en sont ensuite inspirés, et le jeu de société coopératif est devenu un genre à part entière. La plupart de ces jeux utilisent le même mécanisme de base – une pioche d’événements néfastes – les « cartes noires » - arrivant dans un ordre plus ou moins aléatoire, une pioche de « cartes blanches » permettant aux joueurs de régler les problèmes. Les jeux les plus réussis, comme Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, sont ceux qui parviennent à créer une réelle interaction entre les joueurs et à faire sans cesse remonter la tension, maintenant le petit univers du jeu sur le fil du rasoir. Ce sont aussi ceux dont les mécanismes sont suffisamment variés et aléatoires pour permettre un renouvellement des parties et éviter les automatismes. Les jeux de coopération semblent devoir être l’une des grandes tendances des mois à venir, et j’en ai d’ailleurs moi-même un dans les tuyaux.

Pandemic est donc un pur jeu de coopération, dans la lignée du Seigneur des Anneaux. Comme de coutume, le but est de sauver le monde menacé, cette fois, par quatre terribles virus se répandant rapidement sur la planète. Les joueurs sont des scientifiques, bénéficiant chacun d’un petit avantage particulier, qui parcourent le globe tentant tout à la fois de ralentir l’épidémie dans les cités touchées et d’avancer dans la recherche de vaccins ou de remèdes. À la fin de chaque tour d’un joueur, des cartes d’infection sont piochée indiquant dans quelles villes les virus encore actifs se répandent, parfois très rapidement. Les joueurs l’emportent s’ils parviennent à éradiquer les quatre maladies, et perdent si elles échappent entièrement à leur contrôle.

Le thème, sans doute l’un des plus sombres jamais vu dans un jeu de société, pourra certainement choquer. Traité au premier degré, avec un graphisme sombre et sans humour apparent, il parvient cependant à échapper au mauvais goût et à créer une réelle tension, ce qui est la clef du succès pour un jeu de coopération. Les discussions entre joueurs sont tendues, et les choix difficiles. Vaut-il mieux se concentrer sur la recherche ou sur les soins ? Doit-on négliger l’Amérique quelque temps pour tenter tous ensemble d’éradiquer le virus qui s’est répandu en Asie, ou au contraire se répartir sur les différents continents pour pouvoir réagir facilement aux crises ? Peut-on prendre le temps de se rencontrer pour échanger des informations, c’est à dire des cartes, ou doit on compter sur la chance de la pioche ? Ne me demandez pas la bonne réponse, j’ai à ce jour perdu mes trois parties de Pandemic.

Comparé aux autres jeux de coopération parus ces derniers temps, Pandemic est certainement le plus rapide, une partie durant à peine plus d’une demi-heure. C’est aussi l’un des plus simples à jouer, avec des règles logiques et fort bien présentées, mais qui risquent peut-être de manquer de variété après une dizaine de parties. Mais attention, ce n’est certainement pas le plus facile !
---
Cooperative games have long been a minor genre, mostly aimed at young kids. With his big box Lord of the Rings game, Reiner Knizia has reinvented the genre and designed the first modern adult cooperative boardgame. Many authors have followed since, and cooperative game has become a noticeable genre these last years. Most of these games use the same kind of “game engine”, with a drawing deck of bad events – the “black cards” - arriving in a more or less random order, and a drawing deck of “white cards” used by the players to solve the critical situations. The most successful such games, like Shadows over Camelot, have a strong player interaction and a high tension, the small game world always standing on the edge. They also have enough variety and randomness to make every new game different. Cooperative game seem to be a strong trend at the moment, with several scheduled to hit the shelves. I also have one in the pipe.

Pandemic is a pure cooperative game, in the Lord of the Rings style. As usual, the goal is to save the world, this time from four viruses threatening to spread all over the planet. Players are scientists, each one with a specific ability, travelling across the globe trying to treat and slow the infection, and if possible to find cures for the four diseases. At the end of a player’s turn, infection cards are drawn to know in which town the active viruses will multiply, and sometimes spread to neighbouring cities. The players win if they manage to eradicate the four diseases, and lose if they get out of control and overtake the world.

The theme, probably the darkest one ever used in a boardgame, can feel disturbing. It is treated very seriously, with dark and realistic graphics and no apparent hum or, but avoiding bad taste. It also create a strong and always renewed tension, which is the critical point in a cooperative game. The debate between players is always very lively, and the decisions hard to make. Better focus on searching a cure or on treating the infected cities? Better ignore America for a while and all together try to eradicate the Asian disease, or scatter through the world and be ready to jump on any crisis situation? Is it worth taking time and movement to share knowledge, meaning giving or taking a card, or just rely on the luck of the draw ? Don’t ask me what the right answers are – so far, I’ve lost all my games of Pandemic.

Pandemic plays much faster than all other cooperative games, a game lasting little more than half an hour. It also has the simplest and clearest rules, and I’m a bit weary that it can become repetitive after a dozen games. This doesn’t mean, however, that the game is easy.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
"Pandemie" hat schon einige Jahre auf dem Buckel und es brachte schon viele erfolgreiche Ableger hervor. Die bekanntesten unter ihnen werden wohl die drei Legacy Teile "Pandemic Season 1", 2 und 0 sein.
Das Spiel begleitet mich seit nahezu Beginn meiner Spielerkarriere und ich glaube sogar, dass ich damit meine erste kooperative Erfahrung gemacht hatte.
Damals noch im Vertrieb von 'Pegasus Spiele', in einer größeren Schachtel verpackt und mit viel Holzmaterial steht es heute von 'Z-Man Games' mit Plastikpöppeln und -würfeln im Regal. Ich muss schon sagen, dass ich der alten Variante etwas nachtrauere, doch die war mit der zweiten und dritten Erweiterung nicht mehr kompatibel und so habe ich bereits vor Jahren entschieden, auf die neuste Version des Spiels 'upzugraden'.

In "Pandemie" schlüpfen die Spieler in die Rollen von Wissenschaftlern, Ärzten, Krisenmanagern und Co., mit dem Ziel, die Erde, bzw. dessen Bewohner vor vier kursierenden Krankheiten zu schützen.
Die Spieler agieren mit jeweils vier Aktionen pro Zug gegen das Spielsystem, das überwiegend durch Karten getrieben ist.
Mit Aktionen können die Spielfiguren auf dem Globus bewegt, Krankheiten in Form kleiner Würfel aus den Städten entfernt, wissenschaftliche Forschungszentren errichtet und schlussendlich die rettenden Heilmittel erforscht werden.
Einige der Aktionen erfordern zusätzliche Handkarten, deren Kartenfarbe oder sogar Standort wichtig ist. So kann beispielsweise ein Forschungszentrum in der Stadt 'Essen' nur mit der entsprechenden Karte errichtet werden und jede Stadtkarte gibt es im Deck nur ein einziges Mal! Um ein Heilmittel zu erforschen sind sogar fünf Karten der gleichen Farbe nötig! Das ist alles gar nicht so leicht zu bewerkstelligen.

Zu Hilfe kommen die eigenen, individuellen Charaktereigenschaften der Rollenkarten jedes Spielers. So kann beispielsweise die Wissenschaftlerin ein Heilmittel bereits mit vier gleichfarbigen Karten herstellen, was die Sache deutlich vereinfacht. Der Logistiker hingegen darf Spielfiguren der anderen Spieler bewegen, als wären es die eigenen. Und der Sanitäter kann mit nur einer Aktion alle Krankheitswürfel aus seiner Stadt entfernen, statt nur einem.
Am Ende des Zuges zieht der aktive Spieler zwei neue Handkarten vom Spielerdeck und muss danach welche vom Infektionsdeck aufdecken. Die auf diesen Karten angegebenen Städte erhalten jeweils einen (weiteren) Krankheitswürfel. Liegen bereits drei Würfel einer Art dort, geschieht ein Ausbruch und ALLE angrenzenden Städte erhalten je einen Krankheitswürfel!
Dies kann zu Kaskaden führen, die überhaupt nicht gesund sind!
Immer mal wieder tauchen Epidemiekarten auf. Dann muss der Ablagestapel der Infektionskarten gemischt und oben auf deren Nachzugstapel gelegt werden. Nun kommen alle bereits betroffenen Städte wieder an die Reihe!
Das Spiel kann auf unterschiedliche Weise verloren gehen: Beim achten Ausbruch, sobald der Spielerkarten-Nachzugstapel leer ist oder sobald zu viele Würfel einer Krankheit auf dem Brett liegen, also deren Reserve erschöpft ist.
Gewonnen ist es hingegen nur auf eine einzige Weise: Alle vier Heilmittel sind gefunden!

Das Spiel ist großartig. Obwohl es schon so alt ist, hat sich der Mechanismus mit dem Infektionskartenstapel nicht abgenutzt. Dieser fühlt sich immer noch sehr gut an und passt thematisch super zum Spiel. Krankheiten breiten sich vorwiegend in Städten aus, die bereits betroffene Einwohner haben. Doch auch andere Städte kann es hier und da mal treffen. Kümmern sich die Spieler nicht schnell genug um Eindämmung oder Behandlung, kommt es zu unkontrollierbaren Ausbrüchen.
Auch die Charaktere und deren Eigenschaften sind super für das Setting ausgedacht. Sogar die Sondereigenschaften sind stimmig und wirken je nach Spielsituation in etwa gleich stark.
Leider gibt es dennoch sehr starke und sehr schwache Konstellationen.
Ein Beispiel für ein überpowertes Duo:
- Forscherin: kann jede beliebige Handkarte an einen Mitspieler abgeben.
- Wissenschaftlerin: benötigt für die Heilmittelforschung nur vier statt fünf Karten.
Beide Spieler bleiben in der Anfangsstadt Atlanta stehen, der einzigen Stadt, die von Beginn an ein kostenloses Forschungszentrum hat. Alle Aktionspunkte der beiden Spieler werden allein dafür genutzt, Karten von der Forscherin zur Wissenschaftlerin zu geben, um dann mit ihr Heilmittel um Heilmittel zu entdecken.
Was derweil auf der Welt passiert, ist nicht wichtig. Ein paar Ausbrüche vielleicht, doch bevor es wirklich brenzlig wird, wurden alle Heilmittel erforscht und das Spiel ist damit gewonnen, ohne auch nur einen Fuß vor die Tür gesetzt zu haben.
Wer schon einige Partien gespielt hat, weiß um solche Konstellationen und vermeidet sie beim Spielaufbau.

Ich spiele "Pandemie" noch immer sehr gerne.
Auch meine Tochter liebt das Spiel, sodass wir mittlerweile alle Module aus allen Erweiterungen Stück für Stück dem Grundspiel hinzugefügt und ausprobiert haben.
Uns hat das 'Labormodul' sowie das 'Supervirus' sehr gut gefallen. Auch die 'Quarantäne' sowie die neuen Charaktere und Ereignisse sind leicht zu integrieren und spielen zukünftig in jeder Partie mit.

:thumbsup: [b]POSITIVE POINTS:[/b]

++ Very good medium-light weight coop gateway game that is usually really tense until the end.
++ The use of the infection deck that reuse the cities' cards in which infection has already occurred to propagate diseases in a thematically and mechanically sound manner that still include a bit of randomness (by shuffling the discard pile and putting it back on top of the deck).
++ The game user-chosen variable difficulty depending on the number of "Epidemic" cards uses (and can range from easy to nearly impossible).
++ Good replayability because of the randomness of the setup (both for the disease cubes placement but also the "Special cards" used for the game and the variable players' roles.
++ Variable players' power (role) assigned randomly at each game.
++ Great game insert which hold everything in an orderly fashion (base game and expansion, and you can use the OtB expansion insert to store everything in just one box).
++ The "On the Brink" expansion adds a lot of replayability and also challenge as the game difficulty can be enhanced greatly with more "Epidemic" cards, the "Virulent Strain" and the new Purple Virus.
++ There are expansions available for this game (which is useful to refresh the game when we have overplayed it).


:thumbsdown: [b]NEGATIVE POINTS:[/b]

-- A bit long to set up at the beginning of the game.
-- Being a coop game, it is prone to the Alpha Player Syndrome (where an experienced player can dictate other players everything to do to ensure a win).

textfield_comment_value:
I like Pandemic but I think that it fails as a cooperative game. There are two important reasons for this: abstraction and necessity.

The game of Chess is an abstraction. The players are representative of two noble parties in feud as they compete over a given plot of land. The land itself is represented by a logical map and not a physical one. The individual pieces move in accordance with abstract rules, only loosely in keeping with the roles for which they are named - while it is true that a King relies greatly on his subjects or a mounted Knight might be afforded greater mobility, the nature of a Bishop's movement speaks more to play mechanics than it does any interplay between theology and monarchy. Similarly, games like Go and Checkers and even Tic-Tac-Toe are abstractions; they are oppositional games of strategy and tactics. Theme in these sorts of games is superfluous because the players are primarily engaged in left-brain activity.

Despite its dressing, Pandemic is also an abstraction. The theme of epidemiology might easily be substituted with one of farmers faced with the spread of weeds among their crops. The map, while seemingly more realistic than a chess board, remains a logical representation governed by arbitrary rules. Each player, assigned an appropriately themed identity, is granted unique abilities - and these abilities are incorporated to facilitate (or force) player interaction, not because they engender a personal relationship between each player and his or her given role.

The appeal of Chess is not diminished by its abstraction for two reasons: it pits players against one another and, further, it does not necessitate communication among players on the same team.

When you eliminate the opposing player, an abstract game is more akin to a puzzle. There remains no emotional investment of pride. The incentive of winning is reduced to the exercise of skill; and the challenge becomes merely a question of comprehension and complexity.

When you take an abstract puzzle - such as I characterize Pandemic to be - and you introduce the pretense of teamwork, you're going to run into trouble. People don't rally under abstraction. It takes necessity, language and sometimes even symbolism for people to unite.

Simply put: Pandemic allows for two-to-four players, but it only requires one. In fact, the aphorism that two heads are better than one doesn't even apply. Each additional player only introduces additional frustration.

The mechanics of Pandemic are not exceedingly complex. Many have already attested to the fact that on any given turn there exist only a few - sometimes as few as one - reasonable actions of play. Because of the manner in which played cards are reshuffled, a careful player can very easily anticipate and preempt imminent obstacles. The more you understand the mechanics, the easier the game becomes; and by extrapolation, a general solution can be devised and applied.

I approach Pandemic the same way I might approach Sudoku. Both are abstract puzzles, though they initially appear to be otherwise (beginners often mistake Sudoku for a math problem, however, the numbers could just as easily be substituted with the first nine sequential letters of the alphabet).

I suppose you could attempt to solve a Sudoku puzzle with a partner. Having identified the right number for a particular cell you might then explain to your partner why it is so. But your ability to communicate why it is the right number and, further, your partner's ability to understand you has no bearing on the solution itself. The number is either right or it is wrong, and the deciding factor is not dependent on a consensus of the players. What's more, to communicate this way for each cell would become exceedingly tedious.

Pandemic is cooperative in the same sense that Sudoku might be cooperative if you and your partner took turns with the pencil. A given player is no more or less empowered with respect to whose turn it might happen to be; the game is simply played by whomever identifies the next best action.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is the newest in the recent fad of cooperative games, and seems to be one of the more promising entries for fans of straight Euro games.

Pandemic presents a deceptively simple concept: the board is seeded with disease cubes, and after each player's turn, more cards are drawn which create or amplify the disease issues. When an area would have more than 3 cubes placed into it, an outbreak occurs, spreading disease to the surrounding areas and generally causing chaos. The game is based on cooperation, and each player has a special ability that can allow them to combat the diseases in a slightly more efficient way: for instance, the medic allows a player to completely clear a city of disease for 1 action rather tha the 1 cube rate of the other characters.

Over the course of the game, players are also collecting city cards in the 4 coloured suits of the game. When someone has 5 of a colour, they can cash them in at a research station to cure the disease, and then it's just a matter of stamping it out on the board. If that is done successfully, then any cards representing that disease are ignored.

The thing that makes this game insidious is the epidemic mechanic. When an epidemic card is drawn from the "good deck" (which each player receives 2 cards out of each round) then all hell breaks loose on the board: a card is drawn from the bottom of the deck, and that place becomes triple diseased, and then the discard deck and that card are reshuffled and placed ON TOP of the negative deck. What this means is that the same cities keep reappearing, and when you combine that with the negative impact of having more than 3 cubes in a given city, the game can get ugly quickly.

So in terms of concept, this is an interesting game, certainly one of the best coops that I've played. The game is essentially one long puzzle game where each player has 4 action points to spend, and in-depth strategy discussions tend to break out as regularly as the diseases. The game is challenging enough to be interesting as well, which is a key for long-term interest.

The downsides, however, primarily do relate to the difficulty of the game. Though difficulty is partially dictated by the number of epidemic cards that are seeded into the positive deck, the game's difficulty also hinges heavily on how the negative deck ends up stacked. If one area's cards are all clustered at the top of the deck, a single early epidemic card can absolutely ream the players before they can even get going. Conversely, a very dispersed card distribution in the negative deck, or a run of the same colour early in the positive deck can make the game fairly relaxed, as a run of the same colour from the positive deck will result in an easy early cure or two, and dispersed diseases, when they occur, rarely will lead to outbreak chains. This isn't to say that the game is easy to win even given these circumstances, because the end can sneak up on you, but the ideal game experience seems to be somewhere in-between, and I'm not sure if there's a way to artificially manufacture that while still keeping the uncertainty that makes this game interesting.

I think my final feelings on this are pretty positive though. It's a short game with some interesting decisions, and some funny moments. If I'm in the mood for a game in this style (hourish co-op), it would probably be my first pick pretty easily but it's not exactly sitting in a crowded niche, and in a longer time frame I would prefer Knizia's LotR or (with 2) Arkham. 

As of 2016 I'd have to say this is great as a couple's co-op title, but that the Legacy version makes it a pale a bit by comparison.

As an aside: nice component quality: big cubes, thick, weighty cards, a sturdy but not overly glossy board. Kudos to Z Man for the job that was done on this one.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] I tried Pandemic at the start of the pandemic with some friends on Tabletop Simulator. We played one game and won - frankly, it was barely even much of a challenge. What I recall about our experience was that there was a fair bit of quarterbacking which was not even necessarily our fault - the puzzle we were tasked with solving just felt painfully obvious given some of the luck that went our way. We were left with a bit of a "That's it?" impression. 

I never gave Pandemic much of a second look, largely because I came to learn that I would never be able to get Legacy games to the table despite all of the praise I have heard for it. As I have been revisiting a lot of games I had previously played on Board Game Arena, I decided to give it a try. Something I was immediately reminded of was how much I hate the visual design of the rulebook; personally, I believe there is a reason why there is both a "Commonly Overlooked Rules" section of the rulebook and a pinned thread titled "Common Mistakes" on Board Game Geek.

In my first game, someone lamented that I had set "Closed hands" in the settings. The two people with 600+ score proposed we concede during my third teammate's second turn, who had 50 ELO. Friendly reminder that Board Game Arena is not always beginner-friendly, and maybe will not match your expectations (Saboteur flashbacks...). We probably would have lost a few turns later regardless.

I gave it a few more chances playing Solo 2-handed to get more intimate with the mechanics. On my 3rd try, I got a win using Researcher and Scientist - with few exceptions, I barely had to move off my starting research facility. I cured the Black diseases near-instantly off lucky draws before curing Red a few turns later, so I largely dodged the first two epidemics. I cannot say I ever necessarily felt threatened, especially since the rules state that players can cure a disease at any research station; likewise, despite my fumbling, I cannot say I ever really had much of a chance at winning my first two games based on the epidemic triggers that occurred. Those two games went downhill too fast, and the epidemic spread everywhere too quickly to manage.

Sure, I went into Pandemic not expecting much, and here is a wall-of-text just reiterating that I did not feel much while playing. This disinterest is not surprising for me as I recently played Marvel United and was bored through most of it. At the same time, I would much rather be playing Marvel United compared to Pandemic. I own Spirit Island with a few expansions, but I have been struggling to get it to the table (despite keeping up on expansions...). There is no denying that Pandemic was a hugely-important game for modern boardgaming, but I'm willing to completely skip this one. Whether On The Brink!, Legacy Season 1, or Star Wars: Clone Wars would make me have a change of mind, I will probably never know - existence of strategy or not (card-counting will not make Pandemic more fun for me, sorry!), 

My opinion doesn't particularly change - the original Pandemic was woefully underwhelming. Chances are, most Pandemic games will feel particularly prone to 'alpha gaming' for me - with how difficult Pandemic is paired with how restrictive a player's turn is, my feeling is that players need to all be at roughly the same skill level for Pandemic to work. I laughed at someone else's comment describing their miserable experience with Pandemic where they described their experience when playing as the Researcher with experienced players as: "I was basically a doormat" (rating: 2, May 2023).
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Overall, my cooperative game crown still goes to Knizia's Lord of the Rings. But while Lord of the Rings is a co-op game that really requires a group of "gamers", Pandemic is a go-to game for any group of people.

The tension around the table is just palpable playing Pandemic, and the game plays in under an hour, so it's really perfect for a weeknight get together with friends. To succeed, team members must really plan things out together. If each player simply pursues his or her own "plan", then the group is sure to lose the game, especially on Normal or (god forbid) Heroic settings. Pandemic is an ultra-cooperative game. This is its greatest asset, but also the thing about it which I foresee will put me off a bit over time. There is little room for autonomy and self-determination. Success requires the closest sort of collaboration. So be warned: play this only with people you like! If you play it with someone you don't have a lot of patience with, you *will* want to throttle them. Pandemic throws very difficult situations right in the face of the players, and good brainstorming is required to win the game. If someone is being boorish and trying to "quarterback" the whole game, you will be driven to distraction. Likewise if someone is being an utter dolt and failing to grasp the plan that the group came up with.

Again, VERY tense. VERY exciting. LOADS of fun. But play it with the right people. Otherwise Pandemic possesses the potential to devolve into an exercise in frustration. It also shines with 3-4 players, but the tension is significantly less with only 2. This is because 2 players can tightly coordinate their actions, working as a team and moving more or less together around the world in order to cure the diseases. With 3 and 4 players, it's harder to get ahead of the intensity curve - the point where, after a few epidemics, you start infecting new cities without any disease (and hence a lesser chance of outbreaks). Because of this, I think 3-4 player games are actually slightly more challenging than 2 player games.

Components: the board is crap. The disease cubes, pawns, research stations, and cards are all just fine. But I'd shell out another $10 for a decent board. This one warps, wrinkles, smells funny, and peels up from the edge. I like the size of it, I like the art and design. It's the physical quality which is just dismal. That's a shame when it affects such a super game.

Update: this one has settled at a perpetual 7 for me. When I like it, I love it. But it's not really something I'm in the mood for any time, in plenty of situations I'd just rather not play it. You have to be in the mood to do the group-think thing, communicating extensively with the other players at every turn, in order to win. And sometimes, I feel that players can make all the right choices (optimal ones) and still lose due to luck and game balance. If this weren't so, it is true that Pandemic would lose some tension, as it would become a puzzle - solvable by an experienced group of players. That would be a shame, and a downfall. Yet the game falls down anyway, as once you ARE very experienced, it is frustrating to lose a perfectly played game. For some reason, this complaint doesn't arise for me when playing Lord of the Rings. The balance of choices in LotR maintains at least the illusion that your success depends only on your choices.

Anyway, despite my gripes I rate Pandemic a "strong buy" for its accessibility, tension, and short play-time.

[2009-11-25 Rating: n.a. -> 7.5]

Overview:
--------------
Pandemic is a cooperative game where 2 to 4 players try to save the world by curing four deadly diseases. The map of Pandemic depicts the world with various cities. After each players turn, some of these cities are infected by placing cubes in it. If the infection rate of one of the four diseases reaches a cube limit of three in one city and this city gets infected again, an outbreak will occur and the disease will spread.
On their turn, a player can take up to four actions. These actions include:
- Travelling to another city.
- Building a Research Station (these are needed to find the cure for a disease and to travel faster)
- Lowering the infection rate of a city by being in it and removing some of the infection cubes.
- Exchanging city cards with other players.
- Finding a cure by being in a city with a research station and discarding a set number of city cards in the diseases colour.
After their turn, the player draws two new city cards and infects some new cities. After this, the play continues with the next player until one of the game endings conditions is met. These are:
1. Players run out of cubes representing one disease.
2. Players have 8 outbreaks happen.
3. Players run out of cities cards to draw.
4. Players find the cures for all four diseases.
Since Pandemic is a cooperative game, all players win the game when the fourth ending condition is met. If one of the other game ending conditions is met, all players lose and the game wins.

Comments:
---------------
* The card mechanism to infect new cities is really clever and well thought out. Because of its implementation, the same cities get infected again and again. While this puts some pressure on you, this also keeps the game from being too random or too deterministic (and thereby solvable). While you don’t exactly know when an infected city will be infected again, you do know that it will happen for sure. So there is some risk management and push your luck built into the game. I like this.

* The cooperative aspect has it pros and cons. What I like is the fact that I can easily get my non gamer friends to join in for a game of Pandemic. Since all players act together, there is no competition and this is quite appealing to them. The drawback of the missing competition is that some of them are not really involved in the game since they do rely completely on the evaluation of the other participating players. An often heard comment in this regard is: "I like this game because I don’t have to think that much. You can tell me what to do". This kills the fun a little for me.

* After playing my first few games I would have rated this game 9. After more plays with some of my gaming friends my desire to play this game cooled down a little bit. I still enjoy the theme immensely, but with experienced players I discovered the puzzle aspect of the game more and more. Basically the game is won if you manage to optimize your action selection. With experience, it is often times quite easy to see the best play and the discussions about the actions to be taken are replaced by a mutual agreement. I have to see if this issue is addressed in the expansion.

* Great replayability thanks to the different role cards and the great infection mechanism.

* I love the theme and it really helps to get new players to join in for a game of Pandemic.

textfield_comment_value:
(Using BGG star rating system)

What it is
- Herofest - play as a group of everyday heroes taking on a not-so-everyday challenge of saving the world from a pandemic
- Quality - the components are great quality and really help sell the theme for what would otherwise be an abstract probability cruncher 
- Co-op - work together to beat the game

What it isn't
- Easy - variable settings means you can change the difficulty but our group has always struggled even on medium. About 50/50 win ratio at this level
- Nice - this is a mean puzzle and be prepared for strong disagreements around the table on how to beat the virus
- Long - games run true to time and feels fast

Liked
- Saviourism - I feel like I am really trying to save the world. There is enough theme to give an air of seriousness about the endeavour
- Delicate balancing act - so many ways to fail and only one way to succeed
- AI - a simple deck of cards cause terror when reshuffled replacing all of the previous infected destinations at the top of the deck after all of the work you did to clear the virus. Did you manage to clear enough infection cubes to prevent an outbreak?

Disliked
- Disputes - some sour moments when a disagreement on strategy leaves some players feeling marginalised, especially when you lose.
- Replayability - It is somewhat replayable as the destinations which come up mean the puzzle changes every time, but the puzzle is still the same. If you like this game definitely recommend getting an expansion or two to revamp the experience

Play if
- Solid game group - this would not be a great team builder. Rather more of a team tester
- Thrill-seeker - games, win or lose, come down to the wire. So well balanced that way
- Covid revenge - take on the virus and see if you can do it better than the real world leaders

Don't play if
- Looking for a quiet night - it's an exciting, tense experience 
- Trauma-warning - it is a game about viruses killing millions of people. Be cautious about which audience to bring this out with

Evaluation
A fun, tense and quick beat-the-game puzzle dressed in a compelling theme with high quality components. Just be sensitive about the theme with some audiences. This game was released long before the covid pandemic was a thing. I wonder if they would of handled the subject matter differently if it was made today>#? Nothing explicit or disrespectful built-in. 

Why missing out on the 10/10 spot?
Quarterbacking - experienced players will end up calling the shots rather than letting less experienced payers learn the puzzle for themselves. This limits player agency slightly. However, it is more of a nit-pick. A 10/10 would have given some way to have an equal role such as giving players hidden information. 

Similar games
- Risk - but pandemic is way better 
- Diplomacy - for negotiations and strategising 
- Plague Inc - but this time you play as the virus

Gateway Games
- Snakes and ladders - for young children as it trains them in the piece  movement 
- Dam it - teaches asymmetric starting point, dynamic board states and set collection

Recommendation
This is a staple of any board game collection. This was the game that got me into gaming in the first place so take that for what it is. Looking for an exciting co-op puzzle? This game is the best in the business.

Fun Factor: 1 
Components: 7

Theme + Mechanics: 9
Replay Value: 9 (This thing wants you to replay it, nay, dares you.  Problem is, is it really worth it?)
Scaling/Players: 8
Subjective:  -0.50  As cooperative games go, I find this to be more of a multi player logic puzzle than a game.  Arkham Horror on the other hand, is unquestionably a game.  Perhaps great coops fall between this spectrum?

I will go down as a martyr here, but Pandemic just doesn't seem like a game to me. Granted, there are decisions to be made and player interactions to be had-- but really it just feels like one big logic puzzle to me. A puzzle does not a game make. Before somebody charges me with co-op rage, I love cooperative games. The active word being "games"  Cooperative puzzles, not so much.

Games differ from puzzles through:
Player interaction.
Dynamism.
No predetermined outcome.
Superior involvement of skill and chance.
A more active agent of antagonism.

I consider Pandemic to have little player interaction, be very static, and have a relatively predetermined framework within which the players muddle about believing that they can control the outcome. Chance and skill are severely muted within the context of Pandemic, and the agent of antagonism doesn't impress me, because after all it is just a sequence of shuffled cards that regurgitate. Sounds more and more like a puzzle.

Read this quote from Wikipedia on "Jigsaw Puzzle Strategy"...
Quote:
The most common approach to building a puzzle is to start by separating the edges from the inside pieces. Once the edges are built it can become easier to move inward. For those new to puzzles, it is recommended to choose one consisting of multiple areas with contrasting designs and colors. This enables the narrowing down of potential portions of the puzzle where a particular piece will fit.

Some people like to use the picture on the box to help solve the puzzle. Once you have completed the edge, if you can find the location of a particular piece on the picture, you can place it down inside of the overall puzzle at approximately the place it belongs. If you do this enough times, you find pieces eventually will start fitting together.

Another approach is to sort the pieces by color, and work on one color at a time. When you get to large areas with the same color (such as the sky in many landscape puzzles), you can go by shape, or you can place all the pieces in a grid and approach the problem by taking a piece that already has an anchor (such as an edge piece) and trying it against all the pieces laid out.
Strange, but this sounds an awful lot like a game of Pandemic.

The worst part is that you might even be working on a puzzle that cannot be won, so Pandemic probably does not fit the standard for even the most sadistic of puzzles. It is like a jigsaw puzzle that you are working on, and when you are looking the other way, the dog comes in and scarfs down a few pieces. Am I going to keep working the puzzle, or am I astute enough to sit up and take notice that some of my pieces are missing at this point so I might as well chuck this whole "Pandemic" thing in the trash and go play a thoroughly enlivened game of Twilight Struggle?

Also:  HOW IS THIS GAME RANKED SO HIGHLY ON BGG?  FOR SHAME.

textfield_comment_value:
I WANT to love this game, but I just don't. I keep trying and trying, I play it every now and again, but my issues with the game just never get resolved. 1) I hate how it scales...if you play at 4 players, you may not get a 3rd turn...no fun. 2) thematically, and mechanically, running out of resource cards is about the stupidest, contrived, and wholly arbitrary way to end a game as you can get, it's right up there with roll and move if you ask me, why not reshuffle the discards and keep on playing? Hate that. No game should end because you can't draw a freaking card. 3) 9 out of 10 games can basically be scripted as winning or losing simply by how the initial random layout goes (in combo with the first few turns) and/or the distribution of cards at the beginning of the game. If a player lucks into drawing their 3rd and 4th card of one color on their first turn...or the initial distribution is particularly nice...the game can be a breeze...and equally impossible to win, if everyone struggles to get a pair of same color cards turn after turn...and don't get me started on how annoying it is you have to be on the actual city to trade the city card...my god that's stupid. You should be able to at LEAST trade cards of the same color in the region of that color. For me, the game is WAY to dependent on random draws, random distribution of cubes, which means you can basically get easy games and impossible to beat games without any actual game play. 

I love the theme of the game, and the mechanics are great, the outbreaks, the moving around the board...I just think they created arbitrary limitations to gameplay which just jacks up the difficulty of an already difficult game to win. I've played the game dozens of times, won my first game, like 10 games in, solely by lucky draws, and though I have played games where it was fun right up to the end (win or lose), I still found myself frustrated by the dozens of losses that I never felt were a result of my gameplay...they were either unwinnable to begin with, or just one frustration piled upon another. Like when the initial cluster of cubes are all centered around central and eastern asia, and the first outbreak in the region causes a chain reaction that ends the game before the 3rd player in a 3 player game, gets a 2nd turn...that's no fun. There are just too many "no fun" outcomes to this game. I shouldn't have to house rule this game to make it fun. I don't know, maybe it's just the nature of the cooperative beast. I guess I'd just rather play a competitive game where every game there is at least one winner...than a coop game where 90% of the games end up with everyone losing. And again, it's not the winning or losing that make a game fun, I realize that, if I lose the game by the skin of my teeth and was THIS close to winning...that's great. It's losing game after game simply by chance and luck where it doesn't matter how well you play...that's just frustrating and not fun. That's where I am with this game.

Jest bardzo prosta, a więc odpowiednia dla początkujących. To plus. Równocześnie jednak jest za mało wszystkiego - to minus. I nie wynika to tylko z mojego zafiksowania na punkcie masy elementów (im więcej, tym lepiej!). Po prostu często mam wrażenie, że Pandemic jest... pusty. Sterylny. Za mało gracz ma możliwości, za mało jest interakcji między graczami jak na grę kooperacyjną, za mało się dzieje (bo tylko pojawiają się kolejne choroby, a mogłoby się zdarzać coś jeszcze, komplikacje związane z badaniami, reakcje opinii publicznej, cokolwiek). I choć na początku intrygował mnie nieco klimat, pomysł z zespołem badawczym i chorobami, to jednak szybko się przekonałem, że brakuje tutaj tego, na co tak naprawdę liczyłem (kombinowanie z lekarstwami, jakieś poważniejsze działania laboratoryjne), a zamiast tego dostałem symulator pasażera linii lotniczych, który ma zbyt dużo wolnego czasu. Czasami więc mam ochotę Pandemicowi obniżyć ocenę, bo rozgrywka nie sprawia mi radości. [i]Posted: 4/6/10, Rated: 9[/i]
{2P: 9, 3P: 10, 4: 8}

[i]Pandemic[/i] is one of those games that gets a tremendous amount of "buzz" here on the Geek.  It is a cooperative title, which means players are working together to beat the game instead of each other.  In this case, it means they are trying to find cures to four globally-threatening diseases.  The subject matter of global epidemics isn't sexy in the slightest, but it very quickly grows on you all the same.

The amazing feature of [i]Pandemic[/i] is how refined it is.  It embodies Albert Einstein's quote, "Make things as simple as possible, but not simpler."  Each player gets four action points per turn, and can choose from a list of basic and advanced actions.  Reference cards are provided, which is always a nice touch.  She can also use her role's special power; there are five roles provided in the game.  You would think that this recipe is bland enough for the game to feel "solved," but that's not the case.  After having played over 50 games online and in person, I am still surprised by the creativity of some players.

The method of spreading disease has been perfectly implemented.  Reshuffling the discard pile onto the top of the Infection Deck after an epidemic does a wonderful job of making sick places...sicker.  You dread the "Draw 2 Player Cards" phase of your turn as you feel an epidemic lurking around the corner.  There is a sense of urgency to do as much as you can to knock down the "hot spots" before the next one strikes.  Two epidemics in rapid succession can be fatal.

The difficulty of the game can easily scale by adjusting the number of "Epidemic" cards in the Infection Deck.  Player-wise, the game doesn't scale as well: the 2 player game is almost too easy (even at "Hard" difficulty), the 3 player game is perfection, and the 4 player game is very difficult.  Hand management is the differentiator: in a 2p game, it is easier for one player to find a "cure" by collecting five cards of the same color, only four cards if you have the "Researcher" role.  In a 4p game the cards are spread out, and players have to use turns trying to pass cards between each other instead of treating infected cities.  Minus one point for this lack of scalability.  Interestingly, [thing=40849]the expansion's[/thing] introduction of a "Legendary" difficulty provides a solution.

Cooperative games resonate with me, because they offer me a chance to teach a game, and also try to win at the same time.  [i]Pandemic[/i] has a theme which allows for a streamlined rule set which also provides a compelling challenge.  You can even [url=http://www.brettspielwelt.de/Spiele/Pandemie/]play it online for free[/url].  Don't be inoculated by all of the hype: [i]Pandemic[/i] really is a game you should try.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
A couple comments on the components. The cubes and research stations are a little large. The cubes are easier to manage because there will never be more than three of one color at one city. However, if you get three cubes and three pawns and a research facility all in one city, spillover will occur. It isn't that big of a deal, but makes it kind of fiddly. The infection cards are black and I worry about them standing up to repeated playing. They certainly do look sharp though.

The infection / epidemic mechanic is interesting. There are a couple of threads discussing the details. By reading the rules, it does seem counter-intuitive, i.e. drawing off of the bottom during an epidemic. However, through playing it does make sense as this introduces a completely new city to contend with, along with intensifying the need to control the cities currently that have been infected.

A couple of thoughts.  First, this game is accessible to all. The rules are well-written, well-illustrated and don't leave many questions. For some, it may initially appear intimidating, but the system is very elegant. I also believe that being a cooperative game makes it less intimidating - everyone is working together. Second, I am wondering if three people is an optimum number. This gives three roles available in the game and doesn't dilute the player deck too much. Third, I can't see how you can win this game without the researcher. Every game I have played has included the researcher and that player has been the key to getting information to the right players. The medic is nice, but without the medic the strategy becomes controlling the cubes rather than eliminating them. The scientist can be helpful, but usually there are enough cards to pass around that one less isn't a deal breaker. The dispatcher, in my opinion, would be the second most important role. The operations expert is the weakest, and needs a secondary power such as immediately being able to move to any research station from any other city. Finally, the game isn't over until the final cure is reached. Games go from being won in two turns to being lost due to having no more cubes in stock due to outbreaks.

After a couple more plays I have increased my rating of this game. It is fun, and I enjoy playing it. In addition, my wife is already trying to figure out when the next time we will have people over so we can play. I reminded her that we can play with two, and she was ready to set the game up right then.

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is the only coop game I've ever played.  I never really saw the appeal of coop games until somebody brought this in to work.  After my first play through I knew I needed to buy it.

In Pandemic you and the other players are all trying to cure 4 diseases before they outbreak too much and just become unmanageable.  You will start with 9 random cities with disease cubes on them, the first 3 get 3 cubes, the next 3 get 2 cubes and the last 3 get 1 cube.  The world is grouped into 4 regions (denoted by colors) for each of the 4 diseases.  The starting cities get the color of disease cube for the color of city they are.

Each player now takes a special role that will help them specialize in things that will help out in the game.  Now the players need to build research stations, remove disease cubes, share knowledge, and eventually cure all 4 diseases.

The difficulty comes from the constant onslaught of disease cubes.  After each players' turn the next cities are flipped over and receive disease cubes.  If a city gets flipped over and it is already at 3 cubes it then outbreaks giving one cube to each city attached to it.  Throughout the player deck epidemics are included, as these come up you get a brand new city with 3 cubes.  In addition all those cities you've already been adding cubes to, yes those ones you've been removing cubes from as well, get shuffled and thrown right back on top to add even more cubes.

This is a rewarding game.  It is fun to work together and not have to come up with the strategy all by yourself.  It might be good to play the first few times with open hands, but I wouldn't do that for long.  It might be easier, but it seems like it turns into 1 or 2 people running the whole game.

I gave this a 7 because it is quick to play and offers a lot of tough decisions in that short amount of time.  If you lose, at least it was only 15 or 20 minutes so you can easily get in another game to try and win.  If playing with only 4 epidemics becomes to easy, just add one.  Once you get up to 6, which is the most for the base game, things get really tough, so you will never feel like this game is too easy.  I love this game and I am really looking forward to the expansion On the Brink.

textfield_comment_value:
This is an extremely well-designed game with a unique and clever theme that I just don't enjoy all that much.  It's absolutely worth playing if you like co-ops though, just because it's so dang smart.  

The best example of cleverness in this game is that, unlike in so many other co-ops, the bad stuff that happens to you is not [i]completely[/i] random.  After each epidemic, the cities that were infected last round get shuffled and placed on top of the deck.  This means that the same cities will be infected over and over again.  This not only makes the situation more desperate (building tension), but also means that you can really strategize around the cities that you [i]know[/i] will come up (just not exactly when).  Everything seems to be designed around these basic tenets of controlled randomness, building tension, and partial information.

Clearly, I respect this game a lot.  I just don't love it.  The biggest problem for me is an extremely petty one: I hate preparing the deck before each game--shuffling the cards, dealing out the hands, dividing the rest into little stacks, shuffling an epidemic card into each stack, and stacking them all on top of each other. Blah!  If someone else would take this job off my hands, I would like Pandemic much more.  This is evidenced by my greater like for Forbidden Island, which is very similar without the deck building business.

The second problem is that the game just feels "samey" after a while.  Everyone I've introduced it to loves this game, so we play it fairly often, and it just always feels very similar.  The consistency of the game is part of what makes the design so smart, but ultimately it hurts it a bit in my eyes.  You never play a game of Pandemic and say, HOLY CRAP THAT HAS NEVER HAPPENED BEFORE!!!  I'm hesitant to say this is because the game isn't random enough because it's true that you get fluky situations like 5-6 of your first cards all of one color (leading to a quick loss).  I think it has more to do with how constraining the game is in general, leaving not many opportunities for truly creative play by the players.

The expansion does help mix things up quite a bit, and it breathed a bit more life into Pandemic for me.  And of course, as I've already stressed (and is reflected in my score), I think Pandemic is a very smart game in a lot of ways.  I just don't have enough fun while playing it.

---

Update over a decade later: BGA has totally rejuvenated this for me. I play with a group that did two seasons of Pandemic Legacy together, and the vanilla game is still challenging and great fun. We play both async (strategizing in the chat) and occasionally synchronously with Zoom. Not having to prep the decks is also really nice!
