-----------------------------

[i]Pandemic[/i] is a co-operative game where the players are researchers from the Centre for Disease Control in Atlanta, and are attempting to contain the global outbreak of four deadly diseases before the world succumbs to the plague. The game supports 2-4 players, though there is a variant available for a Solitaire game. This game uses networks and a few new ingenious mechanisms to simulate the spread of disease across the globe.

In order to cure the diseases, the players need to collect sets of cards from a deck, and then turn these sets of cards in at research centres around the world. The caveat is that within the deck the players draw cards from, there are special epidemic cards, which intensify the situation on Earth, bringing the players one step closer to their destruction, of which there are three ways that it can happen. These are the players running out of cards to draw from, more than 8 outbreaks occurring, or if there is more disease on the globe than they can cope with, simulated by running out of cubes to put on the board for a specific colour of disease.

[i]Pandemic[/i] is a fun game because of the interaction between the players, and the ideas and discussion that is generated as each person decides what to do on their turn. There have been accusations of [i]Pandemic[/i] being a ‘puzzle’ rather than a game, and I agree, but it is seeing whether you can beat the puzzle with your wits that forms the heart of the game, rather than anything else.  [i]Pandemic[/i] can suffer from one person dominating the game, telling everyone what they should do, and this is a big problem, in fact, one of the main reasons why I do not rate it higher, as it can ruin the discussion that makes this game what it is. It is hard to enjoy yourself when someone, who is usually right, is dictating your every move.

In conclusion, [i]Pandemic[/i] is a game that includes many unique decisions and mechanisms within it, which give it a feel unlike any other game I have played. It is this that keeps me coming back to the game, as well as the immense replayability resulting from the different difficulty settings and variable player amounts. The only problem is the possible domination of the game by a single player, most often occurring with players of varied experience levels.

[b]Pros[/b]
- Variable difficulty levels
- Good interaction and discussion
- Requires good planning and co-ordination

[b]Cons[/b]
- Can be dominated by a single player
- Difficult to play with different expereince levels

textfield_comment_value:
Visual Appeal: (4)
The board and pieces look really nice and streamlined. I have the older version, and from what I have seen, the newer one looks a tad better. One pet peeve is that the map has cities in some odd places. I suppose it is just to fit the words and other graphics comfortably, so I can get over it.
 
Components: (5)
I am playing every game with the first expansion now, and it really enhances some of the components. I love the petri dishes and the smaller pawns are a sensible touch. Cards all feel nice and they aren't wearing too quickly. I like the tracks on the board because they're easy to read and access for all players.

Theme: (5)
Best part of the game is theme. Unlike other games whose theme could be considered nerdy or boring, this one stands out as a player magnet. I can also dig the more-equal-than-usual gender representation in the game. Welcome to the modern age, boardgames, where women do sciencey things too; they don't just pose in futile chain-mail bikinis! Getting back to the topic at hand, the game does a great job making you feel like you are cooperating to save the world from certain doom. Even the likelihood of failure is well simulated. In case you haven't played the game, that is a very HIGH likelihood on harder settings.

Learning: (4)
This is on the list of many people's gateway games. I believe it is rightly on that list because it is easy to learn and fairly low pressure. I mean, the game is hard, but you don't have to worry about experienced players laying the smackdown on you. In fact they will be helping you. Which means, only a short intro is needed before you can jump right in and learn through experiencing the game. Difficulty settings are really well balanced for the casual and hardcore players alike. 

Gameplay: (4)
I only say 4 due to the ever present Alpha Gamer problem in co-op games. Really if you feel the need to control everyone's actions, you shouldn't be playing this type of game, but it happens. Sharing cards is a challenge and provides players with good points of discussion on how to use their actions the most efficiently.

Overall Fun: (5)
This game has been a huge hit with even my non-gamer or casual gamer friends. It is low pressure enough that everyone feels comfortable jumping in. I always enjoy teaching it and watching the horror on new players' faces as the realize how tough some decisions actually can be and what sacrifices need to be made to save the world! This is my go-to Co-operative game without a doubt.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Don't even start with the Alpha-Player argument! 

As an Alpha,having played this game enough times to buy a replacement, don't be a schmuck-ask players questions,include players, and let players play.  By the 3rd game, most players have found their voice and have caught on to the game.  The only times I have ended up grossly Alpha-Playing is when I teach the game to a whole group of new players.  Don't do that.

The great thing about this coop game is that the randomness is predictable and risk assessment good.  At first, it seems like the cards are stacked against you; but as you master the game, you can make calculated risks and weigh your choices.  This means that your choice has value.  When we loose a game, I can generally point to a choice we made that didn't pan out during the game.  That makes me feel in-control; unlike Robinson Crusoe. Additionally, it is that weight and calculated risk that keeps good-players guessing, there is no standard tactic, obvious choice, or methodological mechanics that makes the game rote for good-players; unlike Castle Panic.  This means that every game is different enough so your choice has meaning and your decision will shape the game.  That is a difficult balance in coop games.

Suggestions for Alphas: 
1) Don't teach a whole group of newbies-they will all look to you for decisions, letting you play the game for them.
2) Introduce the game to a group with another player who has played the game.  Let that player go Alpha, you get to be the Obi-wan of the game and be a mentor.  Hint-Ask questions of the new players.
3) If you are introducing Pandemic, then just introduce to a single newbie.  Play the two player game, it will be quick and you can play again, and again, and again, until they really start grasping the game.
4) Don't be the Scientist, Researcher, or Medic; make the newbies be those characters.  These characters abilities directly affect the game and bring a sense of glory during a loosing game.  Contingency Planner is always a good character to take when teaching the game.  
5) Throw the first game.  If the group easily wins the game, then most players will dismiss Pandemic; probably because someone Alpha-played.  If you loose, those competitive players' aggression starts to come out, and then they want to beat the game.  With a bit wise mentoring, these players can encourage other players' voice.  By the end of the night, you got a group of coop gamers talking over each other. Just lovely.

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic pits the players against four diseases (blue, red, black and yellow) spreading over the world. The goal is to find cures for all four before time runs out, the diseases become too widely spread or too many outbreaks occur.

Players need to collect and discard sets of five cards of each different color, one set for each disease. Given that there are twelve cards of each color, a hand limit of seven cards and limitations of trading cards accumulating those cards can be tricky. The cards can also be discarded for faster travel and to build research stations which further reduces the available cards. Players start with four cards each in hand and draw another two from the player deck at the end of their turn. If a player has to draw cards and the player deck is empty, players lose.

The diseases spread each turn by drawing from an infection deck, placing more disease cubes on the map. If the infection cubes of any disease runs out, players lose. Infections can also lead to outbreaks, when a city that is already at three infection cubes is hit. No cube is added to the city, but all cities connected to is are infected, which can lead to chain reactions. If eight total outbreaks occur, players lose.

Apart from the city cards, the player deck also contains event cards that provide benefits to the players and epidemics (5 for a standard game). If an epidemic is drawn, the infection rate is increased, leading to more infection cards being drawn each round. Then an infection card is pulled from the bottom of the deck and infected with the maximum of three infection cubes. Lastly the infection discard pile is shuffled and placed back on top of the infection deck. This means cities already infected will be drawn again.

If the players on the other hand manages to clear all infection cubes of a cured disease, that disease is eradicated and cannot infect again.

The players have to weigh multiple priorities over the course of the game. Treating infected is important, but so is trading city cards between players. Should a player hold on to a card or use it to build a research station or travel by plane to a city threatening to outbreak? What color to hold on to?

Despite being a fairly simple game, it has enormous replay value. At the time of writing I have 77 logged plays and I'm still not tired of it.

Make sure to try it as soon as possible!
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Well we ended up playing this game 9 times in one setting!  There were four of us for the first 4 games or so then we ended up adding a fifth for the remaining games.  None of us had ever played it before.  The game overall is pretty easy to pick up...think I read the manual twice and had about 90% of the game down (looked over some subtle nuances). In terms of playing we went 0-9.  I think the first three maybe four tries everyone was really into it and having a good time.  After that though I think some of the guys started to get a little pissed off at the fact that they were getting their asses handed to them by the board game and insisted on playing another game to try and save a little pride.  In the end though our efforts were fruitless and the game prevailed everytime.

For me though overall I had a great time playing in all 9 games.  The game played out quick and rules were simple enough and you really believe the first few rounds that everything is good...or that you have a fighting chance.  But I will say things sprial out of control real quick.  

I strongly recommend that people new to the game play out the introductory lvl at least once if not a couple of times before progressing.  Part of our problem was that we progressed to the heroic after the first game and of course the heroic lvl is as advertised...quite diffcult!

On a final note this game probably won't make our weekly gaming rotation mostly due to the fact that it is a co-op game. textfield_comment_value:
Kurz: "Pandemie" soll ein kooperatives Spiel sein? Ist das überhaupt Thematisch?  ->Ich erinnere nur an 1,5m-Abstandsregeln, max. 2 Haushalte und Co.  ^^  ...Scherz beiseite. Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
I love the theme. I really feels like a race against time to eradicate nasty, flesh-eating, puking death before it consumes the world around you.
However- this game is a puzzle, and you have to play it cooperatively. That means it has two big strikes against it: 
1. Dominating players will end up telling you what to do.

2. They are frequently right.

There is usually "one best option" to take, and if you don't do it, or maybe you didn't see it at first, the game is OVER. 
It's just OVER, and it's suddenly your fault that Aunt Minnie in Chicago died on the toilet along with half the population of North America.

Similar to Castle Panic, Forbidden Desert, Defenders of the Realm, and other cooperative games -if you don't do the "next right thing," you're toast. Or in this case, a quivering, feces soiled, vomit-covered invalid who just lost the game for everyone because you wanted to take that flight to Buenos Aries to cure the black plague. Who knew the red Captain Tripps virus was about to break out in Moscow?
We knew, you moron. 
And you didn't listen to us.

Get out.

Okay, maybe we were harsh with you, but this game does create a real sense of tension, and when outbreaks occur you almost can hear the screaming humanity.
It's difficult to win, but early on, you will win a few times - mostly because you were playing it wrong.
That happens a lot. 
There are so many house rules for Pandemic, I'm sure Z-Man games is trying to come up with a vaccine for them. It can get a little "fiddly" especially if you forget your characters power, or don't follow the outbreak rules just right. Since it is very hard to win, I think that's where all the house rules pop up. This is often the first co-op game many new players experience, and the concept of losing as a team with the game lurching to sudden halt realy surprises them. Look at everyone's reaction on Will Wheaton's table top when they loose Pandemic. Look at Morgan Webb.  
Yes, let's do that for a while.
Mmmmm. Morgan Webb.

I'd like to buy the On the Brink expansion, but I just don't get to play this game enough to justify the expense. If this is the first game you use to expose your friends to co-operatives, then explain to them about the fun of playing without actually winning. 
It may go down as less of a bitter pill when they loose.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
(Since On the Brink feels basically mandatory, this review is for Pandemic with On the Brink within reach)

My opinion as a gamer:
Pandemic on easy (4 epidemics) and open hands feels very average -- the correct course of action seems obvious at all times. But the premise and art are solid, and it picks up dramatically with the variety that the On the Brink modules add. It's a lightweight gamer's game and serves as a decent gateway. It's easy to teach; it makes sense by the time everyone is done their first turn. It's got a compelling theme and nice pieces. The difficulty is adjustable. Since it's co-op, people with poor sportsmanship won't be sore losers. The game also (usually) runs less than 90 minutes no matter the player count. It's alright.

My opinion as a host:
Although I would rather play Pandemic than Ticket to Ride, I feel something is missing for the more casual audience this is geared towards. On the Brink modules never seem to be a hit with more casual groups. Pandemic in general also seems to take a long time to set up due to the sheer amount of shuffling and dealing and re-shuffling involved. The stock insert sucks and does almost nothing to aid setup. Casual players get easily disappointed by losing, which seems to keep happening at any difficulty above vanilla with four epidemics -- I will start introducing expansions on a Very Easy difficulty to avoid scaring people if this ever hits the table again. It's very easy for inexperienced people, on easy, not to cure enough diseases even if this is my singleminded focus of the group from minute 1 (without alpha-ing the group). The game also has way too much downtime as people repeatedly fumble around with cards and wait for others to move and optimize their turns.

I think that this is a good intro gamer game for gamers, but seems to be missing something that it needs to be a good gateway game for normal people.

As an aside: Pandemic's biggest problem for normal gamers is the alpha gamer (me, usually) who has to fight the urge to coordinate everyone, and On The Brink just lets you slam that player in the bio-terrorist bin where they can have fun being the villain in their own corner. This is a hilariously effective solution.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The basic story for the game is that you are scientists working for the CDC trying to cure four deadly diseases sweeping across the world. Failure results in global eradication of human population... so try not to fail.

At it's base it's a cooperative strategy game which plays out more as group puzzle solving. If you don't play well with others then you are going to want to keep moving. 

In Pandemic each player takes their own turn, what they do is ultimately their decision, but the nice part is that anyone can talk about what actions should be taken during each turn. It makes every turn a group discussion which adds a little length to the game but makes it a team effort. If you have a team working well you can knock out a game in about 45 minutes, but on the flip side it can take a full hour and a half if things aren't going smoothly within the group.

This game is difficult, no sugar coating, but it just makes the actual victories that much sweeter. The game does scale to player skill level so less experienced players can play an intro game and people well versed can play at settings that give the same feeling as the waiting room at your proctologist.

A downsides to the game is that it can lead to someone taking over as table captain. Occasionally someone will feel, for one reason or another, that they are the smartest and therefore their suggestions should be exactly what the entire group should do. My response to this is that the meek should speak up! Just about every school I've been to the teacher always said "There is no such thing as a stupid question" and in Pandemic that is absolutely applicable. Your idea might not be the greatest for the situation, but part of your idea might be useful. I've had many games where I thought A+B=C, then someone suggests A+D=F, to which we then come up with D+B=W... W for winning! Bottom line is you should voice your opinions. If you are a quiet talker then use your legs to kick people until you are heard out. 

Personally I love co-op games. I really enjoy seeing how other people are working on the same puzzle as opposed to how I am working it out. Pandemic scratches that itch to the point my leg involuntarily shakes.
Title: Pandemic

Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
It’s a solid cooperative game, and with an extremely simple set of rules it is a phenomenal gateway into more complex cooperative games.

Though, I feel, it suffers one of the many pitfalls of deck games - it is extremely swingy. Not even that it is too random per se, but rather the cards can literally be stacked against your favor. I found that most play throughs feel like a loss was predetermined, or a win was suspiciously ‘too easy.’ This is a difficult problem to come across in a game, because losses can feel unwarranted and wins do not feel victorious. It’s a tough critique for me to flesh out too - I don’t necessarily think the game’s best actions are too obvious (e.g. Forbidden Island), or that the best actions are too obscured, but rather that you feel like you can never do enough. 4 actions is surprisingly limiting, and pulling bad City cards is brutal, not to mention trading them is a nightmare.

Margins are thin in this game, and it makes the cooperative element less about ‘what can we do by coming together’ and more ‘what can we decide is best together’ - turns taken one at a time become a discussion of what’s the best course of action for a character, instead of a player coming to a conclusion on how to best help the team. This exacerbates the prior critique, that losses feel collectively unjustified, and wins feel collectively undignified.

That is the thrust of my critiques about the game - now for the positives. This game creates, holds, and builds tension excellently. Flipping over cards to reveal Epidemics is ominous and captures everyone’s attention. Reshuffling the infection deck and pulling and outbreak takes the game up a notch. Every game I have played, everyone is always zeroed in on the home stretch. The game is extremely collaborative, and the simplistic rules allow for all players to be engaged and involved in discussion without ever having to pull out a rulebook to better understand what’s going on.

The simplicity really is a marvel - just a glance at the board is all it takes to understand what’s going on. How to go about doing it is an entire other task, and is what makes the game a joy to play with friends.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
““Disease is the retribution of outraged nature.” -Hosea Ballou

I found it on the interweb (not verified). I had to look Hosea up but the quote captures the moment.

GAMEPLAY
A co-operative game where the players try to stop the spread of 4 deadly diseases across the globe in the largest cities in the world. On a player’s turn, you may move around the world, halt the spread of a disease or with gathered resources cure a disease. The game works against the players, but each has a special ability to help slow the spread of the disease, move around the board faster, or more quickly find cures. A common issue with co-op games is that they can really be played by a single person. This is a fair comment and I have played it solo several times, its tons of fun. If you are playing in a group make sure that there is not a single player directing everyone, try to allow each player to have space to decide how to play so that everyone stays engaged.
COMPONENTS
The most important game pieces are the infection cubes in four different colors. I was thinking that it would be cool to have microbes of different shapes but the cubes simplicity keeps the board well organized and a quick visual sweep of the board gives a clear understanding of the crisis. The cards and board are of good quality and the art is clear but not remarkable.
THEME
An excellent unique vision for a game. Cinematic gameplay. The first time I played with my brother it felt as though we were flying around the world to hold off the infectious threat. The tension builds throughout the game as outbreaks build. Every time I have played the outcome has been extremely close. This building tension is a credit to the game mechanics and how the theme integrates extremely well with the rules.
WHO IS IT FOR?
Casual, non-competitive play is found here. With the game rushing the players towards the inevitable doom of mankind, its fairly simple gameplay will be entertaining for most. I have played solo and its fun but its designed for 2 to 4 players. Games last about an hour. This game is not heavy and there is a small amount of determinism as the card stack can prevent victory but not too often.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Generally, I’m not a fan of cooperative games.  They strike me as less of a game and more of just an ‘activity’ to engage in with friends/co-players.  Its a case of, ‘let’s all get together to play a game of solitaire’ and Pandemic is no different.  I guess what makes Pandemic better than most cooperatives is that: it is, what it is, in its purist form with rules and mechanics that are fast, clean, straight-forward, intuitive and very streamlined.  
With an average game length of about one hour, I feel that’s about the right amount of time for a this game (as long as it doesn’t go over 60 minutes).  The game is essentially a puzzle, but even to the most experienced player, whether you win or lose is randomly pre-determined based on how the cards are, literally, stacked-against-you or for-you before the game begins.  
There are several options every round, but really there is always ONE option that is undeniably best and inevitably it’s the most experienced player that sees it (I’m sure even if he actively choose to hold back, it would be frustrating from his perspective and truthfully not really beneficial to winning the game in the end).  And thus, like most cooperative games, I don’t really feel I have any personal vested interest in the game and just want to sit back and let the alpha-player do his magic.  Thus the nature of cooperatives makes us ask, ‘do we fundamentally play games to win, or is it the game-play that is solely fun.’  If we play to win, then let the alpha-player take the lead.  If we play to enjoy the brain-burning aspect of figuring out a puzzle to best of our abilities, then best to play as a solitaire game (I’m sure it would be a frustrating time for the alpha-player to sit back and let players engage in less-efficient options).  
Perhaps this game really works best as a solitaire game (a field that I have zero interest in).  
Among cooperative games, I currently like 2010’s “Forbidden Island” best.  That game’s 30 minutes game time hits a perfect sweet-spot for these types of games/activities and the theme there is a bit more flavourful and imaginative to hold one’s attention.

[u]06-Feb-2013[/u]: I think this was the fist co-op game I played after getting into the hobby, and it has spiraled from there.  First, I do enjoy working together with the other players to defeat the game.  I don't have trouble with the "alpha player problem" since I only play with my family and, on the rare occasion, my two buddies.  Second, I enjoy the puzzle aspect of most co-op games.  That is something that attracts me in games.  And finally, and probably most importantly, I can play them solo controlling any number of players.

So, what about this one in particular?  I think it's fantastic.  I like the theme of fighting against ever spreading diseases around the world.  I like all of the various roles (especially when you include the On The Brink expansion).  The "AI deck" is a fantastic, and brutal, mechanism to play against as it continues to add more and more trouble on the map.  The replayability is very high, in my opinion, as the set up varies from game to game, roles mix and match in interesting ways, the difficulty level can be adjusted, and with On The Brink, three additional options can be added to the base set of rules to really liven things up.

I really can't say anything negative about this game.  However, I think you can give yourself help if you "count cards."  Personally, I don't do that.  Of course, I'll have a general idea of what may be coming up next, but I try not to memorize everything that has happened with the AI deck and what is still to come.  I like being surprised and that tension of not exactly knowing what will happen next.  Maybe that's just me.

[u]24-Jan-2014[/u]:  Man, I can't believe it's been six months since I've played this...what is wrong with me?  Such a great co-op game.  I still hold this one in high regard even though so many co-ops have arrived...and landed in my collection...since.  I would easily recommend this one to any gamer, new or otherwise, interested in a solid, challenging co-op experience.  Oh, and definitely pick up the first expansion for additional options and even more replayability.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
After all these years I'm still torn on my opinion of Pandemic.  On one hand I cannot like it that much as I've sought out many a replacement be it Defenders of the Realm or even something like Zombie State.  In the end though I've lost interest in those alternatives while still not disliking Pandemic.  I think perhaps my issue is in not having liked Pandemic quite enough to have explored the expansions to which I hear the On the Brink one can be considered quite essential.  Perhaps it didn't exist back when I played it with others who were far bigger fans (and perhaps we suffered too much from Alpha Gamers bossing us around at the time!).

I do know that the base game by itself I don't really prefer vs. Forbidden Desert which also has similar role cards and cooperative mechanics.  My wife also finds the theme of Pandemic very morbid while our son tolerates it when I explain it differently.  I do prefer certain things about Pandemic in the way outbreaks occur and are managed but, at least in the 3 player game, we've found it hard to eradicate a cured virus altogether such that it almost seems not worth the effort.

Overall I think there is now a permanent place for it in our collection though, along with Pandemic Lite (Forbidden Desert) and a Pandemic Thematic (Currently looking at Defenders of the Last Stand).  So I'm hoping to think more highly of Pandemic once I acquire some expansions and view it as more of an Advanced Game version.

Odd to find a place for 3 different versions of the same game in a collection when none of them are particularly my favorite but I guess over time the pandemic sort of gameplay has become not unlike worker placement or deck building or something like that which is easily something you'd have a few different versions of even if not quite your favorite thing.

I really like the new box cover art for the entire Pandemic series.  Nice job there.  The current editions bits looks really great as well and the card quality is perfect.  I think that might have helped my opinion of the game a little bit.

11/07/08: Tried a 5p game with 4 Epidemics. We won, pretty easily in fact. Also played 3p Heroic, and finished the game with all 4 diseases eradicated and not a single outbreak!

3/20/08: Played 2 games with 3 players on Heroic tonight, and it had a similar feel to 4 player Normal. I think I like it better with 3 players though, less waiting and fewer people to cause bickering.

3/17/08: Played 2 more 4p/Normal games, lost both soon before curing the 4th disease. Outbreak city!

3/15/08: We played x2 with 4 players on Heroic, and we got owned! Then we played 4 players on Normal and lost 1 turn from victory twice. Finally we played 3 player on Normal and won easily. I'm concerned about the percentage of games that are probably unwinnable from the outset, which I suspect is high with 4 players (especially on Heroic)

3/14/08: I've played about 4 times and have yet to really lose. This game seems kinda easy... maybe I'm just getting lucky. It seems like the game is either winnable or not from the outset, of course you don't know that. It could be the case that the game setup is simply unwinnable. I've not really lost yet, so I don't know how true that is.Pandemic is a very slick attempt at a cooperative game. The main problem with it isn't a problem with the game perse, it's a problem with the Genre. Some people complain that games like Race for the Galaxy are Multiplayer Solitaire... this game isn't Mulitplayer Solitaire, it's just Solitaire!All the cooperative games I can think of suffer from this same problem. One domineering, loud, or stubborn player basically plays everyone's hand. In fact, in order to maximize the chances of winning this is really the optimal strategy. Ideally, everyone collaborates to determine the best course for everyone, but that one loud guy can ruin the fun for the other players by saying "you do this, you do this, and you do this!" The best (or at least a sufficient) coarse of action can be easily constructed by any one person, there's no real need for collaborative input.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Pandemic is an excellent game that is worthy of shelf space for several reasons:
1) It's very different from the usual Euro.  Co-op play is such a different dynamic.  It is not one that I want all the time, but it offers a nice change of pace, and is also highly suitable for gaming with "non-gamers".
2) The theme is really, really well done.  And it's not set in Renaissance Europe.  Again, a nice change of pace.
3) Plays well with 2, and is, again, a great change from games in which you or your spouse have been a little bit dominant in recent times, leading to a blacklisting of said game.  Hypothetically speaking.
4) The game mechanics that you are playing against offer scaleable difficulty, and give a real challenge.  I think it's probably very difficult to design a game which will give a satisfying challenge to players of all skill levels, but Pandemic accomplishes this admirably.

Bottom line: It's Co-op.  This is good, and bad, but mainly, it's very different.  Pandemic is a really, really well done Co-op game.  If you never want to play cooperatively, this is not for you.  But, for most of us, Pandemic is a great option in many situations, and provides a welcome change of pace.

Expect games to go 30-45 minutes, with time decreasing with experience (and also when you get a brutal draw, and lose in the first three turns).  Replayability is very good.  Suitability for 2 players is high. 

Update: after 10 plays, I've upgraded my rating from 8 to 9: Always want to play.  This comes with something of an asterisk - I think there are many games I would pick over this, if it was just up to me, because I like competition more than co-op, and I prefer deeper games.  But, there are many situations where Pandemic is just the best game for the situation, because of the other players.  And, so far, this one has not worn out it's welcome.  So it's fair to say that, in those situations that call for a gateway game, or a co-op game, or a lighter game, I will always want to play Pandemic.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
Jogo bastante imersivo, onde as mecânicas casam perfeitamente bem com o tema. Doenças surgem inicialmente em algumas cidades pelo mundo e vão se espalhando pelas cidades vizinhas, e todos os jogadores, interpretando profissionais úteis de áreas diversas, precisam unir esforços para conter esse crescimento das doenças, que pode avançar de forma incrivelmente rápida, causando desespero, horror e caos em toda a humanidade. E se isso acontecer, seus esforços foram em vão e o jogo acabou para vocês. Lindo!

O tempo de partida respeita o que está escrito na caixa (45 min) e, contra intuitivamente ao que se espera dos jogos de tabuleiro, este jogo tende a ser ligeiramente mais longo com menos jogadores, De mesa cheia ficará dentro dos 45 min ou menos, e em dois jogadores pode chegar a 1h (máximo). Tudo isso independentemente de ganhar ou perder. O que também é incomum em jogos cooperativos.

Também é um jogo mais difícil de ganhar de mesa cheia. Não consigo ganhar nem com apenas quatro cartas de epidemia. Parece ser impossível ganhar esse jogo, mas adoro! E jogo sempre com rigor máximo nas regras, pois creio que isso é indispensável em um cooperativo. Possui bastante minúcias de regra: se você ganhou fácil uma partida de Pandemic, releia o manual, pois provavelmente errou alguma regra importante. Já jogo ele há quatro anos e até hoje nunca consegui ganhar em mais de dois jogadores.

Obra prima eterna.

textfield_comment_value:
My favorite board game of all time, not including one-time games like Pandemic Legacy or escape-room games.

The more you play, the more you realize how tight the game mechanics are.  All mechanics are very tightly intermeshed:  there's not an ounce of fat in there.  What gives the game so much replayability are all the different roles and events that you can randomly place into the game.  Therefore, I recommend getting all the expansions, including On the Brink, In the Lab, and State of Emergency, which all add new roles and events to the base game and give endless variety.

I've never played any of the expansion games except for In the Lab's "Lab Challenge" game, which is also excellent.

My favorite mode is solo, with three roles.  Since I like winning, I play "Intro" difficulty.  I feel adding more epidemic cards to the deck simply increases the randomness of the game.  I add my own goals to add spice to the game:  a favorite is attempting to eradicate all four diseases.

The Dispatcher role is hands-down the best; it may actually be a bit overpowered.  It synergizes extremely well with many other roles in the game, though my favorite is Dispatcher-Medic.

The app is also fantastic...I play it all the time, perhaps over 1000 times.  Sadly it doesn't include all the expansions, so you don't get access to all the roles and events.  Tip:  to speed up game setup in the app, tap the screen repeatedly.

A note on bling:
I love the Meeple Source meeples, including the "character germ set" and the character meeples.

Broken Token's "Biohazard Containment Unit" is very nice, but I wish they'd made the card area 1-2 mm wider to accommodate FFG-sleeved cards; FFG's sleeves are pretty large.

Update (2021):  They broke the mobile app, so to me it's basically unplayable.  Wish I could go back to the original version of the app.  The PC version is awful.

The physical board game is still just as good, though I got all the expansions just to get max variety of roles and events.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
The first co-op I truly, truly loved. The base game is a little easy unless you're playing on Hero (where luck is obviously the determining factor), but goddamn if this isn't a well-designed game.

First off, SAVING THE WORLD FROM DISEASE! is a fun theme that feels appropriately epic and heroic. Watching the board get overrun by disease and losing feels uniquely disappointing (I mean this as a positive).

Pandemic perfects the "randomized puzzle" style of co-ops for me. Sometimes I just want to try and solve a puzzle with my friends. Trying to figure out the best way to optimize your turns as a team is fun. There's heaps of tension, and the way Epidemics (specifically the Intensify step) works is just downright genius - allowing you to see how the game mitigates some luck and makes things even more scary in the process is just fantastic.

Some people hate on co-ops because they play with jerks who like to dictate everyone's turns for them. Pandemic is a game that certainly would allow you to do that, so if you play with jerks stay away. BUT even if you don't play with jerks... it is true that it is very, very difficult for someone new to the game/genre to play with an otherwise super experienced group. Even if your group allows everyone to vocalize their opinions, etc., it's hard for a newbie to contribute anything meaningful in a group of seasoned players and that can ruin the experience for them. For that reason, it's really best played with people of equal skill level.

Update: Upgraded this + OtB both for aesthetic purposes (I think we can all agree these blow the original out of the water under THAT criteria) but mostly to be compatible with In the Lab. Worth it!

Update: Years later, this is still my favorite co-op. Ghost Stories is pretty equally fun to base game Pandemic, but I have to give Pandemic the edge just on the basis of expansions - so far they've managed to release universally excellent expansions that only improve the base game.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
For how popular it is, I expected a little bit more, but Pandemic is an okay game that's worth owning if you don't have other co-op titles. 

Working together to figure out the best moves can be a lot of fun, but often leads to one person ordering the others around - not out of malice or anything, but whoever understands games the best naturally takes over and, even for them, it can feel tedious. So 3 of the party feel like they don't have agency, and the final person feels like they're doing all the work.

The admin is also legit over half the game. As in: you will spend more time flipping infection cards and placing cubes than you will spend actually taking your turn, which isn't a super big deal, but it does make the game feel like it's playing itself.

My final point of contention is this game is really hard to play consistently. What I mean is even after you understand the game and its strategies, you'll still feel helpless against the random system from time to time. Such as the bad luck of going to 1 place to stop the spread and then, while you're there, somewhere on the other side of the world gets dumped on by the infection deck and leads to a nearly unstoppable outbreak that you can't do much about. You simultaneously want everyone to spread out to deal with that stuff and all stay together so you can share knowledge and which is better to do at any point is totally up to chance.

I know I only said negative stuff, but that's because there is so much positive about the game I felt like it was more useful to point out its flaws. I do think Pandemic is a good game. It's good for family game nights since it's pretty simple to teach and play - it's rather lightweight. Playing something that won't leave anyone feeling sour with each other after a loss is also a plus. The flexible action system is fun to puzzle around as you try and optimize your turns to be as effective as possible. So while it may have some big flaws, it's still fun to play.
Title: Pandemic

textfield_comment_value:
[b] Logged plays split between base game and On the Brink expansion[/b]

Rated "8" after one solo play. Curious to see how this rating changes when playing with others. I lost first time through... this is harder than I expected! And, I found myself getting a little angry--in a good way. There's a pressure that develops to "beat the clock." As a true collaborative or solo game, it's more about puzzle solving than playing other players, but at the same time it's a pretty darn intriguing puzzle.

I like the challenge. But, if I keep losing and never win, I'll get angry--in a bad way!

Update: Yay! I finally beat it as a solo game. I can safely like this game now. The strategies are becoming more apparent. I'll be curious to see how many plays this game offers before it becomes a bit repetitive. That's certainly not the case yet.

Update after 25 plays: every play has been solo so far, and I still enjoy this. At some point, I might pick up the expansion to breathe more life into this, but this is much more mileage out of the game than I expected. If only every game held up for 25 plays!

Update: My 50th play, and it was the first time playing with other people. That's a bit tricky, as a pure cooperative game is hard to play if there is great disparity in people's familiarity with the game. I still had a good time, but 49 solo plays means that I have to restrain from bossing others around. Still, Pandemic is easily the only game I've enjoyed playing solo, and for that reason alone, I'm happy to own it.

Update: traded it away along with the expansion for Thebes. After 50 plays, I called it quits. This for me was a great solo game, but I never wanted to play it with a group because of the risk of the "bossing others" factor. It's still a solid game, and I certainly don't regret the purchase! If only every gamed yielded 50 quality plays. But now, I think it's time to "pay it forward."

textfield_comment_value:
My first expeience with a co-op game apart from Lord of the Rings, and I really enjoyed it. Rating is based on a single play and first impression. The game utilizes some very innovative mechanics, not the least of which is when the diseases "intensify" by reshuffling the discard deck and placing them back on top of the draw pile. This is an excellent and clever mechanic that had us scratching our heads at first, until the lightbulb of understanding shone upon us...

UPDATE: I've now played this lots of times, and my rating stands.  It is tense and enjoyable, even if fairly random. The intial placement of 3-cube diseases relative to the players' starting position in Atlanta can have a huge impact, as can the randomly selected player roles, when the first Epedemic card turns up, and when the special cards turn up (if they are near the bottom of the deck, they're not going to be of much help). Despite the random aspects, I still really enjoy it. I think it's one of the most innovative games in years.

textfield_comment_value:
Clever game that, oddly, is much more enjoyable when you lose or have a tough time winning.  There is the potential problem of the "best" or most experienced player kind of directing everyone else what to do in which case it puts a whole new spin on "multiplayer solitaire".  A good gaming group will find the right balance of interaction and personal decision though... at least in my experience.  

EDIT: Down a point over a decade later (during an actual Pandemic) due to other better co-op options including its own legacy versions.  I doubt I will play too much more, but an important game for sure and one I got a lot of enjoyment out of (especially legacy).

:thumbsup: [b]POSITIVE POINTS:[/b]

++ Excellent, medium-light weight strategic and tactical card drafting game, with smooth gameplay, with many paths to victory, and a light engine-building aspect to it.
++ Great scaling between all player counts, by adding more cards. The official "expert 2-players" variant works very well and makes the game more strategic in my opinion (but takes longer to play and affect the gameplay smoothness).
++ It's great that this game can accommodate up to 7 players (or even 8 players with the Cities expansion) and still plays quickly (without being a party game).
++ Great replayability from the variable card draft mechanism, the variable player's Wonder Board used (plus side used, A or B), the limited number of Guild used in the last Age (purple cards), the number of players and your neighbors strategy used during the games.
++ Great exemple of positive player interaction in the trading mechanism where a player can buy ressources to its neighbor for some money, but without depriving these from actual ressources.
++ Easy to teach, fast to set-up and fast to play (even at high player's count when players know how to play).
++ Great game insert which hold everything in an orderly fashion (base game and expansions, but to put everything in the core game box, you'll need to get rid of it unfortunately).
++ Great card graphic design, that is clean and clear.
++ There are expansions available for this game (which is useful to refresh the game when we have overplayed it).
++ The Leaders expansion really add a layer of depth and possible long-term strategy without adding bulk to the base game, as it's essentially just a pre-game draft (to choose our leaders) and then, just one more action per age to do (recruit a leader).
++ The Leaders expansion is also the best kind of expansion in the sense that you can easily decide to play with it (or not), with minimal setup and take-down time.
++ The Cities expansion add more interaction between all the players around the table (and not just your neighbors anymore) by including the black cards. This add a 7th round in each Age, which does add some variability to the game when you have played it a lot (This expansion is best with more players).


:thumbsdown: [b]NEGATIVE POINTS:[/b]

-- Take a lot of table space (beyond 5 players, a normal kitchen table may be not enough!).
-- The replayability in 2-players game can be a bit lower (for the base game only), but is still really high with expansions (especially Leaders).
-- Even though the official "expert 2-players" variant work well and is more strategic, it take longer to play it than a 3+ players game.
-- The components between the base game and the expansions (and between the expansions themselves) have slight color mismatch, thus it easy to know that some cards are from an expansion or not.
-- The real play time is longer than written on the box, more often than not, double the time at around 60 minutes per games.
-- It seems like the expansions are a bit expensive for what we get (especially the Wonder Pack), but if you really like the base game, they are still worth it.
-- Using the Cities expansion add a bit of setup time as we now need to include black cards equal to the number of players for each Age deck (which add to the Purple card setup of the base game).
-- Using the Cities expansion (and thus adding a 7th round) also lengthen the game, but this doesn't bother me much.

Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Kurzrezension:
"7 Wonders" ist wohl eines der ersten und eines der weit verbreiteten Draftingspiele in unserem Hobby. Schlicht und einfach die Weltwunder der Antike zu erschaffen ist das Ziel.

Spielablauf:
Alle Spieler spielen gleichzeitig. Sie erhalten je Zeitalter sieben Karten auf die Hand und wählen gleichzeitig eine davon aus. Sobald alle Spieler gewählt haben, wird simultan aufgedeckt und die Karteneffekte durchgeführt. Viele Karten verlangen eine oder mehrere bestimmte Ressourcen oder Geld, um ausgespielt werden zu können. Ausliegende Karten bringen den Spielern wiederum Ressourcen, Geld, militärische Stärke oder auch Siegpunkte am Ende des Spiels.
Nach dem Ausspielen der Karten werden die restlichen an die Sitznachbarn weitergereicht. Nun sucht sich jeder aus den verbleibenden Karten eine weitere aus, die dann wieder von allen gleichzeitig ausgespielt wird. Dies wiederholt sich sechsmal, wobei die Auswahl natürlich jedes Mal geringer wird.
Alternativ zum Ausspielen kann die gewählte Karte auch verdeckt als Fortschritt der individuellen Weltwunder der Spieler gespielt werden, wobei dann die Kosten des entsprechenden Bauabschnittes bezahlt werden müssen. Bei Geldmangel kann die Karte auch abgeworfen werden, um einfach drei Münzen zu erhalten.
Nach jedem Zeitalter vergleichen die Spieler ihre militärische Stärke mit ihren rechten und linken Nachbarn. Der jeweilige Sieger erhält Siegpunkte, die Verlierer Minuspunkte. Nach dem dritten Zeitalter werden alle gesammelten Punkte addiert und der Spieler mit dem höchsten Ergebnis gewinnt.

Meinung:
"7 Wonders" ist ein sehr einfaches Spiel, das flott gespielt werden kann. Der einfache Draftingmechanismus sorgt dafür, dass die Karten fairer unter den Spielern aufgeteilt werden und minimiert damit den Glücksfaktor. Die einfachen Regeln machen das Spiel zum perfekten Kennerspiel, für alle Spieler mit etwas Spielerfahrung. Außerdem kann das Spiel in jeder Spieleranzahl gespielt werden, ohne dass sich die Spieldauer signifikant erhöht, da alle Spieler gleichzeitig ihren Zug durchführen.
Was dem Spiel etwas im Wege steht, sind die teilweise schlecht zu interpretierenden Symbole. Gerade in den ersten Partien muss immer wieder die Anleitung zur Rate gezogen werden, da die Symbolsprache leider nicht eindeutig ist. Dieser Umstand wird mit den Erweiterungen natürlich nicht weniger, allerdings erweitert jede Einzelne das Grundspiel auf eine schlichte und sehr angenehme Art und Weise, sodass für jeden Spielertyp ein Modus zu finden ist. Mehr Führung, mehr Interaktionen zwischen allen Spielern oder einfach mehr Möglichkeiten, mit den eigenen Karten die Partie zu gestalten ist möglich.
"7 Wonders" macht aber auch bereits im Grundspiel sehr viel Spaß und ich bringe es immer wieder auf den Tisch, um Neulinge an Kennerspiele heranzuführen.

Erweiterungen:
Die "Leaders" Erweiterung führt eine weitere Draftrunde vor den Zeitaltern ein, in denen vier weiße Anführerkarten draftet werden. Nachdem alle Spieler ausgestattet sind, endet diese Phase und das Spiel verläuft über die normalen drei Zeitalter. Allerdings haben die Spieler nun die Möglichkeit zu Beginn jedes Zeitalters einen ihrer Anführer auszuspielen und so noch mehr Möglichkeiten zu erhalten, ihre Strategie zu steuern. Alternativ können Anführer natürlich auch dafür verwendet werden, Baufortschritte am Weltwunder zu machen oder Münzen zu erhalten.
Diese Erweiterung gibt den Spielern von Beginn an eine Strategie vor, welche sie verfolgen können. Dieser Effekt ist zwar nicht sonderlich stark, kann aber für den ein oder anderen zusätzlichen Punkt sorgen! Was wirklich stört, ist die Menge an neuen Symbolen. Nahezu jeder Anführer hat ein eigenes Symbol, welches gelernt werden muss, da es sich bedauerlicherweise nicht von selbst erklärt.
"Leaders" ist für mich eine gute, aber nicht unbedingt nötige Erweiterung.

Die "Citys" Erweiterung bringt 'kompetitive' Spielerinteraktion mit. Sie erlaubt außerdem das Spiel zu acht zu spielen. In der Spielvorbereitung werden in jeden Zeitalterstapel so viele schwarze Stadtkarten hineingemischt, wie Spieler teilnehmen. Diese Karten haben die unterschiedlichsten Effekte, die mit allen anderen Farben interagieren und teilweise auch weit entfernte Spieler beeinflussen. Die Effekte greifen Spieler an und können teilweise Karten zerstören. Daher ist diese Erweiterung für Spieler, die es eher friedlich wünschen, keine Empfehlung. Für alle, die sich nach mehr Interaktion zwischen allen Spielern sehnen, sind mit "Cities" gut beraten.

Die "Babel" Erweiterung erhöht die Spielerinteraktion auf ein unangenehmes Niveau. Sie führt allgemeingültige Regeländerungen ein, die für alle Spieler gelten, allerdings auch von allen Spielern immer und immer wieder geändert werden können. So können sich die Spieler nicht auf wenige gültige Regeln einstimmen und das macht das sonst sehr einfache Spiel unnötig kompliziert. Diese Erweiterung hat es nicht vollständig in die Neuauflage geschafft. Lediglich die guten Elemente sind in "Edifice" enthalten.

Die "Armada" Erweiterung erhöht ebenfalls die Interaktion aller Spieler. Hier werden - wie in der City Erweiterung - weitere Karten in die Zeitalter gemischt. Diese neuen Karten beziehen sich nun meist auf die vielen neuen Elemente, die diese Erweiterung mitbringt. Zum einen wären es die Armada Spielbretter für jeden Spieler, auf dem vier Schiffe unterschiedlicher Farbe am unteren Rand starten. Immer wenn eine bestimmte Kartenfarbe ausspielt wird, darf eine zusätzliche Ressource bezahlt werden, um mit dem entsprechenden Schiff voran zu rücken. Dabei erhält das rote Schiff Seemachtspunkte, die in Seeschlachten zwischen den Zeitaltern eingesetzt werden. Mit dem gelben Schiff wird Geld generiert, mit dem blauen zusätzliche Siegpunkte und mit dem grünen Schiff weitere Sonderkarten und Bonnies.
Diese Erweiterung "zwingt" die Spieler auf die verschiedenen Karten zu spielen und sich nicht zu spezialisieren, wie es in der "Leaders" Erweiterung funktioniert. "Armada" finde ich eine sehr gute Erweiterung, wenn schon einige Partien des Grundspiels gespielt wurden. Allerdings erhöht sie die Regelfülle und Spieldauer merklich.

Die "Edifice" Erweiterung bringt einen Teil der alten "Babel" Erweiterung zurück. Großprojekte in Form großer Karten werden in der Tischmitte ausgelegt. Die Spieler haben während den Runden die Möglichkeit, an diesen Großprojekten teilzuhaben. Werden diese abgeschlossen, erhalten alle Teilhabenden den angegebenen Bonus. Scheitert das Projekt, trifft jeden, die sich nicht beteiligte, der angegebene Malus.
Schlicht und unkompliziert fördert diese Erweiterung die Gesamtinteraktion aller Spieler, unabhängig ihres Sitzplatzes, was mir sehr gut gefällt. Durch die sehr einfachen Regeln kann diese Erweiterung selbst mit absoluten Neulingen sofort integriert werden. "Edifice" ist in meinen Augen die beste Erweiterung und das, obwohl ich "Babel" damals bei weitem als schlechteste empfand, die aber mit zusätzlichen Regeln - welche sich ständig änderten -schlicht zu viel von den Spielern verlangte. "Edifice" ist das perfekte Destillat daraus. Ich liebe sie!
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
[b]IF ALL THE CIVILIZATIONS DEPICTED IN THE GAME HAD BUILT THEIR EMPIRES AND LEFT THEIR MARKINGS ON THE HISTORY BOOKS THE SAME WAY THIS GAME UNFOLDS, I HARDLY BELIEVE THEY WOULD BE ONF ANY RELEVANCE TODAY[/b]

It is not usual for me to come across games I don’t like, for one reason or the other. If those games are about civilization building and historical elements, the probabilities of it not making the cut are astronomical. But then again, if it wasn’t for games like this, I wouldn’t like my historical and building games so much.

7 Wonders, despite the unjustified fuzz about it, is not a great game. In fact, I dare say it’s not even a good one at all. The whole drafting mechanics supporting it are clearly broken and tend to turn the game into an all-out mess on the table when experienced players play with beginners. But in the spirit of fairness, I must say that my experience with this may not be the best base for an objective verdict, especially because I learned to play it with another 6 guys at the table, with a friend of all of us explaining the game. From the get go, the game is clearly the most boring and chaotic experience ever when played with more than five players, maybe even more then four. However, that’s the closest I’ve been to actually playing the game, so writing about it from that perspective is the best one I have. Sadly, I don’t think I will ever play 7 Wonders again. *Sigh*

The draft mechanics are interesting and it was pretty simple for me to understand them since I am a rehabilitated Magic: The Gathering player. The only problem with this is that most of your game depends on the luck of the draw factor that comes with this type of games. If you need a certain card, there’s actually no real certainty that you’ll get it, because after drafting a card in each turn, players get to see what the others choose, so blocking choices for the other players, king-making decisions or radical changes in one’s own strategy (Which for me makes the game nothing but a “win some, lose most” ordeal) forced by not getting certain cards are way too common and frequent in a game that plays almost unnecessarily fast. There’s no actual strategy behind this game, only feeble tactics and very weak decisions.

Maybe with a lot less players, with some time to read the rules quietly and at least a few minutes to make a good, conscience decision on which card to choose and how to use it would make the game a lot more interesting and complex, but for now, I’m keeping away from that game. Too bad, especially because the arts and graphics are gorgeous and the whole them stroke my History buff nerve.

[b][i]I. Criteria[/i][/b]

Mechanics: :d10-5:
Design & Art: :d10-0:
Packing & Presentation: :d10-8:
Theme: :d10-9:
BGG Factor: :d10-8:

[b][i]II. Sliders[/i][/b]

Abstract [b]________[COLOR=#FF0000][9][/COLOR]_[/b] Themed: A Civilization building game based on the 7 Wonders of the Ancient World is definitely my kind of game and despite the fact that the cards in the game are useful for any player and civilization, the idea of all of those cards being so simple and basic are perfect for a game where the players vie for the best Wonder for their people, especially because most civilizations started pretty much in the same way.

Simple [b]___[COLOR=#FF0000][4][/COLOR]______[/b] Complex: When playing with faster players, more experienced ones or whatever, taking your time for each decision is impossible, so you tend to look for the “best” card you have at that moment, without considering if the card itself might help you with other projects or endeavors within your own personal board.

Strategic [b]_______[COLOR=#FF0000][8][/COLOR]__[/b] Tactical: Card-drafting games this quick and unstable are almost impossible to be thought of as “strategic”, since most of the decisions you have are limited by the hands you get from the other players and the previous cards you got on your board. Certainly, some long-term building or collecting could work just fine, but those possibilities are way to constricted by the low chances of getting the exact cards you need or want.

Luck [b]_[COLOR=#FF0000][2][/COLOR]________[/b] Skill: Skill on 7 Wonders is shown not in the cards you choose every time a new set is handed out, but how well you end up using them as a whole in the end. Meanwhile, the luck of the draw factor plays the most central role in this game, with the exception of the draw consists on a set of cards of which one must be chosen, the rest possibly handed out to be permanently lost. There is only an illusion of control in this game.

Fiddly [b]________[COLOR=#FF0000][9][/COLOR]_[/b] Elegant: Something worth mentioning is definitively the elegance of the rulebook and the rule set. The game plays smoothly and it’s almost never a necessity to have the rulebook close by to consult on this or that special rule. The very simple mechanics are very well exploited, and the rest depends on the player’s decisions.

Indirect interaction [b]______[COLOR=#FF0000][7][/COLOR]___[/b] Direct interaction: The military cards in the game are nice and it puts into the game the aggressive competitive element needed in all true civilization building games, which is the armed power. Some cards are better, some cards are cheaper, but it’s always fun to see the reaction on the other players when armies are way too big to be stopped. However, the idea of only being able to attack the players right next to you, makes the whole army side of the game a bit lame and boring, and way too limited in certain occasions. Also, the idea of needing sometimes the resources of your neighboring players is interesting and very adequate, but it happened pretty much the same as what goes on with the army cards.

Cutthroat [b]_______[COLOR=#FF0000][8][/COLOR]__[/b] Friendly: Playing to win, to be the best builder, to be the strongest general, to block other players decisions or just to collect certain cards or colors or whatever the players want at the time is possible, and I suppose it’s fun enough. Decisions in the game are the basis for everything, so playing like a dick just to annoy other players or playing on one’s own terms is just as good.

Heavy use of language [b]________[COLOR=#FF0000][9][/COLOR]_[/b] No language needed: The game is almost in all senses text-free and as mentioned above the elegance of it makes it almost completely unnecessary to reach for the rulebook every time a doubt shows up. Symbols and combinations of symbols are easier to understand and make the game somewhat faster and lighter.

[b][i]III. Number of players recommended[/i][/b]: 4.

[b]CHEERS![/b]
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
An interesting twist on "Screw your neighbor" or "Pass the Trash" poker games. You have seven cards, and after choosing one to play, you must pass the rest to your neighbor to your left (or right depending on the age). The only problem is that ALL of the cards are something you want! The problem is which one will maximize your production or points, while limiting the benefit(s) to your neighbor.

The mechanism is so absurdly simple, making for an extremely light game, or so I thought. There are agonizing decisions to be made with every card. Further, the cards you set up early in Age I will affect your ability to score points in Age III; there's plenty to lament on what you should have done or not!

My only quibble at first is that this game requires some memorization of the available cards in order to do well, similar to Glory to Rome. However, the learning curve is not as severe, as there is very little to read in terms of text on each card; the symbology is straight-forward and easier than Race for the Galaxy.

The game shines in the fact that it can scale up to seven, with no appreciable or proportional increase in downtime, finishing in 30-45 minutes. Card selection and play is simultaneous, so downtime is the relatively same whether there are two or seven people playing (well, there may be more of a chance of an AP-induced straggler with larger groups). Initial rating: '8'.

Update (10/02/11) 10+ plays: This game has definitely peaked. It's still not bad as a quick filler, but people are starting to grumble about the stale nature of the game--people have figured it out. Will an expansion help? I'm beginning to not care too much to get one. Also, teaching non-gamers may be a bit too much for their first game, so this is not as good a gateway game as I thought. I'm dropping this down from an '8' to a '7'.

Update (12/15/11) 19+ plays: I introduced this to my gaming club at work at the annual Xmas party to great success--everybody loved it. A hint to teaching larger groups: teach no more than 3 newbies at first, and then have them teach the next three newbies for a 7-player game (which is what happened). The drafting mechanic and card choices will require a lot of hand-holding for the first Age; having three "veterans" (each with one game under their belt) definitely helps to guide the new-newbies. 

I've concluded that the 7-player is totally chaotic: there just seems very little one can do to "steer" their destiny. It is also somewhat dependent on the left and right player/neighbor binding. Players that are new or inexperienced may not necessarily build optimally (for them), and indirectly may affect what I can build. There seems to be a coupling of what I can build relative to what resources my neighbors are building. If they don't build up, I spend actions building up resources and forgoing juicy victory point buildings. I can't quite articulate it, but something about the player binding really bothers me. I will need to play a number of times more to figure it out.

* * *

After reading the comments of users who rated this a '4' or below, I am beginning to understand the negativity. 7-player is a total crap shoot since you will never see the cards you've passed over. It is a much harder game to grasp for newbies, since they will not know or appreciate the interactions of the cards or the combos that are available.  It probably is a better game at 4-player, since some of the cards will cycle back to you, providing some strategic options, rather than solely tactical ones. The game has a rather short half-life. Still, it was a breath of fresh air when it came out, and one has to give it kudos for the amount of excitement it generated for it's ground-breaking design; it was a candle that burned brightly and quickly at both ends, and now it's time to move on....

Update (05/27/12) 34 plays: If there are 5-7 players, I will grudgingly play, if we are still waiting for more players to arrive. The game is no more than a social vehicle. I don't care anymore if I win or lose, because of the various issues raised earlier, as it just seems pointless to try. Dropping to a '6'.

Update (01/02/2015) 41 plays: Yes, it is fun to play once in awhile and agonize about the cards you want to play. Then, the randomness and chaotic nature of the game starts to seep in, and I see it for what it is. It is a great game in terms of game design, making it a good introduction away from the lighter gateways. However, for gamers looking for meatier play, it soon becomes like a meaningless exercise in futility. It is still a "6".

textfield_comment_value:
Heten játszottuk, ebből egyvalaki ismerte csak előzetesen a játékot. A szabályokat az első játék alatt teljesen sikerült megérteni, szóval könnyen tanulható. Ha a tanulást leszámítjuk, elég pörgős, gyors játék, szerintem nem nagyon lehet 3/4 óránál tovább elhúzni. Minden cselekedet párhuzamosan történik, emiatt egyáltalán nincs benne holtidő, amikor várni kellene a többi játékosra.

A játék alatt mindenki építgeti a saját csodáját, és ha nem lenne elég nyersanyag hozzá, a két szomszédos játékossal lehet kereskedni (ez a kereskedés nem igényel interakciót: egyszerűen odaadod neki a cucc árát, és ennyi (a nyersanyagok nem materializálódott formában léteznek), azaz ha valaki kereskedik veled, akkor ezt abból veszed észre, hogy odarak eléd néhány pénzérmét).
A többi játékossal való kapcsolat kimerül tehát a kereskedésben és abban, hogy próbálsz a lehetséges lapok közül olyat beépíteni a csodádba, amire vagy neked van nagy szükséged, vagy amire a melletted ülő játékosnak lenne, ám te éppen ezért elhasználod előle. A nem közvetlenül melletted ülőkre csak még közvetettebb módon lehet hatni: felhasználni olyan lapot, ami majd két vagy több kör múlva neki nagyon jól jönne... De ezzel nem nagyon foglalkozik szerintem senki, csak a közvetlen szomszédaival és önmagával.

Interaktív elem a játékban tehát alig akad, de mégis sokat kell figyelni a közvetlen szomszédok lépéseit, nem lehet csak magunkra figyelve játszani (vagyis lehet, de tuti nem fogunk nyerni).

Mikre kell figyelni?
1. A saját haderőmre a szomszédaiméhoz viszonyítva (ha erősebb vagyok, plusz pontot kapok, ha gyengébb, mínuszat).
2. A nyersanyagforrásaimra: szinte biztos, hogy legalább egyvalami hiányozni fog, amit a szomszédjaimtól kell majd beszereznem kereskedéssel. Érdemes tehát olyan nyersanyagforrásokat beépíteni a csodánkba, hogy a szomszédjainkéval együtt teljes legyen a paletta.
3. Figyelni kell a technikai mérföldkövekre: saját részre ugyanabból a típusból minél többet összegyűjteni, de a szomszédjaimnak minél kevesebb összegyűjtésére módot adni. Ennél a pontnál érdemes az összes játékos csodáját figyelemmel kísérni, hiszen láthatjuk, hogy az egyes technikai vívmánytípusokat hányan gyűjtik - ha sokan, inkább másik gyűjtésébe érdemes belekezdeni.
4. Sok speciális kártya is van, amik szintén a szomszédjaim lerakott lapjaitól függően juttatnak engem különböző előnyökhöz.

A játék nagyon sokrétű, ez a pontozásnál jól látszik. Mindenkit 6-7 szempont alapján pontozni kell, és e részpontok összege lesz az adott játékos végső pontszáma. Sok pontot lehet szerezni a technikai vívmányok összegyűjtéséből. Sokat ha a seregem nagyobb a szomszédaiménál. Sok összegyűlhet, ha közvetlenül győzelmi pontokat építek a csodámba. Ha a játék végén marad pénzem, az is pontot ér. A sok speciális lap is pontokat ér, a legkülönbözőbb dolgokért lehet velük pontokat szerezni. És akkor egy csomó minden van még, ami most épp nem jut eszembe...

Szóval gyakorlatilag bármit csinálok, pontokat fogok kapni érte. Ha sikerül jobb kombinációkat összehozni, az sok pontot ér.

A játékban a fő döntési helyzet az, hogy az adott körben a legfeljebb 7 lehetőség közül melyiket válasszam beépíteni a csodámba. Ez gyakran nagy dilemmát okoz. Egy kevésbé fontos másodlagos döntési helyzet pedig az, hogy ha mindkét szomszédommal tudok kereskedni, akkor melyiküket válasszam, azaz melyiküket erősítsem a pénzemmel. Egyéb döntési helyzet nincs, de az elsőként leírt tényleg súlyos döntés, hiszen azzal határozom meg, hogy mit csinálok az adott körben - el lehet rajta gondolkozni rendesen, és tipikus, hogy háromszor is meggondolja magát mindenki, miközben kiválasztja a lapot magának.

A játék szinte teljesen nyelvfüggetlen. Néhány csodához tartozik egy egymondatos speciális képesség, ami szövegesen van megfogalmazva, de ez egyáltalán nem okoz nehézséget. Minden mást szimbólumok jelölnek, amik kifejezetten könnyen megjegyezhetőek, egyszerűek. tehát egyedül a szabálykönyv elolvasása igényel nyelvtudást, a játékelemekre lehet mondani, hogy nem.

A játékélmény: pozitív. A főbb tapasztalataim: könnyen tanulható, gyors, folyamatos és valódi döntéseket igénylő játék (azaz nem csak báb a játékos, akinek mindig pontosan tudható, hogy mi az optimális lépése, hanem ténylegesen az ő kezében a döntés a jövőjéről). Tetszik, és akarok vele máskor is játszani! Úgy érzem a további játékok vele növelni fogják a rá adott pontszámomat.

textfield_comment_value:
7 Wonders, c’était un peu un jeu maudit. Je croise assez souvent Antoine Bauza, mais chaque fois que je lui avais demandé de me faire jouer à ce prototype dont j’entendais dire tellement de bien, il ne l’avait pas avec lui. Il m’a donc fallu attendre que le jeu sorte, et que l’éditeur m’en envoie gentiment une boite, pour que je puisse y jouer avec des amis.
7 Wonders est un jeu de cartes étonnant de subtilité, de rapidité et de fluidité. La mécanique de base du jeu, avec des cartes bâtiments produisant des ressources permettant de construire d’autres cartes bâtiments qui rapportent des points de victoire ou donnent des avantages particuliers, n’est pas vraiment nouvelle. Ce qui donne à 7 Wonders un feeling si particulier, c’est la manière dont cette structure classique est associée à un système de « draft », qui permet à tous les joueurs de jouer simultanément, les seules interactions, d’ailleurs très limitées, étant avec ses voisins immédiats de gauche et de droite.
Alors, bien sûr, c’est encore un jeu de cartes où l’on bâtit et développe son domaine chacun dans son coin, à la manière de Race for the Galaxy. De tous les jeux de ce type, 7 Wonders est cependant le plus rapide, le plus fluide, le plus léger, une partie durant rarement plus de quarante minutes, et ce quel que soit le nombre de joueurs puisque tous jouent simultanément. C’est d’ailleurs en partie le peu d’interaction entre les joueurs qui permet cette rapidité, évitant aux joueurs d’avoir à se préoccuper de ce qui se passe de l’autre côté de la table. Les stratégies sont relativement simples, le hasard assez présent dans la distribution des cartes, mais cela aussi contribue à dynamiser les parties.

Reste le gros défaut de ce jeu – un matériel qui ne donne vraiment pas envie de jouer. Je suis même allé vérifier au dos de la boite que c’était bien Miguel Coimbra, le talentueux illustrateur de Smallworld, Intrigo, Cyclades ou Battlelore qui avait commis cette couverture hideuse, et ces illustrations certes très léchées, mais sans charme ni personnalité. C’est dommage, pour un jeu qui méritait quelque chose de plus léger. Les cartes sont en outre particulièrement grandes, ce qui est assez inadapté pour un jeu qui prend énormément de place sur une table.

Novembre 2010
---
Antoine Bauza is a good friend, and I have playtested several of his many designs in progress, but I had never played 7 Wonders before it came out. Having heard that the game was a blast, I have asked him for it every time we met these last months, but he had always forgotten his prototype. SO I had to wait until the game was published and Repos Prod sent me copy which I played with friends in Avignon.
7 Wonders is a surprisingly subtle, fast paced and fluid card game. The basic game engine is nothing original, play building cards which produce resources which will be necessary to build more buildings which bring victory points or special abilities. What makes 7 Wonders different is the “draft” system used to deal these cards. It allows all players to play simultaneously, the only interactions being with one’s immediate left and right neighbor.
Of course, 7 Wonders is one more “building engine” card game in which each player develops his own domain without really considering what others are doing. But of all these games, it’s the fastest, the lightest, the most fluid, a game lasting about 40 minutes, no matter the number of players since all are playing simultaneously. The low interaction is largely the price to pay for this rapidity, since it makes irrelevant to look at what’s happening on the other end of the gaming table. There’s some luck in the dealing of the cards, but this also helps to make the game dynamic.

The only issue with 7 Wonders is the components. The box cover is so ugly that I had to double-check on its back to make sure the artist was the talented Michael Coimbra, who illustrated nice looking games such as Smallworld, Intrigo, Cyclades or Battlelore. The illustrations on the cards are not bad, but they are just bland, style-less. As for the cards, I still wonder why the publisher decided to make them so large when the game needs so much table place.

November 2010

textfield_comment_value:
Strategy vs luck: I think there's a good balance here.  There's definitely a lot of strategy, and the strategy involves what the people next to you are doing a lot, and what the general populous is doing as well (if everyone is going for green cards, then you should definitely not do that strategy, for instance).  But there's also quite a bit of luck, to the point that you can't be guaranteed that the best player always wins.  So I wish the strategy-to-luck ratio were a little bit higher...but hey, this is a gateway game to eurogames, so I don't really consider that a serious problem.  Just a quibble.

And then there's the best part of the game: the drafting mechanic.  It makes the game even more interactive because you're thinking about what you're going to give your opponents.  This might be the best game with the drafting mechanic although it's not the first.

There are multiple paths to victory, but I've noticed that a lot of the time, the person who won had to get VPs from almost every category to do so.  Not all the time though; I just witnessed a winner do it from basically only 3 categories.  So again, that's a quibble.

Replayability: good.  Even without the expansions I've played this many times and not had issue.  I can always go for different hybrid strategies and there are not only 7 wonders, but two sides to each wonder, which each play differently.  Combine that with the fact that I'm dealt different cards each round so no hand will ever be the same, and you have pretty high replayability.  There's also slightly different compositions of cards for different numbers of players.  

Now I will say, replayability isn't perfect because after all, you're pretty much always just building cards.  But that's where the expansions come in; I just played Babel and it's great.  It adds extra options for each turn and gives me a chance to add even more strategy to the mix.  

Are all the paths to victory balanced?  Well, sort of.  But again, it really matters on what people around you are doing.  You could waste a lot of turns on a war with your neighbor to have more red cards.  Or you could waste time doing green cards when other people are also doing them and decreasing what's available for you to score big.  So, while a couple of types of cards are oftentimes stronger, it's very situational, and I like that.  It basically means that this game doesn't have to worry about being extremely well-balanced.  (And from the best I can tell, they are fairly balanced btw.  Maybe reds are a little less than others.)

Theme: I feel the theme pretty strongly, mostly because of the art.  Every card has good art on it and your boards are really nice panoramas.  Now I will say, do all the mechanics necessarily fit thematically?  Such as the drafting mechanic?  No, not perfectly.  But the drafting mechanic is what makes this game great and I'm not sorry for it.  And then there's several other things that contribute to the theme, such as warring and trading with your neighbors, and each country/wonder being a little differentiated, and the global supply.  So I have no complaints on the theme.

Component quality: great.  The only thing that could be better is metal coins; but pretty much no games have those, and hey at least these look like coins even though they're cardboard.  The art is really beautiful too; one of the top 3 games I've ever seen in terms of art.  Overall, they paid attention to detail with these components and nothing seems crappy.

Length is great.  We oftentimes play in only an hour.  It's really impressive to pack an awesome euro-gateway-game in only an hour.  The game basically doesn't get any longer for having more players (unless multiple of them are newbies and you keep having to help them individually).  But even with noobs, it doesn't take more than about an hour.  This is amazing.

It does feel samey after a while without expansions, and the expansions haven't clicked for me yet.

Because this game is so well-rounded, and it is outstanding in the length category (can't think of any game with a lower length-to-strategy ratio), and because I only have 3 minor quibbles with the game, I rate this highly.
