Chaque joueur reçoit 5 cartes Leaders. Le draft se déroule comme L01 mais quand les joueurs reçoivent 2 cartes de leur voisin, il en choisissent une et la deuxième est défaussée (face cachée). Chaque joueur se retrouve donc avec 4 cartes Leaders pour débuter la partie.

Précision pour L02 et L03 : si vous jouez à 7 joueurs, vous avez besoin de 7 x 5 = 35 Leaders à distribuer sans compter les Leaders supplémentaires que nécessitent le plateau « Rome » et éventuellement le plateau « Bruxelles » (A) s’il est placé à côté de « Rome ». Pour éviter la pénurie, les Leaders défaussés lors du draft (L02 et L03) réintègrent la pioche et peuvent être réutilisés par « Rome » et « Bruxelles » durant la partie.

Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] With my recent Board Game Arena binge, I decided to give 7 Wonders a try again. I never really got to play this game much, and I had never been presented the opportunity to try it with expansions. This is a game that I had played a lot with a certain group regularly capable of getting 7 people to the table to play games with; for that reason, when I first played with them, I was never taught the rules properly and got completely lost in the iconography. 

Frankly, I really enjoy 7 Wonders! Unlike the simplicity of other games like Sushi Go, this game devolves into a series of micro-battles with clockwise and counter-clockwise neighbors, all the while battling your own accumulated collection of cards to try to eek out as much as you can for as long as you can (I LOST BY 1 COIN IN THE TIE-BREAKERRRRRR). Neglect specific resources and Round 3 of this game will present a lot of unfavorable options. Take no resource cost reduction cards and everything missing will cost a fortune. Going for a Victory Points-only strategy actually seems quite effective, until you, well, give every neighbor every card they need to succeed while starving yourself of almost every resource in the game. Same goes for Science - except those people are psychos (I kid). Neglect war (or only go for war) and potentially miss out on a ton of resources; go for war next to people hoarding science and VP and you'll basically win the game (no kidding). Also, no one keeps the last card in the draft; there is no such thing as a freebie here, sorry Sushi Go. Ever think you'll just... pay for a resource? Funny thing is, neither neighbor beside you has it either. Worst case, discard a card for 3 coins - hooray. Some games you'll be rich off players paying you dozens; the next you'll be the broke begger asking others "Hey, you have bricks, right?" Don't forget that a player with 20 coins will have no idea how to spend them, so just keep paying them off every chance you get - why bother bringing your other neighbor the chance to get back into the game?

Playing in person will likely remind me of how much of a fiddly mess this game can feel like, but this experience reminded me of the fun 7 Wonders can offer. It's one that's best played over multiple games - a loss is a loss, but there's always a new strategy to explore next time. Though 7 Wonders might as well be multiplayer solitaire, I believe the amount of unique obstacles each player ends up being faced with resulting from completely-diverging engines is what makes 7 Wonders a great drafting game. 

Although, seriously, people, if someone has no resource generation cards, has 3 commercial structures giving 1-cost resources, and has literally taken every green card in the game --- can we stop giving that person more science? I swear I practically lost 3 games in a row to exactly that happening. 

Finally. Finally! I won. Maybe 6, 7 games after being runner-up? It was a 5-player match: I managed to score 26 points off 6 VP cards, managed to win all buy 1 tie on war (because my neighbors had 0 and 1 war all game until the last round, straight neglecting it), and had 4+1+1 Scientific structures... all because I kept reaping the benefits of a Marketplace granting me 1-cost water??/purple??/scrolls?? with barely any other resources.

I adored 7 Wonders: Duel, and drafting games tended to be among some of my favorites. With the right group, I don't think I'd ever be opposed to playing it; however, I do believe there are other games I still prefer. That play was enough for me to (at least temporarily) take 7 Wonders off my "For Trade" pile. Hopefully the expansions will feel like they add to the experience.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Over time I have developed a healthy sceptical attitude towards eveything that gets hyped in an unnatural fashion; and when 7 Wonders fell victim to this ‘disease’ I decided to let the game be until I was able to give the game a go in a quiet setting. So I didn't try at during Spiel 2010, didn't purchase it there either. Without doubt it would be a reasonably nice game, but no more than that, really.

And 7 Wonders turned out to be that, with one or two things which make it stand out from the crowd. First it is very accessible. The main mechanism of passing cards around means you cannot plan very much, and instead have to make do with scavenging and hoping for the best. Ever since Notre Dame used a similar mechanism I've been of the opinion that this [i]doesn't[/i] promote player interaction: players just react to what they're given, build whatever is best to build (which sometimes is a guess), and from time to time take a look at their opponents when there is a [i]really[/i] good card in there. Second, 7 Wonders plays very well at high player numbers, although to be honest the design cheats to accomplish this: it simply limits interaction between players to the immediate neighbours on the left and right. (In other words, there's seven overlapping 3-player games played at the same time.) Still, in clubs and the like the tendency exists to put Citadels on the table when there's 6 or 7 players and there is demand for something quick: that Citadels is not conceived for so many people is besides the issue. Fortunately, that title can now retire in style as 7 Wonders fills the gap nicely.

Those are truly assets for the niche the game fits in. What remains is a simple collect-resources-and-transform-into-VP game with, entirely expected, multiple ways to victory. The basic structure is very simple (as expected again, because of the ease with which you play as a newcomer); on the other hand, it leaves very much open the question what remains of the game when played more than a few dozen times. 7 Wonders is very tactical in nature, and the decision space limited: those are not assets for an extensive longevity. So while I can understand [i]some[/i] of the attention the game is getting, I certainly don't understand this sort of chivalric romanticism:[q="Greg Schloesser"]7 Wonders is an amazing design. There aren't many games that can pack this much tension, decisions and strategy options in a 30 - 45 minute time frame, while accommodating up to seven players. The game seems to have all the elements to give in great longevity in a hobby where most games fade to obscurity after just a few years. It also has all of the elements that should make it a front-runner to capture industry awards such as the Spiel des Jahre and International Gamers Award. Although this is a year wherein there have been numerous promising games published, 7 Wonders seems destined to rise to the top.[/q]There is, however, a genuine mystery surrounding this game: why on Earth gamers were willing to spend €40 on a box containing 7 small player boards, simple wooden discs, some simple cardboard chits, and about 4 packets' worth of playing cards. My suggestion would be to wait until the game takes on a much fairer price of approximately €25—and for that, the game's rating is lowered by 1 point.

[b]Update[/b] I don't really notice the difference when playing with 3. There is a tad more control over what gets played by whom, but not enough to up or lower the rate I've given the game. It remains friendly material, and it beats Citadels... But I won't purchase it myself.

[b]Update 2[/b] That 'owned' flag is not me. It's my partner, you understand.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Quite a few reviews compare this game with Dominion and Race for the Galaxy, but, as a regular player of both, 7 Wonders doesn't play at all like the two. I suppose that, since 7 Wonders has cards which you pick, that makes 7 Wonders similar to both Race and Dominion. Which, in my opinion, it does not. Eurogamers should like 7 Wonders, but, as an erstwhile non-drafting CCG player, I found this game as generic as any other Eurogame (cards and boards have good art, though). The drafting pretty much tweaks the usual tired "multiple paths to victory" Eurogame mechanic. Drafting *does* require you deny cards the player you will pass card on to, but I'm pretty "meh" on this mechanic. As with other "multiple paths to victory" Eurogames, you'll need to "become familiar with" (aka. memorize) the cards -- not to mention scoring system -- a Eurogame tendency which pretty much negates the selling point of the simplicity of the game mechanics. If you're looking for a Eurogame with another novel mechanic (by Eurostandards, at least), I guess this is it. But if 7 Wonders is comparable to Dominion, both are just like Risk.

****

Beats me.

See, I just played it yesterday. And I hated it. The draft mechanic doesn't make the tired old "multiple paths to victory" Euromechanic any better. As for "filler", the game just took too d*mn long for what you did: pick a card and pass the rest along. 

I don't think the game's overrated at all. I *know* many BGG'ers love the "multiple paths" mechanic. I find it all too much to memorize, since you have to [-]memorize[/-] be familiar with the scoring system *and* the card distribution in the deck *and* the cards themselves. Which I find to be a PITA. Drafting, meanwhile, is a new mechanic to the Eurocrowd. Fairy Tales does it, but FT didn't add the "multiple paths" mechanic. 

Eurogamers *should* try this game. I'm not a Eurogamer, so don't have any interest in playing this again.

***

Didn't like 7 Wonders at all:
* Scales terribly with 7 players. You get a new hand of cards each turn, so it's like trying to put a strategy onto a pile of random cards.
* Turns are fast only if you know what you're doing, which means you must know the cards in the deck (assuming you want to win).
* With 7 players, you're mostly denying the next player an optimal move. Passive aggression at its finest.
* Player socialization is limited to looking over your neighbor's shoulder to look at his cards, or passing him a better hand if he or she is you non-gaming spouse.
* Yet another arbitrary "multiple paths to victory" scoring system.

We played a game of seven players, two with some experience. I think I came in second or third, with the winning player and myself saying we wouldn't play the game again.

Citadels: Deduction and outguessing. With bursts of smack talk.
7 Wonders: Deny your opponent an optimal card. Repeat until done.

I probably *would* play 7 Wonders two-player. In two-player, you will receive back the hand you passed to your opponent, so you can do some planning. Also, my two-player CCG opponent would give me the time to AP out a turn.

****

Main problems about the game for the non-gamers:

* Hidden information. *Some* non-gamers don't like the "emotional" conflict of revealing information to a more experienced player (ie. you) while not understanding the cards.

* Icons. Icons are essentially a different language. Yes, I'd like to play my games in Swahili.

That's obviously why Race for the Galaxy isn't a gateway game, while the "other" role selection game, Puerto Rico (sometimes) is.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
I enjoyed 7 Wonders, and if you are a fan of the new wave of euro engine card games (Race for the Galaxy, Dominion and it’s imitators) I would strongly recommend that you try it out. While direct comparisons to those other games are superficial, there’s no denying that it’s becoming a genre.

The main draw is the drafting mechanic. While it’s as old as Magic: the Gathering booster drafts (about 15 years), it hasn’t been heavily explored yet–Fairy Tale is about the only other major game to try it out. It has the virtue of keeping the game moving at a decent pace (everything in 7 Wonders is keyed off what card you draft, including a couple of “pass” actions which require discarding a card). While things can seize up with players who are unfamiliar with the cards (my game was one veteran and five newbies), and experienced group should finish a game in 20-25 minutes, probably faster with a smaller group.

As much as I enjoy 7 Wonders (and I do – I will happily play it again soon), it’s a little hard as a fan of rich, meaty euros not to notice a couple of places where 7 Wonders could have been more interesting. The resource mechanism is a bit dull – it promotes some player interaction and keeps the rules density low, but the decisions are rarely tense. Either your neighbour has what you need or she doesn’t. Frankly, this is a problem with most post-Caylus cube-pushers (7W doesn’t use cubes, but the feel is similar), so it’s hardly fair to single out 7 Wonders, but a problem is a problem.

Also, the elements – military, economic, science, monuments/structures – are distinct silos. With one notable exception, there are no instances where building up your science helps your military or improving your economic power (beyond basic resource production) makes scientific progress more efficient. In some cases, playing a card will let you play a card from another silo for free later, which is a nice touch, but it only comes up if you see the relevant card and if playing it will help you out more than the other cards you have to choose from at the time.

Finally, it’s weird that the purple guild cards – analogous to 10-cost buildings in Puerto Rico or 6-cost developments in Race for the Galaxy – score points based on your neighbours’ position. It creates an incentive for your right-hand neighbour to take a different path than your left-hand neighbour, but the main effect is to give you much less control over which guilds are useful to you. It’s bizarre that the capstones of your game have nothing to do with what you’ve played up until now.

Nevertheless, these are quibbles. The card drafting is fun, that game’s arc is a little forced, but reasonable for a short card game and once you know the cards better, the game will go quickly. Like the start worlds in Race for the Galaxy, the different powers of the different wonders will help to keep the game from feeling *too* much alike from play to play. Unless you are completely europhobic, it’s certainly worth trying out. It may not be every gamer’s cup of tea, but the overhead for trying it out is low.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
[b]Taylor's 100-point rating: [/b]

[b]Enjoyment - 15/20[/b] - This game gets put in a similar category, for me, as Settlers of Catan. I call these games "Gateway Board Games", because similar to "Gateway Drugs" these are the types of board games that a non-board gamer would dip their feet into before getting into really big and heavy games. With that said, the game is very fun, although it is somewhat simplistic in nature. My favorite thing about this game is it's my only non-party game that can play up to 7 players.

[b]Replayability - 13/15[/b] - This game has great, natural, replayability. You can play as 1 of the 7 different wonders, which will give you a different strategy/outlook, and the cards that are passed to you will be different every game, so you'll never play 2 of the exact same game. The reason this didn't receive a perfect score is although it does have some good replayability for the most part, it can still feel very similar game to game.

[b]Game Mechanics - 8/15[/b] - The game mechanics are fun and interesting, but to my taste, lacks some depth. The draft and pass mechanic are fun, but a little overplayed at this point, and the way you score points is fun and diverse enough to add replayability, but there's just something more that I wish was there... and I can't put my finger on it.

[b]Theme/Artwork - 12/15[/b] - It's fun playing with the different wonders of the world, and the card artwork is really good, considering the game came out in 2010. With all that said the game mechanics don't seem to fit the theme as well as I would like, and the artwork, although good, doesn't blow me away.

[b]Gameflow/Pace - 10/10[/b] - These next few categories are where this game will really start to rack up some points, and these next few categories are the reason I recommend this game to people and still play it a fair amount. The game is very quick with little to no downtime and a game can realistically be finished in 30 minutes.

[b]Flexibility - 10/10[/b] - The only knock I can make about the flexibility of this game is the fact that it can't be played solo and is lack luster at 2 players. With that said, it felt wrong to not give this game a perfect score, seeing as it's my only non-party game that can play up to SEVEN players!

[b]Production - 5/5[/b] - I've had, and played, this game for a while and it's kept in good condition. The cards are high quality, and the same with the boards.

[b]Effort To Play - 2/5[/b] - This game is really easy to get off the shelf. It's a very fast setup, and very quick take down as well. It's also especially easy to play seeing as it can be played on so many different player counts.

[b]Accessibility - 2/5[/b] - Like I mentioned before, this game is relatively simplistic and is pretty easy to learn how to play. I would recommend this to even the most inexperienced of gamers.
[b]Total Score: 82/100[/b]

Here's my ratings reference if you want to know what each metric means to me:

Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
7 Wonders is a very 'attractive' game for a variety of reasons. The symbology gives an appearance of complexity, depth and 'geek cred', the game has at least the impression of 'building a civilization', there are unique 'powers' (civilizations) to play with, and it accommodates up to seven players in roughly the same amount of time (which, admittedly, is pretty impressive). Of course, everything comes with a cost, and 7 Wonders is no exception. 

In 7 Wonders' case, the downside comes mainly in the form of [i]interaction[/i] -- or more accurately, the lack thereof. It is difficult to imagine why I would want to play a game with six other players when I only have the ability to interact with the two players adjacent to me. And that interaction is often overly subtle for my tastes. Burying a card in your Wonder to deny it to an opponent is a good strategic play, but it happens so quietly that it simply isn't [i]fun[/i]. And when the player count is >4, any ability to play strategically is also dramatically reduced, making each decision less meaningful.

Furthermore, every decision in 7 Wonders feels essentially the same and [i]feels like it carries the same weight[/i]. It is exceedingly rare, if it ever happens at all, that a turn poses a very difficult, fun decision -- a problem which is exacerbated when the player count reduces the ability to play with any semblance of strategy. Some games offer limited victory points, while others are classified as 'victory point buffet' games. 7 Wonders is an 'action buffet' game -- except all of the courses are the same. Compare this to Settlers of Catan, which offers the same choices every turn, but adds [i]noticeable tension[/i] because you are trying to make that key trade with another player that will help you advance your game. In 7 Wonders, your opponent just silently hands you some cards with an implied "Eh, just take one. I may have taken the one you need, but you'll never even know until the end."

Like Agricola, scoring is also a huge letdown, and is quite anticlimactic. Surely a ~30-minute game could have employed a scoring system that doesn't require a pencil-and-paper version of Excel. The scoring is balanced (perhaps overly so, to the point of being artificial), but uninspired and negative fun.

[url=http://boardgamegeek.com/thread/811970/theres-gotta-be-a-better-way]This review[/url] is an excellent summary of much of my feelings about 7 Wonders: [i][7 Wonders] fills a need that it had to create. ... Nothing about 7 Wonders serves any reasonable game function. Instead of a fun social experience, it offers a way to sit around a table of seven people and never have to speak to them. I can live with that in a game with fewer people, or a game that just felt more satisfying.[/i]

I don't mind playing 7 Wonders a bit, but I don't enjoy it as much as other games, and don't consider it to be nearly as good of a game as it gets credit for.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
7 Wonders is fun and deserved of the hype for the most part.  It is an easy to teach and learn game that can accommodate up to seven players and it does this with little down time.  I rate it a 7 because of these things.  It is only a 7 however because of a few issues I have.   (My 2 plays were both 7 player games)  The card drafting mechanic was intriguing at first, and offers a meager attempt at player interaction, but it only exacerbates the inherent randomness of the game and it reduces the strategy to almost nil by only allowing short tern tactical planning.  

In the two games I played, during the third age every player immediately played the guild card if they were dealt one.  They are inevitably worth a decent amount of VP's and which one(s) you get to play is totally random.  There is no strategy in "play the purple card if you get one".   The green science cards are like a siren's song; the set collection seems like a good idea, but the payout is not enough.  It is easy to block by your opponents and you need too many cards to score enough to be worth more than the blue VP cards.  For example, in one game I collected a set of four of one type squared, that's 16 points, and then one of each of the 3, for 7 points.   So I invested 6 cards for a total of 23 VP's (not a good ratio in this game) and it would have been easy for my opponent to have buried the last card of the set, if he would have done that, I would have scored only 16 points for 5 cards.  Military is simply unbalancing in a 7 player game.  In both games I played, the winner had a mere one or two military cards played, but gained a significant amount of points because the person to the right or left chose not to play military; while the players on the other side of the table each escalated their military, causing a lot of investment with little or no payout. You see, it is almost a given that one player grabs a significant lead in military.  Let us say the player to his left decides, I can't compete with that, I will let him win military and I will concentrate my plays on VP's hopefully out gaining him in that manner.  But this allows the sneaky player to his left to play one military and gain the military points.   So it is the player two chairs away (or across the table) that gains the benefit of someone that invest heavily in Military.  

Most of my faults above would seem to lessen in a game with less players; you would be able to have more choice on Guild cards, you would be closer to the other players for military, you would see science cards more than once and it would be harder for them all to be buried.  So my score of a "7" is only for the 7 player game, I am interested to see if I am right and it is better with fewer players.  All in all it is a 7 as a 7 player game for me.  With its flaws it is deserved due to the easy of play the low downtime and the ability to engage 7 people at one time.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Euro to the core.  It is an optimization exercise that is prevalent in the genre.  You are trying balance a whole lot of doo-hickies:  some give you instant gratification (victory points) while others get you nothing now, but may get you more future gratification (bigger victory points).  Some doo-hickies in combination won't score you VPs until the end of the game, while others keep you from losing VPs during the course of the game.  If you overload in one area, you lose, so you have to balance and optimize.  (I asked on more than one occasion, "Are you SURE Knizia didn't design this?")  It's a common mechanic, but by selecting a card to play from a hand of cards and passing the rest around can keep cards out of the hands of those who may benefit more from them.  It is like [thing=13823][/thing] with more doo-hickies and a [thing=12][/thing]-like scoring system.

If you flip for Euros, you probably own it, and if you don't and this type of optimizing/puzzle-solving is your thing, then why heck don't you already own this?  Don't you know this won a whole bunch of awards that I cannot even pronounce?  

If this isn't your thing, then run far and fast.  Me?  I'm indifferent.  I like optimization puzzles for a couple of tries, but they get old pretty quickly (which is why I'm happy to let others buy them and play their copies).  I'll play it, and for a short filler for 3, I may even [i]recommend[/i] it, but it's not one that I would run out and buy, nor is it one that I'm going to center my game-playing night around ("Sorry, I can't play [thing=91][/thing] right now.  I've been waiting all night to get into this game of 7 Wonders.  Can I take a rain check?")

But in defense of it, it's one of the better Euros that I don't own and maybe the best 3+ player Euro that plays in about 20 minutes.  It's not worthy of "game of the year" hype, since it's really just another Euro, but folks who vote on this probably never played anything but Euros.  For instance, I watched the BGG-produced video in which the lady said, "Don't be intimidated by the complexity."  10 minutes later, when I finally stopped laughing, I commented that she's obviously never played a wargame or anything by Fantasy Flight.  Hint: it ain't complicated. As a matter of fact, it's greatest charm is the combination of its simplicity, it plays in less than 15 minutes, has more choices in it than its peers, and that after about 5 games you should be ready to play with anybody, and because of that, I kind of like it: it's a filler that doesn't [i]feel[/i] like a filler.

If I were rating it against other Euros, it would probably be an 8, but compared to a world of awesome wargames and Ameri-Trash, it gets a 6, but that's how I roll.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
The game's simplicity belies the strategies and decisions that are present.  Players must make decisions as to which cards they seek to construct, realizing that by concentrating on a few categories they will likely be forced to neglect other categories, most likely to their detriment.  Further, this decision is influenced by the strategies being pursued by one's neighbors.  It is also wise to keep an eye on what resources your neighbors are producing -- and what they are not producing -- so you can plan accordingly.  

Choosing which card to keep can be tough, as there are usually multiple cards that are beneficial and fit your strategy.  Plus, the knowledge that you will be passing a desirable card or two to your neighbor is troubling.  Sometimes a card would be so valuable to your neighbor that you opt to keep it instead of a different card that you coveted more.  While these decisions are angst-inducing, their resolution is generally quick, so the game moves along at a brisk pace.

For me, the only knock against the game is that you can only significantly influence and be influenced by the players to your immediate right and left.  You have little real influence on the remaining players and, indeed, may not even be able to see what they are collecting.  Since you are not concerned with these other players, however, it does have the benefit of keeping the game moving along as there is little need to assess their holdings.  

This drawback, however, pales in comparison to the excitement and brilliance of the game.  There is a persistent tension of trying to collect the cards you desire.  Yes, much of this is dependent upon the cards you are passed, but everyone is forced to pass along valuable cards.  So, the odds are good you will be receiving cards that are beneficial.  It is fun and challenging to construct a set of cards that enable you to construct more valuable and beneficial cards as the game progresses.  It is not exactly an "engine building" game, but it has some of the elements.  

7 Wonders is an amazing design.  There aren't many games that can pack this much tension, decisions and strategy options in a 30 - 45 minute time frame, while accommodating up to seven players.  The game seems to have all the elements to give in great longevity in a hobby where most games fade to obscurity after just a few years.  It also has all of the elements that should make it a front-runner to capture industry awards such as the Spiel des Jahre and International Gamers Award.  Although this is a year wherein there have been numerous promising games published, 7 Wonders seems destined to rise to the top.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
I love this game, but I really wish military focused games weren't so stronger than science focused games. Science is, unfortunately, inconsistent to follow as your main strat! I just use it in ancillary manner, for 10 points, usually. Of course blue cards are good, but a lot of the time they do not offer a follow up path, so I don't rely on them as much as other players (only run heavy blue centric strats on occasion). In this game playing "balanced" colors kinda works (mostly), and memorizing is a somewhat big deal (which I should practice more online, to be honest, but I usually do not bother).

Update: While I still think Sci is ancillary, in 3p settings it is a lot easier to do it (getting ~26 is way easier there). I still think mil is essential (in 3p less so, but you are actually focusing on not being behind in 3p, since luck is bigger and you won't win all mil matches). I think I dropped mil only once in my Arena games (for a blue-sci mix win), but only because people around me played mil to their detriment for some odd reason.

IMO, that's a design flaw.

OK, if you drop more than 5 military card you might be in trouble, but otherwise, there are very small amount of situations in which you don't want to drop mil and blue as your whole game - usually the situations are "start with wonders with grey resources", in which case the ancillary Sci strat pays up, since you can have a pretty easy "drop 3 cards for 10 points" style of play, since you need only 1 other grey, and can drop the last card to complete a horizontal set basically whenever you want. So the game basically is a juggle of blue against red, with circumstantial yellow for money (and usually not a lot in the first round, since everybody hunts the 5 coin card and very few people value - the better - Vineyard for some odd reason), denying green to the brave souls trying Sci (should they try their second set, since rarely they'll get to their third), and trying to get the lucky purple (you'll always drop a purple, but not always a lucky one).

This is why I kinda like the 2p version of the game: it is a lot closer to perfect information, and makes thing go more smoothly strategy wise (and, IMO, it is a better arena format all things considered).

About wonders: I also think they are a bit unbalanced. For instance Halicarnasus has such a strong power in the B side there is almost no situation you want to use their A side. Rhodes is a lot harder to play than the other wonders. Alexandria is inconsistent (but the B - stronger - side can have very amazing, crushing games). Babylon is just a bit too weak (because science is weak)... Etc.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
This game is all about "drafting." If you don't know what that is, then think of a large family gathered around the dinner table. 
Dad takes a plate of assorted meats, and picks out the particular cut he wants. He then passes the plate to mother, who does the same, but when it reaches the third or fourth family member, most of the best cuts are gone, or the specific favorite you were looking for is already sitting on brother Biff's plate. 
And Biff,that sniveling but-monkey, will use his prime cut of beef to wage bloody war against you, costing you precious victory points. Maybe you sister took all of the "science" meat that you were trying to accumulate, or you took that one slice of baloney, not because you wanted it, but because you know cousin Freddy desperately wants it, and there's no way you're going to let him have all the baloney, so he can make a sandwich later; a sandwich that lets him get another slice of baloney for free on the next turn.
That's drafting, and that's 7 wonders.
It hangs onto it's civilization building theme about as well as Dominion does - and that means, not very well. You never feel like your actually "building" something. You're just trying to get the right cards to maximize your points, and maybe denying cards to the person on your right or left, depending on which way the card draft is moving.
If you've ever played a game with drafting mechanics, it's probably due to this game, which is the best example of the mechanic, but, it's also the WORST example because it demonstrates how luck-centered drafting games are. It all depends on the draw of cards, and your luck of being on the receiving end of someone else's inattention. 
After all rounds are played, it may be difficult to tell who won, but's it's always easy to tell who LOST. Because when you lose, you usually lose big, and that would be okay if the game had some fun built into it. 
It doesn't.
And the process of determining the winner involves so many calculations and conditions. The game just ends, with a big deafening thud of Math hitting the table.
I know some people who really love this game, and have all the expansions. I get the "game" part of it, and it all functions and works very well, but it just isn't fun, at least, not for me.
It's more like an intellectual exercise pretending to be a game, that isn't very intellectually exact, due to the luck involved.
Those who are good at 7 Wonders, are very good, and they will win again and again, and want to play it again and again, while the rest of us have moved on to things like Ticket to Ride or Shadows over Camelot - games that are actually FUN.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
I have played this game several times with my gaming group, but mostly with large groups. The first several times that I played it, I had thought it was awesome: So many different card types, so many different ways to score points, using resources that either you had previously built or paying for the resource(s) from one of your two neighbors. It was the first card drafting game I had ever played, and it had interesting mechanisms.
Fast forward months later, and it seems that the people at my gaming club have outgrown the game. While we would always play the game about once a week, the game just does not hit the table as much these days.
Because I was able to find it for a cheap enough price, I decided to buy the game myself (I would not have thought that I would have originally, since there are a lot of people in my gaming group who already own the game and I try to buy different games so that I can bring different games to play at the club).
I decided to teach the game to my family. We have played 3 different games so far. 2 of those games were 3 player games and 1 of them was a 5 player game. However, all 3 of those games were won by my father, using almost the exact same strategy every time. He would build a lot (but not all) resources early in the game, and then come Age III (and Age II, to start somewhat) he would gather and build most of the high scoring straight-out blue victory point cards. If you have a bunch of blue cards that you are able to build because of your variety of resources you built early on, and sprinkle in some military, and what do you know you have almost an unstoppable path to victory. I swear, there was one game in which my father gathered 30 victory points just in blue cards (8+6+6+4+3+3=30) While you can also scoring points from science cards, you need to commit and hope for specific cards, and on average / card may only net you 3.5 points/card. Whereas with blue cards, even snagging just one can give you 3 to 4 points minimum, going up from there. Also, my father was also able to execute this strategy in a 5 player game (although 2 of the players were new to the game in that particular case and were just catching on the strategy towards the end of the game), too, so although it could be that only the 3 player game is flawed.
Although I have not played any further games with my family, I believe that this game is so unbalanced, because I believe that the above basic strategy can be executed time and again and become a dominant strategy to winning this game.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
14 plays - not bad - but I think I've hit that point where I'm not enjoying it that much anymore. Apart from the niggling issues of balance and control, I think probably 7 Wonders biggest problem is that the pacing and narrative are wrong. High-stakes decisions are made early with inadequate information, and rather than build to a conclusion 7 Wonders actually becomes less and less interesting, and the game drains tension, with each passing age, until the 3rd Age when almost all the decisions are automatic and little you do matters. Which is a shame. There are of course reasons to break the rules of narrative structure, but you need to really know what you're doing if you want to change things up. I don't think 7 Wonders does.
---
Having now gotten a significant number of plays of this under my belt, I like it. It's great that it packs a fair amount of interest into a 30-minute game that easily scales to 7. But ... I can't shake the feeling that there is less here than meets the eye. Once people get the hang of the game it seems like scores become very clustered (a recent game was 52-51-49-48), which is not really  a good sign. Or, the game can be decided by some guy who never builds any Military and allows a neighbor to score a ton of points off of a single 1-point military card. Given there isn't much depth the underlying game here, it's rather chromy, and it feels like your fate is as much in the hands of others as it is your own - Military and Science can both be swingy. Still, it has many good qualities as well, it's clever and fast and fun and flavorful and colorful, and I expect to be enjoying it for a while.
---
Played twice at BGG.con, fun, but a bit over-hyped. It's a nice medium-weight that plays very fast but doesn't pack the punch of, say, a Beowulf, Blue Moon City, San Juan, Race for the Galaxy, or even Small World. It seems clear that it's going to become pretty samey pretty fast. But it does play fast, and does cleanly support 6-7 players, which is huge - nothing else in my collection keeps 6 or 7 players as engaged and moving as quickly on a game with some substance. This alone will assure it a spot in my collection for some time, I imagine.

I'm really curious as to whether there is a "life extension" plan for expansions for the game. Clearly it'll need something if it's to rise above disposability. Also clearly, new player mats aren't going to do it; we'll ultimately need more variety and range in the decks. The path forward is not entirely clear.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Clever mechanism to keep playing time and particularly downtime low with many players (all players take their turns simultaneously) - an extremely big plus in larger groups! This definitely makes 7 Wonders my most preferred strategy(ish) game for 6 or 7 players (or for 8 with [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgameexpansion/111661/7-wonders-cities]Cities[/url] or [url=https://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgameexpansion/247315/7-wonders-armada]Armada[/url]), because many of the alternatives tend to have problems with too much downtime between turns. But I also like it with fewer players, it is even decent with 2 (although I considerably prefer 7 Wonders Duel for two).

It has a high level of luck compared to most other games I love and is probably more tactical than strategical. But there are still several ways how strategic planning can pay off and deep considerations can be made and give definite advantages.
The still rather high level of luck means the game is well suited to play with and appeal to beginners who have a chance to win even in their first game - but in contrast to many other games for which this is true, it's still also thrilling for the more experienced players, at least for me.

I hate hidden trackable information (HTI) in games (see my profile) and thus don't like the rather strong incentive for the memorization of hands in 7 Wonders - I don't want to play "[url=www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/7688/memory]Memory[/url]". But I'm willing to tolerate it in this otherwise excellent game! Besides, the bigger the group (in which 7 Wonders particularly excels compared to other games), the fewer hands will come back to you and the fewer returns you get from memorizing cards.

Another minus is that the two sides of several of the wonders could clearly and thus should have been balanced better. This is most obvious on Ephesus, where the B side is clearly and reasonably undisputably stronger than the A side. On Rhodes and Alexandria, the B side is too close to clearly dominate the A side as well in my opinion - but at least it isn't as clear as with Ephesus.
I am not quite sure how this could have happened particularly in case of Ephesus as it is really obvious if you add up - wasn't it a design goal to make the two sides of each wonder as equally strong as possible?
This is particularly annoying for me because I prefer to draw only the wonder randomly and let the players choose the side. The game would be better if it were a real choice more often.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
A good game that's fun and more-ish with plenty of decisions to be made in its half an hour playing time. However, you can reach saturation point with it where each game begins to feel samey. 

It's similar to a Magic: the Gathering draft only without having to play the game afterwards. This is clever because the best bit about Limited Magic was card drafting and deck building. What made those drafts great was pack evaluation, signalling possibilities, great variability and the thrill of opening packs. How does 7 Wonders compare on these points?

Pack evaluation: Working out which is the best card in the hand you've been passed, given what you've drafted already and what is likely to come your way. Sometimes what would be the best card in a vacuum is not the best choice given your previous picks. I'm glad this is still present in 7 Wonders, although there aren't so many things to factor in compared to Magic. This is likely to become more important as players get increasingly familiar with the game. The first few games will involve some relatively uninformed picks, but I can see a learning curve here to work through.

Signalling: Much more obvious in 7 Wonders, as players can see what you've picked after every pick. 'Hate drafting' is possible by spending cards your opponents want to build your wonder or to turn into coins.

Variability: Except for the purple scoring cards, the same cards are used in each game, so there's never going to be a game where one particular colour is present in greater numbers than another, or one resource is rarer. Expansions may change this. Without them, some variability comes from the different wonders each player can play and the interactions with different neighbouring wonders. There aren't as many different cards as I'd expected.

Thrill of opening packs: With every pack you open in Magic, there's always the hope that you'll get a ridiculously powerful card (usually rare) that fits right in with the rest of your deck. This is a complete lottery, but it's still exciting. In 7 Wonders, the only thing that matches this is hoping your 3rd Age hand contains a purple card which scores for cards you've already played. Not quite as thrilling, but also less swingy, so probably fairer all round.

It's easy to pick up with a depth that belies its simplicity and has the advantage of accommodating up to 7 people with little increase in time.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
7 Wonders is a surprisingly rich card drafting game. You play three hands of seven cards and each turn you pick a card from your hand and pass on the rest. The turn structure really is that simple. This way you try to build your own civilization and score the most victory points in various ways. A big part of the game is to set up a resource engine that will last your game plan through all three hands, or ages. The Wonders that give this game its name provide players with special abilities which really affect your play. 
Within the game you only interact with your direct neighbors. Mainly, the player interaction is limited to  passing cards, buying resources and comparing military strenght after each age.
7 Wonders is a highly replayable game that needs a few plays to really grow on you. The virtual resource mechanic needs some time to settle in and specific card knowledge helps a great deal to do well. I first rated it a six, but over time I kept adjusting its rating: now, it's one of my few 10 rated games. Games are quick, varied and really a lot of fun. The more I play, the more I want to play and that is probably it's best quality.

The Leaders expansion adds a great deal of strategy while not adding a lot to the complexity. It adds a smaller fourth hand, which you draft at the beginning of the game and which you keep for the entire game. At the start of each age you get to play one of these leader cards. Basically you plot out your strategy at the beginning of the game based on the leaders you're dealt and draft. Hate drafting now happens less often, but is more meaningful. Also, money becomes more important since leaders have to be paid with money. This is a great improvement from the base game, where money was only used for buying resources.

I'd say the Leaders expansion is a must have expansion, whereas the Cities expansion is a very good expansion, but not a mst-have per se. Instead of three hands of seven cards, you now play three hands of eight. The extra cards are a new type of cards which add some more direct player interaction. The new cards shake up your decision tree quite nicely.

The Wonder Pack is another must have expansion, as you can never have enough wonders for extra replayability. Also, these new wonders are awesome and some of the most fun ones to play with.

Owned expansions: Leaders, Cities, Wonder Pack, Catan promo, Esteban promo
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
A slight-step above a gateway game, 7 Wonders is a classic.  I first played this a long time ago in my early days of Euro-gaming with a not-so-friendly group at a meetup and no one would really explain the rules.  However, I was STILL able to get a grasp of the civilization and engine building aspect of accumulating resource cards to build more cards.  It was logical, intuitive and felt very natural.  
Instinctively thinking I should just try my best to diversify, when the scoring came at the end, I actually came somewhere in the middle range compared to the other players.  With the exception of the Science cards, the scoring is very simple and straight forward.   Often when I introduce this to new/non-gamers, they get this déjà vu feeling they’ve played this before; that’s how instinctive this game is (very much like Splendor).  

While my first experience with it was tainted by the players at that particular meetup, I’ve since played it many times at meetups (with friendlier people) and came to love it.  

The game is fast and a fun activity when you have a lot of players who don’t want to split up into two groups.  As far as strategy, well… while experience at knowing what cards will come up during each age has its advantages, it really comes down to the luck of the draw as to what cards are passed to you.  You can try to block or exploit advantages, but there is a lot of luck in the game.  I’ve seen first time players win a number of times (although they almost always had a LOT of help from their neighbours).  And the scoring at the end is a chore (best to get the computer application to do the math for you).   
The amazing artwork is some of the best I’ve ever seen in a game and gives 7 Wonders a very classy feel.  You very much feel you are building a civilization from ancient times.   

Some people may critique the game for its lack of interaction (especially against players on the opposite side of the table), but the simultaneous selection mechanism eliminates downtime and all players are considering their selections concurrently.  Thus it makes the game feel fast as everyone is constantly engaged in play.   There aren’t many games out there that can accommodate 7 players that aren’t straight-up party games.  That said, I’ve never played this game with less than six players and usually play it with the full seven.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Got this to add another highly ranked (yet fairly light) game to my collection and also because I'm looking into civilization-themed games.

The game is pretty slick and easy to play, but as a civ game I'd like a bit more connection to the theme. Most of what you do, in terms of thinking, is deciding which card to draft on a given turn, and there's really no thematic justification for the drafting mechanism. The most thematic thing is the arms race with your immediate neighbors. Most cards you play reduce costs of a later card or have some synergy with what you've already played (built). Science is reduced to a set collection game, which is pretty abstract.

The player interaction seemed just OK to me, coming not just from the arms race but also because you can try to draft cards you think someone else will want, blocking them.

I thought it was odd how the third (of three) eras has no new ways to get resources. You can't stockpile resources (except money), so if you don't produce enough of something, and your neighbors don't produce enough for you to buy and make up the shortfall, you can be quite sure, 2/3rds through the game, that you'll never be able to build certain things, such as stages of your Wonder!

I was disappointed by the lack of differentiation among player positions. I think games will start to seem samey pretty quickly. Over the course of the game you'll play approximately 6x3=18 cards. There are only about five general types of cards. This leaves room for (probably) a few broad strategies, but you're never going to find yourself in a particularly strange or surprising position.

...Upping .5 point to 7.5 after playing a thrown-together variant where I just mixed all the eras and then only played 4 cards per era instead of 6. It definitely wrecks some of the balance, but it was exciting and felt much less scripted.

...Tried playing where instead of drafting normally, there's a market and you put chips on the cards you want to skip over as in If Wishes Were Fishes. Adds some fiddliness but probably also some strategy.

...What I like most is the economy (deciding which resources to have for yourself and which to pay other players for) and after that, the majority game of military. I wish science and VP buildings had interconnections with something else in the engine.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Not a good first impression.  What a mess!  An interesting game, yes, but fails to draw me in for wanting another round... ever... pretty much.  Just because you can succeed at borrowing mechanics from other games and combining them in a new and somewhat interesting way, this doesn't mean you know how to make a good game.  This game does nothing to draw me into any fantasy world regarding the 7 Wonders of the World.  Nor did it stimulate any interesting conversation or interaction among friends.  The only conversation was functional game play chatter.  You're not really drawn into what's laid down on the whole table either.  Monopoly draws more interest in this area.  Huge fail there.  Basically, you focus on all the icons, and can forget the rest of the meaningless art.  Heck, you can forget the icon art too since one widget would be as meaningful as any other.  Then, you focus on the one or two strategies that your early hands present as most likely to succeed.  Maybe diverge a bit as you go.  Meanwhile, the other players could be pursuing a dozen other win strategies.  With so many ways to win it becomes fairly absurd to try to track them and instead the temptation is strong to just go heads-down in your own strategies and simply hope you come out on top at the end.  I think I "got" the game in a group of 7 and scored really well.  But, I'm also suspicious some things might have been lacking and I need to read the rules for myself sometime.
March 2019

UPDATE May 2024: I haven't played again yet, but have some things to add after some more thought and research.  I have recently labeled this game "poly-solitaire" (multi-player solitaire), but that was a loose classification.  Some object to it--and fairly so.  Yes, this game is heavy on discard management (like Canasta) meaning you have to track the strategies of those next to you (for more than just discards, BTW).  But it is still a heads-down game that is at least 90% solitaire... which is enough to call it poly-solitaire (because no multiplayer game has zero interaction [unless you really do just play solitaire next to each other and compare scores at the end]).  Yes, after you ramp up on the many mechanics after a dozen plays, you may be able to look up more... but do I care?..
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
We had been curious about [thing=68448][/thing], especially after all of the attention that it had garnered when it was released.  It sounded almost like a holy grail---this was a game with good decisions and great artwork that scaled from 2-7 players.  How could you not have it in your collection?  So when we found it for a good price, we ended up getting a copy (as well as a copy for my sister).

When my sister visited over the holiday break, we took the three player game for a spin.  I think part of the hype of [thing=68448][/thing] is justified.  It's a very attractive game with great artwork.  My wife and I always enjoy these types of tableau-building games, so we felt more or less at home already.  However, it's still fairly easy to pick up and almost ventures into gateway game territory---my sister is not a hardcore gamer, but she was able to enjoy the game pretty quickly.  At least in the three player game, there's some nice interaction with the card drafting and you have to pay attention to everyone's tableau.  I wasn't a big fan of the iconography (some of them still remain a little confusing to me), but it was still an enjoyable game.  I can see how it would work with more as well.

However, after my sister left, my wife and I broke this out for just the two of us.  Generally, we don't mind dummy players too much---we enjoy [thing=6249][/thing] and [thing=66188][/thing], but the dummy player in both of those games is relatively easy to use.  In [thing=68448][/thing], the dummy player mechanic felt needlessly complicated.  Instead of just looking at your own tableau, you now had to look at the dummy player, so it felt like you were playing two boards.  Instead of just dumping cards, you had to consider all of the options that the dummy player could actually build, which actually took us a little bit of time to calculate all of the available resources, which card would benefit us more than our opponent, etc.  All of this was on top of the same type pf calculations you had to do for your own tableau.  Perhaps it will get better over time, but it felt like too much effort.  

If it was just the two of us, we would probably pass on [thing=68448][/thing], but it's a good game to keep in the collection when more people are over.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Visual Appeal: (4)
Art on the components is beautiful and immersive, even if the theme is fairly shallow. 21 awards displayed on the outside of the box seems a little boastful...

Components: (3)
Average quality cards. I could sleeve them I guess, but I'd expect them to deteriorate anyhow when handled heavily in so many 5-7p games over its lifetime. Wonder boards feel nice and sturdy. No warping here so far.

Theme: (2)
Take a card, pass the rest. Make a set, collect more symbols, repeat. The building of wonders while sacrificing a card fits nicely, and I like the idea of buying resources from your neighbors. The game sacrifices theme for simplicity. I used to draft MtG, and the drafting had more weight to it because your creation had to survive an onslaught from other players. In this game you create a spread of cards for points which just feels flat in comparison.

Learning: (4)
A simple game which is simply taught. One thing that the rule book might have done is provide more suggestions for new gamers who might freeze up when faced with a scoring system as layered as this one. There are 7 sources of points, and this can be intimidating. After a 7 player game with 5 newbies lasted over 90 minutes, I changed my teaching tactics to include some guidance on choosing a card. One might also consider adding a 60 second timer.

Gameplay: (2) Lackluster. Occasionally heated drafting against my neighbors, but when someone 3 seats away from me is running away with the game I can do very little about it. The game feels more controllable with 3-4 players, but if it advertises up to 7 it should play well with 7. I am disappointed that I end up reaching over this game for Resistance or Saboteur at 7 players. The disappointment is soon forgotten though, because they are just more fun than 7 Wonders would have been anyway.

Overall Fun: (2) 
I have some friends who enjoy this game quite a bit, so it comes out every now and again, just not with more than 4 players. Nothing to do while Sammy Slow-picker to your right takes his turn. The inability to actively affect the game state at large player counts. I rarely end the game feeling like I am satisfied, or that I made any difficult choices.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
It does just what it says it does, it plays 3 to 7 WELL and does it in 30 minutes flat. Its a filler with a weak theme so don't expect more, it does play well, it plays fast with no downtime and also keeps you interested. It also has that let's play one more game addictive quality.
 
I was leary about a game of just a pure draft and thats all but it works out quite good and shit it plays 7 players, how many games are decent and play 7 in half an hour?  That and it’s easy to teach mean its a great gateway game and this puts it on the wishlist for me.  

You are building up your player board by drafting cards, once you know the cards (which only takes one game really) you can do some planning on how you want to  build combos on the table (set collection). It's nice that the player boards push the envelope all a little differently too, so one board encourages to play a certain strategy and another board a slightly different one. 

The obvious comparison is to Fairy Tale but I'll do it versus Dominion. Dominion probably has a little more depth just because the cards you are drafting are face up and open to everyone where as here you know what you’ll probably get and probably need but it isn’t as certain. Once you own cards things are kind of flipped around because once built here they are on your board and stay there where as in Dominion the cards randomly come to you and you don’t know how they will combine. They are different games but fill the same niche of a good 30 minute filler, personally I give this one the edge due to scaling and no annoying shuffling, this game will likely make its way to my shelf.  

I do think replay with the current cards is limited to maybe 20 plays tops and some will be bored of the cards after 5 - 10 games. For me this isn't as big as problem since I want it for a filler only and for family outings *BUT* the BIG box and BIG price really mean they should have included a lot more cards which might stop me from buying it at the current price. Note the cards are a good thick stock but black rimmed and not that durable and this means unsightly wear on edges, and the cards are too big for regular sleeves :(
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
This is a great game. It plays extremely fast (around half an hour) and plays 3-7 player in ALMOST exactly the same way - and in the same time!

It's a good light civilization card game which I think fills a unique niche; I cannot really compare 7 Wonders to many other games. The symbols and how the ressources work can be hard for newcomers to figure out at first, but once they have tried a game, they know what to do the next time - which will probably be right after the first game as it's such a fast game! 

Even though it's a fast game, you actually feel that you are building your own small civilization, especially because of your own unique wonder (which are all pretty well balanced, and I like how there are 2 different sides to choose from). 

When playing with 3 players there is much less luck as you will get your starting hand back and everybody have access to the same starting ressources and influence each other militaristic. If you are playing with 6 or 7 players, there is more luck involved as you never know which cards will be passed to you by your neighbour, but I don't mind this aspect. 

Regarding strategy, I think that the different paths are pretty balanced though it does seem that, in our games, the blue civil cards have been granting the most VPs, but the green scientific cards and red military cards have won their fair share of games too. A good mix of the different cards can be okay too sometimes, but it really depends on how many players you are, which wonder you have and which cards you are dealt etc., so you cannot declare a superior strategy... I also like the guild cards and how they are mixed into the deck randomly.

The expansion adds a little something different to the game and I can't wait to see the rest of the expansions. The promo wonders Manneken Pis and Catan are okay wonders but not some I use when playing with fewer than 5 players.

This is one of those games you want to have in your collection. I recommended it a lot - not many games can play 7 players like this in 30 minutes!

My recommended number of players: 3, 4, 5
Best with: 4
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value: My new nickname in my gaming circles is Zevin Wonders - short for Zevin wonders why this game was ever made.   That's not true actually, I do respect the game designers for making such a widely received 7 player game that can play in 30-45 minutes.  What just boggles my mind is why everyone likes it so much?  You have limited control over your strategies.  It's not a true drafting game in 5-7 players(which is the number of people who tend to gravitate towards this game b/c of the lack of game choices with that number) because you will never or rarely draft in anticipation of getting something back.  So there is almost always a best card to draft, little to no strategy in drafting something in one pack because you know it combos well with something in another, and in my experience, if you sit next to one or two pacifists, you have about a 99% better chance of winning the game.  Science is rarely viable except when coupled with the leaders expansion or as previously stated if you're next to some hippies that 1 age I warrior can bash into 18 points in your favor.  Some starting civs are significantly better than others.  This game basically comes down to one giant luck box.  All of which I would be totally okay with if EVERYONE didn't ALWAYS want to play this game.  There are 7 of us left at game night.  Me: "Let's play a 3 and a 4."  Others: "Well 7 Wonders plays   7." Me: "sigh..........."  If everyone else out there wasn't so damn enamored with this game I'd aptly give it a rating of a 7.  But thanks to the mindless zombie rending flesh craving this game triggers in otherwise sane individuals, I felt it my civic duty to all that is rational and just in this world to do my part to keep this game out of the top 10 BGG games.  Thus Zevin Wonders, you have a special place in my heart as the only game I've ever rated a 1!  Mazel Tov!   Addendum - I heard through the grapevine that 1 ratings may get thrown out as spam.  I cannot in good conscious let that happen, thus I shall reluctantly raise my 7 Wonders rating to a 5.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
Though rife with shocking nudity and Masonic devilry, the game functions well enough for what it is, a "super-filler" that hosts up to seven players in 30 minutes.  It's pretty, engaging, and the small decisions are nice.  At the end you're rewarded with an awesome/mediocre/just-plain-sad tableau that tells the story of your soaring/forgotten/broke-ass civilization.

[i]But...[/i]

The game suffers grotesquely when players don't counter-pick—the player who manages to seat themselves between two milquetoasts will win with a shockingly massive score.  We're talkin' 37-42-52-[b]87[/b]-33 shocking. 

"What the hell were you doing?!" I ask Ms. 87's neighbors.

They blink as if slapped.  "I was building my civilization," they say.

"For the love of God," I rave, "Why did you keep passing her [i]exactly what she needed?![/i]"

"Well," they mumble, "I had other things to do."

"Yes," I gurgle through clenched teeth, "Like making sure she doesn't double all our scores!"

So, yeah, this game requires mouth-pooping in order to work.  When everyone keeps a scatalogical eye on their neighbors—and even up- and downstream some—it's a nice little card drafting game that's over quickly enough that you don't notice the undigested corn.

When playing with people who refuse to poop in their neighbor's mouths, I [i]strongly suggest[/i] you sit between two of them in order to maximize your score.

[b]After 25 plays:[/b]  Much better (I'd rate it an 8) with the [gameid=92539] expansion.  Leaders allow you to focus your strategy (just a little), or at least build some synergy.  Or, with a poor selection, have hilariously random historical figures running your show.  [i]Hatshepsut in Rome?![/i]  ~LULZ

textfield_comment_value:
Components: Nice, over-sized cards, though they really start to fill up the table after a bit. Wonderful art. The iconography is clear but too small in the 'costs' corner of the cards, making it difficult to audit my neighbors as the cards are played.

Experience: I went into my first game thinking I would invest heavily in raw and manufactured goods, so that I wouldn't need to rely on commerce with my neighbors. This ended up pushing me toward a brown/gray/blue strategy, since I found myself continually strapped for cash. Other players focused more on commerce, or on science. I hammered my neighbors with military, but they were able to compensate in other ways. Very interesting.

Seems to be well balanced, and I expect that as we become more familiar with the cards, the game will become more competitive. With complete knowledge of all cards in circulation (except for the guilds in Age III), and with better knowledge of the build chains, one could employ different strategies with better clarity than I was in this first outing.

I appreciate that my neighbors can't muck with me too much (other than taking my cards, and vying for military might). Nearly every card is attractive to build. Whereas in Agricola the game mandates that I have a little of everything, this game, like Stone Age, seems to push me more toward extremes: specialize in a few different scoring methods, and let the rest fall to the side, otherwise I end up being mediocre in everything.

I'm beginning to feel like Science is too good, as more often than not the player who scores the most in science is also the winner. I also want a bit more direction in terms of final scoring (somewhat provided by the Leaders), to prevent me from just making the same choices every time.

Like in Kingsburg, there isn't much in this game to make me try new strategies; our group is in a bit of a rut with the types of cards we play.

textfield_comment_value:
Card-drafting civilization building that scales very well and plays quickly.

I can see why people love this game; it plays quick, it has replayability, and it can accomodate 2-7 players (!), plus the theme "fits".  I'm not sure it has much in the way of strategy or control, but again because of the short playtime this is tolerable I guess (any game with card-drafting as the central mechanic seems tactical at best).

Setup/space is a bit of a pain in the ass, considering its a quick card game, so you almost have to have a big table and play several games back-to-back for it to be worth it.  2-player is a bit annoying for this very reason(s); that said, the "dummy" mechanic, which I usually do not enjoy at all, is implemented pretty well.  The cost and box-size/shelf-space is a bit absurd, when you compare it to say, oh Dominion.  This game also seems very expandable, and the Leaders expansion seems to be a must buy for me.  And oh, this is really a very very simple game to jump in and play, despite what the simpleton SdJ jury voters might lead you to believe.

Own the [boardgame=92539]Leaders[/boardgame], [boardgame=111661]Cities[/boardgame], [boardgame=154638]Babel[/boardgame], [boardgame=247315]Armada[/boardgame] and [boardgame=133993]Wonder Pack[/boardgame] expansions, as well as the [boardgame=110308]Catan[/boardgame], [boardgame=83445]Manneken Pis[/boardgame], [boardgame=99315]Stevie[/boardgame], [boardgame=127838]Louis[/boardgame], [boardgame=156119]Wil[/boardgame], [boardgame=166329]Nimrod[/boardgame], [boardgame=130236]Esteban[/boardgame], [boardgame=231167]Leaders Anniversary pack[/boardgame] and [boardgame=231168]Cities Anniversary pack[/boardgame] promos.  This expansion (Leaders) adds another round of drafting, which leaves you with a hand of 4 leaders, 3 of which can be played during the course of the game.  The leaders allow for specialization/ways to score points/quick money etc., and add to the gameplay.  Really a simple addition and a must-have expansion for fans of 7 Wonders.
Title: 7 Wonders

textfield_comment_value:
So after seven plays of 7 Wonders I think it's time to rate it as a solid 7...

...anyway, the idea of drafting cards by passing small decks from player to player is certainly not new, but basing an entire game around it is definetivly special.

A game of 7 Wonders is divided into three ages. In each age, players gets seven cards each, picks one of these to play and then passes the remaining cards to the next player. This is repeated until all cards have been played.
Cards fill different funtions. For instance, brown and grey cards are production that is needed to play cards of differend colour. Other cards represent military, economy, technology, monuments and so on.
Also, cards become progressively better in each age, but you need cards from precious ages to play the later ones.

Just about everything you do in 7 Wonders will score points, but figuring out how to score a lot while at the same time keeping the other players down is certainly not easy. I like how cards scores differently. Blue, green and red cards all score points, but in varying ways. For instance, green is set collecting, while red is a race against your neighbours.

You can also use the cards to build on your unique Wonder, or simply discard them for money.
Finally, you are allowed to use the production of neighbouring players if you pay them.

It's easy to think of this as solitaire, but you need to keep an eye on the other players. Perhaps you don't want to go for green cards if to many other players are doing so, but you might need to do so if only one player is going green...

While there are lot's of different options with the different kind of cards, the best option seems to be to do a little bit of everything. This makes the game a bit too unfocused for me some times.
More importantly, this lack of variation makes the above mentioned solid 7 a lot less solid. It might even border on a 6...

If you add the Leaders expansion you add a bit of focus, making the game jump from 7 to an 8, perhaps even a 9!

textfield_comment_value:
Número de Jogadores: 2 a 7.
Dificuldade: 2,0/5,0
Indicado para Iniciante: Sim
Contras: Não roda legal com poucos jogadores.
Prós: Rápido, comporta uma quantidade boa de jogadores, clássico.
 
Comentários: Esse jogo se tornou um clássico dos jogos modernos e tem envelhecido muito bem!
No jogo cada jogador está construindo a sua civilização, onde pode investir em recursos, força militar, tecnologia e construções civis. O jogo é passado em três eras, cada uma com cartas mais fortes, porém mais difíceis de serem construídas. Na sua vez de jogar ou você constrói a carta pagando os seus recursos ou vende ela. No fim da terceira era, ganha o jogador que fizer a maior pontuação.
Você tem várias maneiras de pontuar, o que deixa o jogo com várias estratégias diferentes a serem seguidas.
A interação no jogo é bem interessante, já que você pode comprar recursos das cidades vizinhas, e ainda, a cada final de era existe uma comparação de forças militares.
Ele é bem rápido, já que todos os jogadores jogam praticamente juntos, seja na hora de escolher a carta no draft ou construí-la.
O jogo possui uma pequena assimetria, pois cada jogador recebe uma maravilha que ao ser construída, recebe uma bonificação diferente.
Para mim um dos pontos mais positivos é número de jogadores que você pode jogar, não sendo um jogo party.
Já o ponto negativo fica por não rodar muito bem em 2 ou 3 jogadores.
Por mais que tenham saído outras versões, vale muito apena adquirir a versão antiga, pois não tem nenhuma falha e a arte é boa.
Recomendo!
7 Wonder x Hadara: Os jogos possuem algumas semelhanças, mas um não anula o outro, sendo os dois muito bons.
7 Wonders: Indico para quem tem grupos grandes e não quer jogar party. O tempo tende a ser mais curto que o Hadara.
Hadara: Possui maior gestão de recursos, sendo um pouco mais complexo que o 7 Wonders.
Gosto de ambos os jogos, mas se for para escolher um, fico com o 7 Wonders por ter uma certa interação, coisa que o Hadara não possui. 
 
Modo Solo: Não existe.

Total Score: 7.1 Came back to this one after an extended vacation, and it was great. Updated the scores to reflect a "non-burnout" mindset.

-Enjoyment - 7.5
Came back to this one recently after a long vacation from it. I am much more experienced in board games now than I was then, and the simplicity of this was refreshing. 

-Components - 6
These are very average for me, nothing shiny, nothing metal, just a bunch of cardboard but they suffice. The insert does a fine job of organizing base game. 

-"Tableability" - 7
The score of how easily/frequently I can get this game to the table. This is a great gateway game. Teaches drafting, military points teach table awareness. It can be a little overwhelming to new players but in my experience it was quickly overcome. For my typical gaming group this is about the right the weight, but a little depth light for me personally. 

-Eagerness to Replay - 7
Would play again soon, love the fact that this is simple enough to squeeze in between meatier games. 

-Mechanics - 8
Easy to understand, fun player interaction with drafting and scoring military. This game just works. What I originally listed as imbalances based on the starting cities, I believe to be more of an adaptive strategy issue that may be difficult for inexperienced players to overcome.

textfield_comment_value:
The initial reason for this high rating was that after the first game, everyone immediately wanted to play again. The game feels _fun_ (and retains that feel after playing more). The game also has longevity, and a subtlety which you only slowly learn to appreciate. I'm much more excited about playing the game now, after 30+ plays, than I was after 5 plays. (Was in fact nearly uninterested in the game after 10 plays.)

Plays very swift, but is not as light / devoid of meaningful choices as one might expect based on other comments, particularly in a 4-player game. There are several opportunities per game of screwing over your neighbours by handing them only bad choices (which can include gleeful taunting), and the different strategies you can follow in the game do each have their own distinct feel. Paying attention to your neighbours is important, but in the end you're going to have to accept that no matter how well you play, luck will remain a factor in this game. As you play the game more often, though, and play with a table of equally experienced players, you'll learn that the choices that lead to a win are subtle and very fine indeed, and the game becomes a very careful balancing act in building up your resources (or ways to acquire them) _just_ far enough to enable to you to more efficiently build a better mix of point-scoring cards. Yet add a single inexperienced player to the table, and it's all thrown out of whack again.

The 2-player version surprisingly works relatively well, and I'd rate that a 7.1

Thus, you'll know what cards are where, but there is a small amount of doubt as to when those cards you haven't seen will show (one of them won't).  You can use the dummy player to enrich yourself and/or screw your opponent, so there's more strategy than with 3+.  This is a fun, fast game, but no matter how you play, no terribly deep.  Great filler, sadly at non-filler prices.  If you pick this one up, be sure to get some sleeves - every Repos game I've owned has had cards that show wear after only a few plays.
