textfield_comment_value:
[2023] King of Tokyo was one of the first modern boardgames I played. Unfortunately, I never got to play it with the Power Up! expansion.

I came to learn two things over the years because of King of Tokyo:

(1) Dice rolling as a central mechanism is not my preferred type of game; 

(2) I am generally not in situations where I am teaching non-gamers boardgames at 4+ player counts, and I'd rather not be the person teaching games to non-gamers (re: this point, I once had three different people begin arguing semantics and wanting to house-rule every faint ambiguity in the game that should otherwise be taken literally as "Oh, but I did not understand, so let's play this way from here on out" before we'd even managed to get one round in, and I was stuck being the *censored* who says "But, that's not how the game is played - we can let it slide, but here's how it is play it going forward" which no one ever seems to like).

As a result, I do not see much reason to keep King of Tokyo. I will never actively volunteer to get it to the table with my regular gaming groups, and I'm not patient enough to teach it to people new to the hobby. For higher player-counts, I'd rather be playing Telestrations, Codenames, or something akin to Just One.



[Update] ----- X -----

I played King of Tokyo again on Board Game Arena, and I noticed that people tend to enable a few specific options: Power-Up! and Berserk. I saw the occasional Costume and Cultists add-ons, but Tokyo Tower and Curse were often omitted. Likewise, Dark Edition was frequently disabled (which is actually the content that what brought me back to playing King of Tokyo on Board Game Arena). 

Go read the review titled "Remember that 1998 remake of Godzilla? This is worse..." as it is actually quite funny.

For my own reference:
- Costume Cards: Each player receives a starting Costume card, and players can steal Costumes from each other by rolling 3 Damage and paying the cost of the Costume (for example: Statue of Liberty gives an extra re-roll with a cost of '4', and Cheerleader gives one player the ability to add a free Damage to any other player's roll);
- Cultists: Gain a tile if rolling four identical faces, and those tiles can be used to gain a Health, an Energy, or an extra roll;
- Tokyo Tower: Claim a tower level by rolling at least four '1' while in Tokyo, and gain bonus health and energy at the beginning of a turn (or, win the game by reaching the top level);
- Curse Cards: Permanent effects applied to all players and a Die of Fate that triggers Ankh or Snake effects;
- Berserk Dice: Roll 4 or more Damage and gain a Berserk die that lasts until healed;
- "Even More Wicked!": Gain wickedness points to get special tiles upon rolling three '1' or three '2'.
- Power-Up!: Adds powers.

Really, I see why Berserk is popular, although I found that the rest are all take-it-or-leave-it. At the same time, Costumes and Power-Up! make the game that bit more wacky. They are both very, very fun.

----- X -----

King of Tokyo is solid enough without the expansion content. It got me into the hobby, and it got me to buying my own copy - as far as dice games go, it is not the most interesting to me. Players either roll victory point dice, energy dice, health dice, or damage dice - the game ends when one player is left standing or when one player reaches 20 points by rolling 3-of-a-kinds on the victory point dice. Even on Board Game Arena, the game features a lot of downtime (and it features a funky interface - the 'locking in' of dice is oddly fiddly because of how smooth it is). 

I am equally reminded by just how unbalanced some of the shop cards are - they are either too strong, too weak, or too situational. For reference: I got a Shrink Ray because I rolled 6 Energy in an early turn; I eventually got forced into Tokyo; my opponent in Tokyo Bay knocked out 3 people with a 5 Damage roll before getting forced out of Tokyo due to player count falling too low; the Alienoid player frantically tried rolling Health to get back in the game from 1 HP; then, I managed to roll 5 Damage again using a Berserk die at the end of the game to knock out my two remaining opponents. Thankfully, playing online means the first three getting knocked out could simply start a new game; in-person, people do not have that privilege. 

For my preferences, dice games work best at low player counts (see: Castles of Burgundy and Spots). King of Tokyo also requires a few too many components to be truly great by my standards - moreover, it's just a weird, fiddly, bookkeeping nightmare sometimes when teaching to certain large groups. The expansions, which all make the teach that bit more complicated and the bookkeeping just that bit worse, all add so much to the experience.

Plus, this is just a footnote: games where no one player gets eliminated and someone wins by points is a very, very weird experience... especially with the expansions. I had a bunch of Costumes and Keep cards and was not able to remotely touch one player who was hiding outside of Tokyo, especially because The King player kept using their Chest Thumping evolution power-up which forced other players out of Tokyo (let me stay so that I could hit that stupid VP player, dangit). Sorry, but strategy dictates that players must not fight and instead go for Victory Point victories. 

----- X -----

In short: Costumes and Power-Up! really add a lot of fun to the base King of Tokyo experience, the Wicked! expansion (similar to the Dark Edition) is a solid implementation, and the Berserk dice is just worth including each time. I see no reason to return to the base King of Tokyo experience, personally.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
[b]GodZILLA-FILLER![/b]


[i]Kong[/i] of the Hill Yahtzee style dice-fest.

[b]When the red moon sets, and the sun rises in the West, two monsters will appear to save the people.[/b] 

1. Huge great chunky dice. Surprisingly meaty in my clunky great paws.
2. Short and sweet rulebook. You only [i]really[/i] need a one-sheet. Trouble is, in this dazzling interweb age, there are so many morons playing games, and asking dumb questions about those games, that game publishers have to try and provide 100-page idiot-proof rules (Mission: Impossible). The rulebook here is clear and colourful. Back in the day, this would have been a photocopied black and white printed wafer-thin sheet, accompanied by a ridiculous questionnaire that needed posting to Atlanta or some-place, and a wargames catalogue of delights.
3. Fantastic giga-monster theme. Everybody loves huge killy monsters. And splashing in muddy puddles.
4. Fast playing. Yeah, it's a filler. McD's cheeseburger-like filler. Sometimes I like me one of those, and I could eat two on the trot.
5. Excellent evocative art on the action cards - are all well named and fit the Toho company B-movie stylee, ensuring dramatic reading during gameplay: [i]He's grown another head! She's had a son! Crikes - look at all the grabby tentacles you now have! It's a absorbing all the energy. He's eating a skyscraper! Christ, it's growing even bigger! Shit - he's breathing radioactive fire at me![/i] type of thing.
6. Box and contents feel classy, not cheapo.
7. Simple and straightforward mechanisms.
8. Gateway game, certainly. Might even see if my GF will try it - I know my daughter will be a potential target for KoT when she's a teeny bit older.
9. There's room for light strategic play in here. Do I play passively or aggressively or build up my super powers? Obviously you switch it any way you like, dice depending.
10. Interesting decisions. Each turn you'll agonise over whether to concentrate on healing, fighting, energy conservation, or go on a victory point drive. Plus there's the choice of special powers to buy or save up for. Another thing (decision) is whether to stay as King of Tokyo, fighting back with your mega-paws the pretenders to your urban throne (while you hoover up valuable victory points), or yield like a surrender monkey, letting a helmeted 300' high spider-legged alien into Tokyo city.
11. Fun - in a laugh-out-loud manner occasionally. Especially if idiots like me make silly monster screeches during play, or your friends make declarations like "Now I have a massive new brain!"
12. Can cope with up to six players - ensuring, with 5-6 friends, that you will have two 'hills' to fight over: Tokyo city and Tokyo bay.
13. Fast to learn. Takes minutes, and everyone knows how to throw dice - so it feels intuitive and smooth.


[b]O' Godzilla! Destroy the people of Japan, who once tried to conquer the Azumi Tribe! You will be the instrument of our revenge! O' Godzilla![/b]

1. Yeah - you could be slaughtered before getting to do much, in a 4+ player game, but the game's short, and trashy, enough that an [i]elegant[/i] solution to that 'wasn't thought up'/'or needed' - delete as your confirmation bias allows.
2. Luck of the dice can be cruel. You get at least 2 re-rolls, but it's still luck. Managed luck, to a degree, however. BUT, you're not just rolling bones here, folks, you also have to manage your energy (represented by cubes) and your special monster powers (represented by cards). So there's that.
3. Shame it's not an actual Godzilla-themed game, but that's not a biggie for me - there's enough daft monsters to keep most people happy, with all the major monster 'stereotypes' covered; you know, big lizard, mecha lizard, giant monkey, huge fighty robot of destruction, etc.
4. Because it's a King of the Hill game, you are beating up on the leader each turn; but, as the leader, you beat back heavier on those lesser monsters who wanna muscle in on your Tokyo throne.
5. Not convinced on the greatness of the 2-player game. If you need an exciting and fun pastime before cracking out Dune for your group, I'd heartily recommend KoT.
6. Similar to Yahtzee and some other games. Knizia's [i]Scarab Lords[/i] has a 'wait a turn before grabbing any points' system too. I liked it there, and I like it here, but I will not eat green eggs and ham, Sam I am!

 
TRIVIA: Did you know that Godzilla even has his own star on the Hollywood walk of fame? Well, he does.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
King of Tokyo is a game that I have enjoyed with both my board gaming group as well as my family because it is pretty easy to pick up. It's essentially a better version of Yahtzee where you compete with the other players to be the King of Tokyo. You can roll out of 6 dice to get fists (Deals 1 damage per), hearts (Heals 1 health per), lightning (Gains 1 $ per), and 1/2/3 (Gives that many victory points for every 3 you roll + 1 victory point for each additional die [Such as 3 1's = 1 victory point + 2 more 1's = 3 victory points]). You can buy cards with the lightning that you accumulate and they will either be "discard" cards that you play right away or "keep" cards that you keep equipped to your character. You have a maximum of 10 health unless you have a card that says otherwise. Be the first one to 20 victory points or be the last one standing as the King of Tokyo!

The Power Up! expansion makes each character unique instead of just choosing them for aesthetic reasons and also adds Pandakai, a new character! When you roll 3 hearts, you can now draw a card from your character's Evolution deck which is specific to each character. This also makes it so that hearts aren't completely worthless when you are inside of Tokyo. The powers are pretty evenly balanced and are definitely a welcome addition to the game which builds off of its core principles. I would love it if they released a Dark Edition version of this so that it matches up with the theme of it instead of potentially using an odd mix of artwork.

The Halloween expansion adds 2 more character options as well as Evolution cards for them which are both pretty fun to play and have cool artwork. It also adds 6 orange dice for the Halloween theme and costumes which are a new version of keep cards that can actually be stolen from a player (If you roll 3 fists and choose to steal it instead of dealing damage to them). If you are looking for more variety for replayability, the new characters and costumes definitely add that.

The Dark Edition is better than the base game, but it doesn't support the Halloween and Power Up! expansions since their themes don't match. If you really wanted to, you could probably use them with it though. The Dark Edition is pretty much the same as the base game but with a darker theme. The biggest difference is a "wickedness track" which allows you to pick a card from a stack at 3, 6, and 10 on the track. You move up the track 2 spaces if you roll 3 1's on top of the victory points and you move up the track 1 space if you roll 3 2's on top of the victory points, so no matter which number you roll, you always receive 3 of something whether it is moving up the wickedness track and/or gaining victory points. It makes it much more worth it to get 33% of the rolls on the dice (1's and 2's). It's a straight up improvement over the base game and I would highly recommend it for fans of the game.

TL;DR: King of Tokyo is a great game whether you get the original or the Dark Edition and is easily accessible for people that are looking to get a good gateway game. It even has a second edition that includes a new character and updated artwork to choose from. I would recommend the Dark Edition over the base game every time though because it just makes the 1's and 2's that you roll (33% of each die) worth it compared to how they were before.

**Side note: I've moved my regular King of Tokyo plays over into the Dark Edition.

textfield_comment_value:
A relatively simple game with big, chunky dice and gorgeous window dressing. The artwork drew me in first, and the large six-sided dice and humorous power-up and bonus cards kept me in. Half the game is its visual charm and light humor, but I can't say I felt like I was truly a giant monster stomping around, destroying buildings and having epic battles. Rather, it's a competitive points-acquisition/dice-rolling game centered around a king of the hill mechanic. 

Conceptually, where are the other monsters if they're not "in" Tokyo (the tiny board that comes with the game)? Why does one monster's attacks within a giant city impact every other monster not in the city next to him/her? It doesn't make much sense, but it's so pretty and simple you don't mind. Humorous and ridiculous scenarios on the item and bonus cards (often showing monsters that aren't one of the base set you can play as) help spur your imagination and visualize epic battles.

You can win by acquiring 20 points first or by eliminating all the other monsters. If you get knocked out of the game by losing all your life points, however, you hope for the remaining players/monsters to wrap it up quickly, which may or may not happen with the tug of war that can happen with certain item cards' hail Mary moves.

As for whether to get the expansions, I'd definitely recommend the (Panda-kai) Powered Up expansion as it makes the selection of monster actually have meaning. The Powered Up expansion provides unique ability cards that each monster can earn by rolling three hearts. Only in this way does each monster have a unique ability set and personality. Otherwise, the depth of your monster selection in the base game has about as much meaning and impact as the rest of the theme-- it's pure window dressing. That being said, Powered Up's monster-specific cards don't do as much as I'd like, as the odds of you acquiring and using more than one or two of them (out of a set of 12) in a given game is slim.

Thankfully, the base game, and the ability to roll and re-roll dice to your liking is fun enough on its own. King of Tokyo is a great gateway game-- light and pretty-- and a nice way to start up or end a night of gaming. Recommended.

Positives
- Easy to pick up and play
- Fantastic graphic design and theme
- Plays fast, encouraging "just one more round"
- For a game centered on dice rolling, it's nice you can always re-roll as many dice as you like at least twice

Negatives
- Theme is only skin-deep
- Monsters aren't unique without Powered Up expansion
- Easy to get knocked out of the game early and be sitting around waiting for it to end
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Comme Zombie Dice, King of Tokyo s’inspire du yam’s, du moins en ce qui concerne la méthode de lancer des dés. Trois lancers, avec après chaque lancer la possibilité de conserver ou relancer les dés de son choix. La meilleure stratégie consiste à avoir de la chance aux dés, en obtenant des brelans et, selon les besoins du moment, des baffes ou des soins. Le seul vrai choix tactique consiste à savoir si c’est bien le moment d’entrer dans Tokyo, en posant sa figurine au centre du plateau, afin de pouvoir frapper tout le monde et prétendre à la victoire, mais au risque de se faire frapper par tous.

King of Tokyo un jeu de dés assez basique et brutal, dans une édition superbe mais peut-être inutilement luxueuse. Les nombreuses et puissantes cartes action, la possibilité d’entrer dans Tokyo ou de quitter la ville, donnent au jeu un côté un peu baroque, un peu délirant, que n’ont pas d’autres jeux de dés. Surtout, King of Tokyo apporte un élément réjouissant absent de la plupart des jeux de ce type, la possibilité de mettre des baffes à ses voisins.

Le genre yam’s amélioré et thématisé est dans l’air, même s’il n’est pas vraiment nouveau. Zombie Dice, et le plus ancien jeu des cochons, ont pour eux une certaine sobriété, une simplicité classique. King of Tokyo, à l’inverse, fait le choix de l’orientalisme baroque. En plus sophistiqué et plus tactique, il y a aussi Dice Town ou Alea Jacta Est. À chacun de choisir selon ses goûts.

Mai 2011
---
Like Zombie Dice, King of Tokyo is built on the Yahtzee dice rolling rule – one can roll dice three times, and keep the dice he wants after each roll. The basic strategy in King of Tokyo is to have lucky rolls, with lots of hits and three of a kind. The only real, and relatively obvious, tactical choice is whether to enter Tokyo, in order to hit all opponents at once and try to seize the victory, but with the risk of being hit by everyone.

At its heart, King of Tokyo is a fast, basic and brutal dice game, deliberately overproduced. The many action cards, and the possibility to enter or leave the town, make it a bit more zany and complex. A nice point is the possibility to directly hit opponents, something not possible in most Yahtzee variations.

Yahtzee variants with some chrome and a fun theme are not a new thing, but they seem to be in the air. Zombie Dice and Pass the Pigs are simple classics, reduced to the core. King of Tokyo is a baroque orientalist construction. There are also more tactical and sophisticated games such as Dice Town or Alea Jacta Est. Depending on your taste, you can get one or another.

May 2011
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Reduced rating from 8.5 to 7.5 because the base rules really lead to an uninspired game play where whoever rolls 3's wins. I'd raise it to 8.5 or perhaps 9 if I could figure out the right combination of house-rules to improve the game.

(original comment) Just a lot of dice-rolling fun.  The theme goes a LONG way with me, and the short time making the inevitable vagaracies of luck more bearable.

Only problem with the rules to me was the lack of victory points for staying in Tokyo 1 whole turn. 2 measly VPs for surviving that many attacks (in larger player games) is not nearly enough motivation to suffer so much risk.

After thinking about it, I want to try the number of VP's = # of players still in the game
For example, if there's 2 players, it's 2 VPs.
4 players, 4 VP's for starting the turn in Tokyo.
And for 6 players, it's 6 VP.
Yes, this sounds overpowering. However, I strongly feel the game should be decided by whoever conquers Tokyo the most/longest, AND even 6 VP's is not that much compared to "3" rolls and cards, AND you have to take your lumps and stay in Tokyo all the way to your next turn. It should give motivation to the players to beat the crap out of the ballsy monster in the city. In a 6-player game, a monster would have to stay in Tokyo till their 5th straight turn to win!

Other possible house rules:
Nobody is going to use 3 1's to score one measly VP unless they are the last dice to come up. 
All 1's should be Energy. Energy is the entire currency which is required to make the game more than just a dice-throwing luck-fest. There needs to be more energy available to the players, and eliminating the 1 and making it an Energy seems an easy way to do that.

Oh - house rule #3 : 
All players start with 3 Energy. Gets the action and choices happening faster.

Other potential house rules:
a) Use 5 face-up cards instead of 3 (or maybe 1 per player?)
b) Wings may be overpowered - remove the card from the game
c) At beginning of game, draw 5 cards and keep up to 7 Energy's worth of cards  OR  Everyone starts with 1 Keep card and gets Energy equal to the difference between their card and the highest player's card.
d) Cards may be bought before you roll dice.
e) A rolled Energy is worth 2 Energy cubes, not 1.
(not actively considering the following) f) Every opponent's turn you are in Tokyo, you get 1 Energy.
g) When in Tokyo, after resolving dice, you get 1 free wipe of the cards, if desired.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Ein 'Würfelspiel' à la "Kniffel", nur mit gegenseitigem Angriff und großen Monstern und so :).

Wer an der Reihe ist, würfelt mit allen sechs Würfeln bis zu dreimal und darf jedes Mal beliebige davon beiseitelegen. Spätestens nach dem dritten Wurf müssen alle Ergebnisse genutzt werden.
Mit der 'Tatze' wird Schaden auf die Monster der anderen Spieler verteilt.
Mit 'Energie' erhält man Energieressourcen, mit denen Karten, mit diversen Sondereigenschaften, aus der offenen Auslage gekauft werden können.
'Herzen' sind dafür da, das eigene Monster von Schaden zu heilen und für Drillinge der Zahlenwerte '1', '2' oder '3' werden entsprechende Siegpunkte generiert.
Auf diese Weise ist ein Spieler nach dem anderen am Zug, bis es einer auf 20 Siegpunkte schafft oder als letztes, überlebendes Monster übrig bleibt. Der ultimative Sieg gehört natürlich demjenigen, der beide Bedingungen gleichzeitig erfüllt! ;)

"King of Tokyo" ist sehr kurzweilig und spielt sich überaus schnell. Durch die kurze Spieldauer ist der hohe Glücksfaktor, sowie das Ausscheiden von Mitspielern gar nicht mal so tragisch, wenn auch weiterhin keine gute Spielmechanik.
Knifflig und spannend sind Entscheidungen wie: 'Bleibe ich mit fünf Lebensenergien noch in Tokyo oder ziehe ich mich lieber zurück?'
Wer entscheidet drin zu bleiben, erhält wertvolle Punkte, läuft aber Gefahr von den anderen Spielern ausgeschaltet zu werden!
Ein sehr schönes Spiel für den Ausklang oder den Start eines Spieleabends, aber auch sehr zu empfehlen, um neue Spieler ins Hobby zu ziehen.

Mit der Erweiterung "Power Up" erhalten die Spieler bei jedem Wurf von drei oder mehr 'Herzen' eine Power-Up Karte des eigenen Monsters, die mit individuellen Fähigkeiten aufwartet und so eine schöne Asynchronität und Individualität für die verschiedenen Monster ins Spiel bringen.
Eine richtig gute Erweiterung.

Die Minierweiterung "Noch Boshafter!" führt nun auch endlich die Bosheit-Skala der "Dark Edition" in die bunte Version ein. Sie erlaubt ein Voranschreiten bei einem '1-er'* oder '2-er' Drilling, was die relativ schwachen Würfelergebnisse etwas aufwertet. Sobald ein Spieler eine bestimmte Schwelle auf der Leiste erreicht, schaltet er sich eine mächtige Sonderfähigkeit nach eigener Wahl frei! Diese Fähigkeiten werden von Schwelle zu Schwelle stärker und spielentscheidender. Doch die Schritte müssen auch erst mal erwürfelt werden!
Ebenfalls eine sehr gute Erweiterung.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
““Nuclear waste turned him from a harmless grub into a 350 foot tall monster that attacked Tokyo.” - President Hathaway

GAMEPLAY
Players take on the role of giant monsters set on rampaging through Tokyo and bashing each other. Each turn the players roll 6 dice Yahtzee style with 2 re-rolls to build energy, attack other players, score victory points, and heal. The objective of the games is to build up 20 victory points or destroy all of the other monsters. Buying power cards with stored energy brings in victory points, augments your dice rolls, or interferes with other players. Stomping into Tokyo builds your victory points but it makes you the center of attention. The game board consists of only the single space (two for 5 to 6 player games) which creates the dramatic tension of the game mechanic. One of the great decisions mid-game after there are fewer players is whether to hold the middle. Games move quickly form turn to turn and none of my games has taken longer than 30 minutes to finish making it possible to play several times or as a filler while waiting for other people to show.

COMPONENTS
The art style is fun and evocative. Monster stands are of thick card and all the images have strong colors. I would have like to see miniatures for the monsters but that isn’t really the point of the game. The box insert is just right for the existing components in the box but there is already one expansion so I don’t think it will fit.

THEME
Giant monsters attack Tokyo. Simple, easy to understand and fun. Monsters are easy to recognize and mimic many trademarked monsters from movies through the decades. The power cards are all over the map from destroying building for victory points to getting an extra head for more dice rolling.

WHO IS IT FOR?
KoT is easy to bring out with a broad range of players. Young kids can enjoy this game. There is some reading involved but if the adults are keeping the game moving kids as young as 6 should have fun. The game is for 2 to 6 players and can get pretty wild with a full group. Because the game is short (20 to 30 minutes) and the rules are basic, it can be played with anyone passingly interested in sitting down. Monster noises encouraged.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Correct game with short simple rules that delivers a fair amount of fun adding powers to your monster while you need to adapt your dice re-roll focus to the always changing situations. However, willing or not, scoring 20 stars happens always all of a sudden too fast and too easy, which ends the game too soon for my taste, before you or others had really much time to buy enough cards or enjoy the few ones you were able to get in that short time (because some of them feel a bit expensive sometimes, or its effect not that good really).

Despite the many ways to heal wounds the nasty "Player Elimination mechanism" is still there and it's either a mechanism you love or you won't really enjoy that eliminating or being eliminated part. In fact, my nieces HATE whenever a monster dies (not just theirs!). They seem to like a lot the whole re-rolling thing, getting lots of energy cubes (even more than actually using them to buy some of the cards, I would say) and wouldn't want the game to ever end, so they tend to re-roll all thier hits and do all sort of rule bendings/breakings to avoid monsters death at all costs. They seem to enjoy more the wealth accumulation side the game offers rather than the whole fighting, damaging and "eliminating" aspects of it. Maybe they are too young for a game like this, or too compassionate, or too greedy, or all together.

Without out-of-the-box asimetry, adding new unique powers from the cards is the substance of King of Tokyo, yet with some of their energy costs and renewal rate they are kind of hard to get in very short gameplays. I believe tweaking its cards market (to resemble that of "Stone Age" or "Through the Ages") to allow for eventually cheaper cards (and perhaps starting with a bit of energy to buy the first 2 cards or saving it for a more expensive one later) and of course setting a higher victory points goal (or adding the ability to slightly wound the stars marker too sometimes! instead of always the life marker!)... with such rules variants (some of which we have successfully tested already) I could rate "King of Tokyo" near the 8 perhaps, but it's still a good game as it is and I'm usually willing to play it ...if in the mood.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Two Player Value = Fair. Good game, just better with more players.


King of Tokyo is a simple dice game turned into a free-for-all brawl. It is silly and light. Nothing fancy or complicated.

In King of Tokyo players fight to victory. There are two methods of victory, the first to 20 points or eliminating all other players. Easy.

The whole game revolves around the dice roll. On your turn you get 3 rolls to build the best "hand" of dice. Then you use those dice to effect the game. You can attacks other players, heal yourself, score points or buy powerful cards to help you are hurt others. Players can also score points by controlling Tokyo.

The design is simple and efficient. The game is very basic, but it is meant to be. That is what makes it fun. It is supposed to be silly and light party game.

Everything else is fine, but not incredible. Rules. Artwork. Components. Theme. 

This game is very good with younger and new gamers.


Pros - 
- Easy to teach and learn
- Good party game


Cons - 
- Very simple game play could turn some away

Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
(New edition)

This is harmless, dice-rolling fun with a bit of a monster flavour paste job on top of it. It is only sort of a board game, as the board is only used to show whether players are in the Tokyo zone, or in the "not in Tokyo" zone. All of the monsters are identical but for the theme gloss, that said, don't try to take my Space Penguin away from me or there will be consequences.

The game is primarily about trying to roll sets of like dice using a pool of 6, 6-sided dice ala Yahtzee. You want sets of 3 for the VPs to score, whereas the lightning bolts power up your guy, the hearts heal him, and the claws allow you to deal damage to the players who are in the zone opposite of yours.

The victory mechanism is multi-faceted in that you can try to just go after VPs straight up (mostly by rolling number sets or occupying Tokyo by beating on the current monster there enough to make them want to leave) or you can try to get aggressive and knock the other players out instead. This second option seems to primarily be included as a potential way for people to catch up against a leader with a strong early VP lead.

The only real additional gloss on this game is the power cards. These are cute, and you only see a few of them each game so the mix should add some long term variety to the play. The downside, however, is that the cards are fairly pricey and the game is so short that it's hard to get full use out of them in some cases.

Anyway, it's nothing absolutely amazing, but it's charming filler and one that I am glad to have around in my collection. I would have liked a bit of a tweak to the cards, as I do think they don't come into play quite as much as I would like (as they do add variety) but overall it's hard to fault it. Short and fun.

The Power Up expansion is a pretty compulsory add to the game at this point for me as it differentiates the monsters by giving each of them additional powers. For anything but rank novice, young players it is something you can add to the game immediately and it adds a significant amount of interest.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
If you're looking for a party game with simple rules and relatively quick play-time, or if you're in the market for a game to introduce to your young child (maybe 6 or 7+ yrs old), this is the game for you.

KoT is extremely easy to learn, very smooth to play, and packs a lot of humor and whimsy in a small box. There isn't any real bean-counting that has to be done, as the little player "plaque" you have uses two sturdy little counter dials to keep track of your health and VP.

I can't say this enough: the theme and artwork are one of the strongest aspects of this game. Garfield et al clearly have a deep appreciation of the kaiju/monster movie genre, and it shows through in technicolor. My wife and I were giggling and reading out the flavor text on each power-up card that was flipped, and we've only seen 1/10th of the deck. I can't wait to see what other silly cards and beautiful designs lay in there!

The mechanics are a mix of push-your-luck dice-rolling, direct aggression, and some light strategy. Do you roll in an attempt to get energy cubes, or try and get more health? Or perhaps attack the monster in Tokyo, or [if YOU are that monster] attack everyone else? What about VP? Maybe you should roll for that!

The power-up cards are entertaining, and (as the name suggests) some are quite powerful! In another game, it might annoy me that some of the cards feel overpowered/unbalanced, but in KoT, it is all in service of the chaos and unpredictability of the game. Much like Love Letter or Ticket to Ride, people in the lead don't have an iron grip on their advantage, and the cards do much to shake up the ladder of players.

I love KoT, and I recommend it for anyone looking for a fun, light, and silly game to add to their collection. Eclipse or Power Grid this is not, so if Munchkin-style luck and aggression annoys you, you may wish to steer clear. However, if the theme appeals to you, and you have a spot in your collection for a simpler, lighter title, you can't go wrong with KoT.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Played this game several times and I honestly don't understand, why it's rated way higher than CV. In my opinion game is just overrated. 
First of all, I just hate player elimination mechanic. It's kinda ok, if it happens near game end, but here it may happen at the beginning of the game and eliminated player has to sit alone somewhere for 30 minutes, while other play. This is unacceptable for "party game".
Second thing I just don't like here is too much randomness. You cannot expect much of a strategy from a dice rolling game, but in CV you can buy cards (and do it easilly, after first turn), which grant you additional tokens or can help you transform rolled tokens into others, in other words to decrease randomness. 
Here you also can buy cards, but they usually don't provide bonuses to change rolled symbols, plus good luck buying them during the first turns. 

And to illustrate this problems, I'm going to tell you about my last playthrough. We played with 6 persons and we had a base game.
So during the first roll, I didn't get anything useful at all (just got numbers and heart tokens, even after reroll), one of the players got 3 VP and 3 cash tokens (3,3,3 plus 3 dices with lightning), so he bought a card granting him +2 damage, if he rolls 2,2,2.
One of the players also got to the one of the city spots.
On my next turn I rolled 1 damage token. I tried to reroll it, but after all rerolls, I still had damage token, so I had to go to the city, 
The player, who bought a card, rolled 2,2,2 and 3 damage, so he gave me a 5 damage (so I lost half of my hitpoints), I swapped place in a city with him (other player remained in the city), then 2nd player in a city rolled 5 damage and one lightning, so he dealt 5 damage to everyone, who was outside the city, so I lost my 2nd half of hitpoints and got eliminated in first 5 minutes of the game. 
Really "fun" game.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
The very first time I played King of Tokyo I fear I made myself look a bit like nerdy Sheldon for not wanting to continue a statistically completely lost position (meaning I'd end up second, not a bad result for sure). Well, my opponents retorted, isn't it cool that you then win through sheer luck??! No, I replied, that's just dumb, as rolling beter is not really an achievement I want to rely on. And so I proclaimed the other player the deserved #1 (she had a wonderful combo lying in front of her), and we went on playing a different game. After that I did not expect to play King of Tokyo anymore, but a friend of mine bought it, and 'made' me play. To my bemusement, and the other players' annoyance, I found I'm quite good at it, finishing first or second nearly every time. So when I'm challenged again, I always mockingly joke that the players [i]must[/i] have a thing for masochism, seeing that they enjoy being beaten up so thoroughly every time. This infuriates them to the point of taking too many risks, and me beating the crap out of them once more. 

Game-technically King of Tokyo is of course just another Yahtzee-clone, spiced up with fictional Big Monster artwork. Poor Tokyo is just backdrop; and to be honest, once the game is done, I'm not sure there'd be much of the city left to crown the victor 'King of Tokyo'. It's 'King of What Is Left of Tokyo', I fear. There isn't much to talk about it, save, perhaps, the player elimination. The game is short enough that it can be stomached, although it is pushing matters in the 6 player-game. Apart from that, relax, and eat radioactive dice attack!

[b]Update[/b] Many years after what I wrote above I found myelf taking on the role of Cyberkitty... who beat the rest to a bloody pulp in seven or eight turns flat. Still got it :sauron:...

Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
By all rights a dice game with lots of luck using player elimination shouldn't be fun. This one is great. Player elimination is used in just the right way. The dice rolling has enough strategy in it that the luck adds excitement not meaninglessness, the components are fun, appropraite and likable. People have complain that a given game doesn't use very many of the cards available... how is this bad? This means any given game your unlikely to repeat the same cards over and over and there's always plenty of variety. The expansion is strong though it doesn't add much--the expansion should be a better value--but this is often the case with small expansions. This game is one of the few board games that actually plays well as a "party" game of 6 people without resorting to not having a board. For family, for adults having parties, for gatherings, I can't recommend this game highly enough for how strong it is. People have complained that certain strategies just trump others; this is not the case. If you think you can just "roll for numbers" this is easily countered once someone realizes what you're doing. Likewise, just going for kills doesn't always make sense either. There is no "cheat" or "perfect" strategy for this game and you have to adapt. If a strategy seemed perfect its only because your opponents failed to adapt to it. Luck is a factor but don't let dice make you think this has more luck than many euro games that incorporate luck but dont even have dice. Overall, great game. I rate this according to the criteria BGG provides.

This game continues to just be a fairly shallow but incredibly awesome and fun crowd pleaser. An essential game for my collection.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
King of Tokyo is one of a number of light-weight dice games to come out in the last couple years.  It's got master designer, Richard Garfield's considerable talent behind it which gives it a leg up against other games competing for the same space in my closet.

KoT is a game of King of the Hill mixed with classic Yahtzee.  Rolling dice will do damage to other players, heal your own wounds, or give you points or energy.

Almost all dice games can suffer if they go on too long and this can certainly happen in King of Tokyo.  Games will usually only last about 30 minutes, but the ones that go longer feel WAY too long.

This is a problem made worse by the fact that King of Tokyo does have player elimination.  In my mind player elimination is always a weakness in a design.  It's a flaw that can be mitigated by short play-time, but I pretty much always dislike it when players get knocked out of a game.

So what I end up with is a somewhat uneven impression of the game.  When it is working -- when you have a buncha monsters slugging it out with lots of cool special powers on the table, and when the game is short (under 30 minutes), it's a very fun and very easy-to-play filler.  

but there are games that drag on for too long and end up being sort of boring.

the one bit of warning I would offer is that if all players are ONLY focusing on killing the other monsters (which is probably most gamers' natural tendency), the game has a much better chance of dragging on for too long.  The "victory by points" is a pretty reliable timer as long as one or two players at the table are keeping that as an option for winning.

Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
King of Tokyo is a light, beer-and-pretzels style game with a quick playing time and a healthy dose of luck. It also scales wonderfully from 2-6 players, though I think it's just plain more fun with more monsters - ah, I mean, players.

The premise of the game is basically the same as [thing=17835][/thing]. That is to say, it's not JUST Godzilla or King Kong, it's ALL THE MONSTERS and they are going to kill each other, not just the planet. The cardboard stand-ups of the monsters are high-quality and have great cartoony illustrations. It has a bunch of custom dice and some special power cards which are really what make the game shine.

Just as in Yahtzee or [thing=37380]Roll Through the Ages[/thing], you take a fistful of dice and get three rolls, keeping whatever you want from the previous roll and re-rolling the rest. The goal is to either kill all the other monsters or get 20 points. The dice have various combinations that get you points, healing, attacks on other monsters or energy. Energy is the currency of the game and is used to buy special cards.

As you would expect from Richard Garfield, these cards all break the game in various ways, changing the rules just for your monster so he has a leg up on the other critters. There are tons of these cards; it will probably take 4-5 games (depending on the number of players) to see them all, even if you set aside the ones you already used. 

If I had to describe this game in one word it would be "addicting". I can't think of another game that creates more of a feeling of "just one more game" than this one.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
Maybe you have some non-gamer friends. Maybe they have no interest in playing games whatsoever. Maybe you haven't been able to play games with them because you know they'd think board games are lame.

King of Tokyo is the game you want to show them. You tell them it's a game about smashing each other, you explain the rules in two minutes, and you start playing.

And it will be awesome, 100% guaranteed.

I've never played a game that delivers what it promises as consistently as King of Tokyo. Yeah, it's filler. But it's filler that lets you pursue different strategies, has a lot of direct player interaction, and has enough variety to play several games in a single night and never be bored.

There's a lot to like about this game, but the best thing is that it's simple enough to be played (and enjoyed!) by almost anyone while still complex enough to provide all but the most complexity-craving experts with interesting decisions. The second best thing (or best, depending on your viewpoint) is that it's short (30 mins max). This makes the player elimination less of a problem.

[EDIT: I played this with a different group and it was not short. They took foreeeeeeeeever. It made te game way less fun...you really need to keep the game moving for this one to work]

King of Tokyo is a great game that can appeal to a very wide range of players. I absolutely recommend trying this no matter what type of player you are, and that's not something I can say for very many games.

#3 on personal list "Top 10 games for a new gamer to own"
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
This game is simple, quick and pretty fun.  I play with kids, and I imagine that if you play with a lively group of adults it could be over-the-top fun.  As it is, we're enjoying it more and more as we get more familiar with the different power-up cards and the best way to exploit them.  It's also very nice to look at in a playful way.  One knock against it is that all the monsters are the same -- it seems like the monsters could have balanced, special powers that make choosing your avatar more meaningful than just prefering the look of your cardboard counter.  But as it is, the game mechanic is still unique and a lot of fun and involves some risk management and meaningful decision making, and KOT is one of those games where you really never know who is going to win or be eliminated until it actually happens.  You can have a guy about to win on VP get suddenly eliminated from the game by a hot attack role from an opponent.  That always keeps a game interesting to the end.  I don't like games (Monopoly, Conquest of Nerath, etc) where you can get into a hole and know you are never climbing out, but you have to keep slogging on waiting to lose.  One drawback, however, is that a player (or more) can get eliminated early and have nothing to do while the game goes on.

Also, setup is very fast and the games are short, and it's important to have a few games like that in the house for the days when you don't have hours to spend.

textfield_comment_value: I played it several times with my regular group, both vanilla and with several expansions. I believe the game is best with 3 or 4 players, since with 5 or 6 it get's long and tedious. While the mechanics are very simple and you can teach the game within few minutes, it does provide enough entertainment value. In the basegame it practically doesn't matter which monster you pick as they are merely cosmetic choices. The luck component is pretty high in this game, which might not be an issue for some but a major-turn off for others: The core mechanic is casting a set of dice yahtzee-style (roll once, re-roll any number of dice up to two times). Depending on your results, you either attack other monsters, heal, gain points required for victory or gain energy required to buy cards. A major issue of the game, however, is that players whose monster was defeated are eliminated from the game and spend the remaining time waiting. This is often not that much of an issue in small groups, but in a 5 or 6 player game, waiting for an hour might be a bit frustrating and boring. Other than that, the game is pretty fast-paced and usually doesn't take too long to play if you play with a maximum of 4 players, so it's a good filler if you have some spare time after a longer gaming session, but it provides too little diversity to be in the spotlight of a boardgame-session by itself.

textfield_comment_value:
Good monster fighting game.  The goal of the game is to be the first player to reach 20 victory point or to be the only one alive.

On your turn, you have to roll the 6 dice up to 3 times (you can keep dice between roll).  The dice have the following faces :
1 : gives you 1 victory point if you have 3 (+1 VP for each other 1).
2 : gives you 2 VP if you have 3 (+1 VP for each other 2).
3 : gives you 3 VP if you have 3 (+1 VP for each other 3).
Energy : each of those gives you 1 energy cube (can be use to purchase card that gives you special power).
Heart symbol : each of those gives you 1 health point back.
Monster hand : each of those cause 1 point of damage to the monster(s) you're attacking.

Your monster can be in Tokyo or outside Tokyo.  When in Tokyo, the monster can't use heart symbol to heal.  There's only place for one monster in Tokyo (except for 5-6 player game).  Attack are made to the monster(s) that are not at the same place as you are (if you're in Tokyo, you attack all the monster that aren't in Tokyo and vice versa).
Each time the monster in Tokyo is attacked, he chooses to stay or leave.  If he leaves, the monster that attack him goes in Tokyo.
Each time a monster enters Tokyo he gain 1 VP.
Each time a monster is in Tokyo when his turn begin, he gain 2 VP.

The game end when a player reach 20 VP or when there's only one monster alive.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value: Lots of fun with a beautiful theme which helps bring what's really nothing but a dice game to life. A turn is simply rolling 6 dice with 2 re-rolls. Dice can give you VP's (if you get a set of 1's, 2's or 3's), can inflict damage on players not in your location (you're either in Tokyo trying to earn points if you can hang in there until the start of your next turn, or you’re outside Tokyo whaling on those in Tokyo trying to earn points), heal thyself, or earn cubey things, enough of which will allow you to buy a card from the display of 3 with either immediate or ongoing effects. So, go for what you want, re-roll away, whale away, heal thyself, buy good stuff, earn VPs. Die last or get to 20VPs first. Turns are fast. It's a fun decision whether to keep or re-roll damage if it's going in on Tokyo as it's a double-edged sword - they're allowed to move out if they get damage and that forces you in ... at least until you cop it next and you'll be faced with the decision on should you stay or should go ('cause if you go there will be trouble, but if you stay it will be double). So the game is one of trying to stay alive, be on the righteous side of where the damage is going as much as possible and accumulate those VPs as you go. Easy to learn, easy to play, easy to laugh, just a little too much downtime (with lots of players) to really bring it home.

textfield_comment_value:
? Game explanation:
In the popular push your luck game King of Tokyo, you try to defeat opponents to become the boss of Tokyo. Each player chooses a player character with corresponding player board. On your turn, you roll the 6 black dice and they determine your actions. You may roll a maximum of 3 times and you may put dice aside in between and roll again. With the dice you can collect victory points (3 of the same value give you that amount of points), heal your monster (hearts), collect energy (lightning) to buy upgrades (power card) and you can attack other monsters (paw) and thus move to Tokyo. If you stand outside Tokyo, the player in Tokyo loses life points. If you stand in Tokyo, then all players outside Tokyo lose life points. If you stand in Tokyo and lose lives, you may choose to leave Tokyo. If you stand in Tokyo at the beginning of your turn, you receive 2 points, if you move to Tokyo, you also receive one point. If you run out of lives, you have lost. If you are first to reach 20 points or last to remain, you win the game.

⭐ Our review:
King of Tokyo is a well-known game by @iello_fr and plays very smoothly and fun. The game looks cool. However, you do sometimes have to get lucky with throwing the dice, which makes the luck factor definitely play a big role in this game as well. King of Tokyo can be expanded with many expansions.

textfield_comment_value:
Full Review: http://manualgamer.com/king-of-tokyo-review/

Tokyo smashing goodness!  In King of Tokyo, players get to be giant monsters rampaging through Tokyo, causing as much chaos and mayhem as possible.  It is fast, fun and fantastic for families and casual gamers.

Essentially, it is Yahtzee with giant monsters and super powers.

Fun and light, with different strategies depending on what others are doing, and the cards that are available.  Shall I rush Tokyo and smash down my opponents?  Shall I sit in the background and go for point victory?  Shall I power up my character with various abilities?

King of Tokyo is incredibly easy to learn and teach.  The amount of luck involved means that brand new players have plenty of opportunity to win against seasoned veterans.

Sometimes the interaction between particular power-up cards isn’t clear.  Fortunately this is a rare occurrence, and if players can’t agree then there is a fist full of monster dice to help settle any argument.

Players who have difficulty with being eliminated may need some assistance and coaxing to play (adults or children).  However given the short play time and the amount of luck involved in this game, players shouldn’t take elimination too personally.

While this game does play with 2 players, doing so loses much of the interaction that comes with 3 plus players.

textfield_comment_value:
Yathzee-style dice rolling game for action determination.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Theme
+ Artwork and components
+ Yathzee-style dice roll and 2 re-roll (press your luck) for simple action determination
+ Energy cubes needed to buy cards: grant special abilities
+ Simple combat between players (competitive)
+ Plays well with higher player counts
+ Staying in Tokyo grants points, but all players are bashing the monster in Tokyo
+ Quick playing time (about 30m)
+ Easy to teach

[b]Neutrals:[/b]
# Can be mixed with King of New York
# A lot of expansions (new monsters, new evolution cards, different monster abilities)
# Potential gateway or family game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Big game box for a little game
- Player elimination
- Luck prone
- Quite complex for a party game

[b]Similar games:[/b]

* King of New York (very similar gameplay, more complex, buildings and military units, multiple areas to move to)
* Arena: For the Gods! (game ends when the first player dies, no player elimination, grid movement, auction for new equipment with health points)
* Dice Throne (similar gameplay best for 2 player count)
* Yahtzee
* Bang: The Dice Game (Yathzee-style dice game with hidden roles and characters with unique powers)
* Bloodborne: The Card Game (different gameplay, card-driven, similar complexity and game length, take-that, kind of semi-cooperative)

textfield_comment_value:
I love the theme and artwork, but I feel the balance / mechanisms of this game are off in quite a few ways:
1) 2-player game completely does not work (bgg poll reflects this with >80% not recommended, so I won't elaborate).
2) Victory points in center are not proportional to # opponents / allies. So I feel far too little bonus for 4-player game, and far too much for a 2-player game. This changes as players are eliminated, but doesn't make it balanced.
3) Game can be won without ever fighting! This makes me sad since I've seen it happen several times, and it contradicts the entire theme.
4) Power cards feel pretty imbalanced (e.g. sometimes costs most of 2 rounds to get one decent card, other times 2 cheap cards combine to give an easy win).
5) Decisions rarely substantial/difficult. Most of the time my initial roll narrows my reasonable strategic choices pretty drastically (at most one or two possibilities). So I don't feel I'm playing the game nearly as much as the dice are. To be fair, the cards add a bit to this (if multiple are useful). Choosing when to exit Tokyo is usually not a hard choice though.

FWIW I have high-ish win rate (~50% for 4-5 player games) against more serious gamers than myself, so I doubt I'm missing something. Maybe just need to treat the game as a light social activity and not look for depth here.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
This was a HUGE hit with my friends, which is a big bonus for me because it gets everybody together and excited for gaming! The monsters are awesome, the superpowers are full of diversity, and the risk/reward of entering/exiting the city push the intensity skyward. 

I guess the real selling point for me is the fact that I've always loved Yahtzee mechanics, but Yahtzee itself feels so hollow. The different methods of achieving victory also add to why I like it. You can try to go all out with attacks or try for the points or try for some cards that may give you the edge in both scenarios. I wasn't sure I'd really like this game, but when I found it on sale and tried it with some friends, it wasn't until we were playing and then playing again and then playing again that I realized how brilliant and fun it was.

This is a great example of a game that fills a role in my collection. So often, I only desire games that are full of strategy and slow-burn progression, with story elements and special abilities. Those games are usually pretty time-consuming and difficult to get to the table with certain groups, so I need games that I can enjoy when I'm unable to get my favorite fix. And it's to the credit of these kinds of games that they fill that void and do it so well. That's reason enough for it to be high on my list.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
King of Tokyo is a custom Yahtzee dice-chucking, king of the hill style dustup with some resource management and character development, overlaid with a giant monster theme.  My favorite monster is Cyber Bunny.  The goal is to deplete your opponents of all health points, or to gain 20 victory points.  You can also gain energy to purchase cards that add one time or permanent special abilities or effects, the more expensive, the greater the effect on gameplay.  Atop the hill (or "in Tokyo" or "Tokyo Bay" in a 5-6 player game) makes you unable to heal life points, but also capable of damaging all opponents (they can only attack you), and gaining victory points every turn you remain king of the hill.  

There's no reason to get King of New York or the second edition of King of Tokyo.  It's a simple game, but at the time it set the world on fire.  It should be enjoyed for what it is-- a lighthearted romp with giant monsters violently and ridiculously clashing over "victory points" or bopping each other to death.  It features player elimination, which is ok because the games are fast.  If a game goes longer than 20 minutes, something has probably gone wrong.  It was one of the first hobby games I got, and I played it, will probably always keep it in my collection, but don't play it regularly any more.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
All Yahtzee-family games have been dry and boring. Not so with King of Tokyo, where the card upgrades provide an excellent shot in the arm. It also combats the "all faces of the die are good in their own way" syndrome by layering VPs and health on the game as trade-offs. The two objectives conflict through the decision on whether to man up in Tokyo, resulting in great dynamism in deciding what to go for with the dice.

This is the best '3-attempt' dice game by far, and it has brought the fun back to the retread genre.

It doesn't scale very well, however. All Yahtzee descendants play best with 2 or 3 intrinsically due to downtime, but with KoT, the lowered viability of being King in Tokyo with more players further deteriorates the game at higher player counts. It's reached the stage where nobody dares to go into Tokyo. Think about it: with 6 players, that's at least 5 turns of people whacking you, and at least 10 other-player turns before you get a chance to heal, if you want the 2 VP. I want to try the "Gain 1 energy at the start of each player turn while you're in Tokyo" variant if we play with 5 or 6.

[hr]
Nah, I think the player scaling is fine, just different. Live and adapt. It just raises the stakes for going into Tokyo, which all players then account for. Raised design from 4 to 5.

textfield_comment_value:
Let me start by saying that I would kill to have a shirt that has the Urbavore on it (it only eats urban areas!) This is another game I was introduced to at a friend's birthday party. And the first round I was just watching and cheering the destruction on! The people who didn't know me were shocked at how much I was getting into the game (Crush that monster! You call two damage a lot? Go back to the slime pit you crawled out of!) But come on, who doesn't love the cheesy old giant monster movies? Gamera anyone? 

This game combines my favorite things: clever cards, cute art, and utter DESTRUCTION! The first time I got to play, I got crushed before I could even have a turn – which admittedly did make me angry – but I calmed down, got back in the game, and played jointly with my husband (who is great at calming my wild rages). And while we didn't win the next game either, it was a ton of fun. 

But the third game was the one that we rocked! We had to perfect storm of cards – a card that allowed us to reroll all “3”s and a card where if you roll one of every symbol on six dice we gain 10 points. We did that twice. 20 points from two otherwise useless rolls. It was glorious. The cards really can change the dynamic of the game. And this is one I will definitely be playing again.

textfield_comment_value: A lightweight Cosmic Encounter, with a lot less of that direct and humorously bizarre player interaction. It feels like "no one asked for this" applies, but, maybe with the goofy art and simple dice chucking Yahtzee mechanics, this game works for the young ones. It is also nicely thematic, but in an "oh that's neat" kind of way--its theme really doesn't add much or paint you a story in your mind. Each of the monsters are very different, and have special powers, and are 100% balanced (oh, definitely not, but what freak is try-harding this game? deal them out randomly). It's biggest Achilles heel is certainly the fact that it is an area control game with two locations. Your home base and Tokyo. You are either center stage, wrecking Tokyo, losing health but scoring points, or charging up your batteries back at home. It has a very action-figure, toy-like feel with this arrangement. The problem is when everyone is just taking pot-shots with special abilities and what not from outside the city. It's just kind of random--you won't know how long you can stay, and its that weird combo of having a pretty much no hidden info in a game, and yet way too much shit to predict. You want to form and plan but you just give in. It's not so much a game, but an excuse to play with some toys.
Title: King of Tokyo

textfield_comment_value:
In the late '00s, there was a wave of criticism of the then current crop of Eurogames as being JASE (just another soulless euro).  There was definitely truth to this, as many euro designs were heading down the path of jumbling together a bunch of cube pushing mechanisms that worked well but lacked theme or immersion or the ephemeral "fun."

Well, the pendulum has now swung completely in the opposite direction with King of Tokyo.  Monsters!  Yay!  It has theme!  But ... it is basically Yahtzee with 95% or more of the decisions removed.  So what has been created here is not the themeless game, but the gameless theme.  Once you get over the fact that it has monsters battling in Tokyo (which surprisingly few seem to be able to look past) you find ... nothing.  There is no real game here.  I'm completely baffled that it gets so much love.  No real decisions at all, the always intriguing prospect of getting eliminated so you can watch two others roll dice at each other for 15 minutes, and did I mention no decisions?  If you're really in the mood for something this pointless and mindless, why not just turn off your brain entirely and watch some reality tv?  Just to keep your games played log numbers up?

But ... it has monster!  Yay!  So I'll bump it up from a 1 rating to a 2.

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] I played Splendor years ago and I remember strongly disliking it. Even still, having replayed it on Board Game Arena, I can say I still do not enjoy playing Splendor. 

Gather cards and collect spices to generate an engine capable of racing other people toward scoring cards? I love it (Century: Spice Road). Race for cards to establish rail roads along a track, connecting different points and denying opponents of different scoring opportunities of long railroad tracks? Enjoy it (Ticket to Ride). Establish colonies in sectors using cards to advance your gold and victory point production engines based on probabilities and dice rolls? I get it, but I just don't seem to generally enjoy dice games (Space Base). Forge dice to directly change the odds of your resource generation? I get it, but I'm not a dice person (Dice Forge). 

I seem to understand the flow of Splendor and I can recognize why, for example, reserving cards is actually incredibly beneficial. I can tell that strategies need to remain malleable for players to remain competitive. I can also tell that there exists a solid amount of luck, but *generally* that luck is, at least, manageable. At the same time, playing Splendor like an engine-builder will likely make you regret making certain choices when the cards necessary to put your engine to use suddenly vanish from the shop, or the game will be over by the time you're done setting up. 

The review titled "Splendor after 70 plays: observations and strategic tidbits" notes a few things to which I wish to pull from:
(1) "Splendor is not an engine-building game, nor is it about doggedly pursuing that one Moby Dick of a 5 VP card. It’s a game of getting to 15 VP before your opponent(s), and 15 VP is an intentionally awkward number."
(2) "The fun is in responding, not (or at least not wholly) in scheming";
(3) "Neither the game nor your opponents will let you pursue your agenda unchallenged, and it often feels like a puzzle with a time limit and no definite solution. You either embrace this feeling or you don’t."

The 'situational enjoyment' (as Kurt described it 8 years ago) was clearly not to my liking. It reminds me of some older dexterity games that require players to spontaneously react to things in front of them instead of a deep, strategic experience. Sure, maybe Splendor is not random and not anti-strategic, but I cannot look past the dry exterior of Splendor to find that fun, spontaneous game play. This is not a game that I can relish in the chaos of ever-changing dynamics - and, part of it I think is that nothing ever feels in control. Whether I win or I lose, there's something bothering me about the experience; like, the best I get out of Splendor is a sigh of relief that it is over. I don't get to say "So close - maybe if I took that red thingimajig sooner to duplicate my blue doohickey to produce my yellow thingummywhat sooner, then maybe I could have scored enough to secure the final whatchamacallum" like after playing many engine builders. I don't find myself holding my head out of sheer exasperation that something like the end-game arcs of Ticket to Ride or Castles of Burgundy would induce. I don't go jumping out of my chair in the final stages of a close point salad game like Barenpark where victory is usually only a couple of points apart. Part of that may be because 15 victory points is completely arbitrary - not only is it awkward, it's a lot less easily identifiable compared to something like Century's 5 victory point cards, to which perhaps scoring only 3 high-value cards might be better than racing to fulfill the end-game condition. There are little tidbits that playing Splendor with better opponents will steadily teach you about the flow of the game at a higher-level, but I'm not sure I care enough to ever find out.

To me, it just feels as over as it started - it's like you're making progress in solving some complex calculus problem and the teacher yells "pencils down!" because Timmy finished the test first and Timmy remembered the solution to half of the questions from the homework questions he reviewed 5 minutes prior. Do not ask me why I thought this example makes any sense - perhaps mild PTSD from my years in school. I would be probably be looking at Timmy calling him a lucky weasel ruining it for the rest of us.

For example, in one game: all 4 nobles consisted of Black/Red/White, and but my dumb brain decided to heavily invest in Blue for... no reason. I just did not properly recognize what the cards I was gathering were working me toward until at least the mid-game, where I realized my two opponents were likely in a fierce battle for those three aforementioned colors (before one just started securing Green cards for no apparent reason). On the top row was a 7 Blue card and a 7 Blue 3 Green card that I realized my opponents were never going to work toward; eventually, a 5 Blue and a 6 Blue showed up in the middle row granting... more Blue. I won the game in what felt like 5 back-to-back turns just by being at the right place at the right time. Hooray, I guess? The game crawled its way past the early-game setup, and right as people started making moves, the game was over.

In the end, Splendor just made me want to play a game like Jaipur or Lost Cities instead - simple, streamlined hand management set collection games. Or, it just made me want to play an engine builder - Century: Spice Road and Gizmos come to mind. Somehow, Splendor even made me just want to play Ticket to Ride, which is not a comparison I was ever expecting to make. My love for 7 Wonders: Duel and my enjoyment of Jaipur and Lost Cities is actually tempting me to give Splendor: Duel a shot, as I'm hoping it'll be a tighter experience really highlighting the uniqueness of Splendor. 

Splendor, itself? Easy skip for me.

textfield_comment_value:
:star: [b] Samo's worst game ever played.[/b] :star:
[i]The game that is pure EEVIL[/i]

I hate this one for political reasons. [i]No ... I don't mean ... look ... [/i] political in the sense that I read Splendour to be a [i]counterrevolutionary game[/i]. By the end of 2000s casual games realised eurogames hate them. Euros became arcane mechanical gizmos that pretty much all played the same way. Thus, casual gamers turned to games more in line with what normal people want from boardgames: light social fun. There were microgames, new party games and the entire social deduction genre returned from obscurity (courtesy of The Resistance). Suddenly there were many new beer and pretzel games, German family games became a factor. And this meant that "gateway" game as an idea was dead. Suddenly there were no light accessible games which would double as a introduction to the mechanistic MPS complex clockworks the euros have become. Casual players were happy playing casual games, not "progressing" towards the eurogaming nerdvana. This was not good. Something had to be done.

Enter Splendour. 
Eurogaming equivalent of Empire Strikes Back.

Splendour is accessible, Splendour is simple, Splendour as is asocial as it gets. It's taking your generic euro engine building and removing from it anything remotely interesting to the point that it looks like an early prototype version. Suddenly you have a MPS engine gizmo you can drop on innocent nongamers and there's a high 0.5% chance they'll turn into gamerz! And then there are CHITs. [i]Ahhh! It's PLASTIC! I needz! [/i]Spledour is a hobbyist wet dream: combining plastic bits with the hope of turning nongamers into gamers. This combo also justifies putting a simple deck of cards in a relatively huge box and charging a premium for it.

[b]"Hello, development? Marketing here. I'm calling regarding this game you sent us to promote. 'Splendor' I'm not sure what can we do with it."[/b]
[i]"What seems to be the problem?"[/i]
[b]"Selling it, obviously. We're not sure how to make it attractive. It's a generic snowball engine thing, exactly the kind of thing the market is already full of. Only it's simpler, so we guess casual gamers are the target? However the casual gamer market's already full of games way more exciting. Not sure what you were going for."[/b]
[i]"Well as you said, casual gamers games are not anymore the kind hobbyists need to get nongamers into their hobby."[/i]
[b]"So you want to sell this to hobbyists?"[/b]
[i]"Yes, so they can get nongamers into... err... what you called ."'snowball engine thing'"[/i]
[b]"Okay. Yes, I could see this. But this would only work if hobbyists buy the game in the first place. We need more bling."[/b]
[i]"Excuse me?"[/i]
[b]"Well, the hobbyist market's saturated, innit? We need something to stand out. They love many mechanics, but this has one. Illustrations are quite generic, okay, it's not Menzel, but still. As for the title, let's just say we're relived you didn't go with 'Gem Collector', not that it's much better. We're also not happy with the box."[/b]
[i]"What's wrong with the box?"[/i]
[b]"We want a bigger one, obviously. Stands out more. Can put higher price on it. But can't justify it with just a pack of cards and some cardboard chits."[/b]
[i]"Hmmm. What if we replace cardboard chits with those heavy plastic poker chits?"[/i]
[b]"Seems interesting. Those are quite heavy right? We can make the game box much bigger."[/b]
[i]"And the hobbyists love them. Might just be the bling to grab them."[/i]
[b]"Great idea! We'll run the numbers and get back to you. This might just work!"[/b]

[hr]

From my original rating notes. 

[i]Somewhere in the middle I looked at my tableau, plateau thingy and went "whee, I'm snowballing". What joy.

So, firstly, there's no game in here, it's just a puzzle exercise. Secondly the game plays itself. Thirdly no theme, no dramaturgy (apart from whee snowballing), they didn't even try getting some theme that would make sense. Fourthly the graphics are terribly uninspired - like somebody just drew over photographs.

About Knizian adjective this game gets and undeservedly so. While it's simple and sorta kinda has tension, there's no tension arriving from the players, no shared space, it's a MPS. Tension is there, but what kind of tension? It's a tension you get from withdrawal symptom. Your engine is snowballing and you want just more and more and one more gem and one more card, and why did you take that, it's mine, mine, mine, precious! A friend (Martin) made a really clever comparison to game apps played on phones and tablets and such which makes sense both in what this game is and why is it liked. The tension of the game doesn't come from tense choices or risk taking, it comes from addiction. And addiction is not social, there's no common space players share here, it's just people tring to get their fix. 

t felt to me like somebody took your average MPS engine buiding euro and streamlined it by cutting off anything remotely interesting. It even feels to me like a prototype, something than would need to be properly developed. [/i]

textfield_comment_value:
[thing=148228][/thing] is a light set collection type of game. In your turn you have a small set of options:
- take two chips of the same color (if there are at least 4 chips in the stack);
- take 3 chips, all of different colors;
- take one card from the rows and one gold chip (maximum of three cards separated - you must always pay the cost of these cards, you can't just put them back in the rows);
- pay the cost of one card and put it in front of you.

The cards are divided in three rows, accordingly to the amount of chips necessarry to build them. The less chips, the easier to pay its costs. Every card will have the kind of chips necessary to pay for it, and also will have a type of precious stone - once you take it, the cost of that type of color will reduce in one. So, for example, if the card you took has 1 green gem on it, the next time you will pay for some card that needs green, you will pay one less (up to zero).

Some of the cards are worth victory points, and also there are nobles, which are worth 3 points and require a set of colors to "visit" the first player that complete the set. The game ends when someone reaches 15 points, when this happen, the players will finish the round of play so that everyone has had the same number of turns. The winner will be the player with the most points.

As one can see, [thing=148228][/thing] is a game that can be explained in few minutes and played by anyone that grasped games like [thing=9209][/thing], beign as light as this one. And it plays even faster: usually you will have your turn figure out way before the game returns to you. When we played, one AP player was always surprise to see that the play had already returned to him. Even with this, we played the whole game in around 40 minutes. I won't be surprise at all if the plays, once everyone has the flow of the game set in, will last around only 30 minutes.

It is an easy going game, with some indirect confrontation (I can take a card I see you want to take, or I can hold chips of one color in order to prevent, for some time, other to build cards of that color), nothing major, so, even if you play with family or players that dislike confront, they will probably still enjoy [thing=148228][/thing].

The game has some luck in its play: for instance, if you take several cards that lower the cost one, say white (diamonds) cards, and the ones that are worth points requiring a high number of white don't show up, well... So it is best, as far as I can see, the spread your options, taking, at least in the beginning, cards of almost every color, in order to be somewhat prepare for everything that shows up later. Even with luck, usually the player that played the best will win - something that is always great.

As it was said many time, [thing=148228][/thing] has some [b]awesome[/b] chips - they are sturdy, heavy - a friend of mine thought they were made of metal (but no). Yes, the box is huge for what comes inside, but everything stay in its place, the cards fit even when sleeved (a major plus for me) - so I can't complain about the box. The cards are OK and the noble tiles are thick. Overall, an excellent production value - it makes well worth the price of it (which isn't cheap, considering the game doesn't came with a big lot of components).

So, [thing=148228][/thing] has proven itself as a great option of filler, giving several things to consider in every turn, but none of them overwhelmingly hard nor requiring several minutes of ponderation. It isn't as portable as, say, [thing=172][/thing], nor it accepts as many players as [thing=37759][/thing], but it is a heavier than both, and it will probably be a good choice for players that want more meat in their fillers.

Recommended!
