Codenames review: 

Codenames review by Daniel Cope
Introduction 
Agents as you will be aware communications have broken down here at HQ, and we need to be in contact with our operatives in the field. Your mission is to go out in the city and find our covert operatives and inform them of their new instructions, you will have to use all your skills of deduction as due to the poor lines of communication and the sensitivity of this mission the Spymasters can only provide you with one-word clues.
What are you waiting for? Strap up and move out!
Oh, one more thing as this mission of security status Black, should you or any of your force be caught or killed, the Home Secretary & Head of the Agency will disavow any knowledge of your actions and existence. Good luck agents!
Overview
Codenames created by Vlaada Chvatil is a team collaborative word association game for 2+ players were one member of the team will play the spymaster giving clues to try and find the operatives as quick as possible and the rest of the team will have to use these clues to deduce from the words / agent cards which agents are your colleagues but be aware you have civilians and enemy agents who you want to avoid, we have also received intel that an assassin is at large who will wipe us out as an agency if we are not careful. 
Mission supplies?
Agents due to the sensitive nature of this mission you will not be issued with your usual high-tech equipment such as you Laser lipstick, umbrella shield and bullet-proof car. Due to the assassin and other enemy agents at large, we cannot risk exposure of these critical assets, instead we will be issuing you with the following equipment for the field:
 
Eight Red Agent Cards.
Eight Blue Agent Cards.
One Double Agent Card.
Seven Innocent Bystander Cards.
One Assassin Card.
40 Key Cards.
200 Double-Sided Codename Cards.
One Sand Timer.
 
Game Play
How to setup the game?
Setup for Codenames is quick, easy and simple to learn and will take you no more than 1 to 2 minutes, shuffle your 200 codename cards and place 25 cards of the cards in the centre table easy visible by all players in a 5 by 5 grid, leave a 1 to 2-centimetre gap between the cards to enable players to touch the card and place the corresponding card on top, each card will have a random word on both sides of the card.

Once you have made your 5 by 5 grid, shuffle your key cards which depict were your agents are located on the 5 by 5 grid, place one key in the plastic holder the lights on the edge of the card will either be red or blue this shows which team is the first player, whoever is the first player give the person the double agent as they are going first they will need to find an additional agent. 

How to Play?
One player in the team will be the spymaster who will direct their agents due to the limited communication the spymaster may only use one word to try to reference to the agents in field 
One example would be 3 of your agents in the field codenames are:
     
You could state:
Unlimited (Advanced clue)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
3
---------------------------------------------------------------------
2
---------------------------------------------------------------------
1
---------------------------------------------------------------------
0 – (Advanced Clue)
The number refers to how many agents are in the fields alongside number of agents you can approach this turn, for example our clue could is, 3 Tree, tree refers to all 3 through association like so, bark of the tree, nuts grow on trees and squirrels climb trees, your agents will then discuss which cards they feel meet the clue once they touch a card in the grid, the guess is final and must be revealed truthfully, if the team got the guess right they may continue, if it was an enemy agent the turn end and the other spymaster starts their turn, if it’s a member of the general public / civilian this means you have tried to approach a member of the public saying “Agent Nut” and they are confused and have no idea, what you mean so your turn end, if you find the assassin the game ends as your code has been cracked and your agents are killed meaning the other spymaster and team wins.
When playing as the spymaster the luck and strategy of the game all come together when you give your clues, you must keep a straight face, not as easy as it sounds as not reacting to the discussion from your agents when there on the wrong path is hard, but you must resist any additional clues, facial expressions etc which may help the agents hints to what cards to choose, remember that communication has broken down! and the spymaster is in the HQ while the agents are in the field and in reality, the spymaster would not be able to pass on additional information.
One of the advanced rules allow you to say unlimited which means your agents can pick as many agents on the 5 by 5 grid as they wish, you may use is for example as a final bid to find your agents before the other spymaster if you have given several clues and then agents have not been found by the team due to confusion or risk and this been resolved due to the word which might have conflicted with you clue being removed / found by the other spymaster’s team. Another advanced clue you can use is zero meaning no word / agents refer to this clue when using this rule, you must still pick a card to find and agent but you may have several words which conflict using the zero clue may help you reduce the confusion.
At times the clues you give may be names, or two words and this can be agreed between the two spymasters, as sometimes clues can be hard to give but the official rules sate one-word clues, if you are struggling remember to have fun and not to be too strict on the rules. 
Finial Thoughts
Codenames is a great, fun, simple, family friendly game for groups working best in my view with six or more who are up for a bit of jovial banter. The game can be a good time filler as it is a relatively short game so works well in-between some heavier games.
The components, of the game are card based with very basic artwork and graphics, given the games comes with 200 agent cards given the number of words included you would struggle to play the same game twice.
I personality do like this game and can be great for parties but I do feel there are better word games which use similar mechanics.

Codenames is the perfect game to bring out at pretty much any board game night because it's easy to understand but oftentimes challenging to play. The premise is simple... if you're the clue-giver for your team, you want your team to correctly identify 8-9 words out of a random 25-word grid, using only one-word clues to tie multiple of them together for your clue each turn. For example, if the words "TV" and "Stream" were out there that you needed your team to guess, you might say "Netflix... for two!"  Indicating "Netflix is your clue, and it applies to two of the words on the grid." That's it! Turns alternate back-and-forth between clue-givers until one team correctly identifies all the words they need to on the board, or the other team dies trying by accidentally selecting the "black word" (a single word that ends the game immediately in a loss for whichever team selected it).

What this all typically leads to is multiple rounds of a very fun game that pretty much anyone can enjoy, and one that has endless replay ability. The 25-word grid is completely random each time, made up of a handful of selections from 100 or so double-sided cards. The "overlay" card (that identifies which words your team needs to identify, vs. the opposing team) is completely different each game, so combining those with the grid words results in so many different combinations you'll never come close to playing the same game twice. I have played this game with my 10-year-old son, my board-game loving friends, my casual-game loving family and in-laws, and even some of our elderly relatives. Truly, it's a game that everyone can enjoy, and it leads to so many great moments... "This is a complete stretch... no WAY you figured that out!" (FYI... you'll hear that "stretch" comment a lot - so many clues have to be a stretch to tie words together because what does, say, a toilet have in common with Switzerland?).

The hardest part about the game is clue-giving - but it's also the most rewarding when you've successfully led your team to victory with great clues and awareness of the board (what to say, what not to say, how to avoid the "black" word, understanding how your opponents are doing). If you don't want to clue-give though, because it's too much pressure, then don't! Guessing the clues is still fun as you either praise the great clue-giving of your teammate, or question how in the world they expected you to understand that "Ketchup," "Jim," and "Comic" are all tied together (this is a real example from one of our games - my dad tried tying those all together with the word "Kerry..." maybe you'll figure it out, but at the time, us non-political family members had no idea what he was getting at!).

This is a great game. It's not one of my personal favorites (probably because I've played hundreds of rounds of it), but it's certainly one of the favorites to bring to any given board game night. If I had any gripe... it's that sometimes you can get the perfect, or worst possible, random overlay of words on the board where someone can easily tie together 4-5 words in one clue like "Animal," whereas you have a steep uphill battle with no words that seemingly tie together. Games that lopsided in the board layout seem to rarely happen though, and if they do, hey, more of a challenge to you! I've seen clue-givers think it'd be easy more times than once where they lead their team to defeat by not thinking through their clues good enough, as they thought it'd be "too easy." I've also seen ridiculous, no-way-that-happened comebacks in the eleventh hour when a team had to take a chance at 4 words or so and somehow correctly identified them all to snake a win from the superior team that round. You're always in the game, and it's always fun - there's that risk-reward of "Do I give my team a single, assured clue to identify this particularly challenging word? Or do I risk it, and give them a harder clue, but it ties to 2-3 words that would give us an advantage on the other team?" (Risking it, as a heads up, is almost always the better call, unless your clue is so outlandish nobody could reasonably be expected to figure it out!).

Definitely bring Codenames to any board game night. Your friends and family, the serious and the casual... they'll thank you for it!

Codenames is a two-team game that features wordplay. A 5x5 tableau of cards is layed out, each card consisting of a word (except sometimes there are two words, like ice cream). One player for each team is the spymaster, and has access to a hidden tableau showing which words correspond to that team's agents. The spymasters take turns giving clues, consisting of a single word (which relates to some number of words on the table) and the number of words that correspond to that clue word. The other players on the team then have to choose (by physically touching the word card) which cards they think are their agents. If they're correct, the card is covered with an agent tile of the correct color, otherwise, their turn ends because they've found a non-agent, an agent of the other team, or the sole assassin which autowins the game for the other player. Players must choose at least one card each turn, but may choose a number of cards equal to the number the spymaster gave them plus one. This allows for them to use this extra pick to snatch up cards that they missed out on in earlier turns. First team to find all their agents wins.

So. This is a game where the spymasters have to come up with word association, and then hope that this word association conveys itself properly to the lesser members of their team. So in essence, this is a word game that could be softly compared to games like Taboo, Train of Thought, and even Dixit in some ways, as the subtext of the word association can often be as helpful or hindering as the obvious associations.

But all I can think about is how this games design, mechanically, at its core... feels... obvious.

Saying that a game feels obvious makes ME feel like I'm that one obnoxiously pretentious panelist on a celebrity reality cooking show. I know. I'm so sorry. 

But if you recall, I compared this game to games like Taboo, or Train of Thought, or other types of word puzzle games. Because that's what this game is. The physical game is just a big random word generator, and random tableaus. The actual game emerges when you tell us to do word association. Dixit in many ways does a similar thing but with the tableau of words being a tableau of avant-garde pictures (I don't actually know what avant-garde means, so sorry for that oblique description), and with that game I love the art more than I love the game (which goes to say something considering my usually low opinion of art; in truth I just like pictures of things that are pleasant, which is why I'm so disappointed the ants battling on a pile of coins is not a picture ants battling on a pile of flapjacks). I don't think this is a bad game. I don't think it's a lazy game. But I think it is an obvious game. It's a game of word association. It's put together neatly, and does what it does well, but what it does is word association.

Codenames is a word game. There are lots of well known, and well ranked word games out there. But think about the places where you play word games, and think about the places you play other types of hobby games. There is certainly overlap, but they are not the same.

[i][u]Disclaimer:[/u][/i] This is a [color=#000099][b]standalone game[/b][/color]. Its rating is based on [color=#000099][b]desire to play[/b][/color].

[b]Codenames[/b] is the new classic of word games, a true phenomenon that I see everywhere nowadays, even in non-gamers houses. I find this title to be mostly deserved, although I don't rate it as highly as others.

There's a lot to like about this game. There's risk management, a concept that you rarely see in this type of games, both present in the spymaster dance around the forbidden word and also in the way his team can choose to guess one more word than their captain asked them to. The game also scales incredibly well with more players, it allows people to drop in and out without trouble, and doesn't drag on longer than it needs to.

Now for the more controversial part: here's what I dislike in [b]Codenames[/b], starting with a minor nitpick about the way our good sir Vlaada chose to mitigate the first player advantage. To account for their headstart, the team that guess first needs to find 9 words in the grid, while the second team only needs 8.

Here's the issue, though. The way the game works - at least in my playing groups - it's generally quite easy to get your team to guess two words correctly, and much harder to find a common clue for three.

When you piece together all of this, what you get is that the onus to try something difficult is almost entirely on the first spymaster, because if both teams chain 2-word clues, he will end up losing. The second team, on the other hand, is pretty much locked in a 4x2 gameplan because managing to communicate a triplet does them no good if they can't repeat this feat soon after.

Of course there are exceptions. I have seen the elusive 4-word clue be rewarded, and sometimes a poor spymaster can't do better than a one-word association. But in general, what I said holds true, and I dislike how taking risks isn't rewarded for the second team.

Now for the other problem I see in the design: I have found it very hard for a group of people to respect the rules of [b]Codenames[/b] without killing the mood. Here's the thing: if you play with a smart group of people, almost anything people say, excluding clues and guesses, can be used to gain an advantage. So then you're faced with a dilemma: you either try to play fair and get a mostly silent affair which I don't think is the goal when [b]Codenames[/b] is chosen; or you let people talk and make jokes and so on, but invariably you end up with people saying too much and the game integrity being damaged, which frustrates me more than it should.

I think [b]Codenames[/b] exists is some sort of uncanny valley. It is certainly a good game, but the first issue I raised prevents it from being a great serious word game (I'd say [i]Decrypto[/i] has my preference in this category), and the second from being a great party game (I would nominate [i]Timebomb[/i] here). With how popular it is, I anticipate that I will play it a bunch in the years to come, so there's plenty of time for me to change my mind about this.

textfield_comment_value:
No doubt one of the best party games out there with a high player count. Players divide themselves up into two teams and go head to head with each other trying to be the first team to get all their clues correct to win the game. Codenames require a little more thinking than your average party game, however we found that most people do enjoy clue giving/guessing games,especially in larger groups. It is definitely more fun to play the spymaster as they need to think not only about the clues they give and word associations but also about the clues not to give. After they give their clue, they can sit back and watch their teams squirm as they try to figure out which words fit together. The mechanic where teams may guess other teams' clues is brilliant, as it makes the spymaster ever more cautious to the clues they decide to give. In our experience, the more people play, the more enjoyable the experience will be. A lot of laughter and a lot of social interaction, a simple yet very fun game. 

Aesthetics – 6.5
The components are good quality and the art is fine. The game mainly consists of cards and a few cardboard pieces. 

Replayability – 8.5
It is excellent with a variety of group sizes and usually players would immediately want to play another round. There are more than enough clue cards to ensure a different game each time and this is one of those games people just want to play again and again. And to be honest that’s the only reason this game doesn’t get a perfect 10 from us, it’s because we played this game so many times in one night it gets boring for us after the 100th time. 

Theme – 6
The spy theme is basically only there for aesthetics. The most thematic part of the game is when you choose “the assassin” word and instantly lose the game. Although the game is enjoyable, there is not much theme to the game. 

Fun Factor – 8
Credit where credit is due, this is an amazingly fun little game and quickly lifts everyone's spirits around the table and gets them involved into the discussion. It is a little group dependent as the game relies heavily on language and word association skills

Downtime and rules – 7
Very very easy to learn, but some spymasters can take their sweet time figuring out the right clue to give and that could bring the game down a bit. We found this less enjoyable as not everyone plays at the same pace. But having said that the game does come with a sand timer and can be used to eliminate this problem. In our opinion, the timer is a must.

OVERALL RATING 7.5

I had heard a lot of buzz around this game before I got the chance to play it, and at the time I didn't get what all the excitement was about.  Having now played it, I have to say... I still don't get it.  Well, maybe I can see why other people like it, but it just doesn't do it for me.

The game is very thin on theme which, being a Eurogamer, doesn't usually bother me so long as the game is interesting mechanically, but this one falls flat in that regard as well.  This game is highly prone to analysis paralysis if you don't use a timer (which I didn't in any of my plays), resulting in most players sitting around doing nothing while one or a small portion of players thinks long and hard.  The play time on the box says 15 minutes, but our games took more like 30, and it felt like more than 30 due to the down time.  There's very little thinking or planning you can do outside of your own turn unless you are a clue-giver, which makes the down time more pronounced.

The limitation of single word clues is highly restrictive, and trying to give clues about a randomly selected group of words is even more restrictive.  It's extremely difficult to come up with clues that will lead to more than 2 answers unless the board favors such clues, and even if you could come up with such a clue, odds are it would be so obscure or convoluted that your teammate(s) would never guess it.  Typically the best you can hope to accomplish in a turn is to get two answers correct, usually with the second one being a bit of a toss-up.  I usually agree with the adage that restrictions breed creativity, but the restrictions in this game feel so much so that it chokes out creativity.

Additionally, it's very hard to carry any information over from turn to turn.  Usually you will find the clues your teammate was going for, meaning you are back to square one the next round.  Blindly guessing is not a valid strategy except in desperate situations as you can hit an opponent's word or, worse, hit the assassin and lose straight out (which is not only disappointing for the losing team, but is a rather lame way to win).

I generally find Vlaada Chvatil games overly fiddly with an excessive number of rules, and while I don't find this game fiddly, I do find it too confining.  I don't know whether it would be better off with more rules or less, but I do know this isn't a game for me.  If I want to play a game that involves giving clues and trying to think like someone else, I will reach for Dixit or Mysterium instead.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
This game is great for non-gamers. It's light, easy to teach, encourages communication, gives lots of moments of laughter, and can also give some real head-scratching moments where you just look at the spymaster and can't figure out what the hell they're talking about. Everything about the game says that this should be a great time with family/friends. So why cant I seem to enjoy myself while playing it?

I think part of what stifles this game for me (personally) is just how utterly slow and tedious each turn feels. There's so much waiting to do, especially if you play with AP prone people. The game does include an optional timer to 'fix' this but it often gets people to swing too far the other way where they give 1 word clues (which is super boring for the spies) round after round until the game ends by attrition. There's also the not-so-little matter of having the spymaster keep a pokerface. Some people can do this just fine, but if your (or worse so, your opponent's) spymaster has an obvious tell, then lots of tension is removed from the game. Although not allowed by the rules it's very hard to keep people from staring down the spymaster while they decide upon clues or while you're making guesses and adjusting according to their reactions. It's even harder to keep some of the spymaster's mouths shut while they're revealing the results of a guess. I can't tell you how many times I've heard "Oh, that's not what I meant, but you guessed a word anyway". Again, this is expressly forbidden in the rules and yet its hard to fault players (especially new ones) for doing so. Which brings me to the last ding against the game... this is supposed to be a party game and yet two of your players are supposed to be nearly silent with poker faces like statues. This is completely at odds with what a party is like! On the spy side, players can joke and converse freely, but the poor spymasters are segregated from the rest of the group by this artificial wall the game puts up. It makes it difficult to really enjoy the company of others in this (ostensibly) jovial setting when you can only talk to people in one word clues and can't show any emotion.

Codenames is mechanically sound. The concepts are good and the components are wonderful, but the gameplay is just at odds with the settings that it wants to be played in. I'd still play it if someone asks for it, but ultimately it's too light for a game night and too "gamey"  for parties, so it fails to find it's niche among my collection.

Components - .9/1 Cards are fine, rules are quite straightforward. Knock is probably petty but the box doesn't really store the components in an easy format. It means setup takes a little longer than it feels like it should.

Fun - .8/1 For such a simple concept it really gets you hooked. Trying to come up with clues that are meaningful yet a single word gets you really thinking. Trying to parse your teammates thought process can be equally enjoyable. The biggest downside is there is a little bit of a lengthy downtime when starting because the clue giver needs time to analyze all 25 words and which side they are on before they can give a clue that won't accidentally help the other team. There isn't a great way around this and most people still have had a great time, it just is a small barrier to the fun.

Replayability - .9/1 There are a load of cards, double sided, and a bunch of different keys (to state which cards each side is trying to identify) so every time you play it will be different. We easily play 6+ games every time we play. 

Strategic - .6/1 The clue-giver needs to come up with something that maximizes their haul. In addition there is some strategy around trying to keep your words that are most like your opponents out for longer time to impede their clues. That being said, I would argue it is on the lighter side of things.

Theme - .4/1 There is definitely some effort in the visuals, but playing the game doesn't really convey much in the way of theme.

Codenames is a new party game that I've wanted to try for a while now. I was pretty sure that I'd like the game as it falls into a category of party game that I like... ones where you give clues to get your team to guess the right word.

What's unique about Codenames is that there is a 5 x 5 grid of words that is visible to both teams. Each team has a spymaster. Both spymasters can see a card that shows which words in the grid are for the blue team, red team, neutral or the deadly insta-death assassin card. On a team's turn, the spymaster gives a one word clue and a number. The number tells the team how many words in the grid the clue applies to. Then the team has to guess word by word, which words match the clue. They can guess as many words as the number that was given and one extra guess (to try and get previous clues). If they get a word correct they cover it with their team marker (either red or blue). As soon as they get a word wrong the turn is over and it is the other teams turn. If the wrong word was the other teams it gets the appropriate marker on it, and if it was a neutral word it gets a beige marker on it. When one team gets all their words correct the game is over. Or if anyone guesses the assassin word, they instantly lose.

The game is a lot of fun. It's challenging to come up with clues that match multiple words without matching the wrong words. Interestingly, the opposing team can help you out... if they guess a word for their clue it will be covered (right or wrong) and so is out of play. Maybe you wanted to give garden as a clue for slug, grass and stick, but were worried that your team would guess yard in error. When the other team guesses yard, your clue is now perfect. The hardest part of the game seems to be when the spymaster doesn't realize that their clue might apply to words they didn't mean them to. Sometimes this is just an oversight, sometimes it is because they didn't go as deep as the team did, and sometimes it's an association that they just didn't know. In our game one player had never heard the expression "to pound sand".

The game is a lot of fun and does something new in the word association party game genre. It encourages you to be clever in trying to tie multiple words to a single clue... something that only occasionally happens in other similar games. I like what this adds to the genre and look forward to playing it more.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
I really love the game dynamic of codenames. At first, you're frantically looking over the board, trying to make sure that your clues won't accidentally trigger the wrong ideas in your teammates. Towards the end, the options fade, and you're generally left trying to connect two almost randomly selected ideas in a web of triple-meanings and obscure references. Creative wordplay can be used by the betting types to give bigger clues with more tenuous associations, trusting that even if it doesn't work out initially, it might seed the right idea down the line. The bonus mechanic in this game really helps to make the bets more worthwhile, which I think contributes to overall more exciting and entertaining gameplay. And finally, the assassin exists to ground everything and keep the group on their toes until the very end; the game could be decided by one overlooked word association or one errant thought at any point.

Where Codenames starts to go astray is that it seems to be meant as a social, party-style game. The simple, straightforward rules and quick playtime reinforce this well. But more than half the table is pointedly quiet at any given time, and 2 players are encouraged to have no emotional tics displayed at all. The game is also remarkably brutal - when you fail, there isn't any randomness to hide behind, or thematic trappings to partake in. You failed because you messed up, you gave a bad clue, you interpreted something wrong. This naked blame doesn't really seem to fit the light party game at all. Additionally, the game really does need a timer to work - both for the interests of fairness and to keep the game moving for everyone. But giving clues can be quite hard, especially for new players, and the time pressure sometimes helps people shut down more than helping them think fast. What started as a fun game night continues as one team's guessers go  "Well c'mon, just give us any clue - let's go" and the spymaster can't seem to decide on anything. It's not fun to watch or be a part of.

But that's ultimately worst case scenario, and a bit of a player problem as well. When codenames is played lightheartedly, quickly, and between teams that know each other all about the same, it's a remarkably good game. It dares to have a bit of meat on it, something other light games find it difficult to boast. And I love it a bit more than the others for it.

Um jogo pequeno que não dá margem a muitos comentários. Só mesmo sentindo a diversão extrema entrando pela mente.

Melhor jogar com tempo. Para o turno completo de cada equipe 1,5 min (um minuto e meio) que é o tempo da ampulheta que vem com o jogo. O app é mais prático para o controle do tempo e ainda ajuda a criar tensão com avisos.

Embora este tempo pareça muito, pode ser realmente difícil para o Espião Mestre dar dicas dependendo da situação, e ele pode tomar bastante deste tempo total pensando. Isto pode deixar os anciosos da mesa inquietos e os desavisados com sensação de frustração, então é interessante, antes da partida começar, frisar que isto pode ocorrer e que é bom relevar para que o jogo se torne o mais competitivo possível. Em último caso, com o aplicativo, é possível também ajustar este tempo.

O mais difícil é evitar que as pessoas trapaceiem, mesmo que não intencionalmente. Porque o mecanismo do jogo exige uma certa disciplina por parte dos jogadores (principalmente do Espião Mestre) para que ele flua plenamente. E quando se trata de um jogo festivo onde todo tipo de gente consegue jogar como este, pode ser difícil manter essa disciplina as vezes. Um olhar, um pequeno gesto, um pigarro etc, qualquer coisa pode passar uma pista. E tem pessoas que, no calor do momento, acabam esquecendo as regras ou mesmo inconscientemente passando alguma pista indevida. Tem horas que dá vontade de obrigar os Mestres a jogarem de máscara por exemplo. Huahuahaua!

Conseguindo superar esse detalhe, o jogo é só alegria e é praticamente impossível jogar só uma partida. E a rejogabilidade é virtualmente infinita. Aqui foram mais de 40 partidas com o mesmo grupo em 1 ano e sempre que vai pra mesa todos se divertem. Não enjoa.

Esse tem lugar cativo no coração.
Genial!

textfield_comment_value:
This is a great social game. I've played about a dozen times so far, and had a blast playing it every time. I've played it with colleagues, kids, teens, and non-native speakers. For the last group we had to go over all the words at the start of the game to make sure everyone understands the words, and more often then not, multiple meanings of the words.  

Codenames is easy to set up, quick to get started, and the rules are easy to explain. Some folks may have a harder time then others following the rules (e.g. giving absolutely no hints as clue-givers), but that is beyond game's control. 

The game is also a great ice breaker if you don't know the other players very well, and it is also a great way to get to get know them better (if they actively participate). 

The game has cooperative and competitive elements, which allows different folks to find satisfaction and/or drive from either or both aspects of the game. I enjoy both, so it works great for me. 

Codenames also allows for various levels of participation. If someone just wants to hang around, and throw in a suggestion here and there, they can still feel like they are a part of the game, while not feeling like they are on the spot. This draws participation even from folks who typically shy away form games in general. 

If you have only one pair of players who are very close (e.g. siblings, spouses) it is best to split them into different teams, to help balance things out. Common experiences and background help tremendously when trying to come up with associations. 

The gameplay can suffer from an alpha player or someone jumping to conclusions, not giving others a chance to form or voice their opinions. The game mechanic where by you have to touch the card to indicate your selection helps with this, as it allows others to stop the alpha from making the decision prematurely.  

I have found myself to be able to get into the game, find cool connections between words, stretch my brain, and successfully challenge others with somewhat outlandish clues. However, I was not "on" every time, and there were games and/or groups I played with, where I just couldn't open up my brain in the right way to connect with the words and the group. 

I found 8 players to be the optimal, with 4 on each side, but 6 and 10 can work just fine as well.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
This game is quite an achievement, the small scale Holy Grail of "A party game that Jeff actually looks forward to playing". The rules are the epitome of simplicity and can be explained in 2 minutes, even in a room full of drunks.

The gist is one player tries to find a way to connect 8 or 9 randomly selected words using as few clues as possible, with each clue consisting of a single word and a number. The number represents how many of the random words are linked by that particular clue. His team then tries to guess as many words as they can (from the displayed list of 25 total words).

A second player and his or her team does the same, using the same set of 25 words, but with a different selection of the 8 or 9 words as targets. Then teams alternate attempts, eliminating words as they correctly guess them. The first team to guess all of their target words wins immediately.

This all sounds pretty easy, but there's a catch. One of the words is a trap. If anyone chooses the trap word, their team automatically loses.

It's a lot of fun and I have to say, being the clue giver is much harder than you might expect. Linking the words is fairly easy, but not also linking to words that belong to the other team or the trap word is much more difficult. Often you will focus so intently on creating a clever clue, you will miss an obviously wrong answer match, trapping your team.

The other thing I enjoy is how well it scales to player count. Usually the more eyes you can get on a puzzle, the easier it becomes to solve. Not this one...In fact, the more minds you add to the think tank, the more clouded the answers become. All sorts of questionable relationships start popping up, as more and more outlandish connections start to be made between the random words.

It takes about ten to fifteen minutes to play a game, but once you start it's easy to lose a couple of hours, especially when a metagame starts to form around different ways to link the words using movies, shared experiences and inside jokes. It's an awesome amount of laughs, but still manages to be a challenging an engaging puzzle. I would not feel bad about a copy of this being in every gamer's collection, from casual social gamer to heavy lifting GMT guy.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
I don't always give 10 star reviews.... but when I do, they are for the game 'Codenames.'

It brings me great joy when a game like this comes along - pretty much universally enjoyed, easy to learn, approachable to a wide range of people, and a perfect blend of fun & strategic.

Pros:
-Brilliant concept, huge satisfaction in giving a great clue (and in correctly guessing!)
-An element of (fun) intensity due to the presence of the assassin word (and the possibility of inadvertently giving clues for an opposing team's words!)
-The occasional opportunity to give a clue that hints at something only your partner will know, or that approaches the word in a particularly innovative way (though I am personally notorious for trying to stretch things TOO far and trying to be TOO aggressive when giving clues...)
-Love that the grid configurations are pretty much endless, when you take into account the different configuration cards, the different ways they can be oriented, plus the natural mixing of the words on the grid, etc.

Cons:
-You do have to be careful not to make it painfully obvious which card(s) you are looking at, particularly as the playing field gets narrowed down
-If you play a ton, you do start seeing the same words pop up - thankfully, there are tons of different combinations (so the connections themselves will typically be different), but we have indeed found that, if you play with the same group over-and-over, some clues tend to get repeated (for the same word(s)). Bring on a straight-up expansion pack!!
-You do have to really keep the group honest in terms on not reacting to things, commenting on what they really meant by a given clue after it is guessed, etc. (since you want to keep it up in the air as to whether the intended words were actually guessed as intended, or if the guessers just got lucky with what they picked!)

I personally prefer this game with 4 people, but it can also work with 6 or 8 (though we've seen it result in some more intense disagreements with 6-8.... particularly when the guessers are divided on which word to pick!! It can make it interesting though.... ;) )

All-in-all, a great game that you absolutely should pick up if you haven't already.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
I’ve said it before, but I will say it again: Chvatil is probably the most talented and diverse game designer who has ever lived. I actually don’t care much for many of his games, although I do like some of them, and I think Uwe is the best designer ever. Still, hats off to Chvatil. This time he has designed a surprisingly simple party game which has gotten a lot of hype. I have had my eyes on it for a while, but due to the hype I went out and got it earlier than expected and paid a little more. And overall I’m glad that I did.

I’m definitely not a huge fan of this game and speak about it at every chance I get, as it seems a lot of people currently do, but I like it. It’s a deceptively simple word game in which you’re trying to get your team to guess 8 or 9 words which are placed randomly in a grid of 5 times 5 cards. 

The tension comes mainly when you’re the Spymaster and need to come up with a clever clue which allows your teammates to guess 2 or 3 answers in one shot! Also, the game is tense as you need to “outwit” your opponents, while still trying to make sure that your teammates don’t misinterpret (easier said than done…) so they don’t guess an incorrect neutral word – or, even worse, the other team’s words. Or, of course, the worst thing of all: the assassin, which makes you lose the game instantly… So far I’ve never seen this happen (in more than 10 games), but I definitely think it will happen eventually.
It works well with 4, 6 and 8 players – and also with 2, which I have greatly enjoyed as a coop with my wife!

The reason I’m not totally sold on this party game is because it’s missing a little bit to be a “party” game. It’s very intriguing, but when the spymasters sit and try to think of clever clues, and when the other team is guessing, there is basically nothing you can do and it can get a little boring… This has happened several times, and the term “boring” is obviously not something you want in a party game! Still, I think it’s a very good game. Perhaps not as innovative as some claim as the overall mechanic has been seen in older games before, but Chvatil put a different twist on it, and it is a good game overall.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Der Name des Spiels "Codenames" ist Programm! Zwei Geheimdienstchefs versuchen in diesem Wortspiel Codewörter an ihre Agenten - ihre Teammitglieder - zu übermitteln, ohne dass diese die falschen Rückschlüsse ziehen, aber dennoch schnell auf die Lösung kommen.

In diesem Spiel teilen sich die Spieler in zwei gleich große Gruppen auf, die gegeneinander antreten. In jedem Team wird ein Gruppenführer bestimmt.
Die beiden Gruppenführer sind Geheimdienstchefs und bekommen gemeinsam eine Karte zu sehen, auf der ein Raster an roten und blauen Feldern abgebildet ist. Dieses Raster spiegelt die Kartenauslage in der Tischmitte wider, welche verschiedene Wörter zeigt. Die Aufgabe der Chefs ist es, mit einem einzelnen Wort möglichst viele Begriffe der eigenen Farbe zusammenzufassen, sodass das eigene Team über so wenig Runden wie möglich, auf die eigenen Begriffe kommt und diese errät.
Das Wörterfeld beinhaltet neben den Teambezogenen Wörtern auch neutrale und einen schwarzen Begriff, keinesfalls getippt werden darf!
Sobald ein Team alle eigenen Begriffe erraten hat, beendet und gewinnt es das Spiel. Wenn ein Team den schwarzen Begriff errät, verliert es stattdessen sofort!

"Codenames" war seinerzeit (2015) genial. Ich bin dem Spiel mittlerweile überdrüssig geworden, auch wenn das Spielkonzept bis heute immer noch einzigartig ist.
Leider ist die Downtime des Spiels verhältnismäßig hoch, wenn die Teamchefs sich über einen zusammenfassenden Begriff Gedanken machen. Meist kommt dann ein Begriff heraus, der gerade mal zwei Wörter verbindet. Die richtig genialen 4er oder gar 5er-Zusammenhänge lassen größtenteils auf sich warten.
Außerdem haben in jeder Partie immer nur zwei Spieler die Möglichkeit, Teamchefs zu sein. Auch wenn das Erraten der Begriffe auch reizvoll sein kann, ist gerade die verantwortungsvolle und kreative Aufgabe der beider Chefs das, was "Codenames" für mich interessant macht.
Wenn es jemand kennenlernen möchte und es gerade keine Alternative gibt, bin ich bereit es auf den Tisch zu bringen. In jedem anderen Fall finde ich ein besseres Spiel, auch für viele Mitspieler.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Some thoughts I had after two different evenings (6-7 games): Neat game, but overpriced for what you get. By the end of the first evening, a couple of us had figured out that the game turns and sort of breaks when you get someone as a codemaster who is really good at concept association (and thus good at being the ghost in Mysterium, the clue giver in Concept, etc). The people who just did straight association of words (e.g. "Musicians, 2" and yields "Kid, Rock") had a much rougher/tense go at it than the people who did conceptual linking to examples (e.g. "Jurisdiction, 6" and ended up with London, New York, Australia, Bermuda, etc which just sort of ends the game). The difference is you can still get screwed by interpretation of the dream cards in Mysterium (or just get a shitty draw) where as it just sort of falls over here. Reminds me of Set in that regard (where skill imbalance is a key factor). Second, the game dragged ass above 9 players. The discussion phase lags because you're waiting in lock step for a clue to be given where as in Mysterium you can be working on someone else's clue while you wait for your own. Our best games we had in that regard were at 5p, maybe 6p. Above that, and I'd probably break up into two groups and play something else. I think one of the most telling things is that with Mysterium, we played that until they made us go home every week for like 6 weeks, where as this, we played for maybe 2 hours and everyone was ready for something new after just the first week (both groups on different days even...) It's a game I'll play if it shows up (and there isn't anything else to play right off hand), but I'd never buy it.

almost a year later, I find it's just ok, but it improves some if you use dixit cards instead of words which is where I think Mysterium achieves a better "group guess the interpretation" setup. Baring that, I think it should be a requirement that there are no single guess clues.

textfield_comment_value:
The quality of the components is average. The sand timer was broken and the cardstock is not great. It should not be a problem because the cards will not sustain heavy use.

Codenames is a word association game not related in any way to spies. The rules are very, very simple, and the setup is fast. You will be playing 5 minutes after opening the box. And you will have fun. Because it plays out better than expected when you read the rules.

There's a couple of issues with Codenames:
[b]AP[/b]: There's a risk of serious AP here. Obviously, the more time you think, the more likely you are to come up with better word associations. The sand timer will be a must with certain players.
[b]Catch-up[/b]: If one team fails and chooses a spot belonging to their rivals, it will be almost impossible for them to come back from that. It's not a big issue, because rounds are short.
[b]Clues[/b]: There can be some dissensions about what might constitute a legal clue, and what not. The rulebook already advances some of them.
[b]Rule of silence[/b]: There are many comments or reactions from the clue-givers that can be interpreted as a [n illegal] clue (rightly so). 

None of these issues spoils the fun as long as you don't play in an hyper-competitive way. I personally prefer not enforcing the "rule of silence"; I enjoy more when people laughs and comments on what happens in the game.

It has an unlimited replayability and I think 6 players is the sweet spot. But it works well with 8 too, and although it's not ideal, an uneven number of players (5-7) will work too. I have not tried it,but it might be fine with more or less players too.

Overall, it's a great party game based on a very simple idea. Another masterwork of Vlaada in a new genre for him.

textfield_comment_value:
Codenames is essentially a party type word game in which you are attempting to solve the riddle of uncovering your teams agents - each represented by a single word - on a 5x5 grid of cards.  In actuality,  what this game has done,  is solve the age old riddle of longevity in the party game genre.

There has always been one caveat attached to most of the glowing reviews one might read,  concerning the party game genre - and that is - the fun contained within,  always came with an expiration date.

Take for example,  a highly popular party game - and one of my personal favorites - Wits and Wagers.  While being a great game,  it has a finite amount of cards,  which once you become familiar with,  render them essentially useless.  It is hard to deny the fact that this problem is basically inherent in the genre itself.

Codenames deftly skirts that issue by using 25 cards at a time.  Because of word associations,  the variable mix,  the key cards and the orientation of those cards - the usual stigma that is affiliated with this type of game - disappears,  like a stack of chips at a casino.  Add to that,  the fact that there are no definitive answers - that everything relies on individual interpretation - and you have stumbled upon something that is truly unique for this game model.

If all this game managed to do was break the mold,  it might deserve accolades for,  at long last,  simply performing that feat.  But there is more on display here than that...much more.  Beyond it's near limitless replay value,  there is much fun to be unearthed in that small box of sparse components.

This quickly became my number one word / party game of all time - although if you don't have an affinity for words,  I suggest you proceed with caution.  The game system itself,  is ingenious and versatile enough to allow one to widen it's scope.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Un très bon jeu d'ambiance, rapide à comprendre et à jouer.

Le jeu se joue en deux équipes et il n'y a pas de limite théorique au nombre de joueurs par équipe. De plus, n'importe qui peut joindre ou quitter la table à tout moment. Le gameplay est vraiment intéressant et demande d'être malin, il y a des petites stratégies tacites à mettre en place. Il y a peu de manipulation de matériel après la mise en place (qui est elle-même simplissime).

Concernant les points de discorde possibles, on retiendra un premier potentiel problème, faisant partie intégrante du gameplay, qui est la nécessité pour une équipe de se mettre d'accord sur une réponse (risque de phénomène du joueur alpha). Le second élément qui risque de faire grincer des dents concerne les capitaines des équipes, qui seraient un peu trop communicatifs. En effet, le jeu ne fonctionne que s'ils sont capables de garder leur "poker face" et de ne pas parler à leur équipe, et ce n'est pas si facile, même pour des gens comme moi qui font attention à respecter les règles, surtout dans un cadre bruyant et festif (par exemple si vous donnez l'indice "ballon" et que vous faites la forme d'une sphère avec vos mains, c'est déjà de la triche car vous orientez la pensée de vos coéquipiers vers cette signification précise du mot "ballon").

À noter qu'il est impossible d'avoir des mises en place similaires de partie en partie, et il n'y a pas la problématique de reconnaitre des cartes abimées ou de connaitre des cartes par cœur. Le jeu ne perd donc pas d'intérêt à force d'y jouer.

Pour moi c'est un indispensable des party games :
- Facile à expliquer et à comprendre
- Rapide à mettre en place et à jouer
- Possédant un gameplay vraiment intéressant
- Sans limite de joueurs ni problème d'équilibrage
- Avec la possibilité de quitter ou rejoindre la table à tout moment de la partie
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value: One of the rare guess-the-word(s) party games I actually enjoy playing, Codenames sets itself apart from the pack by boasting a surprising depth of strategy.  This is a race to have your teammates identify all your secret words before your opponents guess theirs, and the key to success is clue economy: cleverly choosing a word that will point to multiple correct answers without leading to costly misidentification.  Missteps and oversights are what give Codenames its humorous flavor; it never gets old watching a clue-giver wince as they notice how the clue they just uttered has some sideways connection to an opponent’s card.  And unlike so many games in the genre, this one is an actual competition - a true GAME - where the score matters, victory feels earned and defeat stings a bit.  So many times I’ve found myself playing Just One, Herd Mentality, Blank Slate, Family Feud, or another such word-based party game, increasingly frustrated and bored as it devolves into a time-passing activity that a couple of people (occasionally guilty) use as an opportunity to prove how funny they (think they) are.  Not Codenames.  If you’re playing this one, you’re playing to win.  Like Dixit (which I love) and Concept (which I loathe), Codenames requires a centralized play area around which participants must congregate - there’s no picking your favorite comfy chair at opposite ends of the living room and scribbling on personal white boards or passing a box of cards.  It’s a party game with board game trappings, so it’s intrinsically more difficult to get people to join in.  Hence, its greatest strength is also its Achilles’ heal.  With the right people, however, Codenames is boisterous and funny, tense and thinky.  Like Dixit, it gathers a lot of dust on my shelf; but I’m always happy to play a game.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Codenames adds a different type of game to my collection.  I'm more of a math type of guy and like games with theme - especially those where you build something (a city, an empire, a business, etc).  Now along comes Codenames that, the first time I saw it, seemed like a party game.  As a general rule, I'm not that in to party games ("Not that there's anything wrong with that.") but it's getting a lot of love around here so I figure I'll give it a try.  And you know what, I like it.

Why?  First, I am enjoying the logic puzzle of trying to communicate something to another person that makes them select certain words and not others.  I like trying to decide how to modify my clues depending on my partner (my wife, my 12 year old son, a friend in her early fifties).  All of these people have very different backgrounds and life experiences which make them interpret clues differently, so it's fun for me to try and customize my clues.  An example of me not doing a good job of this was using a clue of "Flash :2".  I was counting on the 17 year old I was playing with getting "Bolt" which he did, but he totally didn't get "Dance".  Being in my 40's and growing up in the 80's, most people had heard of the movie "Flash Dance" in my circle of friends.  After he failed to make that connection, I realized I had projected myself onto an 18 year old - one that was too young to have heard of the movie "Flashdance".  Doh.

I digress.  I will finish by saying that Codenames is a game that, in my experience, has broad appeal with its short running time and ease of understanding.  It's a game that I can play with people not typically in my gaming circle - my parents or other non gamer friends seem not to be intimidated by it.  Gaming with more people?  That's a win in my book.

JOGAR COM AS CARTAS DO PATUSCADA

Party game para 4 a ~10 jogadores, divididos em duas equipes. Do mesmo designer do [listitem=5715096]Through the Ages[/listitem], apesar de estar no extremo oposto do espectro de complexidade.

Cada equipe tem um capitão, e ambos os capitães podem ver (através de uma imagem escondida) quais cartas, em uma grade 5x5, pertencem à sua equipe, quais são neutras, e qual é a única carta "assassino".

Na sua vez, o capitão dá a seus companheiros de equipe uma pista composta por uma palavra e um número, como "Bolsonaro 4". Estes, por sua vez, selecionam as cartas (até o número dado) que eles acham que o capitão pode ter em mente para a pista (por exemplo, "Laranja", "Mínion", "Genocídio" e "Cocô")*. Escolher uma palavra que não corresponde à sua equipe encerra a sua vez, e escolher a palavra atrelada ao assassino faz sua equipe perder imediatamente. Se nenhuma equipe escolher o assassino, vence a primeira equipe a descobrir todas as suas próprias palavras.

Tenho também o [thing=198773][/thing], que usa cartas com imagens em vez de palavras, e o [thing=224037][/thing], que tem um conjunto diferente de palavras e adiciona regras para jogar de forma co-operativa em 2 ou 4 pessoas. Dá pra misturar todas as cartas também.

textfield_comment_value:
Delightfully easy to explain and launch into with just about anybody - almost any age and any level of gaming interest. Wonderful fun coming up with the clues and being on the other side trying to guess them. Deciphering the clues can lead to some good conversation and a lot of laughs.

There's lots of player interaction as teammates discuss what they know about the spymaster (warning - it can get hilariously personal), 400 words and many agent combinations to mix games up, and a neat timer nudge along mechanism to politely prod anyone dawdling on their turn.

This is the best group game I've played and it makes for a terrific gift for families. Winning is secondary to coming up with a really good multiword clue. But if you like the game bit then there's pressure you can apply to your opponents to catch up, a timing aspect as you wait until giving some clues (based upon other words confusing your team while they're still available), and if you really concentrate then some clue reading on your opponent's turn.

Children will learn some new words, a lot of synonyms and it's a good, fun mental exercise for everyone at the table. One game takes about 10-15 minutes and you'll have a hard time stopping at just one. Every house should have a copy.

(Pity we can't be sure of buying a non-pirated copy anymore to give away as presents. It's appalling that this game is now imported in bulk and sold off through the usual online stores that have no problem flouting copyright laws. I feel for the legitimate publishers. This should be their Settlers of Catan, their Ticket to Ride - the game that brings in the dependable income so they can spend more time and resources on bringing their new creations to gamers. They're sadly being ripped off here.)
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Another party game that I think works better as a computer game due to what people say easily giving away extra information (though since the rules say only one word it's not as easy to game as say Dixit), but despite this being a word guessing game this is a most excellently designed game of the genre, and while party games are far from my favorite board game category I understand why this game has risen so quickly. There is a great challenge balancing giving specific clues but having a lower ceiling of number of correct answers in one turn and a high number of guesses but having to give vague clues in order to apply to more phrases. You could also purposefully lie on the number of words matching a clue to try to get more guesses (or say 0 to get infinite). As the spymaster it's also fun to watch your team come haphazardly close to guessing the instant lose word or as the opposing team attempt to goad your team to choose a word that is clearly not related to your clue, but is also a word they need to eventually guess. You need to consider choosing your clues based on the non spymasters' discussion, either so your team doesn't choose a word due to a misinterpretation of a previous clue, or by timing which clues you give when so that if the opposition is on the cusp of guessing one of your words for you, you choose to give clues to alternate words first to your team. 

Despite the game having teams 7 players worked pretty well (although unless there is a variant 5 would be weird since you would have no one to deliberate with), and having a little more than 8 would probably be fine.

EDIT: It is fun the first time once in a while, but I'm finding I dislike it when played even a few times a month. Reduced rating to a 5.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Chvatil is frequently called an innovator and a creator of lots of unique games, but the games I've tried from him (Through the Ages, Tash-Kalar, and Codenames) have all seemed to be transplants of existing ideas into new milieus. TTA abstracted and simplified the Civilization computer series into a 4-hour competitive game, which I appreciated. Tash-Kalar added random goals, input randomness, assymetry, and Euro-style theme to an abstract, which I appreciated much less. I'd place Codenames somewhere in between the two.

Codenames takes the controlled-communication party game style of Dixit, Concept, or Catchphrase and makes them a competitive team game. This means that the system needs to be tightly controlled -every in-game action must be carefully indicated, and each "guess" has a chance to lose you the game. The communication, too, is carefully controlled; you can't use characteristics of words themselves, only the meaning, and the number you use can't be used to clue anything. The words are carefully chosen to create overlap, and potential first-player advantage is carefully avoided.

I'm sure somebody who hates party games and loves competitive ones would appreciate this game a lot. As somebody who appreciates both, I find it less successful. I don't mind the looseness and inherently variable difficulty of traditional party games, and Codenames adds very little to the competitive game -it's more about what's removed than what's added. While some concepts are neat (the assassin, the variable number of guesses, attempting to avoid opponent's clues), I don't feel the game has much to offer to somebody who gets their fill of cluegiving from party games.

Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Codenames is not a party game in the conventional sense.  It may be a party game in that large groups can play it, and there are elements of teamwork and competition.  But this game is more serious, more cerebral, and has more downtime than almost any party game available.  In theory, the downtime should be a major drawback.  Ambiguity in the rules should be another.

Yet Codenames might be the [i]best[/i] party game available.  There are several reasons for this.  First and most importantly, everyone seems to like it.  I have not found anyone who dislikes the game.  This is remarkable given the wide variety of settings and player counts at which I have played it.  Second, it promotes enough thoughtfulness in play to satisfy strategy gamers while remaining entirely accessible to everyone else.  The rules ambiguity is not a real problem.  Gamers will pay more attention to the rules than others, and groups will deal with disputes as they arise, but they rarely do.  There is a spirit to the game that everyone seems to understand.  Third, everyone is always engaged.  Downtime is filled with tension and curiosity.  While one team is taking their turn, the other is thinking or obfuscating or making snide remarks.  What happens adapts with the group.  It is never dull.  Lastly, like Dixit Codenames provokes insights into how other people think.  It brings people closer together.  What more could you ask for from a board game?

Incidentally, I think it would work as well with asynchronous online play as face to face, though you would lose the interaction of face to face play.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
This is a massively popular party game, based on teams trying to guide each other through a tableau of words. A 5x5 grid of cards are laid out on the table, each one having a word ([i]Codenames[/i]) or ambiguous picture ([i]Codenames: Pictures[/i]). One person on each team (there's two teams) sees a grid of correct and incorrect cards for their team, including one "assassin" spot that results in an automatic loss when chosen. They give a single-word clue to their team, along with a number of cards that could match the clue. The other members of the team then collectively pick the cards, one-by-one, until they stop or an incorrect guess is made. 

Obviously, there is downtime involved in waiting for the clues to be thought of, and answered, so play [i]Codenames[/i] in a casual setting. That said, there are some strategic choices to made: several cards are neutral, so guessing them won't result in a point for the other team. That means that some wrong guesses are safer than others. There's also the temptation to make clues for big-scoring turns (3 or more cards), which carry the risk of disaster. This is especially true in the early part of the game where most of the cards are still available.

My family has played both the English and Spanish versions, and they've both been hits. This game put Apples to Apples out of its misery. Like just about every other party game, we got to the point where we collectively had enough [i]Codenames,[/i] but we did get many uses out of it. This is an easy choice for a starter game collection.

Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
This is probably one of the most popular party games in recent history, and for good reason. Codenames is a very simple game in the vein of Taboo or Catchphrase where two teams try to guess the clues a representative from their team tries to give them for different words. At the start of a round, twenty-five cards with words on them are placed in a 5x5 grid in front of everyone, and the two Spymasters are given the words on the table they need their teams to guess. Since the first team to correctly guess all of their words wins the round, it becomes a competition between who can get their team to guess the most words using only a single-word clue each time. Correctly guessing a word means the team gets to go again, but guessing incorrectly ends a team's turn. Worse still, sometimes a team might guess one of their opponents' words, giving them a slight advantage! Finally, a single word on every grid is the "assassin", meaning that any team guessing that word instantly loses the game.

What I love about this game so much is that it's partly a brainteaser for the Spymaster and partly a game of how well the spies can interpret the Spymaster's clues. Both Spymasters are constantly juggling new clues to wrack up word combos in their minds while avoiding the assassin and their opponents' words, but all this can get turned on its head when players misinterpret the "very obvious" clues the Spymaster thought they were giving them. Even non-gamers will probably get a ton of enjoyment out of this one. Highly recommended!

textfield_comment_value:

some reasons (some relating to the game, others to the players):

4. the single word clues are incredibly restrictive. While some people may find this enhances creativity and forces people to think outside of the box, for us it felt a bit dull and counterproductive in a "party game" that should be encouraging interaction, which leads to

Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value: Great game of limited communication, and its popularity was probably also helped by its incredibly accessible price point. However, that is not to say that Codenames isn't a fun, puzzle-y and sometimes agonisingly difficult party game. It certainly doesn't create a loud and riotous atmosphere, but the perfect time to play this game is either Christmas with the family or at the pub with friends - so it firmly sits in that category for me. The game has also been great as an icebreaker at new game groups too. Articulating exactly what makes this game so much better than the other games like it is very difficult - but the agony of choice and the in-jokes you can make with you friends around the table all go towards putting this in a league of its own. The final reason I love this game, and have racked up 70+ plays so far is how balanced every grid in the game is. It possibly sounds daft to say it, but a hell of a lot of playtesting must have gone in to selecting all the words in the box - to the point where the mechanically identical Codenames: Deep Undercover is nowhere near as enjoyable, because it is too hard to create tenuously successful combos, because all the words in that edition are a bad combination of being far too similar or completely disparate ideas (or parts of the anatomy). Codenames, however, hits the nail right on the head. There always seems to be a risk that you'll reveal the assassin but you're very rarely so stumped for links that you have to resort to one-answer clues.

textfield_comment_value:
One of the hit games of 2015. This is now my first-choice gateway game for introducing to non-gamers. I have now played it as a gateway game with dozens of non-gamers and almost all are hooked and tell me they are going to buy a copy to play with their friends and family. Several find it such a revelation that I get begged to recommend other games they should try. Unlike most 'word' games (eg: Scrabble), it requires some actual understanding of the words. It is quick to teach and learn. Main problem is that the 25-word starting grid makes for an often painfully slow start, with the Spymasters having initially to take a lot in. The game has endless possibilities for development: it is easy to add your own words, and it can be used as an educational tool for language learners by slipping in foreign vocabulary. I have also been experimenting with variants to appeal to wider audiences; for example, you can play with movie buffs by demanding that all clues must be movie titles.

Among 'expansions' for this game, I have a Bonus Pack of cards (EN01) that was a promo in Spielbox 01/17. The Bonus Pack is subtitled 'Board Gaming' but it is playable because the words aren't titles and authors of board games (as in an earlier largely useless expansion) but words with a gaming association (like Euro and Family).

BGG doesn't separately list them but I also have the XXL edition and what I'd have to term the XXXL edition (a giant box XXL produced to demo the game at conventions and in retail stores).
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
Codenames is a team vs. team based Password (the game show) style guessing game in which players have to guess correctly a small group of words from a larger group laid out in a 5x5 grid based on a single clue from a rotating clue-giver.  The clues must help the players associate a number of words together, and a number delivered with the clue helps the guessers know how many words the clue giver believes are associated.  If you guess wrong, the penalties range from loss of turn to giving the other team a word to instant loss.  The theme is a thinly layered on story about spies.  

The art and accessibility of the game is in making the single clues inclusive enough to guess as many words as possible, but not so inclusive that your teammates add words that have nothing to do with the intent of your clue.  Too conservative and the other team beats you to the punch.  Too aggressive and you bust.  If you've seen Password (the game show), you know that word guessing is the ultimate in broad accessibility.  Anybody can be a clue giver because you can try to make associations based on any criteria-- word meaning, stems, personal experiences you've had.  The emergent experience is that it is absolutely hilarious to see how your friends and family think about things or to try to make connections with people you don't know very well.  I enjoy it, and Vlaada's genius was finding the exact combination of accessible gameplay with novel mechanisms to create a Spiel winner.
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
When I first saw this game in the store, it really looked dumb to me.  You lay out cards with common words on them and try to come up with one-word clues to give your teammates in hopes that they will pick all the cards that relate to your clue.  Like if you wanted them to guess “Car” and “Bicycle”, you would say “Wheels” and they would clearly pick the two things with wheels.  Seemed like a game you would teach first graders to help them learn word associations.  

Then I found out, weeks later, that it was atop the best party games on BGG.  That got my attention!  I bought a copy and tried it and we loved it!  It was so much more challenging and fun than I ever imagined it could be!

And if you usually only have two players and the “party game” category this has fallen into immediately disinterests you, know that this game has a fun variant for two players (described in the rule book).  The first night I tried it out, it was just me and my brother and we did the two player variant and really enjoyed it.  We played like 5 games in a row, taking turns being the clue-giver.  Also there is a separate, stand-alone version of the game called Codenames: Duet, which really perfects the two player experience.

This game designer, by the way, is brilliant.  He also designed one of my favorite all time strategy games (Through the Ages).  To go from that to creating such a simple, yet captivating party game takes the mind of a genius.  

Kudos Vlaada Chvatil!
Title: Codenames

textfield_comment_value:
If there's one game that's become a staple at our gatherings, it's Codenames. With over 20 different people in our circle giving it a go, the verdict is unanimous: everyone loves it. 

What makes Codenames stand out is its universal appeal. Kids, grandparents, and everyone in between find themselves drawn into the fun, making it the perfect choice for family game nights or casual get-togethers with friends.

One of the best things about Codenames is its simplicity. The game is light, with rules that can be explained in just a couple of minutes, and setup is a breeze. This ease of access means you can go from opening the box to deep in gameplay in no time at all. Plus, it packs a good punch of replayability. Even if you start recognizing words from previous games, the dynamic nature of the clues and the infinite combinations keep the game fresh and engaging.

However, no game is without its flaws, and Codenames does have a minor one. The downtime between turns for the guessing teams can sometimes stretch a bit longer than some might like. But, in a way, this can also be seen as a hidden blessing. It gives players a chance to relax, strategize, or just enjoy the banter and anticipation of the next round, making the gameplay experience a bit more laid-back compared to more high-octane party games.

In essence, Codenames is a fantastic addition to any game collection, perfectly balancing simplicity, excitement, and inclusivity.

textfield_comment_value:
1/5/17 - This game is good in theory, and probably fine for people who are good with words/language, but as a math/science/numbers guy - I hated this. It was tolerable as a guesser (once there was actually something to guess), but it was just awful as the clue-giver. There's so many words on the board and you have to think of a phrase that suits your own words but not the opponent's, and it either winds up taking forever to go through all the words and come up with a good clue, or you just hurry up to move the game along and don't make much progress because the clue you give isn't as useful as it could/should have been if you'd had more time to think about it. This would be much better in a different format, like an online message board maybe, where you could drag the game out much longer and take several hours to come up with the clue. Trying to do it live in just a few minutes is just terrible because everyone is basically just sitting around waiting for the next clue, which is boring.

2/16/22 - Bumped it up from 2 to 4. We found a website where you can play this online and it is much better digitally. It's just easier to visualize what cards are yours and what aren't, and easier to come up with clues for them. Still not sure I'd like to play the "real" game on tabletop, but the online one is fine. I still would never pick to play this if another board game was possible, but it's ok during virtual game nights over zoom.

textfield_comment_value:
As mentally engaging as you do or don't want it to be. A true team affair, with everyone getting their chance to both let their partners down and make an epic late-game save-the-day play. 

Opens avenues for cleverness and creativity in ways rarely seen in gaming. I personally love this, and the game shines when you’re with those who get a similar joy from creativity under pressures The main flaw of this design (and I hesitate to even classify it as a blemish) is that I’ve seen people buckle under pressure, with games playing out with single-card clues (which sort of goes against the whole point of the game). 

The cleverest bit of the game — and one I should just use in any game — is the timer that anyone at any time can flip over if they get bored. Love it.

Codenames has gotten more plays than probably any game in my collection, and I anticipate it will remain an evergreen for us in the “family reunion” and “family holidays” game space. Solid SdJ pick.

[2023] Depending on the game group, Codenames could be great fun. For all the complaints people could leverage that the two clue-givers need to sit emotionless for most of the time, there are some great laughs to be had.

As a notable example, players somehow managed to figure out every way to pair "Dog" when it was the assassin as the very first guess they would have considered despite much, much better options existing (Mail 3 - Mailman so "Dog", Space 3 - "Space Dog", Undomesticated 2 - dogs are domestic, so undomesticated "Dog"). Ultimately, better options were decided; however, both players trying to contain their composure would often end up breaking in those circumstances. It's just funny.

When I play, I tend to be rather annoying to some people as I enjoy coming up with crazy plays - clue of "Pull 2" made me think of the fact that in 1998, The Undertaker threw Mankind off Hell In A Cell, and plummeted 16 ft through an announcer's table. It worked out - everyone at the table thought I was stupid. That included the clue giver.

In some ways, I prefer Codenames to Codenames: Pictures when playing with fluent English speakers. There's a bit more insanity that Codenames permits - Pictures may be more accessible, but the challenge of word games is more enjoyable for me personally.
