Kurzrezension
"Flügelschlag" ist im Grunde ein Set Collection Spiel, verknüpft mit einem kleinen Arbeiter-Einsatz-Mechanismus. Die Spielmechanik steht aber nicht im Vordergrund, vielmehr sind es die wunderschönen Vogelkarten, von denen jede einzelne einzigartig illustriert und mit Hintergrundwissen versehen ist.

Spielablauf
Das Spiel verläuft über vier Runden.
Wer an der Reihe ist, wählt eine von vier zur Verfügung stehenden Aktionen:
1. Eine Vogelkarte in eine der drei Reihen (Wald, Steppe, Wasser) ausspielen: Dies kostet die auf der Vogelkarte geforderten Ressourcen und je nach Position eine bestimmte Menge Eier.
2. Ressourcen nehmen: Mit dieser Aktion können Ressourcen aus der Spielfeldmitte genommen werden. Je mehr Vogelkarten im Wald ausliegen, desto mehr Ressourcen erhält der Spieler.
3. Eier nehmen: Die Menge an Eiern, die der Spieler erhält, hängt von der Anzahl der gespielten Vögel in der Steppe ab.
4. Neue Vogelkarten auf die Hand nehmen: Und auch die letzte Aktion belohnt den Spieler, der mehr Vögel in seinem Wassergebiet ausgespielt hat.
Nach einer Aktion, werden alle Bonusaktionen der Vogelkarten, die bereits in der entsprechenden Reihe ausliegen, abgehandelt und der nächste Spieler ist an der Reihe.
Nachdem jeder alle Aktionssteine verbraucht hat, endet die Runde mit einer Zwischenwertung, in der jeder einen Aktionsstein verliert, sodass in der Folgerunde mit einem weniger auszukommen ist.
Das Spiel endet nach vier Runden mit der Schlusswertung, in der die ausgespielten Vögel, die Zwischenwertungen sowie übrige Eier und gefressene Beute als Punkte zusammengezählt werden.
Der Spieler mit den meisten Punkten gewinnt.

Erweiterungen
Die Erweiterung "Europa" fügt dem Stapel Vogelkarten nochmals einige Arten hinzu, die neue Fähigkeiten mitbringen, ohne die Spielregeln erweitern zu müssen. Ebenfalls sind neue Zielplättchen und Bonuskarten enthalten, um die Wiederspielbarkeit zu erhöhen.
"Oceanien" bereichert das Grundspiel nicht einfach nur mit mehr vom gleichen. Sie erweitert vor allem das Nahrungsangebot mit neuen Futtermarkern – dem Nektar – welchen einige Vögel in Australien zu sich nehmen. Für die Spielmechanik stellt Nektar eine Joker-Ressource dar, die beim Ausspielen von Vogelkarten als beliebiges Futter eingesetzt werden kann und bringt am Ende des Spiels einen zusätzlichen Mehrheiten-Mechanismus mit, der das Einsetzen des neuen Futters belohnt.
Dafür benötigen einige der neuen Vögel speziell diese Art der Ernährung und der Nektar darf nicht in die nächste Runde mitgenommen werden, sondern verfällt, wenn er nicht genutzt wurde.
Neben den neuen Futtermarkern, wurden auch die Nahrungswürfel und Spielbretter angepasst. Auf ihnen finden sich jetzt Möglichkeiten zum Erwerb des neuen Futters bzw. Aktionen, um die allgemeine Kartenauslage oder den Futtervorrat während einer Runde zu erneuern.
"Ozenaien" bietet natürlich ebenfalls zusätzliche Zielplättchen, Bonuskarten und reichlich neue Vogelkarten. Letztere mischen sich unter die anderen Vögel und enthalten neue Effekte, die teilweise erst am Spielende ausgeführt werden.
Die dritte Erweiterung "Asien" enthält - neben den üblichen neuen Zielplättchen, Vogel- und Bonuskarten ein neues Spielbrett speziell für die Zweispielervariante. Auf ihm werden die Eigenschaften der ausgespielten Vögel markiert, was bei den Wertungen zusätzliche Punkte generiert. Neben dem 2er-Spiel ist auch eine Variante für bis zu sieben Spielern enthalten. In dieser Variante teilen sich die Spieler im Grunde auf zwei Vogeltränken und zwei Futterhäuschen auf und es spielen immer zwei Spieler parallel ihren Zug. Warum man nicht gleich zwei unabhängige Partien spielen sollte, bleibt mir allerdings ein Rätsel.

Meinung
„Flügelschlag“ konnte mich in der Erstpartie auf der Messe 'SpielDoch' in Duisburg überhaupt nicht überzeugen. Es plätscherte vor sich hin und von Interaktion war keine Spur zu sehen. Vielleicht bin ich etwas reifer geworden, vielleicht ergötze ich mich aber mittlerweile einfach nur an den wunderschönen Spielkarten und dem Spielmaterial. Denn nach ein paar weiteren Partien hat mich das Spiel doch noch in seinen Bann gezogen!
Das Spielmaterial ist solide. Pappmarker und Karten haben eine angenehme Dicke. Mich stört allerdings die Vogeltränke - ein Plastikteil, auf dem die zur Verfügung stehenden Vogelkarten ausliegen. Sie passt optisch leider überhaupt nicht zum restlichen Spielmaterial. Dagegen ist das Vogelhäuschen - welches als Würfelturm dient - zwar sehr stimmig, steht dafür aber recht wackelig und unpraktisch auf dem Tisch herum. Beide Komponenten habe ich aus meinen Partien verbannt und lege die Karten und Würfel einfach direkt auf den Tisch!
Die Regeln sind leicht zu verstehen und das Spiel bietet ein schönes Spielerlebnis, ohne allzu komplex zu werden. Die Interaktion ist wirklich nicht sehr hoch und beschränkt sich fast ausschließlich auf die Ziele zwischen den Runden. „Flügelschlag“ ist aber eines der Spiele, bei dem ich nicht benennen könnte, wer die letzte Partie gewonnen hat, weil es mir schlicht egal ist! Dabei spiele ich sehr wohl auf einen Sieg, aber mir reichen die wunderschönen Kartenillustrationen und der einfache Spielfluss aus, um einfach großen Spaß bereits während der laufenden Partie zu haben.
Die Spielmechanik ist sehr gut ausgetüftelt. Zu Beginn der Partie stehen den Spielern verhältnismäßig viele Aktionen, aber wenig Bonnies ihrer Vögel zur Verfügung. Im Spielverlauf dreht sich dieses Verhältnis um, sodass sich die Runden nicht in die Länge ziehen, sondern annähernd gleich lange bleiben.
Vergleiche ich „Flügelschlag“ mit der neuen Inkarnation „Schwingenschlag“, muss ich zugeben, dass letzteres eine deutliche Verbesserung im Spieldesign vorweisen kann. Dafür ist es aber auch komplexer und es fehlt ihm die Leichtigkeit, die mich beim ursprünglichen Spiel so beflügelte. Für mich ist „Flügelschlag“ das bessere der beiden Spiele. Es konnte mich mit jeder Partie und mit jeder Erweiterung immer weiter überzeugen und hat mittlerweile einen festen Platz in meiner Sammlung und meinem Herzen verdient.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
[i][u]Disclaimer:[/u][/i] This is a [color=#000099][b]standalone game[/b][/color]. Its rating is based on [color=#000099][b]desire to play[/b][/color].

Due to the incredible hype surrounding it, I received my copy of [b]Wingspan[/b] very late, several months after I ordered the game. Overall, I would say it was worth the wait: [b]Wingspan[/b] is a very good game. But in my opinion, it falls just short of being a great one, as I will explain later.

First of all the game is absolutely gorgeous. The art is spectacular, the birds are beautiful, the colors are vibrant, and the material is great as well: the cards have a linen finish that makes them very satisfying to manipulate, the eggs pastel colors are very soothing, and the birdfeeder is a joy to use everytime the food needs to be rerolled.

The mechanisms are also fun to play with, and there is a real sense of progression throughout the game. You start with small actions (drawing one card, gaining one food) and often end up with a fantastic engine, drawing 3 cards and activating 3 or 4 bird powers on the way. But as the rounds go by, your stock of actions available diminishes, which ensures the game plays quickly and usually leaves you with something more to do when it ends (like a good magician, stopping when the crowd asks for one more trick). I can't count the times my father said to me "I wish I had one or two more actions to complete this", which prompted a request for a rematch.

As with most card-based games, [b]Wingspan[/b] rewards adaptability more than a fixed strategy, which I very much like. You must be ready to change your course of action if a particular bird shows up in the market, or start working on the next objective if your opponent has taken an insurmountable lead in the current round competition. There is a nice variety of strategies available and some cool combos between birds, although I wish there was a little less redundancy between them. The European Expansion really improves the game on that front, by the way, giving players a lot more avenues towards victory with special end-of round bird powers. Finally, the rules are clear and leave very little room for error (just make sure you know about the ruling regarding rerolls of the birdfeeder: they can be made in the middle of a food action, as each die is treated separately) and I appreciate the fact that the game allows 5 players, a rare enough feature among Eurogames.

Now let's talk about the few issues I have with the game: there are mostly two. First and foremost, the interaction between players is extremely limited. I'm not a fan of "take-that" mechanisms and I appreciate a peaceful competition between players, but I think [b]Wingspan[/b] pushes that cursor a bit too far and ends up on the verge of multiplayer-solitaire. You still need to pay attention to what your opponents are doing for the end-of-round objectives, but there is very little you can do to affect them, let alone try and derail their plans.

The other issue I have is more minor, but deserves a small paragraph nonetheless. Some of the birds (four out of 170, to be precise) are truly overpowered, and if one of them happens to be in the opening hand of a good player, the game is pretty much over from the start. This doesn't occur very frequently, but is annoying when it does, especially since two of those birds warp the game in a very unpleasant way: by allowing you to trade one egg for two food of your choice, they make it so that you don't have to get food from the birdfeeder ever. This is absolutely brutal in a 2-player game: the raven player's opponent is now stuck with the dicerolls he or she gets from the birdfeeder. I encourage you to read this thread if you wish to learn more about the issue : https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/2247955/problem-ravens/page/1

There is a silver lining hiding with these birds, though. When teaching the game to new players, I use them to level the playing field by allowing them to choose one of the OP birds in their opening hand. It has worked great so far and produced some close games without recourse to more artifical measures such as a 10-point or 5-food headstart.

One last thing of particular importance in these COVID-troubled times: the solo mode is fantastic. It provides a great challenge in the hardest difficulty, and does so without altering the game too much (so that you mostly play the same way you would in a multiplayer game, but still have to reevaluate some birds in the context of an Automa opponent). I also love the way the Automa competes for objectives, which is both fair and unpredictable, leading to great moments of unexpected triumph. I can honestly say I had some of my best solo experiences with [b]Wingspan[/b]: experimentation with birds I would never consider in multiplayer, ferocious battles for end-of-round objectives, and already two tense games decided by a single point.

[u]2023 update:[/u] After a few years, I must admit that I'm finding the base game of [b]Wingspan[/b] a bit repetitive, mostly due to the end of round objective that revolve too much around eggs. Between "eggs in a specific habitat" and "eggs in a specific type of nest" objectives, laying eggs is very rewarded and in my opinion too much so. To make things worse, in the last round laying eggs is very strong as well because of the sheer victory points it gives when you lay four of them, and it is quite a disappointing ending when all the players do it. Because of this, while I'm still thrilled to play a game of [b]Wingspan[/b] with an expansion anytime, I'll only play the base game as a gateway experience for new players, so I'm downgrading its rating to 7/10.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
A Wingspan egy jó játék. Boldog vagyok, hogy kipróbálhattam és játszhattam vele néhányat. De nem vásárolnám meg. Legfőképp az ára miatt, illetve azon aránytalanság miatt, ami az egyébként tényleg remek játékmenet és az ár (no meg a hype) között feszül.

Game design tekintetében nem lehet sok panasz a játékra. Egy kiválóan megalkotott ún. engine builder játék ötletes megoldásokkal, fokozódó kihívással. Számomra az ötletek legjobbika a körönként csökkenő akciószám, bár a kivitelezése a színes kockákkal messze nem olyan nagyszerű. Tetszik még a dobókockák újradobásának érdekes feltételrendszere és végül az is, ahogyan ezt a mechanikus rendszert sikerült összekapcsolni a madarak tulajdonságaival.

Mert senki ne értse félre: a játék nem tematikus. Madaras. De nem tematikus. Épp olyan, mint a címe: jól hangzik (inkább angolul, mint magyarul), de semmit nem mond el a játékmenetről. A Wingspan-ben nem vagyunk madarak, de nem vagyunk sem madárfigyelők, vadászok, vagy ornitológusok sem. A játék csupán azt kínálja fel, hogy az akciószekvenciákat madaras témában játsszuk végig. Azaz madáreleségeket szerzünk be, tojások kerülnek a lapkákra, néha egy-egy ragadózómadár (de nem csak azok!) maguk alá gyűrnek kisebb (fesztávú - lám itt a kapcsolat!) madarakat, de az ezek közötti kapcsolat olyan távoli, hogy akár teljesen cserélhető volna. Mondok példát: az egyik madár például (aktiválásakor) minden játékosnak szerez egy egység gabonát, miközben ő nem fogyaszt ilyesmit, ugyanis az élelem nem a táblára felhelyezett madarak életben tartására szolgál, hanem csak a kártyák első kijátszásának feltétele. Mondjam úgy, hogy az így, egy madár által szerzett élelemmel más madarak elhelyezését támogatjuk? Vagy: ha a tojás akciót választjuk, előbb eldől, hogy 2-4 tojás tojatik az akció során, de hogy mely madár tojja azokat, az egy játékosdöntés kérdése. Hogy melyik tojik végül? Aminek a kártyájára fér még tojás a megjelölt limiten belül. Vannak tehát apró kapcsolatok a mechanika és a madarak általános tulajdonságai (fészekrakás, élőhely, szaporaság, táplálkozás stb.), de ilyen alapon egy bármilyen rendszerrel - a számítógép alkatrészektől a 80-as évek popzenekaraiig - összeköthető lett volna. (És ismeretterjesztőnek se nevezze nekem senki: az ötpontos kurzív betűvel leírt, sosem több, mint egymondatos infóval senki nem megy messzire a madárismeretben!)

Látványra a Wingspan igen vegyes képet nyújt. Van a szép borító, a szép (bár sokszor túl kis betűkkel és jelekkel operáló) madárkártyák, a csinos fatojások és a teljesen átlagos, de jól működő élelemtokenek. De ami ezen túl van, az szinte említésre sem értelmes. És ezek között ott van a tábla (pontosabban a játékostábla, hiszen központi tábla nincs a Wingspan-ben), a bónuszkártyák, a fordulók céljait mutató kis tábla, a teljesen felesleges dobótorony, vagy az értékelőlap - de még a kártyalapok hátoldala is ide sorolandó. Látszik egy átgondolt koncepció, de ez nem segít az összbenyomáson. Az egyes elemek néhol már prototípus szinten minimalizáltak - és csúfak. Magát  játékot (az apró, nehezen beazonosítható ikonok kivételével) nem nehezítik, de a kétségtelenül megjegyezhető színvilág és összkép nem okoz kellemes élményt. 

A Wingspan előnye tehát a játékmenet, és még sokan említhetnék a variabilitást, ami a rettenetes kártyamennyiségből kiszámítható. Ez így van, kétségkívül impozáns a másfél száz különböző madárrajz és -tulajdonság, de ez azért kissé megtévesztő. Képességben ugyanis ezek a madárkártyák nagyon is hasonlítanak egymásra. Lehet, hogy két azonos madárkártya nincs a pakliban, azonban sok van, ami ugyanazzal a képességgel bír, miközben legfeljebb a tojásrakási limitje vagy a fészektípusa, esetleg a fesztávja különbözik kevéssel. Ez természetesen a változatosságot nagyban szolgálja, de nem a tervezhetőség oldalon, hanem pusztán a véletlen tekintetében. A Wingspan egyetlen igazi hátránya (a gyenge tematika mellett) a viszonylag magas szerencsefaktor. Ez elsősorban a kártyahúzásnál érinti meg a játékost (hiába próbálja csökkenteni a jelentőségét a három közszemlére kirakott, választható, nyílt kártya), de az élelem tekintetében a dobókockák hatása is mindenható - bár kétségtelenül e hatás csökkentésére is vannak megoldásjavaslatok a szabályban.

A játék sokat emlegetett szoliter jellegét én nem utálom. Egyrészt mert ilyen van, és tulajdonképpen sok játékban van, csak legfeljebb jobban igyekeznek takargatni. Másrészt mert azért van interakció a játékosok között. Persze ha úgy jönnek ki a lapok... Az egyik partira jellemző volt, a másikra egyáltalán nem. Aztán megint jött egy parti, ahol igen...

A Wingspan egy relatíve gyors, fordulatos, családi játéknak mondható engine builder. Egy olyan középkategóriás játék, amilyennel bármikor szívesen játszom, és szerintem van is a polcon egy tucat hasonló kategóriájú szerzeményem már. No de azok a Wingspan árának feléért, használtan harmadáért megvásárolhatók! Lehet, hogy nincs egyikben sem 160+ különböző kártyalap (mert nem is kell), nincsenek pasztellszínű fatojások (mert nem muszáj) és kartonból készült madáretető, mint kockatorony (hiszen felesleges) - nem beszélve a "linen finished" kiképzésű szabályfüzetről (ami meg már egyenesen röhejes). De ezek egyikéért sem adnék még legalább annyit, mint magáért a játékért adtam. Van ebben valami taszító mókusvakítás, ami messze nem róható fel a szerzőnek - legfeljebb a kiadónak/fejlesztőknek, akik a végső formák kialakításáért felelősek.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
BESONDERS EMPFEHLENSWERT

In "WINGSPAN (FLÜGELSCHLAG)" sind wir Vogelliebhaber. Unser Ziel ist es, möglichst viele Vögel in unser Gebiet zu locken und sie Eier legen zu lassen.

Auf den ersten Blick fällt auf: das Spiel hat einen einmalig schönen Look und wundervolle Illustrationen. Mechanisch ist das Spiel im wesentlichen ein kartengetriebener Engine-Builder, durch das Thema und durch das bezaubernde Design wurde dieses Spiel zum spektakulären Erfolg, der die unterschiedlichsten Spielertypen anspricht. Die Auszeichnung Kenner-Spiel des Jahres war da nur folgerichtig.

Gemacht wurde das Spiel von Elizabeth Hargrave, einer Politanalystin, Hobby-Ornithologin und Spieleautorin. Und die Liebe zu Vögeln merkt man bei jedem Aspekt des Spieles. Die Illustratorinnen Ana María Martínez Jaramillo, Natalia Rojas und Beth Sobel haben auch einen fantastischen Job gemacht. Bei den wunderschönen Grafiken denkt man sofort an klassische Tierillustrationen. Auch wenn ich eigentlich geschlechterspezifische Bewertungen gar nicht mag: man merkt, daß vier Frauen das Spiel gestaltet haben. Soviel einfühlsame Detailliebe findet sich in der Brettspiel-Welt nur selten.

Man kann das Spiel zu zweit, mit bis zu fünf Spielern oder sogar alleine spielen und es funktioniert in allen Konstellationen. Das liegt vor allem daran, daß man meist damit beschäftigt ist, seine eigene Engine auszubauen. Momente, in denen man andere behindert gibt es so gut wie gar nicht. Das könnte auch einer der wenigen Kritikpunkte sein, denn man spielt spielmechanisch fast gar nicht miteinander. Allerdings merkt man bei Partien sehr schnell, daß das Diskutieren über einzelne Vögel mehr als genug Interaktion bietet. Konkurrenzaktionen gibt es kaum. Gewonnen hat der, der in der Schlußabrechnung am meisten Punkte gemacht hat. Aber irgendwie kommt es bei "Flügelschlag" gar nicht so darauf an, wer gewinnt, das Spielen selber ist viel relevanter.

Zu Spielbeginn ziehen wir fünf der zahlreichen einzigartigen Vogelkarten und nehmen uns fünf Nahrungsplättchen. Fünf der zehn Gegenstände müssen wir wieder ablegen.

Jeder hat sein eigenes Spielfeld, auf dem vier Aktionsleisten abgebildet sind. Pro Runde können wir eine Aktion machen. Wir können einen Vogel legen, Nahrung nehmen, Eier legen oder Vogelkarten nachziehen. Die Vögel haben drei Lebensräume: den Wald, das Grasland und das Wassergebiet.

Jeder Vogel hat bestimmte Eigenschaften, kann nur in bestimmte Lebensräume gelegt werden, hat eine definierte Nestart, eine Höchstzahl an Eiern, eine Größe und eine besondere Eigenschaft, die entweder beim Ausspielen oder bei einer Aktion seinem Lebensraum aktiviert wird. Außerdem muß zum Auslegen eines Vogels eine bestimmte Nahrungs-kombination bezahlt werden.

DIe Engine funktioniert durch eine Kombination aus Lebensraum und Aktion. Holen wir uns Nahrung, aktivieren wir alle nacheinander alle Vögel, die sich im Waldgebiet befinden. Legen wir Eier aktivieren wir nacheinander alle Vögel, die in der Graslandschaft gelegt wurden. Und ziehen wir neue Vogelkarten aktivieren wir nacheinander alle Vögel, die wir im Wassergebiet auf unser Spielfeld ausgelegt haben.

Die aktivierten Fähigkeiten können sehr unterschiedlich sein. So dürfen wir zum Beispiel Eier legen oder Nahrung nehmen. Raubvögel haben meist eine Jagdaktion, bei der wir eine neue Karte ziehen. Ist der gezogene Vogel kleiner als auf der Raubvogelkarte angegeben, schlägt unser Raubvogel sein Opfer. Die Karte des gefressenen Vogels wird dann unter die Raubvogelkarte gelegt und zählt bei Spielende als Siegpunkt. Viele Vögel haben auch Aktionen, die dann auslösen, wenn die Mitspieler etwas Bestimmtes machen.

Sehr schön ist noch der Nahrungsmittelmechanismus. Fünf Würfel zeigen die gerade verfügbare Nahrung an. Wählen wir die Aktion Nahrung nehmen, wählen wir einen der Würfel und bekommen das angezeigte Nahrungsplättchen. Ist nur noch eine Nahrungsart auf den Würfeln vorhanden, darf neu gewürfelt werden.

Gespielt wird in vier schlanken Runden. Jede Runde hat ein zufälliges Rundenziel, wie etwa gelegte Eier in einer bestimmten Nestart, das Extrapunkte liefert. Zudem gibt es auch noch Bonuskarten, die bestimmte Spielziele vorgeben, die am Ende auch Punkte bringen. Zum Beispiel möglichst viele Vögel mit Namen, die Körperteile beinhalten zu legen.

Das klingt jetzt alles komplizierter als es in Wirklichkeit ist. "Flügelschlag" ist ein recht zugänglicher Enginebuilder, bei dem man schnell während des Spielens die Regeln begreift. 

"Flügelschlag" ist ein Phänomen, denn es verführt auch Brettspielmuffel zum spielen. Und, ganz nebenbei, lernt man sogar auch etwas und ist erstaunt über sich selber, wenn man an der nächsten Straßenecke versonnen dem hochfliegenden Krähenschwarm nachschaut. 

Und genau deswegen gebührt "Flügelschlag" die höchste Punktzahl. Es mag spielmechanisch einige bessere Spiele geben, aber bei kaum einem anderen Spiel ist die Freude, es zu spielen, wenn man es vorschlägt, bei so vielen unterschiedlichen Menschen so ausnehmend groß.

Fazit:
Bestmögliche Umsetzung eines hochfliegenden Brettspiels.

Kategorie: zugänglicher Engine-Builder, Kennerspiel
Spielerzahl: 1-5
Spieldauer: 40-70 min.
Autor: Elizabeth Hargrave
Illustratoren: Beth Sobel, Natalia Rojas, Ana Maria Martinez
Erscheinungsjahr: 2019
Verlag: Feuerland

10/10 Gesamtwertung
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
12/13/2022

Talk about a game that quickly got exposed to the general audience, for good reason, and that quickly made an impact on the board gaming industry. Between a solid engine building design, beautiful presentation of components and art, and honestly one the most inviting themes made this an eye catching marvel worth trying.

Before I dive in to all the previously mentioned aspects, I also want to give this game huge kudos since this was made from someone who was new to the board game design scene and that it was a female led designer backed by female artists as well. And while I don't know how everyone identifies and who everyone involved is, this space often feels male dominated in terms of who we often bring up in conversations, so I definitely want to bring attention how huge this game has become due to quality and that a gender diverse team made this with so much detail, that I'm honestly very grateful to have such a beautiful vision make an impact to a hobby that I love. Even with any criticisms I have for the game design, I want to thank anyone who made this project happen. Y'all are terrific!

That aside, the engine building design is probably why there's always an itch to come back and play more. With so many bird cards to fill up your habitat, your personal tableau, the engine you're bound to come across will always have different nuances and a game play loop. And the fact that each bird brings a thematic, educational, and game affecting component is very clever design. The options are truly endless. Which is also a double edge sword. Sometimes the abundance of birds can make cycling for a bird that may optimize your habitat a inconsistent chore. Especially for an engine building game where you want to feel satisfied with what you created, it can often feel up to chance if you came across the right bird. What I feel often happens is that if I try to be too competitive in this game, I'm left feeling a little disappointed because I knew what I needed and my luck to pivot to a different strategy feels random at best due to my previous complaint on the sheer abundance of cards. But if I play this for the thematic presentation and educational vision, than I'm always impressed to see how everything is incorporated to make up the game design. I know the expansions fix this to a certain degree, but I want to weigh this for the base game alone plus I still think this issue is present with other expansions to a certain degree.

There's a couple other criticisms that I have, and I rather get these out of the way. Some cards never feel relevant due to the high feed cost and how many turns it takes to get it into my habitat. This is definitely fixed by the Oceania expansion, which is fantastic, but for the base game it feels like I'm often ignoring birds when I want to appreciate them instead. And while this isn't a true criticism, I often wish this game had one additional round. Cause the clever thing is that each round gets shorter as you score each round objective, and there's the grand total of four rounds. By the fourth round I'm just repeating a couple actions over and over again, when I want to fine tune my engine that I struggle to get to, and I want to use the theoretical last round for me to finally play with the engine I made. The game plays fine how it is, but it is a repeated feeling I have when I do get to the final round since the end happens so quick.

With all of that out of the way, this game is definitely one of the most appealing and inviting games to play at a glance. Each bird card gives you a brief, but detailed, summary of the bird it's representing. The diet, habitat, size, how many eggs they lay, and what these birds can do that support the game play. It's amazing how all of these get represented and all you want to do is share this with someone who has never played before. Plus you know this is a labor of love because there are goal cards you get at the beginning, so there's something you can individually aim for from the start, and it gives you the percentage of how many birds can help you accomplish this certain goal. And what makes this incredible is that they accounted the percentage for each expansion that has come out and made sure the cards wouldn't skew the odds in any way. When I say this game has been meticulously considered, I truly mean it. Without this theme, there's no alternative for Wingspan. Some games you can change a ruling, the theme, or something in between, yet with Wingspan it's the whole collective of what makes up this game that makes it so unique and irreplaceable.

I recommend this game to most. If it's someone totally new to this hobby or someone younger, I honestly think it's pretty complex. I know people love showing this one off cause how could you not, but it has a lot of overwhelming aspects to the gaming illiterate. If you play games, generally, you'll eventually pick it up after a couple of turns. I want people to play this game, but I don't want to scare them away from it. Maybe introduce them to Stone Age, show them basic game mechanics, then upgrade them to this. ESPECIALLY if they love birds.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Exactly not my sort of game.

First impressions after my first (and with any luck, only) game. It's a pretty, themefree and tedious solo game played simultaneously with one or more other people who happen to be seated at the table and playing the same game. The loser is the one who gets a bad opening hand and then can't get the dice or the cards they need.

I've heard that it's easy to learn. Not for everyone. Not for me. I find this kind of arbitrary-interlocking-moving-parts game horribly confusing.

The first principle that I failed to see is that you should try to get as many cards on your player mat as possible. Nobody will tell you this. You heard it here first. The reason is that the more cards you have placed, the more effective each of your moves becomes. And if you care about winning, you need your moves to be as effective as possible. 

It costs tokens to play a card from your hand. Some cards cost 1 token, some 2 and some 3. Getting 3 tokens, especially at the start of the game, is ruinously difficult. Because you want to get cards out on the mat as quickly as you can, at the start of the game you want to aim for the cheapest cards possible and get rid of those expensive ones. Don't be like me.

The player mat consists of four rows. One row controls how many tokens you acquire for a single move.

Tokens become easier to acquire once you have one or more cards in the token-control row. That's really important because without tokens you can essentially do nothing. I found that out all by myself.

The tokens come in several suits (rats, berries, fish, grain, invertebrates). To play most cards from your hand onto your mat, you have to pay a token of a specified suit, or in the case of the more expensive cards, a combination of suits.

You are in direct competition with the other players for one thing only - tokens. It is likely that you will be trying to collect tokens in the same suit as other players. The supply of tokens in the various suits is strictly and severely limited, but it is always possible to convert two tokens of any suit into a single token of a suit required to place a card on the mat. Thus it is more sensible to collect tokens of any suit at all than it is to wait for the right suit to offer itself to you. This is obvious to anyone who has grasped the game. Unlike me.

In general, cards with a brown stripe improve your effectiveness more than cards without. So once you have some cards on the mat, it's probably sensible to aim to collect (and play!) brown striped cards. 

Cards also have various other characteristics that limit the way they can be played or offer opportunities for various ways of scoring. Stay with me, now. Stay with me. Hello? Stay with me. As the game goes on, you will also need to focus on playing cards with particular characteristics. But you do not want to wait until the game goes on to start collecting them, because if you do it will be too late. 

Most cards carry a restriction on which row they can be played on. Once played, most cards cannot be moved. 

At the start of the game your hand will contain a card that offers a reward for a particular achievement. This is a trap. Your first decision will be to pick certain cards to discard. Do not allow the "achievement" card to influence your decision more than marginally at most. Focus on getting cheap cards onto the mat fast. You'll probably get your achievement by mistake anyway.

The second card in a row costs tokens as before, but also requires you to pay a token of a different kind, called an egg. It's called an egg because theme and it's shaped like an egg. Cool, eh? These tokens are undifferentiated, having no suits. By placing these tokens on specific cards you also contribute to certain other goals. Capice?

On the issue of other goals, as if the miscellaneous plates you have to keep revolving on sticks wasn't enough, the game offers several other ways to score - for example by collecting sets of particular kinds of cards in specific rows or with eggs on them.

To me, this entire mechanic is a complicated mess. My mind just doesn't work like this - all interlocking cogs with varying influences on each other and random payoffs unrelated to anything. 

The theme is not just irrelevant but obstructive for someone like me, a literal thinker for whom metaphor has great significance. The game wouldn't change one iota if it were about computers, motherboards and hard drives, mobile phones and apps, or archaeological digs. It might be better if it were themeless, though. It'd be less pretty, but.

Have you ever been stoned and confused? Really confused, where climbing onto a bicycle is just too complicated? Hold on to that state of mind; you're picturing me playing Wingspan. Apart from mounting misery, my main emotions were humiliation, and great relief when I finally played my last cube.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
[2023] I was working at a game store around the time that Wingspan was coming out. The hype was unbelievable - I had people coming in saying that they had read about this game in a New York Times article and they wanted to buy a copy (re: March 11, 2019, "She Invented a Board Game With Scientific Integrity. It’s Taking Off."). When does that ever happen? There are many reasons to celebrate the existence of Wingspan (although I am now annoyed with how many abstract nature-themed games exist), including just how wonderful this artwork is. If someone would ever show the slightest bit of interest upon seeing me play a boardgame with someone, I would usually show them Wingspan as an idea of "Here's what a game -can- look like". Dear God is the production gorgeous. Many times, they pull the phone out of my hands because they want to keep looking at the pretty art of the birds. 

I remember how excited I was when I got my copy on special-order. I also remember the first time I opened it up and felt all of the premium materials. I then remember how disappointed I was when I played it: I... just didn't get the appeal. 

I tried it again, maybe a year later with the same game group - did not see the appeal. As I came to learn, I coincidentally had not enjoyed many of the games I played with that group. Board Game Arena has an implementation? Let me try it!

Turns out, same deal. The downtime in this game can be obnoxiously long, even for a digital implementation. Then, when the turn order gets back to me, I look to my actions - nothing I want in the birdfeeder, I don't have any reason to lay eggs, there are no face-up cards I like, and I cannot afford any of the cards in my hand. Further, nearly no one else is actually interested in resetting the birdfeeder despite them seeming to have bottomless amounts of food available to them. Also, there is always that -one- player who managed to get some crazy 3-card combo going very early in the game, meaning their engine is off to the races while you're struggling to get yours going in first gear. Who cares about "Most birds with eggs in cavity nests" or having cards named after people when you have to keep taking empty "Draw Bird Cards" action? While I managed to get a half-way decent engine going, I simply wound up only getting it online after losing the first two rounds (and tying the third), in which the game was basically over at that point. Also: my objective was Prairie Manager, which is to place "Birds that can only live in Grassland" - small problem which is that my opponent placed 3 of those, and I swear that I had not seen any (with the vast majority being Wetland-only, Wetland/Grasslands, or Forest-only). That bonus was worth a maximum of 8 points, but my opponent gets 2 points per card that has the wild symbol that can be any cost? Seriously? I had 4 of those in my tableau and I wasn't even trying for that objective!

I don't understand how, but the Board Game Arena timers in this recent game were consistently reaching 1:00 or passing into the negative. It was basically an hour-long slog. I just wanted this game over with. Besides, it was clear that one of my opponents had an 'egg' engine online by the start of the 3rd round and my 'tuck' engine would not be remotely capable of catching up... all because I tried competing for the "Most wetland birds" round bonus that I ended up tying.

I want to love this game, I really do. I keep thinking to myself "Maybe it'll be fun -this time-" like it will be different from any other time, or "Maybe if I tried the expansion" but threads on BoardGameGeek are as conflicted on those as with the base game. For the time this game takes, I would just rather be playing something like Terraforming Mars with the Prelude expansion, or Gizmos, or literally anything else. For this reason, I am planning on selling Wingspan; however, doing so will pain me greatly when I actually do. Nothing about this experience feels properly -tight- to me, so trying to sink my teeth into it just leaves me progressively more frustrated each time.

What Wingspan needs is a Prelude-esque expansion, or at least house rules to start 1 space further on our tableau. A friend of mine mentioned Board Game Arena is perhaps the worst way of playing this game as you need to feel the cards and become engrossed in the theme and iconography (which I very much disagree with), before conceding this game does feel like a bit of a slog. What he then noted was the following: "What this game needs is something like Sushi Go where people could play their hands at the same time". Sadly, due to cards being so reliant on the deck and the resources being so reliant on the birdfeeder, that suggestion is not particularly feasible.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
This is my favourite, with over 100 plays in it. I also have all expansions, and I will talk about all of it; although largely, all the points below apply to the base game alone.

Things I find great:
    - A non aggressive game were each player cannot hurt other players (except very passively such as taking food the other player wants, refusing activating areas to prevent pink powers, or taking the "good" bird from the bird tray).
    - There are dozens of available strategies that one can go for and there is very little influence on the starting hand as the game progresses. (Although, one needs to know the game sufficiently well to realise that a "bad" starting hand has little to no impact in the game overall.)
    - Art is beautiful, and quality of  materials is great. And while the bird feeder is a bit gimmicky, it adds a lot of utility in the game; specifically, since the player mats occupy a lot of space, it is quite nice that the roll of dice can be done in a confined space that will not move pieces around accidentally.
    - The amount of cards is so large that no two games are alike.
    - The variety of powers is so large that one is always doing actions, even when it is not one's turn (pink, teal and yellow powers active off-turns).
    - It is quite hard to keep track of who is ahead of other players, so at the end, one usually ends surprised in how close we all end up. This, however, requires familiarity with the game for some new players do complain how some experienced players have accumulated more points (e.g. because they have eggs or token or tucked cards).
    - Asian Expansion introduced the Duet mode which is wonderful for two players. It makes two player games much more enjoyable, and it refreshes the game a lot without spoiling anything that makes wingspan wonderful.
    - Solo mode is also very good, and solo duet mode is fantastic. It is quite challenging and it allows you to hone your skills.

Things that require improvement:
    - Many birds of prey from North America (base game) have "When Activated" (brown powers) that are too weak. For example, some birds ask you to roll all dice not in bird feeder and if any is a fish, you get 1 fish (regardless of how many fishes showed up). From basic elementary probability, we know that such a bird will give you an expected number of fishes equal to 0 for 0 die available, 1/6 for 1 die available, 2/6 for 2 dice, 3/6 for 3 die and 4/6 for 4 die (there can never be more than 4 die available). Assuming 0,1,2,3, and 4 dice appear equally likely, each with 20% chance, we get that such a card will give you in average 0.2(1/6+2/6+3/6+4/6) = 5/6 points per activation. Newer cards give you easily 1 or 2 points per activation. Thus, some cards in the base game are absolute trash while new cards are over powered in comparison.
    - Oceania expansion introduced nectar, this is great for experienced players making surpassing the 150 final score rather probable, but it is exceedingly punishing for new players. Furthermore, all ravens become broken cards with nectar (i.e. from being quite strong to outright broken since what hold them back was the 3 food cost, easily doable with wild nectar).
    - The are so many cards that sleeving the game is quite expensive (it costs as much as buying a new base game). I wish Stonemaier would just sell replacement components as is (the bird feeder is the first one to take a large beat up). Also, the deck is so large that sleeving it increases its already immense height three fold.
    - Newer or less experienced players may get "lucky" the first time around and may want to repeat an strategy; this is not quite doable with wingspan since there are so many birds, chances you get a similar strategy twice is quite unlikely. I have done the strategy of placing as many birds with as many eggs only twice in maybe 100 plays. This is so because some good birds for some strategies will not show up again. So newer players often find the game restrictive (it is quite the opposite in fact). One needs to adapt and be open to try what the game gives you.
    - Newer players do not realise that the bulk of points (between 30 and 50 percent) come from feather points, while most of the other points are taken in the last round. So, some new players may feel they already lost by the end of 3rd round when they very much are likely to win.
    - The name of the expansions is not consistent; they are called "European Expansion", "Oceania Expansion" and "Asia." I much rather have them named "Europe Expansion", "Oceania Expansion" and "Asia Expansion" (although just using Europe, Oceania and Asia is fine too; or using the denomyns European, Oceanian and Asian is also fine)
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
As a big fan of birds and board games, Wingspan has very quickly become one of my favorite board games. An engine-building competitive bird collecting game is the perfect description. You play through 4 rounds of playing new birds, acquiring food sources for those birds, laying eggs to score points and play new birds, and drawing new bird cards so you can play them or use them as victory points. You also have end of round goals at the end of each of the 4 rounds such as having the most birds played or having the most eggs laid in the forest. 

The board is laid out into 3 rows: The forest which is where you acquire resources, the prairie which is where you can lay eggs, and the wetlands which is where you can draw more bird cards. You can also play up to 5 birds which cost eggs depending on how many you play in each habitat. 

When you decide to play a bird, you should consider the different characteristics that it has. It will have a food/resource cost (bug, fish, fruit, grain, and/or rodent), the habitat(s) that they can be placed in, a nest type, victory points that they are worth at the end of the game, a wingspan, and an effect. The food/resource cost is what you will have to have gathered in order to play your bird. If you play a bird after the first column, you will also have to pay 1 egg for columns 2 and 3 or 2 eggs for columns 4 and 5. Their costs will range from 1 of a resource up to 3. The habitat(s) that they can be played in will also be displayed with corresponding symbol(s) to the habitats on the board. They will also have a nest type which will interact with other birds' abilities and end of round goals. Each bird is worth the amount of victory points (feathers) displayed on their card as well. Each bird card has a listed wingspan (The name of the game), which will be relevant based on certain birds' abilities and bonus cards.

Birds can have "when played" effects which activate immediately, "when activated" effects which occur whenever you take the action in that habitat (Such as acquiring resources in the forest will activate all birds in the forest), and "in between rounds" effects which activate when your opponents do something. You use your "when activated" and "in between rounds" effects to create your engine and build your path to victory while also using a good mix of the "when played" abilities to kickstart your plays.

Acquiring resources lets you choose resources that are face-up on dice which will periodically get rerolled. It starts with 1 resource and increases with the more birds that you play in the forest. Laying eggs starts with laying 2 eggs and increases with the more birds that you play in the prairie. Drawing bird cards starts with 1 card and increases with more birds that you play in the wetlands.

You gain points based off of the values of the birds that you have played, a point for every egg on your board, the number of bird cards tucked behind your played bird cards (You will gain these from birds' effects), the number of food/resources cached on played bird cards (You will gain these from birds' effects), and points from bonus cards (Which you will start with 1 at the beginning of the game and some bird cards will allow you to draw more). You play until the end of the 4 rounds and then add up everyone's total victory points to determine the winner.

The European expansion greatly adds replayability by incorporating new cards and also includes 2 new types of card effects: "Game end" and "round end." "Game end" effects are usually quite strong and only activate once the final turn of the game occurs. "Round end" effects activate at the end of each of the 4 rounds and adds to the variety of ways that you can build your engine to get your plays going.

I have only used most of the new bird cards from the Oceania expansion so far and have not used the new boards, dice, or cards that involve nectar which is a new resource. I will review this expansion further at a later date once I have been able to test it out.

As you can see, I greatly enjoyed Wingspan and will continue to enjoy it for many games to come. It is a very fun and highly replayable game that has a fairly low complexity so that it can be enjoyed by people that aren't frequent board gamers or are a younger age. The European and Oceania expansions are also great additions if you are a fan of the base game as well. I can't recommend this game highly enough and I wish I were able to get my hands on it in 2019 when it came out (Sadly, I wasn't able to get a copy of this until the summer of 2020 due to it being constantly sold out which is a sign in its own right).
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Let's talk about birds for a minute! I'm not sure which version of this popular game I prefer more... this, or Wyrmspan (centered around dragons) which came later. Wingspan is certainly simpler, yet still not easy, for introducing to a new group of players. The idea of it is simple enough... build out three rows of bird cards, score points on the cards themselves, the eggs they lay, different round bonuses, tucked cards, stached food, and bonus points cards. I think that's it? Not looking at the game right now, but forgive me if I'm missing one!

Each row essentially gives you an advantage in one of three areas... the ability to get food, which you need to lay your bird cards and do different abilities, the ability to get eggs, which you need to lay later round bird cards and also score a lot of points (typically in later rounds), and the ability to get bird cards - which is helpful for a multitude of reasons, but not the least of which is obtaining cards from the center pile before your opponents who also may want them for their board. Winning typically requires balancing these row buildouts well, while paying attention to the bonuses being given each round, and your bird "powers." Those "powers" are activated each time you play a row... so if I play a "gain food" row token, I will first gain food, then go through each of my cards I've laid in that row previously, earning more points / benefit from them. Using that same example... if I do the "gain food" option - and have two other cards in that row - then I would first gain food, then do the action on the furthest right card in that row (say, "lay an egg for free on another bird,") then would do the last card in that row's action as well (say, "tuck a card here if the wingspan of the bird is less than 100 cm"). You can see already how this works over the duration of the game... what will largely separate the winners from the losers is how well you build out those rows, because with constantly chaining actions, you can amount a massive point advantage over your opponents if you play it right!

Currently, I probably prefer Wingspan to Wyrmspan, in that it's simpler (yet, not simple), with less mechanics (yet, still plenty of mechanics to track). It's the better game for trying to get you non-gamer friends to play with you, and only your most die-hard board game friends are likely to play Wyrmspan with you by comparison. The cards and presentation in both games is beautiful, and it's fun seeing information on each of these real-life birds as you play (where they live, what they look like, fun tidbits, etc.). Most of the people I've played this game with have enjoyed it, and it's an easy winner to bring out at our house.

My only real gripes... 

1) You're largely depending on other players to properly track their score and rounds. This can cause problems with several mechanics to track - so if they spend an entire game doing something wrong, then that can mess up their end-game score and possibly give them an undeserved win off that (Wyrmspan is a much worse offender of this from what I can tell though), or it can prevent you from benefitting off their bird card when perhaps you should have each round (some birds award bonuses to other players). Generally, this isn't a problem - though I have seen it.

2) A much bigger issue... there is a straight-up broken strategy in this game. Supposedly, it has been fixed in an expansion to the base game, but if you know it, it's pretty much impossible to beat. That said... it would likely take you several rounds of playing to see it (don't Google it!), you still could be thwarted by not getting the cards needed to pull it off (become a % chance of getting what you need), and it's so not fun for everyone else when you do it that the best call for anyone looking to have a fun board game night with friends and knows about it is to simply not do it. All that to say... I can look past it. I've done it once to see if it was as broken as advertised, and yes, it absolutely is. My wife and I didn't even bother finishing that game because (in a four round game) I probably had her beat after two rounds. Not fun, and stupid!

So yeah... Wingspan is an easy recommendation! It's not simple - don't introduce this to your Uno-loving friend - but it's not as complicated as Terraforming Mars either. It fits in that middle ground along with games like 7 Wonders, Red Rising and Pandemic. Strategy fans who like multiple ways of scoring and having to think through each turn will generally enjoy it. Give it a go!
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
1 play.

I enjoyed myself, and had a few sequences of several turns where I hatched a plan, executed it, and felt satisfied. The mechanisms for building the engine are pretty thematic, which is satisfying -- getting the food that that bird eats, playing the bird which requires that food and maybe an egg, placing it in its habitat, and then being able to execute its special abilities. Those abilities are thematic, for the most part -- being able to attack other birds under a certain size, collecting food, sneaking eggs into other birds' nests. The components are very good.

But overall, I felt a bit unsatisfied. Rather than feeling coherent, like I was building a fish-creating engine and getting more and more waterfowl and fish, it all felt a bit miscellaneous. The randomness of the goals added to this sense of arbitrariness, as did the point salad at the end of the game. It helps that you can see the eggs and cached food visibly; it would help if you could more clearly see the bird points, like maybe higher values could be larger and more colorful. I will need more plays to see if more familiarity makes it feel more coherent.

I did like several mechanics a lot: being able to draw from the three visible birds, or to draw a random bird; having both publicly visible goals and secret goals; having limited food and needing to strike fast to get the food before other birds do. 

The instructions are bad, with three completely separate documents all claiming to be the ones that you should read for your first play, and conflicting advice about shared goals for beginners (play the "default" side, or play the, um, other side?). The game isn't very complicated, really, and doesn't need the confusing separate pack of beginner cards. 

First of all, the instructions around the four types of move you can make each turn are far too complicated! Instead of starting by listing the option to play a bird card (which raises the question, which habitat would you want to play onto?), it should start by explaining that you can ALWAYS a) collect food; b) lay eggs; or c) draw cards. But, you start with each of these being slow -- just one food, just two eggs, just one card. Want to use the faster options, to the right? Then you'll need to choose option d), placing a bird card in your habitat. Why play bird cards? Well, the a/b/c actions that you can take in each row is the leftmost one showing, so placing birds onto that row will make it more powerful. You can place a bird if you qualify for three constraints: 1) you have to place it in the habitat it lives in, in the leftmost open space; 2) you have to pay the food it eats, when you place it; and 3) you have to pay some number of eggs for it to hatch (usually one egg; for the first bird in each habitat, zero eggs.) 

For another thing, the action tokens are almost completely unnecessary; their only function in a typical turn is 1) to count the turns remaining, and 2) to act as a pointer, like a reading finger, as you go down your row of birds using their abilities. The first thing the instructions could do is tell you, in large letters, that the action tokens are only to help you remember the steps of your turn, and have no actual function in gameplay! Just instruct players to put them onto the left side of their habitat board. In a note later, you can suggest that players use the right-to-left trick, which does help track their turn, but changes nothing about actual gameplay.

Bird cards are a crucial element of the game, but there isn't a prominent place near the start of the instructions that diagrams a typical bird card and explains what the various areas of the card mean.

There are also many rule ambiguities, and these could be addressed with clearer language, and maybe a few prominent frequently asked questions. Do you "activate" a bird when it's played? (No; players in my game weren't sure.) Can you spend "cached" food? (No; we were 10 turns in before we realized this.) Do birds with wild card food count for goal cards that describe birds that eat a particular food? (No; this could simply be made explicit on these cards themselves.) Does "drawing" a bird card mean you can take it from either the display or the deck? Does the "deck" include the tableau of three public cards? Etc.

Heaviness: 3 out of 5. Really not very complicated, if explained well.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
[EDIT] More games didn't changed my overall idea of this game that much. However, it became apparent to me that this is not a game that you can play by picking one strategy and going with it, but rather you have to adapt your game to whatever best you can get from your starting hand, and hope luck will swing your way with your next draws (that is, hoping that your next draws will somehow combine sufficiently enough with what you have played so far) . However even after accepting that, the game still feels woefully unbalanced. Cards that gives resources to your opponents at the cost of your action are incredibly underpowered (mostly because you always end up giving more resources to your opponents than you would get), while cards that gives extra resources (food, eggs and cards) only to you as part of activate them are or more or less essential to cope with the scarcity of options you have in the early turns. All in all, the cards of this game needed to be divided by some kind of logic tied to the phases of the game (as an example: engine cards at start, points/engine cards in the mid game, points card in the end game). It's simply stupid, for a game that want you to build some kind of engine, to allow players to be punished from the very start because they may not have got any card that can build such an engine. This flaw may be more tolerable if the game was shorter and less prone to AP, but that's not the case. In 4-5 players, the game can be quite lengthy (expecially when activated abilities begins to pile up) and the lack of interaction makes waiting for your turn more and more a hassle. So, again, this game is beautifully made and, overall, works sufficiently good, too bad that it's really not balanced enough to feel you are not constantly at risk of being screwed by randomness.

Beautiful game, but the game itself feels a bit like an accessory to the package, rather than being the real deal. It's mostly random, it's non interactive (and no, it's not like this game can't have players interaction because interaction it's all about "take that" effects, and this is supposed a "peaceful" game. I don't know why this misconception seems so strong in the case of this game. You can have tons of interactions between players in any game without necessarily getting on the nerves of anyone in the process), and some design choices are simply questionable, even only from a flavor standpoint. This is supposed to be a game focused on getting birds on the table, but the action you use to do that it's the only one you can't empower in any way, the reason, probably, being that adding birds to your board already gives you points (usually) and add a piece to your engine. This means that, more or less in the middle of the game, you will have some actions that will reap a considerable amounts of things to you, while playing a bird will do nothing but place that bird, and that's that. Moreover, laying eggs is the only action that is guarantee to give you points (cards in hands and unused food are worth nothing at the end of the game), which means that every player will be naturally inclined to build around that, and in the later stages of the game it will be almost impossible to have "better" actions to do (laying eggs comes at no cost, and in the process you may very well activate other birds abilities that may net you even more points). Adding to that, placing birds in the rightmost sposts of the board charges you eggs, which is again a completely counterintuitive step: i may want to place a bird to get its points, but i have to pay points to do that? Assuming i need to use at least one action to get the food i need before being able to do that, i may very well lay eggs twice and almost certainly get more points. The fact that in the last part of the game you get less actions to do for some reason, it's not helping either, because you will be hard pressed to get the most possible points out of them and forget totally about the birds (unless you are lucky and get the perfect ones you need, of course). In other words, Wingspan it's a wonderful visual experience thanks to the incredible quality of the art and components, too bad that the game almost works against it, and it does not reach the same quality anyway.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Initial Impressions: Rating is assuming non-AP players (as this game seems like it would be really AP prone and I don't think this game is complex enough to be fun if it goes above 75 minutes), and that the game feels fresh after multiple plays (which I'm a little concerned about since while every card is technically unique that is often achieved by having one have a slightly tweaked blob of numbers compared to another, and so I'm not sure there is actually that many paths to victory in the game). 

Wingspan is certainly not anything special mechanically, and I generally am soured by hype rather easily (although that doesn't necessarily affect my ratings, see e.g. Scythe or Terraforming Mars, which while I have negative feelings towards I still rate above average because in a vacuum I would enjoy them). From Wingspan I was expecting a derivative, vacuous light tableau builder that has been hugely overhyped due to its unique theme (ugh why do so many publishers play it safe with theme) and great art. And, well, Wingspan is an overhyped derivative light tableau builder propped up by its theme and art, but I also found its decisions to be surprisingly tough. Thematically how the different "habitats" tie together and how you can spend eggs from anywhere make no sense, but mechanically it works quite well. You can boost certain actions by playing more cards, but the more you improve a track the more it costs. Also, you ideally want to improve the action you are going to do the most of, but often if you are doing a lot of an action you need to use it less, as you will be getting larger quantities of its benefit. Moreover, timing when you do what and chaining them in a way that is the most efficient is also important. In this vein it is like a lighter Imperial Settlers (which has more interesting cards but feels more railroaded), Alicematic Heroes, or Deus (the latter two also having different tableau tracks, but also having a board element).

I certainly wouldn't have chosen this game as 2019's most innovative game of the year, although I completely agree with Elizabeth Hargrave (I also don't think it should have been nominated for strategy game, but am fine with card game, as it is effectively a tableau builder + some light resource management). Regardless I love me some card chaining of different card powers, and Wingspan definitely has that. While I don't appreciate Wingspan as much as I do some of e.g. Knizia's designs, I currently find Wingspan more fan than most of Knizia's games.

There is technically interaction in this game, but it feels more like incidental jostling in line to grab things first, rather than intentional interaction of area control games, the parasitic leeching of Trains or Race for the Galaxy, jockeying for the ability to stall the longest in Condotierre, or even the game of chicken of how much resources are you willing to let accumulate before wasting an action to take them in Agricola.

I thought I would mind the diminishing number of actions each round, as I don't like feeling stressed in games, and that mechanism seemed like it would cause such stress. Luckily that wasn't the case, although I would probably say that the mechanism is a slight negative cause it feels tacked on, even though I understand it is necessary to prevent snowballing.

Overall my Want to Play of Wingspan is currently very high, but I get addicted to card chaining and comboing games easily, and I will need more plays to see if it will stay fresh over multiple plays. The egg resource mechanism in particular feels very thematically disconnected, and I'm not sure how much you could play a strategy of e.g. a few high point cards vs. egg producing machine vs. playing 15 cheap birds, and if those different approaches would even feel interesting, or if it would feel more tactical and just optimizing for whatever I was dealt with.

EDIT: Played Everdell, and it has more card chaining while only playing in slightly longer time, so reducing my rating of this.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Collect food, lay eggs, and attract the highest-value among these 170 birds to build the best bird sanctuary. (With 1 expansion, it ranks 8, but the solo mode lifts the game to a 9 rank.)

PROS: Wingspan has beautiful art and components - and I'm excited to finally find an engine builder (which I like) that depends on text-heavy cards (which I don't always like). For replayability, I enjoy trying different strategies of card-combination (depending on which random cards appear) and efficiency-building in the 4 actions. I LOVE the educational, personally-appealing, and unusual Nature theme, which broadens the number of people who would be willing to play it with me (as does the medium-light weight). The low-interaction, build-your-own-preserve feel is relaxing. Finally, the solo play is incredibly tight and well-designed. 

CONS: When teaching new players, the game runs long. Higher (4/5) player counts, at least with novice players, can have excessive downtime and may feel like there is too little interaction (with no pink cards or slower play) to keep your attention. More players also makes it likely that you will run out of eggs (we substitute extra food tokens). The text on the cards is small and can be hard to read, especially at a distance. The dice tower opening in the back, instead of the top, makes it harder to use from any direction - and it's cardboard nature requires some reinforcing glue to remain sturdy. There is no clear way to mark when you've used a "Once Between Turns" power. I can imagine eventually playing enough times that I run out of interesting strategies to try (though I think the promised expansions may help with this). There is a lot of luck of the draw in this game, making it potentially quite swingy. Allowing a draft in your initial card choice can somewhat mitigate any starting advantage based on better/worse cards. For those who like to build, this may be a bit like the scarcity vs. abundance debate in Agricola vs. Caverna, at least for how hard it is to get your food engine going. Finally, the physical moves you make with your worker cube - from right to left in specific rows - seem unintuitive (at least to novices) and I find it hard to fit them into the narrative of the game.

TEACHING STORY:
You are in charge of a wildlife preserve that wants to have the most birds [show bird card stacks], have the best birds [show feather victory points on a bird card], and for those birds to thrive by laying lots of eggs [show eggs] in their nests, storing extra food [show food tokens], or bringing other birds into their habitat [tuck a card under another]. At the end of 4 years (or rounds), you will be rewarded with donations (known as points) from your foundational grants for having the best sanctuary according to these criteria.

In addition, there are small, fickle donors [show bonus cards] that have specific birding interests (like birds with colors in their names) and medium, more reliable donors [show end of round goals] that have more general interests (like increasing bird populations in the wetlands). But don't focus too much on the smaller donors, as your foundational grants give you the most rewards.

Over the course of 4 years, you use your limited number of workers [show action cubes] to build up your sanctuary in 3 different habitats [have players open playmats/preserves]: the forest, grassland, and wetland.

Each habitat let's a worker do a task that is important for the growth of your preserve: gain food, lay eggs and get bird cards. Let's look at each of these actions, which workers take from the right to the left of your board, in a specific habitat.

[This is where I would explain the various actions and gameplay.]

At the end of each year, your sanctuary is more efficient and can run with fewer workers, so 1 worker takes a job with that year's medium size donor.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
UPDATE: after a tepid second game, I bought the digital version. This game actually rocks, so disregard the initial impressions below.

First impressions: A beautiful looking game, duh.
And the design of the game, I feel is very elegant and streamlined for what it has you doing. I was able to teach this game to 2 other people without a hitch, and I just learned it myself that day. I used no teaching aids. That is a brava moment. There’s a lot of simpler games that I cannot say the same, because they have some weird fiddly rules, etc., that I’ll always need to reference.
Wingspan is not that at all. I feel like I’ll always know how to play this game. Amazing design job in that sense.

But then we have the strategy…this is where I’m not so sure it was that deep or interesting.
You have access to so few cards in the first third of the game, by which point, you probably should have committed to some type of engine already.
My goal card made me go a particular (and arbitrary) direction that earned me 8 points. 2 of the 4 cards for that goal came out of my starting hand. The other initial birds I played to my habitat I only played because that’s all I could afford, or it helped with that particular round’s end goal.

So already, these random objectives (read: not thematic) seem to have an outsized influence on how you develop your habitat.

I played 3 forest birds in one turn & that maxed my feeding action, and helped net a come-from-behind victory. And that was by accident. But then, so were all the objectives I achieved that had nothing to do with birds.
And they call this game thematic?

Why are my food actions tied solely to the forest? Why am I laying eggs, which only excite the grassland birds? Why does drawing new bird cards send only the wetland creatures in a tizzy?

Oh but it’s so educational, right?
I mean, is Snapple bottle cap trivia the pinnacle of learning these days? No, of course not. The bird trivia is simply part of the smoke and mirrors (things that have nothing to do with gameplay) that are best illustrated by its (over)production value.

We played at 3 and agreed that 4+ would be pointless. I don’t personally like the game to play it at 2 when there are so many 2P bangers to get through.

I am not inherently against multiplayer solitaire, but those games need to be on the shorter, punchier side for me to really get on board with them. With Wingspan, you’re at the mercy of whatever birds happen to show up during your turn, and you pray that they relate to the random objective you receive in the beginning of the game.

FINAL JUDGMENT: Wingspan most excels in its production. The design has some wonderful aspects to it, but overall, it’s largely driven by arbitrary forces outside your control. It really doesn’t deliver a thematic experience, or any strong feelings whatsoever. There are no dramatic moments. No Aha’s! or Gotcha! Just a bunch of dorks with their heads down matching worm symbols and turning eggs into cards into food into other resources.

People claim that this is relaxing, but it wasn’t for me. There was no world at the heart of Wingspan. Nothing unfolded to show you that there was more to this game or this idea. It was just another resource conversion euro with pretty paint, except the strategy is super diluted by randomness.

I would play if askew want kitty 
. I wouldn’t ever request it. I couldn’t confidently recommend this to anyone, because I know no one who actually enjoys birds or pretend-strategy games that much.

Also can someone tell me why they only had 4 plastic trays to put our 5 resources into? Also some of the resource tokens were fraying. Those are my only small production gripes.

Thank you for coming to my TED talk.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
By the time I finally experienced it, Wingspan had long since become the Titanic of board games.  Appreciating how influential hype can be, I put on my Cloak of Objectivity and bought a copy.  What I found was a game that lived up  to both its praise and criticism.  It is certainly not inexpensive, but the beautiful components nearly justify the $60 suggested retail price.  On top of the well-loved resin eggs, bird feeder dice tower, custom wooden dice and tons of unique linen-finish bird cards, you get more in the box than they needed to include: four plastic containers with lids that can function as component trays for gameplay and storage, a three-compartment plastic tray for laying out birds and cradling the draw piles, and an inventive “Swift Start” system that really does make the game a breeze to learn.  It takes a couple of plays to understand all the card powers and how to chain them together, and it is at this point that one might notice that many of the point scoring avenues are actually dead ends.  The bonus cards with private goals bring in very few points for the effort and resources it takes to achieve them.  Predator cards that involve rolling dice to possibly cache food are capricious, and the little pile of food is not worth much at the end of the game.  Nor should one fight too hard to win the end-of-round goals, since a first place finish earns just three points more than second.  In stark contrast to all this dink-and-dunk scoring is the egg system.  Each egg is worth a point at game’s end, so the last round is usually best spent simply laying eggs over and over.  Going into the final round, you will sometimes have a really cool bird in your hand that you are excited to play.  It might even work toward one of the goals on a bonus card.  But after quickly crunching a few numbers, you realize that it will be better to just keep this bird in your hand and lay more eggs instead.  This is Wingspan’s biggest flaw, because it gives each game an anticlimax.  Some cards are overpowered (e.g. ravens, crows, killdeer, and Franklin’s gull), usually because they can be played in the grasslands row where the “lay eggs” action resides.  These cards can turn the grasslands into a triple threat, generating food, cards, and eggs all for the cost of one action cube.  When this occurs, it creates a boring game state for the player reaping its rewards, and a disenchanting obstacle for everyone else.  After playing the outstanding Automa solo variant a number of times, I made peace with these shortcomings and used my knowledge to prepare for them.  There are still times when a very lucky or unlucky opening hand can pretty much determine the outcome before the game even starts, but I truly believe that experienced players will rarely find themselves in a helpless predicament.  Luck of the draw will always be a factor, but will rarely swing the entire game.  Wingspan scales well.  I have not played it at five, but it is excellent at all other player counts, though each is idiosyncratic.  The pink bird powers are most affected by player count: they are highly effective in solo mode, practically useless in a duel, and increasingly productive the more people are in the game.  Thematically speaking, it falls short of similar games like Everdell and Meadow, but I appreciate its tranquil nature and don’t find it particularly lacking.  When my falcon eats a chickadee, I feel the theme plenty.  Wingspan continues to grow on me with every play.  I like it.

Update: Increasing my rating from eight to nine after playing Wyrmspan, which made me appreciate even the hairiest aspects of Hargrave’s 2019 classic.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Rating is for base game only.

Plays (base game only): 14 (1 at 3p, rest at 2p)
Win ratio: 70%

Part of me wishes I could give this game a lower rating to counter balance the hype.

Unfortunately, I have to agree it is a very good game.

- Is it overpriced? Well, there's components up to 5 players and even an apparently elaborate solo automa, so, no, the price is right.
- Is it overproduced? Definitely! You most certainly don't need all the many eggs, the SM trays, the bird feeder dice tower, etc. But I do believe they add to the aesthetics, toy factor and overall enjoyment of the game.
- Is it good value then? I'd say yes. At this price point one sort of expects a more elaborate game. Wingspan is a fairly light game compared to most other games (euros) at this price point. 

As I said I consider the base game to be very good and enjoyable.
I believe Wingspan's popularity comes from its outstanding combination of length, strategy, complexity, aesthetics, etc. It's like all of these factors are tuned to the "just right" setting.

It is *not* a heavy game. It is *not* an uber strategic game. There *is* a good deal of randomness (sometimes too much) and there *are* some obvious strategies (lay eggs FTW). But we still choose to play it lots and enjoy it every time.

I heavily disagree Wingspan is a family game. IMO it certainly isn't.

Also do keep in mind I love birds and we find the arts and components overall super cute. The theme is certainly there as many of the birds' actions correspond to how they are and behave in real life. But obviously it isn't the most thematic game either.

There ARE a few downsides to the base game of Wingspan: some pretty major, most of them minor.
- Some birds are undoubtedly OP and, if you get them early, you will certainly win by a good margin (search in the forums for Franklin's Gull, the ravens, etc). This really needs fixing if you play enough.
- Building towards a lay eggs loop in the last round is certainly the way to win 99% of the times in base Wingspan. To me, this is fine. The base game is obviously a lighter experience and I don't think the game sells itself as having dramatically diverse strategic avenues (now, how you get to that end, does vary from game to game).
- Other than the above, replayability is very good, thanks to the private and public goals, the variety of cards, etc.
- The 2p mode is very good except for the public goals. The objectives are clearly created for the green (the more competitive) side of the scoring, which is too swingy in the 2p mode. We always play on the blue side (everyone scores based on how they did towards the goal, not compared to the other player) but unfortunately many of the goals don't really work well with the point scaling. Something like amount of birds played, it's almost impossible not to have 5 birds played by the last round...
- The private goals can sometimes be pretty swingy which sometimes is annoying (same as when you draw a ticket that you have, by complete chance, already fulfilled in any Ticket To Ride).

Otherwise, I must admit that Wingspan is indeed a very good game even just the base game. Does it deserve the crazy amount of hype it got/gets? No, I definitely don't think so. But the birds are adorable (although I do like the art in Piepmatz better! Those are more realistic) and I'm happy to see a game with this theme be so popular.

Also see my comments for the European Expansion.
