engine builder game with bird collecting theme
overrated
decent but not that great

I played it maybe 4 times and then it wasn't that interesting anymore.

cute theme
I actually like birds very much and think it's a cool idea to use collecting birds as theme for a board game.
Problem is, the game doesn't seem thematic! It's quite mechanical (fixed rows, fixed order, triggered effects, get engine running or lose, tight resources).
Engine Building can be cool, but what has it to do with birds in nature??

+ birds, raises awareness for birds and nature
+ great components and bird artworks (although important symbols on cards are a bit too small)
+ engine building, some good game mechanics
+ replayability with the big deck of singleton cards and variable scoring ?
+ somewhat attractive to non-gamers (mainly wifes I guess) ?
- very mechanical, not thematic
- very luck-dependent (getting the bird cards and food you need, conditional effects) (!)
- not enough player interaction, almost multiplayer solitaire (!)
- balancing issues (eggs dominant, some bird cards) (!)
- heavily card-based (sleeves necessary)
- regional (only North American birds in base game)
- expensive

I wonder if there are enough bird lovers that like engine building to make this game popular. I would expect that bird lovers dislike the complexity and mechanical feel of the game, while most engine building fans find the theme boring.


Smart idea to reduce action points each round while the engine becomes more powerful.
The different round goals and bonus goals are nice.

A problem is that the bird cards aren't that different and memorable, so it is hard to learn all the cards to not have to rely on reading the text every time. It also doesn't make it that apparent what your opponent(s) do.

Card draw and resources are tight.
Laying eggs is central and more powerful than collecting food and drawing cards. Dominant strategy seems to be getting the Lay Eggs Row good and activate often.
Gameplay drags a bit at least during the first few games.
End game (in the last round) is a bit flat (only eggs and birds with lots of points are good at that stage).
Some said the game is light-headed, but I can't agree. The resources are very tight and decisions can be tough, sometimes almost AP, especially when deciding to discard cards. It was too complex for my mother.

How they translated "Wingspan" into "Flügelschlag" is beyond me. Keeping the English name would have been the way to go. Makes marketing easier and more impactful. In the Internet Age it is weird to have different names in different countries for the same thing.

I'm not a fan of the plastic card box with three display slots.
And the SM resource containers are just impossible to open without the contents flying through the room. :/

This seems a lot simpler than "Terraforming Mars" so the comparison doesn't really fit.

I would probably prefer to play with drafting starting cards, 5 cards instead of 3 in display and 1 free extra card for each player at start of game to reduce the luck factor and to make resources less tight in the first round. More cards on display might even increase interaction a tiny bit.
Fixing the eggs problem is a bit tougher. Maybe make eggs count only half a point beyond a certain number (5 or maybe the number of birds that can have eggs or round(n/2)+1)!?

Still not getting over that the grassland lays eggs onto birds.

4/13/19:  Gaining more familiarity with the birds. Thus, forming better chains, and aiming for birds with better bonuses and worth more VPs.   Therefore, the strategy factor is increasing. Three plays in. Two with Automa.  I highly recommend familiarizing yourself with solo play even if it’s not your preference.  It works very well, is quick and allows you to learn what the birds have to offer. 

4/19/19:  played first 3P game.  This is where the game shines.  More competition for goals, additional opportunity to trigger pink activation.   More bird cards in play over the course of the game.  Still, the game does not lose that tight feel, where you need to optimize your decisions and work efficiently.  In this particular game, player one quickly got a cache bird down and really hit that card often for nine additional points at game end. High VP bird cards were quickly grabbed and made it to the mat by round four. The game was teachable in under 10 minutes. Game flow was smooth, even with a newbie. The tactile feel of the game, the consistent game play and decision making provide for an excellent game experience. This game lives up to its hype. I’ve seen some negative reviews for this game and one that said the game was brought to a game night but others were not interested in playing. I find these comments difficult to accept as the game is beautiful to look at and incredibly accessible. I have found it enjoyable at 1, 2 or 3 players, with 3 really letting this game fly.

Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Such a great game. I love how smooth and streamlined the gameplay is, as on your turn you're just activating one habitat of four possible choices, making the game really easy to teach and get into. However there's also an extremely satisfying ramping up element in the game since as you're playing more and more birds into your tableau, your actions get both more varied and more powerful, and you start to discover interesting and cool card combos. You also really get to active and use the engine you've built multiple times during the game, which is highly satisfying.

It's also a fascinating efficiency puzzle because you have a set number of actions available for the whole game, but your plan and situation is constantly in flux depending on the state of the birdfeeder, the birds others have played, the end of round goals, and the cards you happen to draw. It's very much a game to which you cannot go in with a specific strategy in mind from the very start, you just have to see where birds and the bonuses take you, meaning the game provides you with a new pathways to consider each turn, while also not being so overwhelming that it ends up disrupting the flow of the game.

The game is undeniably a little bit solitary but since the turns are so quick it doesn't end up being an issue, though interestingly for some reason this "multiplayer solitaire" element is always massively overstated as a negative for Wingspan specifically. I find it a bit odd, since the game is not different to any other euros where the only interaction dynamic is "I took something / went there before you did". If anything the game actually has more interaction than those games since you might be benefitting or leeching off from the actions of others because of certain bird abilities.

The visual look of the game combined with the high production value is also fantastic, as they really complement the theme, which also feels quite well integrated to the actual gameplay mechanics. The experience is also most definitely being elevated by it's unique theme which is approachable and interesting, and it wouldn't be the same if it was something generic about spaceships in space or fantasy characters in fantasyland. 

The expansions are also great, with the European expansion mostly just adding more birds and more variety to the end of round goals, and Oceania expansion additionally overhauling the player boards and introduces nectar as a new wild food type. The new player boards are fantastic and provide a welcome change with nerfing the grassland habitat and making the forest and the wetlands habitats more powerful, but I'm not sure how much I enjoy the addition of the nectar. It almost makes the game too easy as it removes some of the tightness from the resource management and you also get points for using it. However it also removes some of the luck of the draw from the game and means that frustrating games where you don't manage to get your engine going don't really happen anymore, which is not a bad thing.

Overall a stellar production, stellar design, stellar theme. I was pretty much always destined to love this game since the production quality is top-notch, the gameplay combines hand-management and resource management with extremely satisfying and streamlined tableau-building, and the theme is something I really enjoy.

Definitely the best board game i have played so far.......
There is a large amount of cards, all made out of a high quality material, aswell as the eggs, the different colours make it nice aswell.

The whole game has been produced using high quality materials. The game provides alot of strategy and is different every time, and the expansions make it even better.

This game provides you to think about getting points in different ways. You can win through bonuses, goals, birds, or other powers, so there are many different strategies you can play to win, unlike some games where there is only one way to ensure a win. 

This game is one of the least luck-based games i have played, the dice doesnt affect the game much, so you are required to think alot.

The only reasons i have docked this as a 8.5 instead of a 10 is because of four reasons:
1. There are not mahy goal tiles. I have played this game about a dozen or so times and even with the expansion tiles the goals can get repetitive, and there are alot more options to make them. Hopefully more will come with the new expansions.
2. The rulebook is hard to understand. I had trouble understanding it, i would reccomend watching a youtube video to understand it.
3. Not enough egg/food storage. This is only very minor, but as i have added the expansions, when i am playing the baskets for the egg and food are basically overflowing so it is easy to knock them out of the baskets. A couple of extra baskets in each expansion would have been nice, considering they would only cost about 5-10p each.
4. There is also not enough food either. I was playing a five player game with my family, and when we had about 2 or 3 caching resource cards, we ended up running out of resources in the end. I know it says to use a "suitable replacement" but i dont know how you would signify which resource is which. You wouldnt need many more, only about a dozen of each.

This game is definitely one i would recommend playing to everyone, young and old. It is not too difficult either but it is still challenging to play with experienced players. I am very critical of alot of things, and this is just one of the games that cannot be critiqued. I am not a bird lover, but this game is still the best i have ever played. Despite the errors of not having enough baskets and food, along with too few goal tiles and a confusing rulebook, i simply cannot dock points for minor errors. If they turned this game into a burger i would convert from veganism to being a meat eater it is that good.

However i will say, that the expansions are a definite. Now that i have played with, the base game does seem to lack that little bit of edge, and that is what the two expansions bring to it.

I cannot wait to see the other expansions, since they are planning on having 5 expansions. They should definitely add something like a 5th round or maybe incorporate a 5th action into the game to add another something to make the game even better.

One thing i would also add, is to invest in a six deck card shuffler. You can get a decent one for about £25, and it is really useful, for not just this game, but especially this one, as there is ALOT of cards, and they are hard to shuffle.

2019-06-25

Initial Rating: 5.0 (June 2019)

I was wary of Wingspan as it was an over hyped game, but, in this case the hype was, mostly, correct. Wingspan IS a good game, but still, it is worse than expected :D. That´s the problem with hype, I try to ignore it, but I’m only human so I couldn’t keep my expectations out of the game.

Wingspan´s rules are easy to teach, you can do it under 10 minutes. Gameplay takes around 120 minutes.

The game´s components are pretty good. The eggs look gorgeous on the table. The dice tower also looks gorgeous assembled, but it doesn’t fit inside the box so you need to un-assemble it and the tower suffer due to that. I don’t think I will ever use it again.

The art is very good and some of the artists are from my country, a fact that has hyped even more the game among some friends. I don’t care about nationality, so I don’t care they are from Colombia, I only care that they are very good artists.

Best with 3 players, I tolerate the game with 4 fast players. With 5 players, the downtime is way too much.

Too much downtime with 5 players.

The theme is ok, although unique.

Gameplay is fun even though I was expecting a heavier game. Wingspan is like a mix of Terraforming Mars (engine/combo building) with Deus (the way you activate your cards improving your action) and I love both games. The decisions needed to play the game aren’t very hard, nor very obvious. You do need to think your options and strategies. Every turn you have four options, you can play a card, you can gain food (to play the cards), you can lay eggs, and you can draw cards, that’s it! In each of the latter 3 options, you can “specialize” doing better and better actions, so knowing where to play which card to maximize your returns, is the fun of the game. There is also some global condition to achieve each round which keeps the game interesting. In each subsequent round, players will have one less action per round, I also like this.

There is luck with the cards and the dice, but I feel it is very controlled. With the dice you can use 2 kinds of food for the one you need and for the cards, you can always draw more of them easily to find the ones you want, sometimes a player will get lucky and get some amazing combs with very little effort. The goal cards do have much more luck of the draw than the regular cards, I need more plays to verify if they bother me or not.

I can see why people compare the game to Terraforming Mars, to me, Terraforming Mars is by far the best game though.

Bottom line, Wingspan is a rare example that (kind of) lives to the hype. The game is fun to play and it has interesting decisions (that aren't very hard to process). The game is gorgeous and my SO loved it. I think it´s a good game, so it is (probably) a keeper in my game collection. I would love to play it again soon.

textfield_comment_value:
First impressions:
Typically I'm all for Engine Building games. I typically find it interesting to combo pieces together and see the payout of your investment. However, I feel this game depends too much on luck of the draw if you are actually able to play that game.
And that's because the engine pieces are mostly dictated by the cards you initially get, with birds that trigger if you executed the base action of the row they are in. Birds actions can be economical (give resources, improve action efficiency, draw cards / improved hand management capabilities) or geared towards point generation (create eggs, converting resources into points or have a chance of generating points for you).
The same kind of problem with another game: Terraforming Mars (these 2 games feel similar).

The game lets you take 26 actions, where only between a quarter and a half seemed interesting to me. Which action to take is often dictated by you gameplay state (especially if you are doing poorly), and the actions by themselves I didn't find all that enjoying. Building a bird and deciding where to place it if you have the freedom was mildly entertaining as you got to influence upgrading one of the other basic actions. But the base action of getting some randomly made available resources (or trying to gamble for better ones) or getting eggs don't matter to me unless you also have an engine to trigger with that action. If you have a good engine in that row, it's no longer really an interesting choice but an entertaining turn of 'Look! I get to do some cool stuff! (All the while you get the wait and see me do it)'. Getting cards is also only midly interesting and hardly enjoyable by itself (again, the enjoyment got better for me if I actually had an engine to fire off it).
So I only really enjoy playing the game if I get to fire off a satisfying engine. Which depends on the luck of the card draw if you even get to build one and having to spent (semi-)boring turns playing down cards.

Combined with the fact that I had no investment in what other people are doing on their turn, this game felt like a multi-player solitair (which I don't mind perse). Where waiting for you turn can take a 'long time' if your other players are having relatively decent engines building up and executing regularly to maximize turn efficiency (which they should in order to have a chance at winning the game).

So for me personally, this game doesn't feel dense with enjoyment and on top that enjoyment is swingy due to it depending on the grace of luck you receive at the earlier moments in the game.

However I can see why other people may like it. It feels like a great gateway game for a lot of people, where the game mechanisms are clean and accessible, offering a huge variety per game (you just cannot do the exact same thing over and over again) and mechanisms that motivate / force exploring alternative strategies causing the game to feel fresh to quite some time. It also looks colorful on the table, which is definitely a plus!

I'd rather be playing Imperial Settlers or Dominion than this game if I'm looking to scratch my engine-building itch.

Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Perfectly pleasant engine builder that serves to provide a satisfying experience under narrow circumstances when company is mixed. Perhaps best when the entire table is freshly arrived to board games of its ilk (see my updates below). Is this going to be a game I play with my primary gaming group? No. The rules are simple, the tactics fairly light, and there's some randomness (e.g., hawks that gamble for victory points), but this means it's designed for a certain crowd in mind (hint not medium to heavy gamers). Wingspan, in terms of game play, is more similar to 51st State/Imperial Settlers. In terms of weight, Wingspan is more similar to Splendor. 

While the design aspects fail to express brilliance or novelty, there's some thoughtfulness in the design. In particular, some of the design choices keep the game from sticking around too long (it can be played with experienced players in about 60 minutes with 5 players).  The dwindling action cubes keep all the rounds nicely paced. Further, the game design focuses on smartly allowing the players to fire their engine multiple times throughout the game, while also keeping the activation chains from getting too long and bogging this light game down. Light interaction is present due to the end of round bonuses and some positive effects. There's definitely room for some expansions to up the interest, but overall the design feels well considered for what it's trying to be. 

There are some thematic touches in the card powers and how they link to their real life counterparts. The rest of the supposed theming is nonsense, and is simply attractive window dressing (though the offset card market is annoying).

[Update] So it appears the briskness of play is quite group dependent; moreso than some other games of its weight. I've played a few times with people new to the game, and the combination of card effects and turn choices has caused them to drastically slow the game down. You want this game to play briskly for its level of decisions, so choose who you introduce the game to carefully. 

[Final update] The more we played Wingspan, the less interest we had in the mechanical portions of the game itself, and there was a growing annoyance at a number of mechanical flaws. Like seemingly all Stonemeier games, there are issues in card design and the concomitant mechanisms (e.g., the low amount of market card churn in low player count games, which results in strings of blind draws). But we still can't deny the charm of the art, production, and little moments where a bird effect causes a bit of a smile. The production and art design are definitely handling more than their fair share of weight, and the game is better for it. 

In any event, we moved on from the game entirely. My wife, after a few plays, declared the experience not worth the set up, especially compared to other options we have, and she's quite correct. And with us finding it too sensitive to slow players (we both hate the experience when Wingspan goes long), we can't trust it with inexperienced players.

textfield_comment_value:
I'd heard that this was a new game people were excited about, but didn't know much about it. Someone had said that if you liked Terraforming Mars and Gizmos, you'd like this. I'm not sure that's a true statement, and it's nothing like TM, but I did enjoy it.

It's a beautiful game. Each card is a unique bird (there's a ton of cards) filled with information about that bird. If you are at all interested in birds, this game will probably draw you in.

In the game you're doing one of several things, playing a bird, collecting food, collecting eggs or collecting cards. Playing a bird meaning putting it on your player board. Your player board has three rows, representing three habitats: coasts, grassland and forests. Each row has five spaces. Playing a bird requires you to pay the food cost for the bird, and if you place in the leftmost spot, nothing additional. If you place a second bird in a habitat, it must go to the right of the previous bird and requires that you sacrifice an egg (or possibly two) to place it (as it is further out). Some birds have effects that trigger when placed, but most have activation effects that trigger when you take the other actions.

When you trigger the other actions you place a cube in the appropriate habitat (forests = food, grasslands = eggs, coasts = cards) to the right of the last bird in that row. The further out that is the more powerful your action is. Some actions can be augmented by discarding a card or a food or an egg.

Collecting food allows you to take a die (there's a birdhouse dice tower) and getting the associated food. If there's ever only one food type available (out of five) then you are allowed to reroll all the dice (even the ones that were previously removed) before taking a food. This is true even if you've already selected some food (thus causing only one food type to remain).

Collecting eggs just lets you get however many eggs and put them on birds. Each bird has an egg maximum capacity it can hold. Eggs are worth points at the end of the game.

Collecting cards allows you to draw bird cards from a public display of three cards or randomly from a face down pile.

Each game has four random public goals corresponding to the four rounds of the game. So you might want to have the most birds residing in the coastal region that have eggs on them at the end of round one. At the end of each round the round goal is evaluated and players score points based on whether they were 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th in that competition. Later rounds are worth slightly more than earlier rounds.

Additionally players have some secret objectives (and can get more with the right bird cards) that give them points mostly on if they have gotten the correct bird types and done something with them, like getting eggs on them, etc.

There's a fair bit to think about here and it's very interesting. The game is lovely with great production quality. I really enjoyed my play.

Initial rating (1/2020): 6.0
Updated rating (8/2021): 6.5 

Thoughts about game with Oceania expansion (9/2022): 
The nectar and other additions seem to make the overall experience smoother. I haven't played it enough to notice any balance issues. Haven't had excessive nectar even using all the expansion dice. 

Updated thoughts (8/2021):
Disconnect visuals, audience. Activations, selecting cards, evaluating in hand, taking actions. Feel similar about Parks, Trails an opportunity for more accessible version. 

Initial thoughts (1/2020):
The theme, art, and components are nice. However, overall, I feel the game is overwrought. Similar to my thoughts on the game Museum, it takes a relatively simple concept, overproduces it, and adds layer upon layer on top of it, which is not something that appeals to me. 

The personal and shared objectives are what I find the most interesting about the game, but I think they are undermined by the other ways points are more effectively generated in the game. Generally, objectives help define a game and give it foundation, but to be an effective player in Wingspan it would probably be better to spend only 5% of your consideration on the objectives. Building an effective engine is more likely to achieve your objectives rather than working towards them intentionally. They might be a determining factor in who wins, but it's mostly incidental, as there are other strategies that are more likely to generate you more points. Focusing on the objectives themselves might have you spending time working towards a suboptimal strategy. 

In general, it's good to do things that get you things rather than work towards a particular goal or to simply enjoy the theme because certain birds appeal to you. With lots of things you can do more things that get you things. It's an engine builder, but I feel like I'm just building an engine, rather than playing a game about collecting birds.

The game has a peaceful and appealing theme, but the experience of the game feels more about the mechanisms and combinations. Some of the cards relate their abilities to the type of bird it is, which is a nice touch, but as a whole the theme feels superfluous. It could be entirely removed and my experience of the game would be the same. 

In terms of the experience of playing the game with others, it feels like their actions could be automated and I would have the same overall experience. Although there is some interaction in the game and it's nice to get stuff on other player's turns, I don't feel I'm interacting with them as a player. It's a mostly heads-down experience. 

Although very different, to compare it with another game by Elizabeth Hargrave, Tussie Mussie feels to more strongly evoke the theme of the game and create an environment where players feel like they're playing together.

First play against 3 who had played before. I thought it was okay and won 95-93-80s ish in a 4p game. I hate the bird house and find it inconvenient to roll in. The card draw is random too. I drew 2 bonus that both have 0vp and had to pick one. And the eggs look nice but roll around so it's not good functionally, plus we ran out of egg cards. The card play chaining leads to longer downtime too in a 4p. The card combos were okay but very tactical imo. I may prefer it a smidge more strategic though the beginning was decently strategic with picking a goal card and the starter birds. I think I kept 2 or 3 beginner ones which gradually synced well. It's a bit hard to see other player's birds and their activations. I heard complaints of samey effects and could see that a smidge. I heard the rulebook was nice and felt the linen and it wasn't a huge deal either to me. Overall, I think it was okay. I wish the components were made more functional than pretty/attractive and wasn't blown away by the "multi use card play". For good multi use cards, I prefer Bruges and didn't find this significantly better than San Juan's miniscule "multi use". But in terms of tactics/strategy, it was fine overall despite minor downtime between turns. We played in 90 minutes ish. The 3 different engines and choice between them was semi interesting balancing them and activating stuff. Didn't love the bird theme though and didn't pay much attention to the pictures, as nice as they were. Also surprised this was considered #1 Family game because I think it could be a bit overwhelming for a family game given how much info is on each card and on the board. I kept forgetting and losing track different things I did. Also wasn't crazy for the insert and needing to put things in in a certain way. Appreciated bird food mitigation despite dice rolls.

Anyway, nitpicks aside, it was fine and would play again if offered but I may prefer either deeper/more strategic engine builders or simpler faster ones maybe. And the "high" production doesnt actually grab me that much, nor does the theme. 6.5/10

4p game in second at 89-85-60s-60s and was fine. Does Eat cherry count with Eat wild? Also tied scoring a bit finicky since you add up positions then divide by number of players. Semi high downtime as actions stack and it made me miss Quacks simultaneous bag engine building aspect or Splendor or Century's streamlined engine building speed. Still decent and same rating score but would probably wish there were a way to take faster turns. Also dislike cards that trigger on opponents turns since you gotta watch them like a hawk and it takes some of the relaxed fun out of the game. I think I don't like that sort of 'interaction' it feels more like work than like fun play. Same rating 6.5 though.

textfield_comment_value:
Very nice looking game but when you play it, it's pretty lonely for a multiplayer and not that much fun. I'm really trying to like it because of all the recommendations and the hype all over social media and I do like the theme but the actual gameplay is not really clicking

Pros: 
- Very nice production, lots of items and things to look at. It really has the ability to bring curious people to the table. 
- Not too complicated to explain and start playing. Really nice addition that our box came with the swift start pack already included
- The cards have very nice scientific and curious facts about the birds which contribute to the theme and most actions feel connected to such theme.
- There is immediate feedback after each round so you get more or less an idea of where you are comparing to the others
- Doesn't really fell long if you have few or experienced players and people get the hang of it fairly quickly

Cons:
- Very lonely multiplayer-solitarie game style. There's absolutely cero interaction between players (other than taking someone's desired food from the bird feeder). You really could just be playing in separate rooms and get together at the end to compare results. It brings people to the table but it doesn't bring people 'together'. To somewhat fix this you need people to narrate what they're doing in their turn so you sort of squeeze some interaction
- Once you had a couple of plays, you can clearly see a simple strategy to get lots of points which is 'just lay eggs'. Each egg scoring 1 point vs placing a bird, which takes you 2 or 3 turns bc you have to take a card, get eggs, get food, play a bird, etc makes it very tempting. You could just get 3 or 4 turns laying eggs and get 12 points vs placing a single 5 points bird card. This makes the last two rounds having people hoarding eggs like crazy. Maybe set a house rule that each 2 or 3 eggs gets you a point to help with this
- There is little variety of public objectives. I've heard this gets fixed by getting expansions, but then again they take more money from you.
- You really are not able to use THAT MUCH strategy because of the limitation of bird cards available on the display. It kinda feels more like a reactive damage limitation strategy than a meticulous plan if the cards are just not right. On the other hand if you get (by luck mostly) some powerful birds, then you get a supercharged engine which makes you obliterate the competition. It really feels that the decisions are not really yours.

I really think people like this game more for "how cute it looks" and because "everybody is talking about it" than really the value and fun you get by playing it. It seems to me more like a "sunk cost" bias IMHO. The game is OK and we'll play it if the mood is right but that's it
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Price I paid: $60

Is it worth it: Yes (It's a Stonemeier game, and they're always built fantastically) BUT: if I had to price it, I'd say $50. That's not to disparage it, it's still great, but in terms of the mechanics, that's just more where I price it. Still, great game.

Is it complicated?: No, the gameplay is very easy to get to grasp with, and it's all explained on your personal playmat. However, there's a good amount of depth in the combos that you can pull off with different birds.

A very high-quality game about collecting birds to place in your nature preserve. Almost everything about the construction of this game screams quality. The eggs are wooden, the dice tower is made of heavy card stock, the cards feel textured, the player mats are chunky and vibrant in colour, the bird artwork is (for the most part) absolutely stunning. The only thing that doesn't feel quality is the card holder, which is used as a display area during gameplay. It's made of very cheap and flimsy plastic, and really takes away from the quality of everything else. Still, it's not going to ruin the game or anything. Just annoying.

The gameplay itself is very simple, but it's definitely a game you can replay a lot before you get tired of it. You have a number of cubes each round, and these cubes represent how many turns you get that round. With these cubes you can take a number of actions. 

You'll be rolling dice to determine what bird food you can pick up, then spending that food on birds (either the three that you can see, or a random one from a deck) and adding it to your hand. You'll then play birds onto your playmat and activate any powers that bird has. This might be "play another bird in the same turn" for example. 

Alternatively, you can spend your cubes to take any of the actions present on your playmat. This might be "pick up eggs" for example. Then you'll work your way backward, activating every bird power in that row as you do so. So, after activating all of your birds, you might end up picking up eggs, getting more food and adding eggs to bird's nests, all in one turn! The combos that you can pull off range from very simple to simply insane. 

Or maybe you won't go for the combinations and you'll simply go for big-points birds instead. These don't tend to have any powers, but are worth far more than smaller birds.

There's a lot more to this game that I can't fit in here, but you can obviously tell that I endorse it. Is it my favourite game? No, but is it a game with great replay value, fantastic assets and a gameplay loop that's satisfying? Absolutely. 

This would make a fantastic gift, too. It's big, it's chunky and it's beautiful. Just like you
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value: Wingspan is a beautiful engine-building game where you must fill your tableau with different birds across three different habitats (rows corresponding to different biomes birds can live in, and corresponding to different actions you can take). Birds have different food costs depending on how valuable they are, each providing a number of feathers (point), and having various different abilities such as gaining more points when you take a certain action by tucking another card behind it, moving row to a different habitat, or providing a bonus such as extra food or an extra card when taking the action corresponding to the row the bird is in. Filling up your tableau also inherently increases the power of the action you can take from the corresponding row even if that bird has no particular power, providing a strong engine-building effect that you can really notice over the course of the game. At the beginning of the game, it may take several actions just to get a bird you want, the requisite food for it, and put it in play, while later you'll get much more out of each individual action. End of round goals, shared by everyone where you must compete with other players, for objectives like most birds in a given habitat, or most eggs, give short term goals to work towards, while each player has their own bonus cards providing long-term objectives to work towards over the course of the game, both varying what you should aim for with your strategy. To be a bit critical though, there are two main problems I find with Wingspan: the first is a well known problem where with your final actions of the game, typically spamming lay eggs will simply be the best option as this provides points directly, where gaining food or drawing cards are no longer useful as they require several actions to be effective. People say the expansion helps with this, though from the game I played it was still largely the same and makes the final turns of the game a rather dull affair with no real decisions to be made. The other problem is to do with the snowball effect related to engine-building aspect of the game, as mentioned before your early actions are quite incremental, so whether or not you get a good bird early-game to get your food engine up quickly (e.g. the Common Raven) can give you a big advantage to avoid spending several actions on gaining 1 or 2 food each that other players will have to do. Wingspan is also mostly a solitary experience, there's little in the way of direct interaction which may put some people off. Still, Wingspan is a great game, though having played a little of both I'd say I prefer Everdell for the moment as a better engine-building game.
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
Love the original theme, art and production. Although the bird house and card container is form over function, and even redundant once you add expansions. Would have preferred more function, I.e fit expansions in the core box, and/or a lower price. Not well thought out. 

The game doesn't do anything that's new really, although the triggering of rows is not done that many times before. but does it in a streamlined way. Don't let the theme fool you. It’s tougher and more unforgiving than it looks which I find intriguing and annoying at the same time. 

The BIG negatives are that you can have simply bad luck which makes you lose the game without much control. The main way to mitigate this is to unlock card draw powers, but I prefer card games that offer more card control from the getgo instead of making me unlock that as a strategy. Also the birds themselves don't offer much options in card control.
In a game that sees so few cards you can definitely get 1 or 2 cards in your starting hand that makes it very hard for the other players to win. 
The same with the end game bonuses. It's not unlikely you get 2 tough bonus cards which, as it turned out after the game, weren't even achievable at all vs some player who get them all very easily. Add the dice to gain food and the randomness is complete. 
Also it just turns out in mass egg collection in the end. There are almost no other viable things to do in the last round. Although Oceania apparently solves these issues. I have the expansion. Just not played yet (only with base + Europe). 
And the bonus card saying "all birds from this region or this name" with a whole list to monitor is just crazy. Could have easily solved with a color marking or icon on the cards instead. 

You'll have to be able to live with that. It's made up with the fact it's just fun and kind of relaxing to play in terms of art, theme and flow of the game. When things come your way It does really feel satisfying and anyone can win. So it's a good next step up from a family style game. It also plays quick enough to not get super frustrated. 

I adjusted the rating quite a bit because of the balancing and luck issues. It says a lot how much impact a proper theme can have on an actually mediocre and unbalanced game. If this were a fantasy or space themed game I probably would have burned it by now. It has something charming an calming that makes it still enjoyable to play. 

Tip: We decided to draft the starting cards just like in TFM To mitigate luck somewhat and add some more strategy. And also give more bonus cards or decide later when to pick one (like nemesis or AN does it too). It makes the game more playable. \

textfield_comment_value:
For me, I love games with Engine building, individual player game boards, and beautiful artwork. 

Perhaps I'm biased because if a game has a nice theme and has great artwork I'm moved to overlook flaws.. which I think is a little bit of a factor with Wingspan. 

Don't get me wrong, I really enjoy this game if I play it lighthearted without worrying if I lose because of bad card draws... But after having played it 3 times:

1. (I learnt as I played with 2 experienced players)
2.(I played with 1 experienced player and 1 new player)
3.(I played just with 1 experienced player) 

This game takes significantly longer than it should if there is a new player. For example, the 3rd game took literally about 30 minutes compared with 1.5 - 2 hours 

Additionally.... and I sincerely enjoy what this game trying to do... there are some flaws in the mechanics... 

Only getting one action per turn that in itself doesn't really feel like a great deal is accomplished by it, can make it feel like you're taking a lot of time to not accomplish a lot. 

The brown powers are interesting.. but really are just chance that you get a few together that work properly together for even just a basic working engine. 
And if you don't draw the right cards you'll finish the game basically without an Engine at all, but wondering where you went wrong.. when in reality it was just chance of the cards and less skill and planning of the player.

How to sum it all up? Maybe like this.. This game makes you excited that there's loads of ideas that you could do!....and then when you don't draw any cards that work together you're left 2 hours later feeling rather anticlimactic. I think this game has an incredible BASE potential.. but I don't feel like it's been released without having the Mechanics given a couple more reviews to polish. 

Maybe if this is rereleased in a year or so with a fair bit of polishing to the mechanics then this could be a game that Avid Strategy Gamers will find much more interesting.

textfield_comment_value:
Wingspan is a light-medium weight engine building game about attracting different species of birds into your aviary.  

Players can choose between 4 available actions each turn: Play a bird card, get food, lay eggs, or draw bird cards.  These actions (except playing a bird card) get progressively stronger as bird cards are played into their associated environments.  The bird cards have different powers, point values, egg capacities, and even their wingspan become a point of interaction for certain bird-hunting birds of prey. 

There is a strong element of luck in terms of card draw for bird cards and bonus cards, as well as in the roll of the food dice.  So looking for specific cards to build a pre-determined type of engine is probably not the optimal way to play.  The game lends itself more as a tactical evaluation of what you have in your hand and what is available to you in the face-up bird cards.

This game is somewhat of a multiplayer solitaire, as the player interactions are mostly indirect (ie. taking a food die or bird card that your opponent may want) and mostly positive (ie. gaining food or egg when your opponent does X).  

As typical of most Stonemaier games, Wingspan is wonderfully produced; from the thick card stock, rulebook texture, wooden eggs, and beautiful bird art on the cards.

Overall, I found Wingspan to be a very enjoyable experience, from the game play to the little facts about each bird on their cards.  The game plays fairly quickly, and has a theme that is more welcoming to those averse to sci fi or fantasy settings.  

Highly recommended!
Title: Wingspan

textfield_comment_value:
One of our go-to games. It is beautiful, easy to learn, and fun to play without being too complex. Lots of fun and the production values are simply astounding. 

Your ability to win is impacted by luck of the draw, though. You can't build a good engine if drafting from the deck feeds you junk. There's a wide range of bird powers some of which are clearly better than others.

This would be a good intro for people who haven't played modern board games. It's easy to teach, and easy for newcomers to play.

textfield_comment_value:
Wingspan stole my heart immediately and is one of my most-played games.  I still love it, though I'm perhaps a little less enamored than I was initially.  Almost everyone I've introduced it to enjoys it (and requests it again), which is something I can't say about every game.  I find a lot of engine builders boring (Splendor, Century, Gizmos), yet Wingspan adds enough to actually make it fun.

For me, Wingspan is about having a great experience.  It has amazing table presence, gives you a lot to think about as you figure out how to create an engine with the cards you have, and there's enough bird variety (especially with expansions) that I rarely find it feeling stale since I feel like I see something new every time I play.  Yes, the egg strategy is dominant in the base game.  That said, I still almost never pursue it because I find other aspects of the game more fun - and sometimes other strategies can still beat an egg strategy.
